paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
context_brief: Products of toric diagrams and B-models
original_question: Graded quivers can be constructed from the topological B-model, and products of toric diagrams produce higher-dimensional Gorenstein singularities from lower-dimensional ones. Is there a correspondence between the product construction for toric diagrams and B-model approaches to graded quivers?
self_contained_problem:
A graded quiver with superpotential of order m+1 consists of a finite quiver Q whose arrows carry an integer grading c ∈ {1,2,…,m}, together with a superpotential W that is a formal sum of cycles satisfying a grading condition (degree m+1) and modulo signed cyclic equivalence. Such graded quivers arise as the open-string sector of the topological B-model on local Calabi–Yau (m+2)-fold singularities; in particular, for toric Gorenstein (m+2)-fold singularities X, the associated graded quiver theory can be derived from a B-model construction on X. 

On the other hand, there is a purely combinatorial product operation on toric diagrams: given a Gorenstein toric singularity X of complex dimension d₁ with toric diagram Δ₁ ⊂ ℤ^{d₁-1} and another Gorenstein toric singularity Y of complex dimension d₂ with toric diagram Δ₂ ⊂ ℤ^{d₂-1}, one forms a (d₁+d₂−1)-dimensional toric Gorenstein singularity whose toric diagram Δ₁ × Δ₂ is obtained by an appropriate fibered product of the two diagrams. This product lifts to a construction on the corresponding graded quivers with superpotential, producing a graded quiver associated to Δ₁ × Δ₂ from those associated to Δ₁ and Δ₂.

Problem: Establish a precise correspondence, intrinsic to the topological B-model, between the combinatorial product of toric diagrams and the B-model construction of graded quivers. Concretely, given the B-model graded-quiver data for Gorenstein toric singularities X and Y, identify a B-model operation that produces the graded-quiver data attached to the product toric singularity X × Y (in the sense of the toric-diagram product above), and prove that the resulting graded quiver with superpotential coincides, up to the relevant equivalence, with the one obtained by the combinatorial product of the two graded quivers.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Brane tilings carry a modular parameter tau_R coming from isoradial embedding and R-charges, while the associated Belyi pair defines a modular parameter tau_B. In which situations does the equality tau_B = tau_R hold?
self_contained_problem:
A brane tiling is a bipartite graph drawn on a two-dimensional torus that encodes the data of a four-dimensional N=1 superconformal quiver gauge theory associated with a toric Calabi–Yau threefold. Two complex structures (modular parameters of the torus) can be attached to such a tiling:

(1) The R-charge modular parameter τ_R. By a-maximization, every chiral field of the gauge theory acquires an R-charge R_i ∈ (0,1). An isoradial embedding of the brane tiling places every edge as a chord of a unit circle so that the angle subtended at each white/black node by the edge corresponding to a field of R-charge R_i equals πR_i. The fundamental domain of this embedding is a parallelogram in the plane whose ratio of sides (with the appropriate orientation) defines a point τ_R in the upper half-plane, well-defined modulo SL(2,Z).

(2) The Belyi modular parameter τ_B. The combinatorial data of the brane tiling (its permutation triple, or equivalently the associated dessin d'enfant on the torus) determines a Belyi pair (E, β), where E is an elliptic curve and β : E → P^1 is a holomorphic map ramified only over {0, 1, ∞}. The complex structure of E gives a modular parameter τ_B in the upper half-plane, well-defined modulo SL(2,Z).

Problem: Characterize the brane tilings (equivalently, the toric Calabi–Yau threefolds and their associated dessins d'enfants on the torus) for which the equality τ_B = τ_R holds in SL(2,Z)\H. In particular, identify necessary and sufficient combinatorial or geometric conditions on the brane tiling that guarantee this equality.

A brane tiling is a bipartite graph G drawn on a two-torus T^2 = R^2/Z^2 whose faces are 2-coloured. To each edge e of G one assigns a positive real number R_e in (0,1), called an R-charge, such that for every vertex v one has sum_{e ni v} R_e = 1 (the marginality condition) and for every face f one has sum_{e in partial f} (1 - R_e) = 2 (the anomaly cancellation condition). Given such an R-charge distribution, the tiling admits an isoradial embedding in which every edge e subtends an angle pi R_e at the center of each adjacent face; this construction realises G as the bipartite graph dual to a dessin d'enfant on a Riemann surface, and the complex structure on the resulting elliptic curve is encoded by a modular parameter tau_R in the upper half-plane H, well-defined modulo PSL(2,Z), depending only on the data (G, {R_e}).

More concretely: does the orbit of tau_R under Gal(Qbar/Q) lie in the modular orbit of the j-invariant of the corresponding Belyi pair, and can tau_R be used to distinguish Galois orbits of dessins?

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
context_brief: Physical meaning of common Galois orbit
original_question: When two brane tiling theories have bipartite graphs that, viewed as dessins d’enfants, lie in the same Galois orbit, does that relationship have physical significance?
self_contained_problem:
A brane tiling is a bipartite graph drawn on a two–torus (or, more generally, on a Riemann surface) which encodes a four-dimensional N=1 supersymmetric quiver gauge theory whose mesonic moduli space is a toric Calabi–Yau cone. Any such bipartite graph on a compact Riemann surface can be regarded as a dessin d'enfant in the sense of Grothendieck: there exists an associated Belyi map, i.e. a meromorphic function ramified only over {0,1,∞}, with the black vertices being the preimages of 0, the white vertices the preimages of 1, and the faces the preimages of ∞. By Belyi's theorem the underlying Riemann surface and Belyi map are defined over the algebraic numbers, and the absolute Galois group Gal(Q̄/Q) acts on the set of all dessins, partitioning them into finite orbits.

Two brane tiling theories T₁ and T₂ are said to lie in the same Galois orbit if their bipartite graphs, viewed as dessins d'enfants, are related by some element of Gal(Q̄/Q).

Problem. Determine whether the relation "lying in the same Galois orbit of dessins d'enfants" carries intrinsic physical significance for the corresponding quiver gauge theories. More precisely: identify physical invariants, dualities, or quantitative relationships (for example among R-charges of chiral fields, central charges, superconformal indices, Seiberg-duality classes, or normalized volumes of the dual Sasaki–Einstein geometries) that are shared, or that transform in a controlled way, between brane tiling theories whose dessins lie in a common Galois orbit.
status_search_result: The question appears to remain open. Existing work (e.g., Hanany–He–Jejjala and follow-ups on gauge theories and dessins d'enfants beyond the torus) has established that certain algebraic invariants such as the degree of the field of definition over Q are Seiberg-duality invariants, but the precise physical interpretation of common Galois orbits—particularly how the Galois action affects R-charges, isoradial embeddings, and normalized volumes of the dual Sasaki–Einstein geometries—is explicitly stated to remain to be understood, with no comprehensive resolution found in the literature.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: How are N = 1 vacua obtained from deformations of Seiberg-Witten curves explicitly linked to dessins d’enfants?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $G$ be a simple gauge group and consider an $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric gauge theory in four dimensions whose Coulomb branch is described by a Seiberg-Witten curve $\Sigma\to\mathbb{P}^1$ together with a meromorphic Seiberg-Witten differential $\lambda$. Adding a generic superpotential deformation that breaks supersymmetry from $\mathcal{N}=2$ to $\mathcal{N}=1$ confines the theory to isolated vacua, which are described by factorizations of the Seiberg-Witten curve in which the branch points coalesce so that $\Sigma$ degenerates to a rational curve with prescribed double points. To each such factorization one associates the corresponding rational map $\varphi:\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^1$ obtained from the degenerated curve.

A Grothendieck dessin d'enfant is a bipartite graph embedded in a compact oriented surface that arises as $\varphi^{-1}([0,1])$ for a Belyi map $\varphi:X\to\mathbb{P}^1$, i.e. a rational map ramified only over $\{0,1,\infty\}$. Belyi's theorem implies that $X$ admits a model over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, and the absolute Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ acts faithfully on the set of dessins.

Problem. Construct an explicit and canonical correspondence
\[
\bigl\{\,\mathcal{N}=1\text{ vacua obtained from superpotential deformations of a given Seiberg-Witten curve}\,\bigr\}\;\longleftrightarrow\;\bigl\{\,\text{dessins d'enfants}\bigr\},
\]
specifying, for each $\mathcal{N}=1$ vacuum, which Belyi pair $(X,\varphi)$ it produces and, conversely, which factorization data of the Seiberg-Witten curve correspond to a given dessin. The correspondence should identify gauge-theoretic invariants distinguishing branches of $\mathcal{N}=1$ vacua with arithmetic invariants distinguishing Galois orbits of dessins, and should be compatible with the natural moduli of the Coulomb branch.
status_search_result: An explicit link has been developed in several works, beginning with "Children's Drawings From Seiberg-Witten Curves" (2006) and substantially extended in "Dessins d'enfants, Seiberg-Witten curves and conformal blocks" (JHEP 2021), where Belyi maps are identified with degenerated Seiberg-Witten curves and combined with AGT to produce conformal blocks; a machine-learning exploration also exists. The correspondence is constructed in specific families (e.g. trivalent dessins with 4 punctures on the sphere) and connects gauge-theoretic branch invariants to Galois-orbit invariants, but a fully general, canonical dictionary remains incomplete.

original_question: Can one establish a complete correspondence between tropical geometry and neural networks, especially the piecewise-linear functions arising from ReLU architectures?
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. Zhang–Naitzat–Lim (2018) showed that feedforward ReLU networks with integer weights are equivalent to tropical rational maps, relating linear regions to vertices of Newton polytopes and decision boundaries to tropical hypersurfaces. Subsequent work (e.g., Brandenburg–Loho–Montúfar, 2024, "The Real Tropical Geometry of Neural Networks") extends this to real weights via real tropical geometry, embedding the parameter space of ReLU networks as a semialgebraic subset of tropical rational function space. A fully complete dictionary including all architectural and geometric invariants is still being developed, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
original_question: Can the empirical success of machine-learning methods be explained using techniques from quantum field theory, such as ideas related to renormalization-group flow and fixed points?
self_contained_problem:
Provide a rigorous theoretical framework, grounded in quantum field theory, that explains the empirical effectiveness of modern machine-learning methods (e.g., deep neural networks). In particular:

(a) Construct a precise correspondence between the training dynamics of a parameterized learning model (such as a deep neural network with weights evolving under gradient descent on a loss functional) and a renormalization-group (RG) flow on a space of effective field theories or effective probability distributions. Specify the analogue of the energy scale, the coarse-graining map, and the space of couplings.

(b) Within this correspondence, identify fixed points of the RG flow and relate them to features of trained models such as generalization, feature learning, or criticality. Prove that the existence and stability properties of these fixed points imply quantitative bounds (e.g., on generalization error, expressivity, or convergence rate) that match observed empirical behavior.

(c) Demonstrate that the framework yields nontrivial, testable predictions about machine-learning systems that are not obtainable from existing statistical-learning-theory tools, and verify at least one such prediction rigorously for a concrete class of models (for instance, infinite-width neural networks, residual networks viewed as discretized flows, or restricted Boltzmann machines).

Either produce such a framework with proofs, or show that no quantum-field-theoretic explanation along these lines can recover the empirical success of machine learning.
status_search_result: The question is a broad conceptual research direction connecting renormalization-group ideas to deep learning. There is an active literature (Mehta–Schwab on RG and deep learning, neural-tangent-kernel / NNGP correspondences, Halverson et al. on neural networks as field theories, Roberts–Yaida principles of deep learning theory) offering partial analogies and specific results, but no consensus or complete QFT-based explanation of machine-learning success. The problem remains open in its general form.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: To what extent do non-additive genetic effects, including epistatic interactions among variants or genes, contribute substantial phenotypic variance in complex human traits, and how should genome-wide association studies, polygenic risk scores, and heritability methods detect and model those effects when existing methods mostly assume additive allele effects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a complex quantitative or disease phenotype $Y$ in a human population, modeled as a function of genotypes $G = (G_1, \ldots, G_M)$ at $M$ genetic variants together with environmental and residual contributions. The standard additive model writes
$$Y = \mu + \sum_{i=1}^M \beta_i G_i + \varepsilon,$$
and the additive (narrow-sense) heritability $h^2$ is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance explained by $\sum_i \beta_i G_i$. A more general decomposition allows non-additive contributions
$$Y = \mu + \sum_i \beta_i G_i + \sum_{i<j} \gamma_{ij}\, f_{ij}(G_i, G_j) + \text{higher-order terms} + \varepsilon,$$
where the dominance terms and the epistatic interaction terms $f_{ij}(G_i,G_j)$ (and their higher-order analogs) capture deviations from additivity. The broad-sense heritability $H^2$ is the fraction of phenotypic variance attributable to all genetic terms.

Address the following:

(a) Determine whether non-additive genetic effects, in particular pairwise (and higher-order) epistatic interactions among variants or genes, contribute a substantial portion of the phenotypic variance $H^2 - h^2$ for typical complex human traits, or whether this gap is generically small.

(b) Develop statistical and computational methodology — applicable to genome-wide association studies, polygenic risk scores, and heritability estimation — that can reliably detect, estimate, and incorporate epistatic interaction terms $\gamma_{ij} f_{ij}(G_i, G_j)$ at genome scale, where naive enumeration over all $\binom{M}{2}$ pairs (with $M$ on the order of $10^6$ variants) is computationally and statistically prohibitive.

(c) Quantify the conditions (sample size, effect-size distribution, allele-frequency spectrum, linkage disequilibrium structure) under which explicitly modeling non-additive effects measurably improves heritability estimates and predictive accuracy of polygenic scores compared with purely additive models.
status_search_result: The question of how much non-additive and epistatic variance contributes to complex human traits, and how to detect such effects at genome scale, remains actively debated as of 2025–2026. Recent work in vertebrate models has uncovered substantial G×G and G×G×E interactions, and 2025 benchmarking studies of non-additive polygenic prediction conclude that it is still unclear when explicit modeling of non-additive SNP effects improves disease risk prediction, with larger datasets needed. No general resolution has been established.

The problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How can large, accessible family-based cohorts and methods that combine family-based and population-based data be built and analyzed so that complex-trait studies can exploit Mendelian transmission and parental genotypes to separate causal from confounding effects and direct from indirect genetic effects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a complex (polygenic) quantitative or binary trait Y measured on individuals in a population, together with their genome-wide genotypes G. In a standard population-based genome-wide association study (GWAS), one estimates, for each variant j, an effect β_j by regressing Y on G_j (with covariates). This estimated effect conflates: (i) the direct genetic effect (the causal effect of the individual's own allele on their own phenotype), (ii) indirect genetic effects (effects of relatives' genotypes acting through the environment, e.g., parental nurture), (iii) effects of population structure, assortative mating, and other sources of gene–environment confounding.

By contrast, in a family-based design with genotyped parent–offspring trios, Mendelian transmission provides, conditional on parental genotypes, a randomized assignment of the transmitted allele to the offspring; regressing offspring phenotype on transmitted vs. non-transmitted parental alleles permits unbiased estimation of direct effects and, via the non-transmitted alleles, of indirect (e.g., parental) effects. Such trio/sibship cohorts are however much smaller than population biobanks.

Formulate and solve the following problem:

(a) Design a statistical estimation framework that takes as input a large population-based cohort of unrelated individuals together with a (substantially smaller) family-based cohort of related individuals (e.g., parent–offspring trios, sibling pairs, or extended pedigrees), each with genome-wide genotypes and trait measurements, and that produces, for every variant or for genome-wide polygenic predictors, separate consistent estimators of (1) the direct genetic effect, (2) the indirect (parental/sibling) genetic effect, and (3) bias terms due to population stratification and assortative mating.

(b) Establish identifiability conditions and derive the asymptotic efficiency of the combined estimator relative to (i) the family-only estimator and (ii) the population-only estimator, as a function of the relative sample sizes, the heritability, and the magnitude of indirect effects and confounding.

(c) Provide a concrete construction (with proofs of consistency) showing how Mendelian transmission within the family subset can be used to debias the larger population-based estimates, including a procedure for constructing polygenic scores whose predictive accuracy reflects only direct genetic effects.

Equivalently: give a method, together with a theoretical guarantee, for using parental genotypes and Mendelian segregation to separate causal direct genetic effects from confounding and indirect genetic effects in complex-trait studies that pool family-based and population-based data.
status_search_result: Methods for separating direct from indirect genetic effects using family-based designs (e.g., Young et al.'s SNIPar/FGWAS, Kong et al.'s non-transmitted alleles approach, and Howe et al.'s within-sibship GWAS) have made substantial progress, and growing family resources (deCODE, MoBa, UK Biobank sibling subsets) have been used to combine family- and population-based signals. However, no general, fully accepted framework yet provides scalable, unbiased separation of direct, indirect, and stratification effects at biobank scale, and the problem is still discussed as open in recent reviews (2023–2025).

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How should complex human phenotypes be defined and measured—such as deciding whether to split or merge diagnoses, whether to use official clinical diagnoses or self-reports, and when to analyze sex-specific subphenotypes—so that genetic studies reduce noise and bias and align phenotype categories with biological mechanisms?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the methodological problem of defining and measuring complex human phenotypes for use in genetic association studies (e.g., genome-wide association studies and heritability analyses). A phenotype is a measurable trait of an individual (such as a disease status, a quantitative biomarker, or a behavioral measure) that is to be related statistically to genetic variation across a population. Develop a principled framework that addresses the following methodological questions and quantifies their impact on the bias, variance, and statistical power of downstream genetic analyses:

1. Splitting versus merging: Given a candidate phenotype category that may correspond to a heterogeneous collection of biological mechanisms (for example, a broad diagnostic class versus its clinical subtypes), determine criteria for when the category should be subdivided into finer subphenotypes and when distinct categories should be merged into a single phenotype, so that the resulting categories better align with underlying biological mechanisms.

2. Diagnostic source: Compare the use of official clinical diagnoses (made by trained professionals according to standardized criteria) versus self-reported disease status (obtained from questionnaires) as the definition of case/control phenotypes. Characterize the random noise and systematic biases each introduces, and provide guidance for choosing or combining these sources.

3. Sex-specific analysis: Provide criteria for deciding when a phenotype should be analyzed separately by sex (i.e., as two sex-specific subphenotypes) rather than pooled, taking into account possible sex-specific genetic architectures and measurement differences.

The goal is to develop methodology and best practices for phenotype definition and measurement that minimize ill-defined phenotype effects, reduce the random noise and systematic biases they introduce into genetic studies, and align phenotype categories with biological mechanisms.
category_tag: phenotype definition in genetic association studies
status_search_result: This is stated as a broad open methodological problem in human trait genetics. It is an ongoing area of active research (phenotype harmonization, deep phenotyping, electronic-health-record phenotyping, PheWAS) rather than a question with a single definitive solution; no consensus framework resolves the splitting/merging, clinical-versus-self-report, and sex-specific analysis questions in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How should researchers interpret and compare heritability estimates from twin studies, genomic-relatedness methods such as GREML and LDSC, and family-based methods, given that these methods use different broad-sense or narrow-sense definitions, rely on different assumptions, are sensitive to biases, and often produce different estimates for the same trait?
self_contained_problem:
For a quantitative human trait Y measured in a population, define the broad-sense heritability as H^2 = Var(G)/Var(Y), where G is the total genetic value, and the narrow-sense heritability as h^2 = Var(A)/Var(Y), where A is the additive genetic component. Three families of statistical estimators are commonly used to estimate heritability from data:

1. Classical twin-study estimators (e.g., the ACE model), which decompose phenotypic variance among monozygotic and dizygotic twin pairs using assumptions about shared environment and additive genetic effects, and typically target H^2 or h^2 under structural assumptions on environmental sharing.

2. Genomic-relatedness-based estimators applied to unrelated individuals genotyped on common SNPs, including (i) GREML/GCTA, which fits a linear mixed model Y = Xβ + g + ε with Cov(g) = σ_g^2 K for a genomic relationship matrix K built from common SNPs, and (ii) LD-score regression (LDSC), which regresses GWAS chi-square statistics on LD scores to estimate SNP-heritability h^2_SNP. These methods target the variance explained by the genotyped (or tagged) variants under specific assumptions about effect-size distributions and LD structure.

3. Family-based estimators (e.g., sib-regression, RDR, relatedness-disequilibrium regression) that exploit within-family variation in realized genomic sharing to estimate h^2 while attempting to control for assortative mating and shared environment.

These estimators rely on different identification assumptions (random mating, no gene-environment correlation, additive effects, distributional assumptions on effect sizes, equal environments for MZ vs DZ twins, etc.), target different estimands (H^2 vs h^2 vs h^2_SNP vs family-h^2), and in practice often yield numerically different estimates for the same trait, with discrepancies persisting even between methods within the same family.

Problem. Provide a rigorous framework for interpreting and comparing heritability estimates produced by these three families of methods. Specifically:

(a) Formulate a unified statistical model under which the estimands targeted by twin, genomic-relatedness (GREML and LDSC), and family-based estimators can be written as explicit functionals of the same underlying joint distribution of genotypes, phenotypes, and environments, making precise how each estimand differs from the others.

(b) Characterize, as a function of model misspecification (assortative mating, dominance, gene-environment correlation, rare-variant contribution, population stratification, LD-effect-size coupling), the bias of each estimator relative to the corresponding population estimand, and derive sharp identifiability conditions under which two given methods must agree asymptotically.

(c) Determine the precise sense (if any) in which a heritability estimate provides an upper bound on the variance explainable by a polygenic risk score constructed from a given class of genetic predictors, and identify which of the estimators above produces the tightest such bound under stated assumptions.
status_search_result: Recent literature continues to debate the comparison and interpretation of heritability estimates from twin, GREML/LDSC, and family-based methods. Methodological papers (e.g., RDR, sib-regression variants, and recent critiques of LDSC and GREML) have clarified individual biases but no unified framework reconciling all three families is established; estimates for the same trait still diverge in practice. The problem remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How can genotype-to-phenotype predictive models, including polygenic risk scores that aggregate many weak genetic signals into an individual-level phenotype or disease-risk prediction, explain substantially more trait variance and reach clinical relevance without relying only on ever-larger cohorts?
self_contained_problem:
Let a quantitative or binary human phenotype Y be modeled as a function of a high-dimensional genotype vector G ∈ {0,1,2}^p (encoding allele counts at p single-nucleotide polymorphism loci, with p on the order of 10^6 to 10^7) together with unobserved environmental, demographic, and non-additive genetic factors. A polygenic risk score (PRS) is any predictor of the form Ŷ(G) = f(G; θ), where θ is learned from a training cohort of N individuals with paired (G, Y) data; the most common instance is the linear score Ŷ(G) = Σ_j β_j G_j, with weights β_j estimated from genome-wide association statistics. Predictive performance is measured by the proportion of phenotypic variance explained on held-out individuals, R²(Ŷ, Y), or by analogous metrics such as AUC for disease traits; the gap between R² and the trait's narrow-sense heritability h² quantifies the "missing prediction."

Develop methodology — for example, by exploiting non-additive interactions, rare variants, functional genomic annotations, cross-trait structure, regularization tailored to linkage disequilibrium, multi-ancestry data, or alternative model classes — such that for a fixed training cohort size N, the held-out predictive R² of the resulting PRS is substantially larger than that achievable by current linear summary-statistic-based scores, and prove quantitative guarantees on the improvement. Concretely: identify conditions on the genetic architecture of a trait (e.g., effect-size distribution, level of epistasis, sparsity, polygenicity) under which a PRS can attain R² close to h² at a sample size N strictly smaller than that required by standard additive linear models, and characterize the optimal achievable R² as a function of (N, p, h², architecture).
status_search_result: Improving polygenic risk score (PRS) accuracy without simply increasing cohort size remains an active and unsolved research problem. Recent work (2022–2025) has proposed methods incorporating functional annotations (e.g., PolyPred, LDpred-funct, PRS-CSx for cross-ancestry), but predictive R² for most complex traits remains well below heritability, and no method has been shown to close this gap at fixed N. The problem is broadly recognized as open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
original_question: How can polygenic risk scores and related genotype-to-phenotype prediction models be made robust when transferred across populations, datasets, and genotyping technologies, and what theoretical framework can predict expected accuracy loss from linkage disequilibrium, allele-frequency or effect-size differences, gene-environment or gene-gene interactions, and batch effects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of genotype-to-phenotype prediction via polygenic risk scores (PRS). A PRS is a linear predictor of a phenotype y for an individual i defined as PRS_i = sum_{j=1}^{M} beta_j * g_{ij}, where g_{ij} is the (possibly imputed or dosage-coded) genotype at single-nucleotide variant j and beta_j is an effect-size estimate obtained from a training cohort (typically via genome-wide association study summary statistics, with optional shrinkage or LD-based adjustment). Suppose the training data are drawn from a source population/cohort/genotyping platform S with linkage-disequilibrium (LD) structure Sigma_S, allele frequencies f_S, causal-effect distribution pi_S, and environmental/interaction structure E_S, while predictions are made on a target setting T with possibly distinct Sigma_T, f_T, pi_T, E_T, and additional measurement/batch noise.

(a) Develop a methodology for constructing PRS-type predictors that remain robust (in the sense of bounded loss of predictive R^2 or AUC) when transferred from S to T, accounting jointly for: (i) LD differences Sigma_S vs Sigma_T, (ii) allele-frequency differences f_S vs f_T, (iii) effect-size heterogeneity pi_S vs pi_T, (iv) gene-environment and gene-gene interaction differences, and (v) genotyping/batch effects.

(b) Derive a theoretical framework that, given quantitative descriptions of (i)-(v) above, predicts the expected accuracy loss Delta = R^2_S - R^2_T (or a comparable transfer-gap functional) of the PRS when applied to T, with explicit dependence on the population-genetic and statistical parameters governing the source and target settings.

Provide either a constructive estimator with provable transfer guarantees, or rigorous bounds/exact expressions for the expected accuracy decay under a well-specified probabilistic model of cross-setting variation.

original_question: Let C be a smooth projective curve over the complex numbers. What is the dimension of each irreducible component of the Brill-Noether locus B(n,d,k)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective irreducible curve of genus $g \ge 2$ over the complex numbers. For integers $n \ge 1$, $d$, and $k \ge 1$, let $M(n,d)$ denote the moduli space of (semi)stable vector bundles on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and define the higher-rank Brill–Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k) \;=\; \{\, [E] \in M(n,d) \,:\, h^0(C,E) \ge k \,\}.$$

$$\beta(n,d,k) \;=\; n^2(g-1) + 1 - k\bigl(k - d + n(g-1)\bigr).$$

Lower bounds (e.g., dim ≥ β when k > d − n(g−1)) and the existence of components of the expected dimension have been established under various hypotheses (Teixidor i Bigas, Mercat, and others), and recent work continues to determine components in further regimes, but a complete answer remains unavailable.

$$\mu_\alpha(E,V)=\frac{d}{n}+\alpha\,\frac{k}{n}.$$
A coherent system $(E,V)$ is called $\alpha$-stable (respectively $\alpha$-semistable) if for every proper coherent subsystem $(E',V')$ (i.e., $E'\subseteq E$ a nonzero subbundle and $V'\subseteq V\cap H^0(C,E')$) one has
$$\mu_\alpha(E',V')<\mu_\alpha(E,V)\quad(\text{resp. }\le).$$
Let $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ denote the moduli space of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$.

Question: For which choices of $C$, $\alpha$, and $(n,d,k)$ is the moduli space $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ smooth? In particular, is $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ smooth whenever it is nonempty?

original_question: For a smooth curve C, is the rank-n Clifford index monotone in rank in the sense that Cliff_n(C) <= Cliff_m(C) whenever n >= m?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve of genus $g \geq 4$ over the complex numbers. For an integer $n \geq 1$, define the rank-$n$ Clifford index of $C$ by
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C) := \min_E \left\{ \frac{1}{n}\bigl(\deg E - 2(h^0(E) - n)\bigr) \right\},$$
where the minimum is taken over all semistable vector bundles $E$ on $C$ of rank $n$ satisfying
- $h^0(E) \geq 2n$, and
- $\mu(E) := \deg(E)/n \leq g - 1$.

(For $n = 1$ this recovers the classical Clifford index of $C$.)

Question: Is it true that for every smooth irreducible projective curve $C$ of genus $g \geq 4$ and for all integers $n \geq m \geq 1$, one has
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C) \leq \mathrm{Cliff}_m(C)?$$
status_search_result: The monotonicity of higher-rank Clifford indices in the rank is posed as an open question in the literature on higher rank Brill–Noether theory and coherent systems. Work by Lange–Newstead introduces these invariants and computes them in special cases, but a general monotonicity result Cliff_n(C) ≤ Cliff_m(C) for n ≥ m does not appear to be established.

original_question: Which vector bundles compute the Clifford index Cliff_n(C), and among them which, if any, are stable bundles?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible complex projective curve of genus $g\geq 2$. For a vector bundle $E$ on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, define the Clifford index of $E$ by
$$\gamma(E) \;=\; \mu(E) - \frac{2}{n}\,h^0(E) + 2 \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\bigl(d - 2(h^0(E)-n)\bigr),$$
where $\mu(E)=d/n$ is the slope. For an integer $n\geq 1$, the rank-$n$ Clifford index of $C$ is
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C) \;=\; \inf\bigl\{\gamma(E) \;:\; E \text{ semistable of rank } n,\ h^0(E)\geq 2n,\ \mu(E)\leq g-1 \bigr\}.$$
A semistable bundle $E$ attaining this infimum is said to compute $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$.

Problem. Characterize the semistable vector bundles $E$ of rank $n$ on $C$ that compute $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$. In particular, determine for which curves $C$ and which ranks $n$ there exists a stable bundle computing $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$, and describe all such stable bundles when they exist.

original_question: If C is a smooth plane curve of degree delta >= 7, are the only vector bundles computing Cliff_n(C) precisely the direct sums of copies of the hyperplane bundle H?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ be a smooth complex projective plane curve of degree $\delta \ge 7$, and let $H = \mathcal{O}_C(1)$ denote the hyperplane bundle on $C$. For a vector bundle $E$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$ on $C$ with $h^0(E) \ge n+1$, define the Clifford index of $E$ by
$$\gamma(E) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\bigl(d - 2(h^0(E) - n)\bigr).$$
For an integer $n \ge 1$, define the rank-$n$ Clifford index of $C$ by
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C) \;=\; \inf\bigl\{\gamma(E) \,:\, E \text{ is a semistable vector bundle on } C \text{ of rank } n,\ h^0(E) \ge 2n,\ \mu(E) \le g(C)-1\bigr\},$$
where $g(C) = \binom{\delta-1}{2}$ is the genus of $C$. We say a vector bundle $E$ on $C$ \emph{computes} $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$ if $E$ satisfies the conditions in this infimum and $\gamma(E) = \mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$.

Question: Is it true that the vector bundles on $C$ that compute $\mathrm{Cliff}_n(C)$ are exactly the direct sums $H^{\oplus n}$ of $n$ copies of the hyperplane bundle?
status_search_result: The question appears in a 2021 survey of open problems in higher-rank Brill–Noether theory and coherent systems. Recent work (e.g., on rank-two Clifford indices and Lazarsfeld–Mukai techniques) computes the value of the higher-rank Clifford index for smooth plane curves of degree $\ge 5$ as $\delta - 4$, achieved by direct sums of the hyperplane bundle, but a complete uniqueness/classification of all bundles attaining this value for $\delta \ge 7$ does not appear in the located literature. original_question: Let K be the canonical bundle of a smooth curve C of genus g >= 2. Whenever the modified Brill-Noether number beta(2,K,k)=3g-3-k(k+1)/2 is nonnegative, must the locus B(2,K,k) of semistable rank-2 bundles with determinant K and at least k sections be nonempty?

Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible complex projective curve of genus $g\geq 2$, and let $K=K_C$ denote its canonical line bundle. original_question: Let C be a general smooth curve of genus g >= 1, and let (E,V) be a general generated coherent system in S_0(n,d,k). Is the dual-span bundle D_{E,V} semistable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a general smooth projective curve of genus $g\ge 1$ over $\mathbb{C}$. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$ is a pair $(E,V)$ where $E$ is a vector bundle on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and $V\subseteq H^0(E)$ is a linear subspace of dimension $k$. The coherent system $(E,V)$ is called generated if the evaluation map $V\otimes \mathcal{O}_C \to E$ is surjective; in this case one has a short exact sequence
$$0 \longrightarrow M_{E,V} \longrightarrow V\otimes \mathcal{O}_C \longrightarrow E \longrightarrow 0,$$
and the dual-span bundle is defined by $D_{E,V} := M_{E,V}^{\vee}$, a vector bundle of rank $k-n$ and degree $d$. Let $S_0(n,d,k)$ denote the moduli space of generated coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$ for which $E$ is semistable (equivalently, for which $h^0(E^*)=0$ so that the dual-span construction yields a coherent system $(D_{E,V}, V^*)$).

Question: for a general curve $C$ of genus $g\ge 1$ and a general $(E,V)\in S_0(n,d,k)$, is the dual-span bundle $D_{E,V}$ semistable?
status_search_result: This is a form of Butler's conjecture on the (semi)stability of the dual span bundle of a general generated coherent system. It remains open in general, but multiple partial results are known: stability has been established in special ranges (e.g. type (2,d,4) and (2,d,5) under linear stability hypotheses), and recent works (2023–2024) continue to make progress using linear stability and α-stability techniques, without resolving the full conjecture.

A coherent system of type (n, d, k) on C is a pair (E, V), where E is a vector bundle on C of rank n and degree d, and V ⊆ H^0(E) is a k-dimensional subspace of global sections. The coherent system (E, V) is called generated if the evaluation map V ⊗ O_C → E is surjective; in that case its dual-span bundle D_{E,V} is defined as the dual of the kernel M_{E,V} of this evaluation map, i.e. one has the exact sequence
   0 → M_{E,V} → V ⊗ O_C → E → 0,  D_{E,V} := M_{E,V}^∨.

A generated coherent system (E, V) of type (n, d, k) (with k > n) is called linearly semistable if for every proper subspace W ⊂ V with 0 < dim W < k generating a subsheaf E_W ⊆ E of rank n_W (the image of W ⊗ O_C → E), one has
   deg(E_W) / (dim W − n_W) ≥ deg(E) / (k − n),
and linearly stable if strict inequality holds for all such W.

Denote by G(n, d, k) the moduli space of α-stable coherent systems of type (n, d, k).

original_question: Suppose on P^1 that d = an - t with a >= 2, 1 <= t <= n-1, and k >= n. If G(alpha;n,d,k) is nonempty for some alpha, must the upper endpoint alpha_M of the interval I(n,d,k) be infinite?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X=\mathbb{P}^1$ be the projective line over an algebraically closed field. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $X$ is a pair $(E,V)$ where $E$ is an algebraic vector bundle on $X$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and $V\subseteq H^0(X,E)$ is a $k$-dimensional linear subspace of sections. For a real parameter $\alpha>0$, the $\alpha$-slope of a coherent system $(E,V)$ is defined by
$$\mu_\alpha(E,V) \;=\; \frac{d}{n} \,+\, \alpha\,\frac{k}{n},$$
and $(E,V)$ is called $\alpha$-stable if for every proper coherent subsystem $(E',V')$ (with $E'\subset E$ a subbundle and $V'\subseteq V\cap H^0(E')$) one has
$$\frac{\deg E'}{\operatorname{rk} E'} + \alpha\,\frac{\dim V'}{\operatorname{rk} E'} \;<\; \mu_\alpha(E,V).$$
Denote by $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ the moduli space of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ on $X$. It is known that the set of values of $\alpha>0$ for which $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ is non-empty forms an interval $I(n,d,k)\subseteq(0,\infty)$, whose upper endpoint is denoted $\alpha_M=\alpha_M(n,d,k)\in(0,\infty]$.

Suppose that $d = an - t$ with integers $a\ge 2$ and $1\le t\le n-1$, and that $k\ge n$. Assume that $G(\alpha;n,d,k)$ is non-empty for some $\alpha>0$. Must $\alpha_M(n,d,k)=\infty$?

original_question: Fix a smooth curve C of genus g >= 2 with specified classical Clifford index Cliff_1(C). What values can the coherent-system Clifford indices Cliff_{alpha,n}(C) attain?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible complex projective curve of genus $g \geq 2$. Recall the classical Clifford index of $C$:
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_1(C) = \min\{ \deg L - 2(h^0(L) - 1) : L \text{ a line bundle on } C \text{ with } h^0(L) \geq 2 \text{ and } h^1(L) \geq 2 \}.$$

A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$ is a pair $(E,V)$ where $E$ is a vector bundle on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$, and $V \subseteq H^0(E)$ is a linear subspace of dimension $k$. For a real number $\alpha > 0$, the $\alpha$-slope of a coherent system $(E,V)$ of type $(n,d,k)$ is
$$\mu_\alpha(E,V) = \frac{d}{n} + \alpha \frac{k}{n},$$
and $(E,V)$ is called $\alpha$-(semi)stable if for every proper coherent subsystem $(E',V') \subset (E,V)$, $\mu_\alpha(E',V') < \mu_\alpha(E,V)$ (resp. $\leq$).

For integers $n \geq 1$ and $\alpha > 0$, define the coherent-system Clifford index
$$\mathrm{Cliff}_{\alpha,n}(C) = \min\left\{ \frac{d}{n} - 2\!\left(\frac{k}{n} - 1\right) : (E,V) \text{ is } \alpha\text{-semistable of type }(n,d,k),\ k \geq n+1,\ \mu(E) \leq g-1 \right\}.$$

Problem: Given a fixed value of the classical Clifford index $\mathrm{Cliff}_1(C)$, determine all possible values that the coherent-system Clifford indices $\mathrm{Cliff}_{\alpha,n}(C)$ can attain as $n$ and $\alpha$ vary, for curves $C$ with that prescribed $\mathrm{Cliff}_1(C)$.

No source verifies a complete answer.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: For a general nodal curve, if (E,V) is a general generated linear series in G(1,d,k), is the dual-span bundle D_{E,V} semistable?
self_contained_problem:
Let C be a general nodal curve (a general irreducible projective curve over the complex numbers having only nodes as singularities, or alternatively a general reducible curve with nodal singularities). Given a coherent system (E,V) consisting of a vector bundle E on C together with a linear subspace V ⊂ H^0(C,E), we say (E,V) is generated if the evaluation map V ⊗ O_C → E is surjective. In that case, the dual-span bundle D_{E,V} is defined by dualizing the short exact sequence

   0 → M_{E,V} → V ⊗ O_C → E → 0,

so that D_{E,V} := M_{E,V}^* fits in

   0 → E^* → V^* ⊗ O_C → D_{E,V} → 0.

Let G(1,d,k) denote the moduli space of generated coherent systems (E,V) on C with E a line bundle of degree d and dim V = k (so that rank D_{E,V} = k−1).

Question: For a general nodal curve C and a general (E,V) ∈ G(1,d,k) that is generated, is the dual-span bundle D_{E,V} semistable?
category_tag: Brill-Noether theory and dual span bundles
status_search_result: The problem is a nodal-curve version of Butler's conjecture on semistability of dual-span (kernel) bundles. Recent work (2023–2024) on linear stability of coherent systems and on kernel bundles over reducible nodal curves provides partial progress in specific rank/degree ranges, but no general resolution for general nodal curves and general generated (E,V) ∈ G(1,d,k) appears in the literature. The question therefore remains open.

paper_title: Higher Rank Brill-Noether Theory and Coherent Systems: Open Questions
original_question: Let C be a smooth curve equipped with the morphism C -> P^1 induced by a line bundle of degree d_{1,2}, the gonality map. Study higher-rank Brill-Noether loci and coherent systems on C through that morphism.
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth irreducible projective curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, of genus $g \ge 2$. Let $d_{1,2}$ denote the gonality of $C$, that is, the minimal degree of a non-constant morphism $C \to \mathbb{P}^1$, and let $L$ be a line bundle on $C$ of degree $d_{1,2}$ with a two-dimensional space of global sections $V \subset H^0(C,L)$, so that the associated gonality morphism $\varphi_L \colon C \to \mathbb{P}^1$ has degree $d_{1,2}$.

For integers $n \ge 1$, $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $k \ge 0$, define the higher-rank Brill–Noether locus
$$B(n,d,k) = \{ E \in M(n,d) : h^0(C,E) \ge k \},$$
where $M(n,d)$ is the moduli space of semistable vector bundles on $C$ of rank $n$ and degree $d$. A coherent system of type $(n,d,k)$ on $C$ is a pair $(E,W)$ where $E$ is a vector bundle of rank $n$ and degree $d$ and $W \subseteq H^0(C,E)$ is a subspace of dimension $k$; let $G(\alpha; n,d,k)$ denote the moduli space of $\alpha$-stable coherent systems of type $(n,d,k)$ for a stability parameter $\alpha > 0$.

Using the gonality morphism $\varphi_L \colon C \to \mathbb{P}^1$ (for instance via push-forward $(\varphi_L)_* E$ to $\mathbb{P}^1$, pull-back of bundles from $\mathbb{P}^1$, kernels of evaluation maps $V \otimes \mathcal{O}_C \to L$, or Lazarsfeld–Mukai type constructions), describe the geometry of the loci $B(n,d,k)$ and of the moduli spaces $G(\alpha; n,d,k)$: in particular, determine their non-emptiness, irreducibility, dimension, and singular loci in terms of the invariants $(n,d,k)$ and the gonality $d_{1,2}$ of $C$.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research direction concerning the use of gonality morphisms to study higher-rank Brill–Noether loci and coherent systems. While related results exist (e.g., work of Lange–Newstead on coherent systems and on bundles related to gonality), a full systematic study answering the question is not available, and the problem appears to remain open as a general program.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
context_brief: neutron-star phase and equation of state
original_question: What phase of QCD matter is realized inside neutron stars, and what is the high-density QCD equation of state needed to determine that phase? More concretely, when baryonic matter is compressed to several times ordinary nuclear density so that neighboring nuclei overlap and it is no longer meaningful to assign quarks to individual nuclei, does the system remain a hadronic or nuclear medium, or does it enter a deconfined quark phase, and what first-principles finite-density QCD calculation can determine the corresponding equation of state?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at zero temperature and large baryon chemical potential, in the regime relevant to the interiors of neutron stars, where the baryon number density reaches several times the nuclear saturation density n_0 ≈ 0.16 fm^{-3}. In this regime, the typical inter-nucleon spacing becomes comparable to or smaller than the nucleon size, so that the wave functions of neighboring baryons overlap and the assignment of quarks and gluons to individual nucleons ceases to be meaningful.

(a) Determine, from first-principles QCD, the equation of state P(ε) (pressure as a function of energy density) for cold strongly interacting matter throughout the density range n ∈ [n_0, ~10 n_0] relevant to neutron-star interiors.

(b) Using this equation of state, determine which phase of QCD matter is realized at the densities reached in neutron-star cores: a confined hadronic/nuclear phase, a deconfined quark (or quark–gluon) phase, a color-superconducting phase, or some other phase, and identify the location and order of any phase transition(s) between them.

A solution should be based on a controlled first-principles QCD calculation valid at finite baryon density (for example, a lattice QCD method that overcomes the fermion sign problem at large μ_B/T, or a rigorously justified continuum approach), rather than on model-dependent phenomenological equations of state.
status_search_result: The phase of QCD matter realized in neutron-star cores and the corresponding cold high-density QCD equation of state remain open problems as of 2025. First-principles lattice QCD at large baryon chemical potential is obstructed by the sign problem, so current studies rely on phenomenological models or indirect astrophysical inference. Recent observational analyses (e.g., evidence for quark-matter cores in massive neutron stars) suggest deconfined behavior is plausible but not established, and unified hadron-quark models continue to be proposed in 2025.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: How do hadron masses, couplings, and related properties change inside nuclei or more generally at finite baryon density, and can partial restoration of chiral symmetry in nuclear matter be determined quantitatively from QCD itself rather than from phenomenological models? This includes determining how changes in the chiral condensate inside nuclear media modify hadronic observables and whether those modifications can be established reliably from first principles.
self_contained_problem:
Consider Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3) gauge theory of quarks and gluons defined by the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QCD}} = -\tfrac{1}{4} G^a_{\mu\nu} G^{a\,\mu\nu} + \sum_f \bar\psi_f (i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m_f)\psi_f\), at nonzero baryon chemical potential \(\mu_B\) (equivalently, in a nuclear medium of finite baryon density \(n_B > 0\)). Let \(\langle \bar q q \rangle_{n_B}\) denote the in-medium chiral (quark) condensate, and for a hadron \(H\) let \(M_H(n_B)\) and \(g_H(n_B)\) denote its in-medium mass and effective couplings, defined via the appropriate two- and three-point correlation functions of interpolating operators evaluated in the finite-density ground state of QCD.

(a) Derive, directly from QCD (e.g., via lattice QCD, QCD sum rules anchored to first-principles inputs, or a rigorous effective field theory matched to QCD), quantitative predictions for the dependence of \(M_H(n_B)\) and \(g_H(n_B)\) on \(n_B\) for representative hadrons (such as the nucleon, the \(\sigma\), \(\rho\), \(\omega\), and \(\phi\) mesons, and heavy-quarkonium states), without recourse to phenomenological hadronic models.

(b) Establish quantitatively, from QCD itself, the partial restoration of chiral symmetry in nuclear matter by computing \(\langle \bar q q \rangle_{n_B}/\langle \bar q q \rangle_{0}\) as a function of \(n_B\) and identifying the precise functional relationship between this ratio and the in-medium modifications \(M_H(n_B) - M_H(0)\) and \(g_H(n_B) - g_H(0)\).

The task is to provide such first-principles, quantitatively reliable determinations, overcoming in particular the sign problem that obstructs direct Monte Carlo simulation of lattice QCD at \(\mu_B \neq 0\).
category_tag: finite-density QCD and chiral symmetry restoration
status_search_result: This is a long-standing open problem in finite-density QCD. The sign problem prevents direct lattice Monte Carlo computation at nonzero baryon chemical potential, and current first-principles determinations of in-medium hadron properties and the in-medium chiral condensate remain limited; the problem is acknowledged as open in current reviews on finite-density lattice QCD and in-medium hadron physics.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Can one devise a genuinely practical method for performing QCD path integrals with complex actions at realistic computational cost, thereby solving the sign problem rather than merely circumventing it in limited regimes? This asks both for a method that remains reliable when the action is highly oscillatory and for a criterion of success based on feasible computational scaling rather than formal correctness alone.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a lattice gauge theory whose partition function is given by a high-dimensional path integral

  Z = ∫ D[U] e^{-S[U]},

where U denotes the gauge link variables on a finite four-dimensional lattice and S[U] is the (Euclidean) lattice QCD action including a chemical-potential term that makes S[U] complex. Because e^{-S[U]} is not a positive real weight, standard Monte Carlo importance sampling cannot be applied; this is known as the sign problem.

Devise a numerical algorithm with the following properties:

1. It computes expectation values ⟨O⟩ = Z^{-1} ∫ D[U] O[U] e^{-S[U]} for physically relevant observables O in lattice QCD at nonzero baryon chemical potential.
2. It remains reliable when the integrand is highly oscillatory (i.e., when |Z|/∫ D[U] |e^{-S[U]}| is exponentially small in the spacetime volume).
3. Its computational cost scales at most polynomially in the lattice four-volume V and in the inverse statistical error 1/ε, for arbitrary values of the chemical potential within the physically interesting regime.

Either exhibit such an algorithm together with a proof (or convincing demonstration) of polynomial scaling, or prove that no such algorithm exists under stated complexity-theoretic assumptions.
status_search_result: The sign problem in finite-density lattice QCD remains an open problem. Numerous approaches (complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimbles, tensor networks, density-of-states, machine-learning contour deformations, etc.) have made progress in restricted regimes, but as of recent reviews no general method with provably feasible computational scaling for full QCD at realistic chemical potentials has been established. The problem is widely considered NP-hard in general (Troyer–Wiese 2005), suggesting no universal polynomial-cost solution is expected.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Can reweighting-based approaches control the overlap problem and complex phase fluctuations well enough to remain reliable at larger chemical potential, larger volume, and near phase-transition regions? More specifically, can one avoid the regime where the reweighting factor becomes dominated by a tiny subset of configurations or where phase cancellations drive the relevant averages effectively to zero?
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice QCD with a finite quark chemical potential $\mu$. The Euclidean path integral partition function is
$$Z(\mu) = \int \mathcal{D}U \, e^{-S_g[U]} \det M(\mu)[U],$$
where $S_g[U]$ is the gauge action and $\det M(\mu)$ is the quark determinant, which for real nonzero $\mu$ is generally complex. A standard reweighting strategy is to sample configurations $U$ with respect to a positive reference measure $d\mu_0[U] \propto e^{-S_g[U]} w_0[U] \, \mathcal{D}U$ (for instance the phase-quenched measure or the $\mu = 0$ measure) and to compute
$$\langle \mathcal{O}\rangle_{\mu} = \frac{\langle \mathcal{O}\, R\rangle_0}{\langle R\rangle_0}, \qquad R[U] = \frac{e^{-S_g[U]}\det M(\mu)[U]}{e^{-S_g[U]} w_0[U]}.$$
Two well-known obstructions are:

(i) The overlap problem: the distribution of $|R|$ over configurations sampled from the reference measure may have a long, heavy tail, so that after $M$ Monte Carlo samples the estimator of $\langle R\rangle_0$ is effectively dominated by a single configuration, reducing the effective sample size from $M$ to $O(1)$.

(ii) The phase (sign) problem: the complex phase of $R[U]$ fluctuates rapidly over configurations, so that $\langle R\rangle_0$ is exponentially close to zero in the four-volume $V$ and in $\mu$, leading to uncontrolled cancellations.

Question. Does there exist a reweighting-based scheme (choice of reference measure and choice of estimator) for lattice QCD at finite real quark chemical potential which provably controls both obstructions (i) and (ii), in the sense that it remains reliable—i.e. yields estimators whose statistical error stays bounded by a polynomial in $V$ for a sample size polynomial in $V$—in the simultaneous regime of (a) chemical potentials $\mu$ of order the QCD scale, (b) thermodynamically large lattice volumes $V$, and (c) the neighborhood of the conjectured finite-density phase transition (including a putative critical endpoint)?
status_search_result: The problem remains open in general. Traditional reweighting from $\mu=0$ or from the phase-quenched ensemble is known to suffer from severe overlap and phase-fluctuation problems at large volume and chemical potential. Recent work (Borsanyi–Fodor–Giordano–Katz–Nogradi–Pasztor, 2021–2022) introduced a "sign reweighting" scheme that eliminates the overlap problem in a discrete two-sector decomposition and is reliable provided $\langle\mathrm{sign}\rangle\neq 0$, but it still degrades exponentially in volume due to the residual sign problem, and no scheme is known to remain reliable in all three regimes (large $\mu$, large $V$, near the transition). Surveys describe the situation as a partially mitigated but still open problem.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: How reliable is analytic continuation from imaginary chemical potential once one moves beyond the small-µ/T regime where different fitting ansätze agree? In particular, can one control the strong fit-function dependence that appears when continuing pseudo-critical lines or other observables into the real-chemical-potential region?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum field theory (lattice QCD with $N_f$ flavors of quarks) whose grand-canonical partition function $Z(\mu)$ depends on a quark chemical potential $\mu \in \mathbb{C}$ at temperature $T>0$. For real $\mu$ the fermion determinant is complex (the sign problem), so direct Monte Carlo simulation is intractable; however, for purely imaginary chemical potential $\mu = i\mu_I$ with $\mu_I \in \mathbb{R}$ the measure is positive and observables $O(\mu_I/T)$ can be computed numerically. By the Roberge–Weiss symmetry, only the interval $\mu_I/T \in [0,\pi/3]$ carries independent information.

Let $O(x)$, $x = \mu/T$, denote an observable that is analytic in a neighborhood of $x=0$ (for instance the pseudo-critical temperature $T_c(\mu)/T_c(0)$ defining the chiral crossover line, or a susceptibility). Given a finite set of noisy numerical values $\{O(ix_k) \pm \sigma_k\}$ on a grid $x_k \in [0,\pi/3]$, one estimates $O$ for real $x$ by fitting an ansatz from a class $\mathcal{F}$ (e.g.\ polynomials in $x^2$, ratios of polynomials, trigonometric polynomials in $\mu_I/T$) and then evaluating the analytic continuation $x \mapsto x$ real.

Empirically, different ansätze in $\mathcal{F}$ yield mutually consistent extrapolations for $x \lesssim 0.3$ but diverge strongly for larger $x$, while the rigorous radius of convergence argument only guarantees control for $|x| < \pi/3$.

Problem. Develop a mathematically controlled procedure for analytic continuation of such observables from the imaginary-$\mu$ axis to the real-$\mu$ axis that:
(a) quantifies the systematic uncertainty arising from the choice of fitting ansatz in $\mathcal{F}$;
(b) provides rigorous error bars valid for $x \gtrsim 0.3$ and ideally up to $x \sim 1$;
(c) is consistent with the analyticity domain and known symmetries (Roberge–Weiss periodicity, charge-conjugation symmetry $O(\mu)=O(-\mu)$).

In particular, determine whether the strong fit-function dependence observed beyond $\mu/T \approx 0.3$ can be tamed, or prove a lower bound showing that with data restricted to $\mu_I/T \in [0,\pi/3]$ and finite precision $\sigma$, the extrapolation error necessarily grows uncontrollably for $\mu/T \gtrsim c$ for some explicit constant $c$.
status_search_result: The reliability of analytic continuation from imaginary chemical potential in finite-density lattice QCD remains an active and unresolved methodological issue. Recent lattice QCD reviews and studies (2022–2025) continue to report ansatz-dependent results for the curvature and higher-order coefficients of the pseudo-critical line beyond $\mu_B/T \gtrsim 2$–$3$ (i.e.\ $\mu_q/T \gtrsim 0.7$–$1$), and no rigorous procedure with controlled systematic error has been established. The problem is generally regarded as open.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Why does the early-onset problem appear in finite-density lattice QCD, with severe phase fluctuations setting in when the quark chemical potential reaches mπ/2, and how can one reliably study the hadron phase beyond that threshold? In particular, what mechanism explains the onset of extreme difficulty at µ = mπ/2 and how can simulations be extended into the physically relevant dense hadronic regime associated with nuclei and neutron stars?
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice QCD at zero temperature and finite quark chemical potential μ, formulated on a Euclidean spacetime lattice with the standard Wilson or staggered fermion action. The grand-canonical partition function

Z(μ) = ∫ DU det M(U,μ) e^{-S_g(U)}

has a fermion determinant det M(U,μ) that is complex for μ ≠ 0, producing a sign (phase) problem. Empirically, in the cold dense regime one observes the following "early-onset" phenomenon: at zero temperature, as the quark chemical potential μ is increased from 0, severe phase fluctuations of det M(U,μ)/det M(U,0) suddenly set in once μ crosses the threshold μ = m_π/2, where m_π is the pion mass. Consequently, reweighting or any approach that relies on gauge configurations generated at μ = 0 (or at μ < m_π/2) breaks down beyond this threshold, even though the physical baryon onset is expected to occur near μ = m_N/3 ≫ m_π/2 (where m_N is the nucleon mass).

Problem. 
(a) Provide a rigorous mechanism, at the level of the eigenvalue distribution of the Dirac operator M(U,μ) and/or of the phase-quenched (isospin-chemical-potential) theory, that explains why μ = m_π/2 is precisely the threshold at which the sign/phase problem becomes severe in the T → 0 limit, and quantify the rate of growth of the phase fluctuations and of the sign-problem severity for μ > m_π/2.
(b) Devise a simulation algorithm (for example based on complex Langevin dynamics, Lefschetz-thimble integration, density-of-states methods, canonical/fugacity expansions, dual variables, tensor networks, or any other framework) that is provably reliable for full lattice QCD with dynamical light quarks in the cold, dense hadronic regime m_π/2 < μ < m_N/3 and beyond, in the sense of yielding controlled estimates of bulk thermodynamic observables (baryon number density, energy density, equation of state) at zero or sufficiently low temperature, with statistical and systematic errors that do not grow exponentially with the spacetime volume.
status_search_result: The early-onset/sign problem in cold dense lattice QCD remains open. The general sign problem is known to be NP-hard, and while partial mechanistic understanding exists (spreading of Dirac eigenvalues in the complex plane and the role of pion-pair excitations in the phase-quenched theory explain the μ = m_π/2 threshold), no algorithm reliably simulates full lattice QCD with dynamical light quarks in the cold dense hadronic regime beyond μ = m_π/2 up to and past the nuclear onset μ ≈ m_N/3. Recent (2024) studies in two-color QCD and ongoing work with complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimbles, and density-of-states methods illustrate continued effort, but the problem for QCD itself is unresolved.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Can the complex Langevin method be made reliable in the low-temperature, finite-density hadron phase of QCD, where the singular drift problem caused by near-zero fermion determinants presently spoils the method? This includes whether deformations, generalized cooling, contour-based hybrids, or other ideas can remove or control the singularity-driven failures without changing the target theory.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice QCD with a nonzero quark chemical potential μ. The Euclidean path-integral weight, after integrating out the quarks, takes the form det M(U;μ) e^{-S_g[U]}, where U denotes the SU(3) gauge link variables, S_g is the gauge action, and M is the lattice Dirac operator including the quark mass. For μ ≠ 0 the fermion determinant det M(U;μ) is in general complex, so standard importance sampling is obstructed (the "sign problem").

The complex Langevin (CL) method addresses this by complexifying the gauge degrees of freedom (U ∈ SL(3,ℂ) instead of SU(3)) and evolving them by a stochastic differential equation in fictitious Langevin time, with drift derived from the complexified action S_eff = S_g − log det M. Expectation values are computed as long-time averages along the CL trajectory.

In the low-temperature, finite-density "hadron phase" regime (in particular for μ ≳ m_π/2 where the sign problem becomes severe), the eigenvalues of M accumulate near zero, making the drift term ∂(log det M) singular. This "singular-drift problem" causes the formal justification of CL to break down and produces biased or incorrect expectation values. Auxiliary techniques such as gauge cooling, deformation of the action followed by extrapolation, contour deformations, and hybrid schemes have been proposed but none is established as fully reliable in this regime.

Problem: Determine whether there exists a modification of the complex Langevin method — for instance via a generalized cooling procedure, a deformation-and-extrapolation scheme, a contour-deformation hybrid, or some other systematically controlled prescription — which (i) does not alter the target lattice QCD theory in its physical limit, (ii) provably or demonstrably evades the singular-drift failure caused by near-zero eigenvalues of the Dirac operator, and (iii) yields correct expectation values throughout the low-temperature, finite-density hadron phase of QCD. Equivalently, prove that no such modification exists.
category_tag: Complex Langevin / lattice QCD sign problem
status_search_result: Recent work (including a 2025 study on CL validity near the deconfining transition) confirms that the complex Langevin method still fails in the low-temperature, finite-density hadron regime due to the singular-drift problem associated with near-zero Dirac eigenvalues. Various mitigations (gauge cooling, deformation technique, etc.) extend the applicable region but none reliably covers the hadron phase. The problem is still open.

paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
original_question: Is there a fundamental lower bound on the computational cost of evaluating physically relevant path integrals with sign problems, and if such a bound exists, how is it related to the P versus NP question in computational complexity? In other words, is an exponentially hard sign problem an unavoidable feature of some theories rather than merely a symptom of inadequate algorithms?
self_contained_problem:
Consider physically relevant path integrals (in the sense of Euclidean lattice formulations of quantum field theories or many-body quantum systems) of the form
   Z = ∑_C w(C),    ⟨O⟩ = (1/Z) ∑_C O(C) w(C),
where the weights w(C) are in general complex or non-positive, so that direct Monte Carlo sampling suffers from a "sign problem" (cancellations causing the signal-to-noise ratio to decay exponentially in the system volume and inverse temperature).

(a) Does there exist a fundamental, theory-dependent lower bound on the computational cost (as a function of system size, inverse temperature, and desired accuracy) for evaluating such path integrals when a sign problem is present? In particular, decide whether for some physically motivated families of theories an exponential growth of computational cost with system size is unavoidable for every possible algorithm (including all possible reformulations, contour deformations, dual variables, etc.), as opposed to merely reflecting limitations of currently known algorithms.

(b) Clarify the relationship between the existence of such a lower bound and the P versus NP problem: i.e., determine whether the impossibility of a generic polynomial-time algorithm for the sign problem can be established conditionally on P ≠ NP, or unconditionally, and identify the precise complexity class that captures the hardness of evaluating these path integrals.
status_search_result: Troyer and Wiese (Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201, 2005) proved that a generic solution to the fermionic sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo is NP-hard, so a polynomial-time generic algorithm would imply P = NP. This conditionally rules out a universal efficient solution. However, the broader question — whether for specific physically relevant theories (e.g. finite-density lattice QCD) an exponentially hard sign problem is provably unavoidable, and the unconditional resolution tied to the still-open P vs NP problem — remains open.

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
context_brief: Finiteness and basin decomposition for generalized Syracuse maps
original_question: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀ for some integer ν₀ ≥ 1. Define T on positive integers by T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 when n is odd. A cycle is a finite orbit Ω with T^k(x)=x for every x in Ω; C(a,b) is the set of all cycles. For a cycle Ω(ω) whose smallest element is ω, let G(ω) be the set of starting values that eventually reach ω, and let G(∞) be the set of starting values whose iterates diverge to infinity. Is C(a,b) always finite, with the positive integers decomposing as the union of the finitely many cycle basins G(ω₁*), …, G(ω_q*) and the possible divergent set G(∞)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a$ and $b$ be odd integers satisfying $a > -b$ and $a + b = 2^{\nu_0}$ for some integer $\nu_0 \geq 1$. Define a map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ on the positive integers by
$$T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even},\\ (an+b)/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}, \end{cases}$$
(assume the parameters are chosen so that $T(\mathbb{N}) \subseteq \mathbb{N}$). A cycle of $T$ is a finite nonempty set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{N}$ together with an integer $k \geq 1$ such that $T^{(k)}(x) = x$ for every $x \in \Omega$; the length of $\Omega$ is the smallest such $k$. Denote by $\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ the collection of all cycles of $T$. For a cycle $\Omega$ with smallest element $\omega$, define its basin
$$G(\omega) = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : \exists\, k \in \mathbb{N},\ T^{(k)}(n) = \omega \},$$
and the divergent set
$$G(\infty) = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} : \lim_{k \to \infty} T^{(k)}(n) = \infty \}.$$
Prove or disprove: for every admissible pair $(a,b)$ as above, $\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ is finite, say $\mathcal{C}(a,b) = \{\Omega(\omega_1^*), \ldots, \Omega(\omega_{q^*}^*)\}$ with $1 \leq q^* < \infty$, and
$$\mathbb{N} = G(\omega_1^*) \cup \cdots \cup G(\omega_{q^*}^*) \cup G(\infty),$$
where $G(\infty)$ may or may not be empty.
status_search_result: This is a generalization of the Collatz (3x+1) problem to a family of affine maps $T(n) = (an+b)/2$ on odd inputs. The classical Collatz conjecture (the case $a=3$, $b=1$) remains famously open; analogous finiteness-of-cycles and basin-decomposition statements for generalized Syracuse maps are widely conjectured but unproven. Tao (2019) showed that almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values, but the full conjecture, including the absence of divergent orbits and finiteness of cycles, is open. No proof of the stated general conjecture is known.

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
original_question: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. If C(a,b) denotes the set of cycles of T on the positive integers, can one find effective estimates or bounds for the cardinality #C(a,b) that are strong enough to determine, or at least confirm, whether C(a,b) is finite?
self_contained_problem:
Let $a$ and $b$ be odd integers satisfying $a > -b$ and $a + b = 2^{\nu_0}$ for some nonnegative integer $\nu_0$. Define the map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by
\[
T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}, \\ (an+b)/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}. \end{cases}
\]
A cycle of $T$ is a finite nonempty subset $\Omega \subset \mathbb{N}$ such that $T$ restricts to a permutation of $\Omega$; equivalently, there exists $k \geq 1$ with $T^{(k)}(x) = x$ for every $x \in \Omega$, and the length of $\Omega$ is the smallest such $k$. Let $\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ denote the set of all cycles of $T$ in $\mathbb{N}$.

Provide effective estimates or bounds for the cardinality $\#\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ which are strong enough to determine — or at least to confirm — whether $\mathcal{C}(a,b)$ is finite.
status_search_result: The classical Collatz/Syracuse problem (the case $a=3$, $b=1$) is famously open, and the finiteness of the set of cycles for generalized $(an+b)/2$ maps with $a \geq 3$ remains unresolved in general. No effective bounds on the number of cycles of such generalized Syracuse maps are known that would settle finiteness.

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
context_brief: Classical Collatz conjecture in Syracuse-map notation
original_question: For the classical Collatz/Syracuse map T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(3n+1)/2 when n is odd, is Ω(1)=(1→2→1) the only cycle, and does every positive integer eventually reach 1, so that N=G(1) and there are no divergent trajectories G(∞)=∅?
self_contained_problem:
Define the Syracuse map $T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ on the positive integers by
$$T(n)=\begin{cases} n/2, & n\equiv 0\pmod 2,\\ (3n+1)/2, & n\equiv 1\pmod 2.\end{cases}$$
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, let $T^{(k)}$ denote the $k$-fold iterate of $T$, with $T^{(0)}(n)=n$. A cycle of $T$ is a finite sequence $(n_0\to n_1\to\cdots\to n_{\ell-1}\to n_0)$ with $n_{i+1}=T(n_i)$ and all $n_i$ distinct; the trivial cycle is $\Omega(1)=(1\to 2\to 1)$. Let $G(1)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\exists k\in\mathbb{N}_0,\ T^{(k)}(n)=1\}$ and let $G(\infty)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: T^{(k)}(n)\to\infty\text{ as }k\to\infty\}$.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:
(a) The trivial cycle $\Omega(1)=(1\to 2\to 1)$ is the unique cycle of $T$ in $\mathbb{N}$.
(b) $G(1)=\mathbb{N}$ and $G(\infty)=\varnothing$; equivalently, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$ with $T^{(k)}(n)=1$.
status_search_result: The statement is the classical Collatz (3x+1) conjecture, which remains open. Partial progress includes Tao's 2019/2022 result that almost all orbits attain almost bounded values, but the full conjecture is unresolved.

paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
context_brief: Uniqueness and divergence for the (2^ν+1)n+(2^ν−1) family
original_question: For every integer ν≥3, define T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=((2^ν+1)n+(2^ν−1))/2 when n is odd. Is the only cycle the trivial cycle Ω(1)=(1→2^ν→2^{ν−1}→…→2→1), so that C(2^ν+1,2^ν−1)={Ω(1)}, and do the positive integers decompose as N=G(1)∪G(∞) with a nonempty divergent set G(∞)?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer $\nu\ge 3$ and define a map $T:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ by
\[
T(n)=\begin{cases} n/2, & n\text{ even},\\[2pt] \dfrac{(2^{\nu}+1)\,n+(2^{\nu}-1)}{2}, & n\text{ odd}. \end{cases}
\]
(Note that when $n$ is odd, $(2^{\nu}+1)n+(2^{\nu}-1)$ is even, so $T(n)\in\mathbb{N}$.) For a positive integer $n$, the orbit of $n$ is the sequence $n,T(n),T^2(n),\ldots$ A cycle of $T$ is a finite tuple $(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_L)$ of distinct positive integers with $T(n_i)=n_{i+1}$ for $1\le i<L$ and $T(n_L)=n_1$. Let $C(2^{\nu}+1,2^{\nu}-1)$ denote the set of all cycles of $T$. Let
\[
\Omega(1)=(1\to 2^{\nu}\to 2^{\nu-1}\to\cdots\to 2\to 1),
\]
the cycle of length $\nu+1$ obtained by iterating $T$ starting from $1$. Define
\[
G(1)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \text{the orbit of }n\text{ under }T\text{ eventually enters }\Omega(1)\},
\]
\[
G(\infty)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: \text{the orbit of }n\text{ under }T\text{ is unbounded}\}.
\]

Prove or disprove the following for every $\nu\ge 3$:
(a) $C(2^{\nu}+1,2^{\nu}-1)=\{\Omega(1)\}$, i.e., $\Omega(1)$ is the unique cycle of $T$;
(b) $\mathbb{N}=G(1)\cup G(\infty)$ (every positive integer either eventually enters $\Omega(1)$ or has an unbounded orbit);
(c) $G(\infty)\neq\emptyset$ (there exists at least one positive integer with unbounded orbit).
status_search_result: The problem is posed as Conjecture 5.2 of a 2021 preprint on a generalized Syracuse problem. As a generalization of the Collatz/Syracuse-type dynamical conjectures (including the existence of divergent orbits, which is unknown even in much-studied cases), no proof or disproof is known; the question appears to remain open.
