paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Combining dynamic maps with temporal delays
original_question: How can one meaningfully combine a dynamic cognitive map of the kind used in Section 2.2 with either discrete or distributed temporal delays, so that movement is influenced both by an evolving memory field and by explicit reference to past times? In particular, can a standard bootstrapping argument be adapted to prove existence and uniqueness for bounded-domain problems that contain both nonlocal perception and discrete or distributed delays?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an animal population whose density u(x,t) on a bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^n (with smooth boundary and zero-flux, homogeneous Neumann, or homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions) evolves under a reaction–diffusion–advection equation in which movement is biased by both (a) a dynamic cognitive map and (b) explicit dependence on the past. Concretely, let the cognitive map k(x,t) satisfy its own evolution equation coupling memory acquisition, decay, and the current density u, e.g.

  ∂_t k(x,t) = α u(x,t) − β k(x,t) + D_k Δk(x,t),

and let movement of u be driven by a nonlocal perceptual gradient ∇(G ∗ k)(x,t), where G is a spatial detection kernel and ∗ denotes spatial convolution on Ω. Couple this perception with temporal delays of either discrete type, k(x,t−τ), τ > 0, or distributed type, ∫_0^∞ w(s) k(x,t−s) ds, with a non-negative weight w satisfying ∫_0^∞ w(s) ds = 1. The full system reads

  ∂_t u = D Δu − ∇·(u χ ∇(G ∗ K_τ[k])(x,t)) + f(u),
  K_τ[k](x,t) = k(x,t−τ)  or  K_τ[k](x,t) = ∫_0^∞ w(s) k(x,t−s) ds,

together with the cognitive-map equation above, suitable initial history on [−∞,0] (or [−τ,0]), and the chosen boundary conditions.

(i) Formulate a coupled PDE model that meaningfully integrates such a dynamic cognitive map with either discrete or distributed temporal delays, in which animal movement is influenced simultaneously by an evolving memory field and by explicit reference to past times.

(ii) Prove, by a bootstrapping (iterative integration over successive delay intervals) argument or otherwise, existence and uniqueness of solutions to this coupled system on Ω with the prescribed boundary conditions, for suitable classes of initial histories, kernels G and w, and nonlinearities f.
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an open problem in a 2023 survey on PDE models with nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping. Related recent work (e.g., on spatio-temporal dynamics with nonlocal spatial memory and coupled nonlocal PDE–ODE systems with spatial memory) develops well-posedness for either memory or delay components separately, but no source found establishes existence and uniqueness via bootstrapping for a bounded-domain model combining a dynamic cognitive map with discrete or distributed delays. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Connection between layered memory and TSLV
original_question: Can a PDE model with both short-term and long-term memory layers be meaningfully related to the empirically motivated notion of time since last visit (TSLV)? More precisely, does including both memory compartments improve predictive power relative to models that have only one memory compartment?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a class of partial differential equation (PDE) models for animal movement in which the population density u(x,t) on a spatial domain Ω evolves under advection–diffusion dynamics whose drift term depends on internal "memory maps" carried by the animals. Specifically, allow the model to include one or two memory compartments:

(a) a short-term memory field m_S(x,t) that decays on a fast timescale τ_S and is reinforced by recent occupancy of location x;
(b) a long-term memory field m_L(x,t) that decays on a slow timescale τ_L ≫ τ_S and accumulates over longer histories of occupancy.

The animals' movement is biased by a (possibly weighted) combination of ∇m_S and ∇m_L. Separately, given an observed (or simulated) trajectory of an animal, define the time-since-last-visit field TSLV(x,t) as the elapsed time since the animal was most recently within a fixed neighborhood of x (with TSLV(x,t) = t if no prior visit has occurred).

Questions:
1. Establish a precise mathematical correspondence between the layered memory variables (m_S, m_L) of the PDE model and the empirical quantity TSLV. For instance, identify conditions (choices of reinforcement kernels and decay rates) under which functionals of (m_S(x,t), m_L(x,t)) recover TSLV(x,t) as a deterministic limit, or under which TSLV serves as a sufficient statistic for the memory state.
2. For a fitting/prediction framework where models are calibrated to movement data, determine whether the two-compartment model (with both m_S and m_L) achieves strictly better predictive performance than the one-compartment analogue (with only m_S or only m_L) — i.e., quantify the gain in predictive likelihood, identifiability of the additional parameters, and the regimes of behavioral data (e.g., foraging, territorial revisitation) in which the two-compartment structure is necessary.
category_tag: memory-driven PDE models in movement ecology
status_search_result: Recent literature on memory-driven animal movement (e.g., step-selection analyses with short- and long-term occurrence distributions, and PDE models with memory-based diffusion) discusses both TSLV-type covariates and layered memory, but no work was found that rigorously links the two-compartment PDE memory framework to TSLV or quantifies its predictive advantage over single-compartment models. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
original_question: For the learning-inspired one-dimensional model ∂_t u = ∂_x(d∂_x u − u∂_x[ω̃(s)m + γ|x − x0|]), where ω̃(s) switches the strength of attraction to resources according to the satisfaction ratio s = m/u and the fixed term γ|x − x0| represents attraction to a den site at x0, in what sense do solutions exist?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional advection–diffusion equation
\[
\partial_t u \;=\; \partial_x\!\left( d\,\partial_x u \;-\; u\,\partial_x\!\big[\tilde\omega(s)\,m(x,t) \;+\; \gamma\,|x-x_0|\big]\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R,\; t>0,
\]
where:
- $u(x,t)\ge 0$ is the population density of a forager,
- $d>0$ is a constant diffusion coefficient,
- $m(x,t)\ge 0$ is a prescribed (sufficiently regular, bounded, nonnegative) resource density,
- $x_0\in\mathbb R$ is a fixed point (a "den site") and $\gamma>0$ measures attraction to it,
- $s(x,t) = m(x,t)/u(x,t)$ is the satisfaction ratio,
- $\tilde\omega:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is a bounded, piecewise constant switching function modelling that the strength of attraction to resources changes once $s$ crosses a fixed threshold (so $\tilde\omega(s)$ takes one value when $s$ is below the threshold and another value when above).

Supplement the equation with a nonnegative initial datum $u(x,0)=u_0(x)\in L^1(\mathbb R)\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R)$ and either no-flux boundary conditions on a bounded domain or suitable decay conditions on $\mathbb R$.

Question: In what functional setting (e.g. classical, strong, weak, mild, or measure-valued solutions) and under what regularity/structural hypotheses on $m$, $u_0$, and $\tilde\omega$ can one prove existence (and, if possible, uniqueness) of solutions $u$ to this initial-boundary value problem, despite the discontinuous, density-dependent switching of $\tilde\omega(s)$ through $s=m/u$?
status_search_result: No published well-posedness result was located for this specific starvation-driven switching advection–diffusion model with a den-site potential. The problem was posed as an open question in the literature on PDE models of animal movement, and no resolution has been found through search; the status appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Dynamics and alternative satisfaction measures for learning model
original_question: For the starvation-driven switching model in which hunger can switch movement between resource-seeking and attraction to a home site, can this switch generate nontrivial spatiotemporal dynamics or patterns? Biologically, would such realistic switching benefit or impair the species, and what other satisfaction measures could play the same role as a behavior-modification mechanism?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a spatially explicit model for a mobile animal population living on a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ (with no-flux boundary conditions) that uses two distinct cognitive movement mechanisms governed by an internal satisfaction (hunger) variable. Let $u(x,t)\ge 0$ denote the population density, $m(x)\ge 0$ a resource (food) distribution, and $H(x_0,t)\ge 0$ an attraction kernel toward a fixed home site $x_0\in\Omega$. Introduce a satisfaction (hunger) state $s(t)\in[0,1]$ that evolves according to the average consumption rate, e.g.
$$\frac{ds}{dt}=\alpha\Big(\int_\Omega m(x)u(x,t)\,dx-c\Big)-\beta s,$$
with positive constants $\alpha,\beta,c$. Define a smooth switching function $\sigma(s)\in[0,1]$ (with $\sigma$ near $1$ when $s$ is small, i.e. when starving, and near $0$ when $s$ is large, i.e. satisfied). Consider the PDE
$$u_t=D\Delta u-\nabla\!\cdot\!\Big(u\big[(1-\sigma(s))\,\chi_1\nabla(K_1*m)+\sigma(s)\,\chi_2\nabla(K_2*H)\big]\Big)+f(u,m),$$
where $K_1,K_2$ are nonlocal perception kernels, $\chi_1,\chi_2>0$ are advection sensitivities, and $f$ is a growth/consumption term (e.g. logistic with resource depletion). The first advective term models foraging (resource-seeking) and dominates when the animal is hungry; the second models home attraction and dominates when the animal is satisfied. Address the following:

(i) Determine whether the starvation-driven switching mechanism $\sigma(s)$ can produce nontrivial spatiotemporal dynamics or stable spatial patterns (e.g. via Hopf or Turing-type bifurcations) that do not occur in the corresponding non-switching limits $\sigma\equiv 0$ or $\sigma\equiv 1$.

(ii) Compare, in terms of long-time persistence, total population size, or resource utilization, the switching model with the pure foraging and pure home-attraction submodels, and decide whether the switching strategy is beneficial or detrimental to the species.

(iii) Identify and analyze alternative satisfaction measures $s$ (other than starvation), such as predation risk, crowding, social information, or memory of past resource intake, that could serve as behavior-modification triggers between cognitive movement mechanisms, and study the resulting dynamics.
category_tag: nonlocal PDE models for animal movement
status_search_result: No publications were located that resolve the questions about pattern formation, ecological benefit, or alternative satisfaction-based switching mechanisms for this starvation-driven foraging/home-attraction PDE model. It appears to remain an open problem.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Existence with truncated kernels near boundaries
original_question: For the nonlocal dynamic-memory problems introduced in Section 2.2.2, suppose one works on a bounded one-dimensional domain and uses a truncated perceptual kernel near the boundary in the style a(x,t) = (1/(R+x))∫_{−x}^R a(x+z,t)dz near the left endpoint, the full average in the interior, and the corresponding truncated average near the right endpoint. Under homogeneous Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions, under what conditions do solutions exist, and how do those results compare with the periodic-boundary case?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a scalar density u(x,t) on a bounded one-dimensional interval Ω = [0, L] evolving according to a nonlocal advection–diffusion equation of the form

  u_t = D u_{xx} − (u · K[a])_x + f(u),  x ∈ (0, L), t > 0,

where K[a] denotes a nonlocal advective velocity driven by a perceptual (memory) field a(x,t) that itself satisfies a dynamic-memory equation

  a_t = g(u, a),  x ∈ Ω, t > 0,

modeling cognitive accumulation of information about u through a finite perceptual radius R > 0. In the interior, the perceptual field is processed by the symmetric averaging operator

  ā(x,t) = (1/(2R)) ∫_{−R}^{R} a(x + z, t) dz,  for x ∈ [R, L − R].

Near the boundaries, the averaging kernel is truncated so that it never samples outside Ω. Specifically, near the left endpoint,

  ā(x,t) = (1/(R + x)) ∫_{−x}^{R} a(x + z, t) dz,  for x ∈ [0, R),

and symmetrically near the right endpoint,

  ā(x,t) = (1/(R + (L − x))) ∫_{−R}^{L − x} a(x + z, t) dz,  for x ∈ (L − R, L].

Impose on u either homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions u_x(0,t) = u_x(L,t) = 0 or homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0, together with suitable initial data u(x,0) = u_0(x) ≥ 0 and a(x,0) = a_0(x).

Determine conditions on D, R, L, the nonlinearities defining K[·], g(u,a), and f(u), and on the initial data, under which classical (or weak) global-in-time nonnegative solutions exist to this coupled system with the truncated boundary kernel above. Compare the existence theory obtained in this bounded-domain setting with the corresponding theory available when Ω is replaced by a one-dimensional torus and the full symmetric kernel ā(x,t) = (1/(2R)) ∫_{−R}^{R} a(x + z, t) dz is used under periodic boundary conditions.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open question in a 2022 survey on PDE models for animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping. No subsequent work resolving the well-posedness of the truncated-kernel formulation under Neumann or Dirichlet conditions has been located.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Net-growth fitness for cognitive movement models
original_question: For cognitive movement models that include reaction terms, what biological consequences and mathematical predictions are obtained from the net-growth measure ∫_{t0}^{tmax}∫_Ω f(x,t,u)dxdt, where f is the birth-death term after the movement terms integrate out? In particular, are there optimal ranges of cognition-related parameters such as perceptual radius or advection strength that increase fitness in this net-growth sense, and how do those predictions compare with a null model lacking cognitive movement?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded smooth domain and consider a population density $u(x,t) \ge 0$ governed by a knowledge-based (cognitive) movement model of the form
$$\partial_t u = \mathcal{M}[u] + f(x,t,u), \qquad x \in \Omega,\ t \in (t_0,t_{\max}),$$
where $\mathcal{M}[u]$ is a conservative movement operator combining diffusion and a nonlocal advection that depends on perceived environmental covariates (e.g. a term of the form $-\nabla\cdot(u\,\mathbf{a}[u])$ with $\mathbf{a}[u]$ a nonlocal functional involving a perceptual kernel of radius $R>0$ and an advection strength $\alpha\ge 0$), and $f(x,t,u)$ is a local birth–death (reaction) term. Assume no-flux boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$ so that the movement operator integrates to zero, i.e. $\int_\Omega \mathcal{M}[u]\,dx = 0$ for all $t$. Define the net-growth fitness functional
$$F(R,\alpha) \;:=\; \int_{t_0}^{t_{\max}}\!\!\int_\Omega f(x,t,u(x,t))\,dx\,dt.$$

(a) Determine the biological consequences and qualitative mathematical predictions implied by $F(R,\alpha)$ for the long-term persistence and spatial distribution of $u$.

(b) Show whether there exist interior optimizers $(R^*,\alpha^*)$ of $F$, i.e. cognition-related parameter values $R$ (perceptual radius) and $\alpha$ (advection strength) that maximize $F$, and characterize them.

(c) Compare $F(R,\alpha)$ with the corresponding value $F_0$ obtained for the null model with no cognitive movement (i.e. $\alpha = 0$ or $\mathcal{M}[u]$ replaced by pure diffusion), and identify regimes of $(R,\alpha)$ in which $F(R,\alpha) > F_0$.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open problem in a 2022 survey on PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement. No subsequent work has been identified that resolves the existence of optimal perceptual radius / advection strength maximizing the net-growth fitness functional, or that completes the comparison with the cognition-free null model. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: For movement models with explicit resources, how do the predictions based on the foraging-success measure ∫∫ u(x,t)m(x,t)dxdt compare with the predictions based on the normalized foraging-efficiency measure built from the Bhattacharyya coefficient ∫∫ √(u(x,t)m(x,t)) dxdt? Do the two measures identify the same movement strategies as optimal, both for the nonlocal perception model based on resource tracking and for knowledge-based movement models more broadly?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a spatial domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ (with appropriate boundary conditions) on a time interval $[0,T]$, and let $u(x,t) \ge 0$ denote the density of a foraging population and $m(x,t) \ge 0$ denote a resource density, both governed by a coupled system of evolution equations. Two strategies for evaluating a movement strategy are compared:

1. The foraging-success measure
$$ S[u,m] \;=\; \int_0^T \!\!\int_\Omega u(x,t)\, m(x,t) \, dx\, dt. $$

2. The foraging-efficiency measure based on the Bhattacharyya coefficient between the (normalized) distributions of $u$ and $m$,
$$ E[u,m] \;=\; \int_0^T \!\!\int_\Omega \sqrt{u(x,t)\, m(x,t)} \, dx\, dt, $$
appropriately normalized so that $u(\cdot,t)$ and $m(\cdot,t)$ are treated as probability densities.

Two classes of models are to be considered:
(a) A nonlocal-perception model in which individuals bias their movement by a spatially averaged (nonlocal) sampling of the resource $m$, e.g.
$$ u_t = 
abla \cdot  ig( D 
abla u - \chi u \, 
abla (G_\sigma * m)  ig), $$
where $G_\sigma$ is a perceptual averaging kernel of radius $\sigma$, together with a dynamics for $m$ (e.g. logistic growth with consumption by $u$).
(b) Knowledge-based movement models more generally, in which the advective bias of $u$ depends on a memory or cognitive map of the resource landscape.

Problem: Determine whether the measures $S$ and $E$ identify the same movement strategies (e.g., the same perceptual radius $\sigma$, taxis strength $\chi$, or memory parameters) as optimal. Specifically, characterize the relationship between the maximizers of $S$ and $E$ over admissible strategies, both for the nonlocal-perception model in (a) and for the broader class of knowledge-based movement models in (b), and describe under what conditions on the model parameters the two measures yield consistent or divergent predictions about optimal foraging strategies.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in a 2022 collection of open problems on PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement. No subsequent work resolving the comparison between the success measure and the Bhattacharyya-type foraging-efficiency measure has been located.

context_brief: Fitness-function analysis for cognitive movement strategies
original_question: Can the pack-fitness framework used for movement models without explicit population dynamics, in which fitness has the form r_u = −μ_0 + ln(σψ) − α∫_Ω uv dx + ln(∫_Ω uH(u,v)dx), be extended to other cognitive movement mechanisms? In particular, how does this kind of fitness measure change when perceptual kernels or perceptual radii are varied, or when other nonlocal cognitive mechanisms are used in place of scent-marking dynamics?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded smooth domain representing a habitat occupied by a single animal pack. Let $u(x,t)\ge 0$ denote the spatial density of pack members and $v(x,t)\ge 0$ denote the density of a cognitive cue (for example, a scent-marking field) deposited and decayed by the pack. Consider a coupled model of the form
$$u_t = 
abla\cdot ig(D
abla u - \chi\, u\, K_\sigma\!*\!
abla v ig),\qquad v_t = \sigma\psi(u) - \mu v,$$
where $K_\sigma$ is a perceptual (nonlocal) kernel of radius $\sigma>0$, $\psi$ models cue deposition by the pack, and $\mu,\sigma,\chi,D>0$ are parameters. Following the pack-fitness framework for movement models without explicit population dynamics, attach to a steady state $(u,v)$ a pack fitness functional of the form
$$r_u \;=\; -\mu_0 + \ln(\sigma\psi) \;-\; \alpha\!\int_\Omega u v\,dx \;+\; \ln\!\Big(\int_\Omega u\, H(u,v)\,dx\Big),$$
where $\mu_0>0$ is baseline mortality, $\alpha>0$ weighs intraspecific interference mediated by the cue, and $H(u,v)$ is a per-capita resource-acquisition rate. 

Question: Can the optimal-movement-strategy analysis based on maximizing $r_u$ over admissible steady states be extended from scent-marking models to other nonlocal cognitive movement mechanisms (such as memory-driven advection, map-based avoidance, or perceptual gradient following)? Specifically, characterize how the maximizer of $r_u$ and the corresponding optimal pack distribution depend on:
(i) the choice of perceptual kernel $K_\sigma$ (e.g., top-hat, Gaussian, exponential);
(ii) the perceptual radius $\sigma$, including the limits $\sigma	o 0$ and $\sigma	o\infty$;
(iii) the replacement of the scent dynamics $v_t=\sigma\psi-\mu v$ by alternative nonlocal cognitive mechanisms.
Provide either explicit optimal strategies, comparison principles relating $r_u$ across different cognitive mechanisms, or counterexamples showing that no such extension is possible.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Optimal strategies for average-based and per-capita resource maps
original_question: For the newly proposed models in which the advective potential is either the resource density divided by the spatial average resource density, m(x,t)/m(t), or the per-capita resource density, m(x,t)/u(x,t), which knowledge-based strategies are optimal according to the foraging-success criterion? How do those predictions compare with the optimal strategies previously found for the simpler nonlocal perception model with a prescribed resource landscape?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary and outward unit normal $\nu$. Let $m(x,t)>0$ denote a prescribed (possibly time-dependent) resource density on $\Omega$, and let $u(x,t)\ge 0$ denote the density of a foraging population. Consider the following two nonlocal-perception, knowledge-based advection–diffusion models for $u$ on $\Omega\times(0,\infty)$ with no-flux boundary conditions:

(I) Average-based map:
$$u_t = \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(d\,\nabla u - \alpha\, u\,\nabla P\!\ast\!(m/\overline m)\bigr) + f(x,u,m),$$
where $\overline m(t)=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega m(x,t)\,dx$.

(II) Per-capita map:
$$u_t = \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(d\,\nabla u - \alpha\, u\,\nabla P\!\ast\!(m/u)\bigr) + f(x,u,m),$$
where the convolution $P\ast\varphi(x)=\int_\Omega P(x-y)\varphi(y)\,dy$ is taken with a fixed nonnegative perception kernel $P$ of finite range, $d>0$ is the diffusion rate, $\alpha>0$ is the advection strength, and $f$ is a logistic-type local growth functional (e.g.\ $f=ru(1-u/m)$).

Define the foraging-success functional
$$\mathcal F[u,m] = \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega g(u(x,t),m(x,t))\,dx\,dt,$$
where $g$ is a fixed payoff density (e.g.\ $g(u,m)=\min\{u,m\}$ or the per-capita intake $u\,m/(u+m)$).

A knowledge-based strategy is specified by the choice of perception kernel $P$ and parameters $(d,\alpha)$ (within an admissible class $\mathcal A$). Determine, for each of the models (I) and (II), the strategy
$$(P^\ast,d^\ast,\alpha^\ast)\in\arg\max_{\mathcal A}\mathcal F[u,m],$$
i.e.\ identify the optimal knowledge-based strategy maximizing foraging success. Compare these optima with the optimal strategies known for the simpler nonlocal-perception model in which the advective potential is the resource density itself,
$$u_t=\nabla\!\cdot\!(d\,\nabla u-\alpha\,u\,\nabla P\!\ast\! m)+f(x,u,m),$$
and decide whether the optima coincide, differ qualitatively, or depend on $P$, on the resource heterogeneity, or on the relative magnitudes of $d$ and $\alpha$.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open problem in a list of unresolved questions about PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement. No published resolution for either the average-based or per-capita advection variants under a foraging-success criterion was located.

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
context_brief: Travelling waves for nonlocal single-species model
original_question: For the single-species nonlocal aggregation-segregation equation ∂_t u = dΔu − γ∇·(u∇u_g,R), do travelling wave solutions exist on an unbounded domain when the detection function is top-hat, exponential, or Gaussian? If such waves exist, can their speed be computed or estimated, and how does that speed depend on the choice of detection function, the perceptual radius, and the advection and diffusion rates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the single-species nonlocal aggregation–diffusion equation on the unbounded real line (or on R^n)
    ∂_t u(x,t) = d Δ u(x,t) − γ ∇·( u(x,t) ∇ u_{g,R}(x,t) ),  x ∈ R^n, t > 0,
where d > 0 is the diffusion rate, γ ∈ R is the advection (aggregation/segregation) rate, R > 0 is a perceptual radius, and u_{g,R} is the nonlocal perception of u defined by the spatial convolution
    u_{g,R}(x,t) = (g_R * u(·,t))(x) = ∫_{R^n} g_R(x − y) u(y,t) dy,
with a non-negative, radially symmetric, integrable detection kernel g_R supported in (or concentrated on) the ball of radius R. Consider in particular the three standard choices:
   (i) Top-hat:  g_R(z) = 1/|B_R| · 1_{|z|≤R};
   (ii) Exponential:  g_R(z) = C_n R^{-n} exp(−|z|/R);
   (iii) Gaussian:  g_R(z) = (2π R^2)^{-n/2} exp(−|z|^2/(2 R^2)),
each normalised so that ∫ g_R = 1.

A travelling wave solution is a solution of the form u(x,t) = U(x · e − c t) for some unit vector e ∈ R^n, profile U : R → [0,∞) with prescribed limits at ±∞ (e.g. U(−∞) = u_- , U(+∞) = u_+ for constant states u_± ≥ 0), and wave speed c ∈ R.

Questions:
(a) For each of the three detection kernels above, determine whether non-trivial travelling wave solutions of the equation exist on the unbounded domain.
(b) Whenever such travelling waves exist, compute or rigorously estimate the admissible wave speeds c.
(c) Describe quantitatively how the wave speed c depends on the choice of detection function g_R, on the perceptual radius R, and on the parameters γ and d.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a published resolution of this specific question on existence and speed of travelling waves for the nonlocal single-species aggregation equation with top-hat, exponential, or Gaussian detection kernels. The problem appears to remain open; related work on nonlocal advection-diffusion models addresses pattern formation and aggregation but not a full travelling-wave analysis with explicit dependence on the detection kernel and perceptual radius.

context_brief: Travelling waves for distributed-delay movement model
original_question: For the distributed-delay scalar movement equation ∂_t u = d1Δu − γ∇·(u∇v_u) + f(u), where v_u is a spatiotemporal convolution against one of the weak or strong temporal kernels and a heat-kernel-based spatial part, do travelling wave solutions exist? If they do, can their speed be computed or estimated, and how does it depend on the delay parameter τ and the advection and diffusion rates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the scalar advection–diffusion–reaction equation with distributed delay on $\mathbb{R}^n$ (typically $n=1$):
$$\partial_t u(x,t) = d_1 \Delta u(x,t) - \gamma \nabla \cdot \bigl(u(x,t)\, \nabla v_u(x,t)\bigr) + f(u(x,t)),$$
where $u(x,t) \ge 0$ is a population density, $d_1>0$ is a diffusion coefficient, $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ is an advection (taxis) rate, and $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth reaction term (e.g. of logistic type $f(u)=ru(1-u/K)$) with $f(0)=0$.

The cognitive map potential $v_u$ is obtained from $u$ via a spatiotemporal convolution
$$v_u(x,t) = \int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} G(x-y,s)\, K_\tau(s)\, u(y,t-s)\, dy\, ds,$$
where $G(x,s) = (4\pi d_2 s)^{-n/2} \exp\!\bigl(-|x|^2/(4 d_2 s)\bigr)$ is the heat kernel with diffusivity $d_2 > 0$, and $K_\tau$ is a temporal memory kernel with mean delay parameter $\tau > 0$, taken to be either
\begin{itemize}
\item the weak (exponential) kernel $K_\tau^{w}(s) = \tau^{-1} e^{-s/\tau}$, or
\item the strong (gamma) kernel $K_\tau^{s}(s) = \tau^{-2} s\, e^{-s/\tau}$.
\end{itemize}

Address the following:

(a) Do travelling wave solutions $u(x,t) = U(x - ct)$ (with $U$ connecting two distinct constant equilibria of $f$, e.g. $U(-\infty) = K$, $U(+\infty)=0$ for monostable $f$) exist for this distributed-delay system, for either choice of temporal kernel?

(b) When such travelling waves exist, compute or estimate the admissible wave speeds $c$ (including the minimal/selected speed in the monostable case).

(c) Determine how the wave speed depends on the delay parameter $\tau$ and on the rates $\gamma$ and $d_1$ (and, where relevant, $d_2$).

paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
original_question: For the scent-mark-type system with a single moving species coupled to a dynamic cognitive map, namely ∂_t u_i = d_iΔu_i − γ_i∇·(u_i∇p_i g,R) and ∂_t p_i = α_ii u_i − μp_i in the one-species case, do travelling wave solutions exist when the detection function is top-hat, exponential, or Gaussian? If they do, can the wave speed be computed or estimated, how does it depend on perception and the other parameters, and can the results be extended from one species to n interacting species?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following nonlocal advection–reaction–diffusion system on $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^d$) modelling a single species $u(x,t)\ge 0$ coupled to a dynamic cognitive map $p(x,t)\ge 0$:
$$
\partial_t u = d\,\Delta u - \gamma\,\nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(u\,\nabla\,\overline{p}^{\,g,R}\bigr),\qquad
\partial_t p = \alpha\,u - \mu\,p,
$$
where $d>0$ is the diffusion rate, $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ is an advection (taxis) coefficient, $\alpha,\mu>0$ are deposition and decay rates of the cognitive map, and the nonlocal spatial averaging operator is
$$
\overline{p}^{\,g,R}(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} g_R(y-x)\,p(y,t)\,dy,
$$
with perceptual radius $R>0$ and detection function $g_R$ chosen as one of:
\begin{enumerate}
\item top-hat: $g_R(z)=\dfrac{1}{|B_R|}\mathbf{1}_{\{|z|\le R\}}$;
\item exponential: $g_R(z)=C_R\,e^{-|z|/R}$;
\item Gaussian: $g_R(z)=C_R\,e^{-|z|^2/R^2}$,
\end{enumerate}
each normalised to integrate to $1$.

(a) Do there exist travelling wave solutions $u(x,t)=U(x-ct)$, $p(x,t)=P(x-ct)$ with appropriate boundary conditions at $\pm\infty$, for each of the three choices of $g_R$?

(b) When such waves exist, can the wave speed $c$ be computed or estimated, and how does $c$ depend on the detection function $g_R$, the perceptual radius $R$, and the parameters $d,\gamma,\alpha,\mu$?

(c) Can these existence and wave-speed results be extended to the $n$-species analogue
$$
\partial_t u_i = d_i\Delta u_i - \gamma_i\nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(u_i\nabla\,\overline{p_i}^{\,g,R}\bigr),\qquad
\partial_t p_i = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_{ij}u_j - \mu_i p_i,\quad i=1,\dots,n?
$$
status_search_result: Recent work has established well-posedness (existence/uniqueness of Hölder-continuous weak solutions in 1D, including the top-hat kernel) for nonlocal single-species reaction-diffusion-advection models with cognitive maps, but no published result establishes existence of travelling waves or computes wave speeds for the specified system with top-hat, exponential, or Gaussian detection functions. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Is there a general numerical method that can efficiently solve the nonlocal bounded-domain problems from Section 2.2.2 when the boundary conditions are not periodic, so that one no longer relies on pseudo-spectral methods tailored to periodic domains?
self_contained_problem:
Consider nonlocal reaction–diffusion–advection equations on a bounded spatial domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ of the general form
$$\partial_t u(x,t) = D\,\Delta u(x,t) - \nabla\!\cdot\!\big(u(x,t)\,\mathbf{v}[u](x,t)\big) + f(u(x,t)), \qquad x\in\Omega,\ t>0,$$
where the advective velocity $\mathbf{v}[u]$ is a nonlocal functional of $u$, typically given by a convolution
$$\mathbf{v}[u](x,t) = \int_{\Omega} K(x,y)\,g(u(y,t))\,dy$$
with a (possibly singular or anisotropic) kernel $K$ modeling perception or cognitive averaging over a neighborhood of $x$. Assume the problem is supplemented with non-periodic boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$ (for instance, no-flux/Neumann, Dirichlet, or Robin conditions), so that pseudo-spectral methods based on Fourier expansions on a periodic torus are not directly applicable.

Question: Does there exist a general numerical method (independent of the specific choice of kernel $K$ and nonlinearities $f$, $g$, and of the geometry of $\Omega$) that efficiently and accurately solves such nonlocal evolution problems on bounded domains under non-periodic boundary conditions, with computational complexity and accuracy comparable to what pseudo-spectral methods achieve in the periodic setting?
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a collection of open problems on PDE models with nonlocal perception. No subsequent work resolving the general question of an efficient, kernel-agnostic numerical scheme for nonlocal bounded-domain problems under non-periodic boundary conditions was located; partial progress exists via finite-volume, finite-element, and reflected-kernel approaches in specific settings, but no general method matching pseudo-spectral efficiency has been established.

original_question: For the current implicit-memory framework, how can one extend the mathematical and dynamical understanding from two interacting populations to three or more? More specifically, what new behaviors become possible when at least three interacting populations are present, and can those higher-population effects be analyzed beyond the limited numerical evidence currently available?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following implicit-memory model for the spatial dynamics of N interacting populations on a bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^d with no-flux boundary conditions. For i = 1,…,N, let u_i(x,t) ≥ 0 denote the density of population i, and let m_i(x,t) ≥ 0 denote a cognitive map associated with population i. The system has the form

    ∂_t u_i = ∇·(D_i ∇u_i  −  u_i ∑_{j≠i} a_{ij} ∇(K * m_j))  +  f_i(u_1,…,u_N),
    ∂_t m_i = g_i(u_1,…,u_N) m_i  −  γ_i m_i  +  h_i(u_1,…,u_N),         i = 1,…,N,

where D_i > 0 are diffusion constants, a_{ij} ∈ ℝ are interspecific advection coefficients (attractive if a_{ij} < 0, repulsive if a_{ij} > 0) prescribed a priori (this is the "implicit memory" assumption), K is a smooth nonlocal perception kernel and (K*m_j)(x,t) = ∫_Ω K(x−y) m_j(y,t) dy, the reaction terms f_i are Lotka–Volterra-type local kinetics, and the memory dynamics are governed by reinforcement rates g_i, decay rates γ_i > 0, and source terms h_i depending on local population interactions.

For N = 2 a fairly complete analytical theory (existence, stability of homogeneous states, linear stability/Turing-type analysis, bifurcations to patterned or oscillatory solutions) is available. The problem is the following:

(a) Develop a corresponding mathematical theory for N ≥ 3. In particular, establish well-posedness, characterize the homogeneous coexistence equilibria, and perform a linear stability and bifurcation analysis of the above system for general N.

(b) Identify dynamical phenomena that genuinely require N ≥ 3 and cannot occur for N = 2 in this class of models. For instance, prove or disprove the existence of sustained spatiotemporal oscillations (limit cycles, periodic travelling waves, or more complex attractors) that arise for some N ≥ 3 but are excluded when N = 2, and classify the bifurcations producing them.

(c) Provide analytical (not merely numerical) criteria, in terms of the parameters {D_i, a_{ij}, γ_i, K, f_i, g_i, h_i}, under which such higher-population effects emerge.

original_question: Let G be a graph homeomorphic to the Petersen graph. If each path in G made of two successive segments is a geodesic, each cycle of G containing five segments has odd length, and all cycles of G containing six segments have equal length, are these three conditions not only sufficient but also necessary for G to be geodetic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ denote the Petersen graph, and let $G$ be a graph homeomorphic to $P$; that is, $G$ is obtained from $P$ by subdividing each edge of $P$ a (possibly zero) number of times. Call the images in $G$ of the original edges of $P$ the segments of $G$. A graph $G$ is called geodetic if between every pair of vertices of $G$ there is a unique shortest path. Consider the following three conditions on $G$:

(1) Every path in $G$ formed by two consecutive segments is a geodesic of $G$.
(2) Every cycle of $G$ that consists of exactly five segments has odd length.
(3) All cycles of $G$ that consist of exactly six segments have the same length.

It is known that conditions (1), (2), and (3) together are sufficient for $G$ to be geodetic. Determine whether these three conditions are also necessary: that is, prove or disprove that every geodetic graph $G$ homeomorphic to the Petersen graph must satisfy (1), (2), and (3).
status_search_result: Search results indicate that the characterization of geodetic graphs homeomorphic to the Petersen graph is an active topic, with the three conditions established as sufficient. No clear published resolution of the necessity direction (the "Petersen necessity conjecture") was found, and the broader characterization problem for geodetic subdivisions is described as still open.

original_question: Can it be proved rigorously that the total number of geodetic graphs of diameter d >= 2 that are homeomorphic to the Petersen graph is (d + 3)C5, meaning the number of combinations of d + 3 elements taken 5 at a time?
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ is called geodetic if between every pair of vertices of $G$ there is a unique shortest path. Two graphs are homeomorphic if both can be obtained from a common graph by subdividing edges (i.e., inserting degree-2 vertices into edges). The Petersen graph $P$ is the 3-regular graph on 10 vertices whose vertices are the 2-element subsets of $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, with two vertices adjacent iff the corresponding subsets are disjoint.

For an integer $d \geq 2$, let $N(d)$ denote the number of (pairwise non-isomorphic) geodetic graphs of diameter $d$ that are homeomorphic to the Petersen graph $P$.

Prove or disprove rigorously the formula
$$N(d) \;=\; \binom{d+3}{5}$$
for every integer $d \geq 2$.

original_question: Do the geodetic systems of Diophantine equations associated with K4, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph share a hidden common structure in the distribution of their variables that would make it possible to construct the corresponding system for generating every geodetic graph homeomorphic to the still-undiscovered Moore graph with k = 57, including that graph itself?
self_contained_problem:
A geodetic graph is a connected graph in which every pair of vertices is joined by a unique shortest path. The complete graph $K_4$, the Petersen graph (the unique 3-regular Moore graph of girth 5 on 10 vertices), and the Hoffman–Singleton graph (the unique 7-regular Moore graph of girth 5 on 50 vertices) are geodetic, and each can be encoded by an associated "geodetic system of Diophantine equations" whose nonnegative integer solutions parametrize the geodetic graphs homeomorphic to it (i.e., obtained by subdividing its edges with internal vertices, where the number of subdivisions on each edge is a variable of the system, subject to the geodetic constraints).

A hypothetical Moore graph of degree $k=57$ would be a 57-regular graph of girth 5 and diameter 2 on $57^2+1=3250$ vertices; its existence is a long-standing open problem.

Question: Does there exist a hidden common structural pattern in the distribution of variables across the geodetic systems of Diophantine equations associated with $K_4$, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman–Singleton graph that, if identified, would allow one to write down explicitly the corresponding geodetic system of Diophantine equations whose solutions generate the class of all geodetic graphs homeomorphic to the (still undiscovered) Moore graph of degree 57, including that Moore graph itself?
status_search_result: The existence of a Moore graph of degree 57 remains a famous open problem in graph theory (confirmed by recent surveys and notes, e.g., the Open Problem Garden entry and the 2022 note "Existence of a Moore graph of degree 57 is still open"). No common Diophantine framework spanning K4, Petersen, and Hoffman–Singleton that would yield the system for the degree-57 case appears to have been established in the literature.

original_question: How does changing the topology of connections in a computer network influence the quality of network performance when the network is modeled by geodetic graphs, especially in terms of systemic hierarchy, diameter, vertex connectivity, reliability, cost, flexibility of topological change, and the number of graphs of a given diameter that represent the same network topology?
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G=(V,E)$ is called geodetic if for every pair of vertices $u,v \in V$ there exists exactly one shortest path between $u$ and $v$. Model a computer network as a finite, simple, connected geodetic graph $G$, where vertices represent nodes and edges represent direct communication links. The quality of network performance is measured by the following indices:

1. systemic hierarchy,
2. diameter $\operatorname{diam}(G)=\max_{u,v\in V} d(u,v)$,
3. vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$,
4. reliability (the probability that the graph remains connected when each edge fails independently with a given probability),
5. cost (e.g., the number of edges $|E|$ weighted appropriately),
6. flexibility of topological change (the ease with which $G$ can be modified to another graph in a prescribed family while preserving its essential properties), and
7. the homeomorphism enumeration count $N(G,d)$, defined as the number of pairwise non-isomorphic geodetic graphs of diameter $d$ that are homeomorphic to $G$ (i.e., represent the same underlying network topology up to subdivision of edges).

Investigate quantitatively how local and global modifications of the topology of $G$ (such as edge additions, edge deletions, edge subdivisions, or vertex contractions that preserve the geodetic property) influence each of the above performance indices. In particular:

(a) Determine, for each fixed diameter $d \geq 2$, the exact value of $N(G,d)$ for a given geodetic graph $G$.

(b) Establish tradeoff inequalities or optimal bounds relating $\kappa(G)$, $\operatorname{diam}(G)$, $|E|$, and reliability over the class of geodetic graphs on $n$ vertices.

(c) Characterize those geodetic graphs which simultaneously optimize (in a Pareto sense) the listed performance indices.
status_search_result: The question is explicitly posed as an open research direction concerning the influence of topological changes on network performance for networks modeled by geodetic graphs. No published resolution was located; the enumeration of geodetic graphs of a given diameter and the precise relationships among the listed performance indices remain active topics in graph theory and discrete optimization.

original_question: Let G be a locally-finite simple geodetic graph and let t be a natural number. If C is an embedded cycle whose diameter exceeds t and whose length is minimal among all such paths in G, must C contain a geodesic subpath of length t + 1?
self_contained_problem:

A cycle $C$ in $G$ is called embedded if it is an induced subgraph (no chords). The diameter of $C$ is the maximum distance, taken in $G$, between two vertices of $C$. A geodesic subpath of $G$ of length $\ell$ is a path with $\ell$ edges that is a shortest path between its endpoints in $G$.

Suppose $C$ is an embedded cycle of $G$ whose diameter in $G$ exceeds $t$, and which has minimal length among all embedded cycles of $G$ with diameter exceeding $t$. paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
original_question: Which nuclear mass component is responsible for the all-particle cosmic-ray knee observed at about 4 × 10^15 eV: a cutoff of the light proton-plus-helium component at a few PeV, or an all-particle knee dominated by heavier nuclei after the light component has already cut off below about 1 PeV?
self_contained_problem:
The all-particle cosmic-ray energy spectrum, when multiplied by E^2.7, exhibits a steepening feature known as the "knee" at a primary energy of approximately 4 × 10^15 eV, where the spectral index changes from about -2.7 to about -3.1. Cosmic-ray primaries are nuclei spanning from protons (Z=1, A=1) up to iron-group elements (Z≈26, A≈56), and the flux of each nuclear species is conventionally assumed to cut off at a characteristic energy E_c(Z) that depends on rigidity R = E/Z (a "rigidity-dependent cutoff"). Two competing scenarios have been proposed to explain the all-particle knee:

(i) Light-component scenario: The knee at 4 × 10^15 eV is produced by the cutoff of the combined proton + helium flux at a few PeV, with heavier components cutting off at proportionally higher energies according to rigidity dependence.

(ii) Heavy-component scenario: The proton (and helium) flux already cuts off well below 1 PeV, so that at 4 × 10^15 eV the all-particle flux is dominated by intermediate and heavy nuclei (CNO, Si, Fe groups), and the observed knee is due to the bending of these heavier components.

Problem: Determine which of these two scenarios correctly describes the elemental composition of cosmic rays in the energy range from roughly 10^14 eV to 10^16 eV, and in particular identify the nuclear mass component (light p+He versus heavier nuclei) responsible for the all-particle knee at approximately 4 × 10^15 eV.
status_search_result: The question is an outstanding open problem in cosmic-ray astrophysics. Experimental results remain conflicting: high-altitude air-shower arrays (Tibet ASγ, ARGO-YBJ, EAS-TOP, CASA-MIA, BASJE-MAS) favor a low-energy (sub-PeV) cutoff of the light component with the all-particle knee dominated by heavier nuclei, while deeper-atmosphere experiments (KASCADE, KASCADE-Grande, IceTop/IceCube, Tunka-133) place the proton/light-component knee at the same energy as the all-particle knee. Recent measurements (e.g., LHAASO, GRAPES-3) continue to address but have not definitively resolved the discrepancy, which is sensitive to the hadronic interaction model used.

paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
original_question: Are supernova remnants capable of supplying the power and magnetic-field amplification needed to accelerate Galactic cosmic-ray protons to PeV energies and beyond, or must the main PeV cosmic-ray sources be a different class of Galactic accelerators?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard picture of Galactic cosmic-ray (CR) origin, the bulk of CRs observed at Earth up to the "knee" of the spectrum (around 3 × 10^15 eV, i.e. a few PeV) are assumed to be accelerated within the Milky Way by diffusive shock acceleration. A "PeVatron" is a Galactic accelerator capable of producing CR protons with energies of at least 1 PeV. Two requirements must be satisfied by any candidate class of sources: (i) the integrated kinetic power supplied to CRs must match the energy density of Galactic CRs given their confinement time (the standard estimate requires roughly 10% of the kinetic power of Galactic supernovae, of order 10^41 erg/s); and (ii) at the accelerator the magnetic field at the shock must be amplified far above interstellar values so that the maximum attainable proton energy E_max, governed in the Bohm regime by E_max ≈ (e/c) · B · u_sh · R_sh (with B the amplified field, u_sh the shock speed and R_sh the shock radius), reaches at least 1 PeV during the active acceleration phase.

Determine whether the class of Galactic supernova remnants (SNRs), treated as diffusive shock accelerators in their standard evolutionary phases (free expansion and Sedov–Taylor), can simultaneously satisfy (i) and (ii) so as to produce the observed population of Galactic CR protons up to and beyond the knee. Equivalently: prove or disprove that SNRs are the dominant sources of Galactic PeV cosmic rays, and if not, identify the class of Galactic accelerators that supplies this population.
status_search_result: Recent LHAASO observations (2021–2024) of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray sources above 100 TeV indicate that standard SNRs such as Cassiopeia A and IC 443 are unlikely to accelerate protons up to PeV energies, with their hadronic gamma-ray spectra consistent with proton cutoffs around 100 TeV. Theoretical and observational work continues to debate whether only exceptional young/energetic SNRs in specific environments, or alternative Galactic accelerators (young massive star clusters, the Galactic Center, superbubbles), are the dominant PeVatrons. The question of the dominant source class for Galactic PeV CR protons remains open as of 2025–2026.

paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
original_question: What unknown systematic uncertainties make direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements of the 100 TeV–100 PeV cosmic-ray spectrum and composition conflict, and how can experiment designs disentangle the effects of altitude, detector coverage, muon measurements, shower-core observables, reconstruction procedures, and hadronic-interaction models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider measurements of the all-particle cosmic-ray energy spectrum and elemental (mass) composition in the energy range 100 TeV to 100 PeV, which spans the so-called "knee" region. Three complementary classes of experiments contribute data:

(a) Direct measurements performed by balloon- or satellite-borne detectors above the atmosphere, which identify primary nuclei directly but have limited exposure;
(b) Indirect ground-based measurements that observe extensive air showers via Cherenkov light, fluorescence, or radio emission;
(c) Ground arrays of surface (and possibly underground) particle detectors, which sample the secondary particle densities of extensive air showers at one or more altitudes, and may include separate muon detectors and/or shower-core ("core observables") sub-arrays.

Reconstruction of primary energy E and primary mass A from indirect data depends on: the observation altitude (atmospheric depth at detection), the detector area and lateral coverage, the choice of observables (e.g., electromagnetic size N_e, muon size N_μ, shower-core particle density, depth of shower maximum X_max), the reconstruction algorithms, and the hadronic-interaction model used in Monte Carlo simulations (e.g., QGSJET-II, EPOS-LHC, SIBYLL).

Currently the published spectra and mass compositions from different experiments in this energy range disagree by amounts exceeding their quoted statistical and known systematic uncertainties, indicating one or more unidentified systematic effects.

Problem. Identify and quantify the unknown systematic uncertainties responsible for the disagreement among direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements of the primary cosmic-ray energy spectrum and elemental composition in the 100 TeV–100 PeV range. Specifically, design an experimental program (including choice of altitude, detector coverage, muon detection capability, shower-core observables, reconstruction procedure, and treatment of hadronic-interaction-model dependence) that can simultaneously and self-consistently disentangle the contributions of each of these factors to the observed discrepancies, and thereby produce a reconciled measurement of the spectrum and composition across the knee region.
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic experimental open problem in cosmic-ray physics. As of recent literature, the discrepancies among direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements in the knee region remain unresolved, with hadronic-interaction-model uncertainties (notably the long-standing muon excess / "muon puzzle") still under active investigation. No experiment has yet definitively disentangled all listed systematics.

paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
original_question: If the knee and related spectral features follow a rigidity-dependent pattern, are they caused primarily by maximum acceleration energy at cosmic-ray sources or by inefficient Galactic confinement and escape, and what measurements of proton and other mass-group spectra up to about 10^17 eV can decide between these rigidity-acceleration and rigidity-confinement interpretations?
self_contained_problem:
Cosmic rays arriving at Earth exhibit an all-particle differential energy spectrum that follows an approximate power law in kinetic energy E but features a steepening, called the "knee," near a few PeV (1 PeV = 10^15 eV). Two broad classes of rigidity-dependent models are proposed for this feature and its high-energy continuation. Here a particle of charge Z has magnetic rigidity R = E/Z, and a "rigidity model" predicts that each elemental mass group i with charge Z_i has a spectrum φ_i(E) whose characteristic spectral break occurs at an energy E_i = Z_i · R_0 for a common rigidity R_0.

(A) Rigidity-acceleration models: the break at rigidity R_0 reflects the maximum rigidity to which Galactic sources can accelerate cosmic rays, so the spectrum of each species exhibits an intrinsic cutoff at E_i = Z_i R_0 imprinted at the source.

(B) Rigidity-confinement models: sources can accelerate particles to rigidities well above R_0 ("super-PeVatron" sources), but Galactic magnetic confinement becomes inefficient above R_0, so the diffusion coefficient D(R) steepens above R_0 and the propagated spectrum of each species softens at E_i = Z_i R_0.

Problem. Working within this two-class framework, determine:
(i) whether the observed knee and the spectral features extending up to about 10^17 eV in the all-particle cosmic-ray spectrum are produced primarily by mechanism (A) or by mechanism (B); and
(ii) which quantitative measurements of the individual mass-group energy spectra φ_i(E) — in particular the proton (Z = 1) spectrum and the spectra of heavier mass groups up to roughly 10^17 eV, including the energy and shape of the proton knee, the dependence of the break energies on Z, and the high-energy behavior beyond the break — suffice to discriminate between (A) and (B).
status_search_result: Recent LHAASO measurements (2024–2025) have precisely identified the cosmic-ray proton component and measured its spectrum from ~0.15 to 12 PeV, locating a sharp proton softening around 3 PeV that aligns with the all-particle knee at ~3.67 PeV. Subsequent analyses (e.g., joint spectrum-and-anisotropy studies, and a 2025 result linking the knee to micro-quasar accelerators) increasingly favor an acceleration-limit (source) interpretation of the knee, with a new high-energy component emerging at PeV energies. The discrimination program is in progress: key proton-knee measurements have been made, but mass-group spectra up to 10^17 eV are not yet fully resolved, so the question is partially solved rather than settled.

paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
original_question: Which super-PeVatrons, if any, exist in the Inner Galaxy and Galactic Center regions, and what wide-field Southern Hemisphere observations are needed to monitor those regions and test whether they contain sources accelerating particles well beyond PeV energies?
self_contained_problem:
A "PeVatron" is an astrophysical source capable of accelerating charged particles (typically protons or nuclei) to energies of at least 1 PeV (10^15 eV); a "super-PeVatron" is a source that accelerates particles to energies well above 1 PeV, and is typically identified via the detection of gamma-ray emission with photon energies exceeding ~100 TeV up to the PeV range. The Inner Galaxy is the region of the Milky Way within roughly ±30° of Galactic longitude around the Galactic Center (Galactic latitude |b| ≲ a few degrees), and the Galactic Center region refers to the central few hundred parsecs surrounding Sagittarius A*. These regions are best observed from the Southern Hemisphere.

Problem. Determine, by means of wide field-of-view ground-based gamma-ray observations of the Inner Galaxy and the Galactic Center conducted from a Southern Hemisphere site:
(a) which (if any) astrophysical sources in these regions are super-PeVatrons, i.e. emit gamma rays with energies substantially above 1 PeV indicating hadronic acceleration well beyond PeV energies;
(b) the instrumental requirements (effective area, angular resolution, gamma/hadron discrimination, duty cycle, sky coverage, and energy threshold/reach) for a wide field-of-view Southern Hemisphere survey instrument that would be sufficient to continuously monitor the Inner Galaxy and the Galactic Center and to confirm or exclude the presence of such super-PeVatrons.
status_search_result: As of 2026, no source in the Inner Galaxy or Galactic Center has been firmly established as a super-PeVatron emitting gamma rays well above 1 PeV; the Galactic Center has been identified by H.E.S.S. as a likely PeVatron candidate, but conclusive identification of super-PeVatrons requires next-generation Southern Hemisphere wide field-of-view observatories such as SWGO (under construction/planning) together with CTA-South. The question therefore remains open.

paper_title: A Survey on Offline Reinforcement Learning: Taxonomy, Review, and Open Problems
original_question: Which off-policy evaluation method can estimate or rank candidate offline reinforcement learning policies robustly enough to work across a wide variety of datasets, so that practitioners can trust it for policy evaluation or model selection instead of relying on environment rollouts?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the offline reinforcement learning setting. A Markov decision process is given by a tuple $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma,ho_0)$ with state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, unknown transition kernel $P(s'\mid s,a)$, reward function $r:\mathcal{S}	imes\mathcal{A}	o\mathbb{R}$, discount factor $\gamma\in[0,1)$, and initial-state distribution $ho_0$. The value of a policy $\pi:\mathcal{S}	o\Delta(\mathcal{A})$ is
$$V(\pi)\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\,r(s_t,a_t)\;\Big|\;s_0\simho_0,\;a_t\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_t),\;s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)ight].$$
An off-policy evaluation (OPE) procedure is a map $\widehat{V}$ that, given only a static dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(s_i,a_i,r_i,s'_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$ generated by one or more unknown behavior policies, and a target policy $\pi$, returns either an estimate $\widehat{V}(\pi;\mathcal{D})\in\mathbb{R}$ of $V(\pi)$ or, given a finite set of candidate policies $\{\pi_1,\dots,\pi_K\}$, a ranking of them by predicted return (off-policy selection).

Question. Design and analyze an OPE / off-policy selection procedure $\widehat{V}$ with the following robustness property: there exist explicit, broadly applicable conditions on $\mathcal{D}$ (e.g. coverage, behavior-policy diversity, function-class assumptions) under which, uniformly across a wide family $\mathcal{F}$ of MDPs and dataset-generating distributions, the procedure achieves
(i) a finite-sample bound $|\widehat{V}(\pi;\mathcal{D}) - V(\pi)| \le \varepsilon(N,\delta,\mathcal{F})$ with probability $1-\delta$, with $\varepsilon	o 0$ as $N	o\infty$, and/or
(ii) a high-probability guarantee that the top-ranked policy among $\{\pi_1,\dots,\pi_K\}$ has value within $\eta$ of $\max_k V(\pi_k)$,
in such a way that the procedure consistently dominates existing OPE estimators (e.g. importance sampling, fitted-Q evaluation, doubly-robust, model-based, and stationary-distribution-ratio methods) on standard benchmark distributions of datasets. Equivalently: does there exist a single OPE method whose worst-case ranking/estimation error over a broad class of offline datasets and policies is provably smaller than that of every existing OPE method, eliminating the need for environment rollouts for policy selection?
category_tag: Off-policy evaluation in offline reinforcement learning
status_search_result: As of recent literature on the DOPE benchmark and follow-up OPE/off-policy selection work, no single off-policy evaluation or selection method has been shown to consistently outperform competitors across diverse offline RL datasets; robust, dataset-agnostic OPE remains an acknowledged open problem in the offline RL community.

paper_title: A Survey on Offline Reinforcement Learning: Taxonomy, Review, and Open Problems
original_question: How should offline reinforcement learning handle nonstationary datasets and then fine-tune the resulting offline policy online, especially in settings where the data distribution or environment changes over time and the method must adapt without discarding what was learned from the static dataset?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a sequential decision-making setting modeled as a (possibly nonstationary) Markov decision process M_t = (S, A, P_t, r_t, γ), where the transition kernel P_t and reward function r_t may vary with time t. Suppose one is given a fixed offline dataset D = {(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)}_{i=1}^N collected under a (possibly time-varying) behavior policy μ_t from environments {M_t} whose dynamics or reward distributions drift over the data-collection horizon. Let π_off denote a policy obtained by an offline reinforcement learning algorithm trained solely on D, where the goal of offline RL is to maximize the expected discounted return E[Σ_{t≥0} γ^t r_t(s_t, a_t)] without further interaction during training.

Develop and analyze an offline-to-online reinforcement learning procedure that:
(a) produces π_off from a nonstationary dataset D while accounting for distributional drift across the data,
(b) subsequently fine-tunes π_off through online interaction with a (possibly further evolving) environment M_t, and
(c) provably retains the knowledge encoded in π_off (i.e., avoids catastrophic forgetting or unlearning of the behavior-supported regions) while improving performance under the new dynamics.

Specifically, design such an algorithm and establish guarantees (e.g., regret, sample complexity, or convergence bounds) characterizing its performance as a function of the magnitude of nonstationarity (suitably quantified, e.g., via a variation budget Σ_t ||P_{t+1} − P_t|| + ||r_{t+1} − r_t||), the size and coverage of D, and the online interaction budget.
status_search_result: The problem of offline RL with nonstationary data combined with offline-to-online fine-tuning is an active and unresolved research direction. Recent works (e.g., on offline-to-online RL such as Cal-QL, PEX, and various nonstationary/continual RL papers) propose partial heuristic solutions and empirical benchmarks, but no general algorithm with provable guarantees under nonstationarity plus fine-tuning without forgetting has been established.

paper_title: A Survey on Offline Reinforcement Learning: Taxonomy, Review, and Open Problems
original_question: How can offline reinforcement learning use unsupervised reinforcement learning or related techniques to exploit large amounts of unlabeled experience when reward labels are scarce or expensive, while still producing effective downstream policies from static data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the offline reinforcement learning setting in which an agent must learn a policy purely from a fixed dataset of previously collected interactions with a Markov decision process (MDP) M = (S, A, P, r, γ), where S is the state space, A the action space, P(s' | s, a) the transition kernel, r : S × A → ℝ the reward function, and γ ∈ [0, 1) the discount factor. Suppose the available data consists of two parts:

1. A large dataset D_u = {(s_i, a_i, s'_i)} of transitions without reward labels.
2. A small dataset D_l = {(s_j, a_j, r_j, s'_j)} of transitions with reward labels, where |D_l| ≪ |D_u|.

No further interaction with the environment is permitted, and reward labeling is assumed to be costly (e.g., requiring human supervision).

Design and analyze an algorithmic framework that uses unsupervised reinforcement learning techniques (such as representation learning, intrinsic-motivation pretraining, skill or option discovery, or self-supervised dynamics modeling) on D_u, together with the labeled subset D_l, to produce a policy π whose expected discounted return J(π) = 𝔼[∑_{t≥0} γ^t r(s_t, a_t)] in M is provably (or empirically) close to that of the optimal policy learnable from a fully reward-labeled dataset of size |D_u| + |D_l|.

Specifically, formulate sufficient conditions on the unlabeled data distribution, the reward function class, and the learning procedure under which the suboptimality J(π*) − J(π) can be bounded as a function of |D_l|, |D_u|, the coverage of D_u over the state–action space, and a measure of complexity of the reward function, in a way that improves over using D_l alone.
category_tag: Offline reinforcement learning with unlabeled data
status_search_result: Leveraging large unlabeled offline datasets together with limited reward-labeled data is an active research direction. Methods such as UDS (Unlabeled Data Sharing) by Yu et al. (2022) and PDS (Provable Data Sharing) by Hu et al. (2023) provide partial progress (zero-reward relabeling, reward pessimism, and theoretical guarantees under coverage assumptions), but a general, simple, and effective framework with tight sample-complexity guarantees remains open.

paper_title: A Survey on Offline Reinforcement Learning: Taxonomy, Review, and Open Problems
original_question: How should the community build offline reinforcement learning benchmarks and datasets that better reflect real deployment conditions by including stochastic dynamics, nonstationarity, risky biases in the data, and multiagent settings, so that algorithms can be evaluated on the kinds of failures and shifts that matter in practice?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the offline reinforcement learning setting in which a learner is given a fixed dataset D = {(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)} of transitions collected from one or more behavior policies interacting with a Markov decision process (MDP) M = (S, A, P, r, γ), and must output a policy π: S → Δ(A) that aims to maximize the expected discounted return E_π[Σ_{t≥0} γ^t r_t] without further interaction with the environment. Standard offline RL benchmarks typically use datasets generated from MDPs with (approximately) deterministic dynamics, stationary transition kernels P, behavior policies that broadly cover state–action space, and a single agent.

Design and formalize a principled benchmark suite (specification of environments, data-collection protocols, evaluation metrics, and statistical evaluation procedures) for offline RL that simultaneously addresses each of the following four desiderata, and demonstrate that meaningful algorithmic distinctions emerge on it:

1. Stochastic dynamics: the environments must include MDPs whose transition kernels P(·|s,a) are genuinely stochastic (high-entropy, heavy-tailed, or with rare high-impact transitions), beyond the Atari Arcade Learning Environment.

2. Nonstationarity: the environments must include processes whose transition or reward functions vary with time, i.e., P_t and r_t with explicit nontrivial drift or regime change, and offline datasets that span multiple regimes.

3. Risky biases in the data: the datasets must be constructed so that certain catastrophic or safety-critical events (e.g., terminal failure states with large negative reward) are absent or strongly under-represented in D, while the evaluation tests whether the learned policy avoids those events at deployment.

4. Multi-agent settings: the suite must include cooperative and/or competitive multi-agent MDPs (Markov games) with offline trajectory data collected from fixed joint behavior policies, and metrics that evaluate offline learning of decentralized or centralized policies.

Provide (a) precise mathematical definitions of each environment class and of the associated dataset-generation distributions, (b) evaluation metrics that quantify performance under distributional shift, robustness to nonstationarity, avoidance of under-represented risky outcomes, and multi-agent coordination quality, and (c) baseline theoretical or empirical results separating known offline RL algorithms on the proposed benchmark.
status_search_result: This is an open research-program-style problem about constructing offline RL benchmarks. While individual partial efforts exist (e.g., D4RL, RL Unplugged, real-world RL suite, NeoRL, off-policy multi-agent datasets), no unified benchmark suite simultaneously addressing stochastic dynamics, nonstationarity, risky data biases, and multi-agent settings has been established as standard, and the question is still treated as open in the offline RL literature.

paper_title: Underwater and Air-Water Wireless Communication: State-of-the-art, Channel Characteristics, Security, and Open Problems
original_question: What are the vulnerabilities, attack models, and effective countermeasures for magnetic-induction-based underwater wireless communication networks, including how confidentiality, authentication, integrity, and availability can be achieved in systems whose predictable channel response may expose them to eavesdropping and spoofing and whose nearby malicious coils may exploit mutual induction?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an underwater wireless communication network in which each node is equipped with a coil antenna and information is transferred between nodes via magnetic induction (MI): a transmitting coil drives a time-varying current that, by mutual inductance, induces a voltage in a receiving coil. Assume the network operates in a conducting aqueous medium where the MI channel response between two coils is essentially deterministic once their geometry (separation, orientation, coil parameters) and the medium's permeability and conductivity are fixed, so that the channel is highly predictable. Adversaries may (i) passively eavesdrop on legitimate transmissions, (ii) spoof legitimate nodes by exploiting the predictable channel, and (iii) place malicious coils in close proximity to legitimate coils to couple to them via mutual induction.

Develop a complete security framework for such an MI-based underwater wireless communication network. Specifically:

1. Formulate a precise threat model that enumerates the vulnerabilities of MI underwater links, including those arising from channel predictability and from mutual-induction coupling with nearby unauthorized coils.

2. Specify attack models (eavesdropping, spoofing, impersonation, denial-of-service via induced interference, and mutual-induction-based information leakage) together with quantitative metrics for their success probability as a function of coil geometry, medium parameters, and noise.

3. Design and rigorously justify countermeasures that simultaneously guarantee
   (a) confidentiality of transmitted messages,
   (b) authentication of legitimate transmitters and receivers,
   (c) integrity of the exchanged data, and
   (d) availability of the communication service,
in the presence of the above adversaries, and prove (or otherwise establish) the security guarantees achieved.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that security of magnetic-induction-based underwater wireless communication networks remains an underexplored research direction. While MI underwater channel modeling and physical-layer studies have advanced, surveys and recent works continue to flag confidentiality, authentication, integrity, and availability for MI underwater WCNs as open problems with no comprehensive solution reported.

paper_title: Underwater and Air-Water Wireless Communication: State-of-the-art, Channel Characteristics, Security, and Open Problems
original_question: How do existing underwater communication technologies behave under smart malicious nodes that can switch between passive and active attack modes on the fly, and how should security be analyzed when those malicious nodes are equipped with state-of-the-art capabilities such as multiple-input multiple-output operation, full duplex, GPUs, and the ability to launch attacks in both air and water media?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an underwater or air-water wireless communication network consisting of legitimate transmitters and receivers that use one or more of the standard underwater channel modalities (acoustic, radio-frequency, optical/visible-light, and magnetic induction links), possibly combined with above-water radio links at the air-water interface. Introduce into this network one or more "smart malicious nodes" defined as follows: a smart malicious node can sense its local channel and traffic environment and adaptively switch, on the fly, between a passive attack mode (e.g., eavesdropping, traffic analysis) and an active attack mode (e.g., jamming, spoofing, message injection, replay, Sybil behavior). Each malicious node is additionally equipped with state-of-the-art capabilities: (i) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) transmission and reception with several antennas/transducers, (ii) full-duplex operation, allowing it to transmit and receive simultaneously on the same band, (iii) high-throughput GPU-based computation enabling real-time signal processing, machine-learning-based attack adaptation, and cryptanalytic effort, and (iv) the ability to operate and launch attacks in both the underwater medium and the air medium, exploiting the air-water interface.

Develop a rigorous security-analysis framework for such networks that:
1. Models the smart malicious node as a decision process that chooses, at each time step and based on observations, between passive and active modes so as to optimize an adversarial objective (e.g., maximize information leakage or disruption while minimizing detection probability).
2. Quantifies, for each existing state-of-the-art underwater communication technology (acoustic, RF, optical, magnetic induction, and hybrid air-water schemes), the achievable secrecy capacity, detection probability, outage probability, and throughput of the legitimate link in the presence of such adversaries, accounting for MIMO degrees of freedom, full-duplex self-interference cancellation, GPU-enabled adaptive attacks, and cross-medium attacks at the air-water boundary.
3. Determines necessary and sufficient conditions on system parameters (number of legitimate and adversarial antennas, transmit power, channel statistics, coding scheme, key-management protocol, etc.) under which secure and reliable communication is provably feasible against this adversary class, and identifies regimes in which no such guarantee is possible.

Provide the complete model, derive the corresponding performance and security bounds, and characterize defensive countermeasures that achieve those bounds.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research direction in the underwater and air-water wireless communication security literature. A brief search does not reveal a comprehensive security analysis of state-of-the-art underwater technologies against smart malicious nodes that adaptively switch between passive and active modes while equipped with MIMO, full-duplex, GPU-based, and cross-medium capabilities; in particular, full-duplex underwater adversaries appear largely unstudied. The problem is therefore taken as open.

paper_title: Underwater and Air-Water Wireless Communication: State-of-the-art, Channel Characteristics, Security, and Open Problems
original_question: How can machine-learning-based security methods that already appear promising in underwater communication, such as learning-based authentication or anti-eavesdropping approaches, be adapted and validated for air-water wireless communication systems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication scenario in which signals must traverse both an aerial channel and an underwater channel, crossing the air–water interface (an "air–water" link). Such a link experiences combined impairments including atmospheric turbulence, refraction and Fresnel reflection at the interface, wave-induced surface roughness, absorption and scattering in the water column, and turbulence-induced fading in the aquatic medium. In purely underwater wireless communication, machine-learning-based security techniques (e.g., learning-based physical-layer authentication using channel features, and learning-based anti-eavesdropping schemes that exploit channel reciprocity or adversarial training) have shown promising performance.

Develop and rigorously validate machine-learning-based security methods—specifically (i) physical-layer authentication and (ii) anti-eavesdropping / secrecy-enhancing schemes—that are tailored to the combined air–water channel. A complete solution should:
1. Provide a tractable statistical or hybrid model of the air–water channel suitable as input/feature space for learning algorithms.
2. Define adversary models (spoofing transmitter and passive/active eavesdropper) at the air side, the water side, and at the interface.
3. Design learning algorithms (supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement-learning based) whose decision statistics exploit features unique to the air–water channel.
4. Provide theoretical guarantees (e.g., bounds on false-acceptance/false-rejection probabilities for authentication, or achievable secrecy rates for anti-eavesdropping) under the proposed channel model.
5. Validate the methods through simulation and/or experimental measurement and compare them against baselines designed for purely underwater or purely aerial links.

The problem is to determine whether such methods can match or exceed the security performance attained in the purely underwater setting.
