paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
context_brief: Necessary model conditions for delaying resistance
original_question: For adaptive cancer therapy, understood as dynamic patient-specific dose modulation or dose timing that maintains treatment-sensitive tumor cells so they competitively suppress treatment-resistant tumor cells, what cancer and model conditions are necessary for adaptive therapy to delay treatment resistance? In particular, when resistance is costly, resistant cells can be suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and therapy reduces sensitive cells, what objectives should define therapeutic success, and do conclusions from simple sensitive/resistant-cell models remain valid when real-tumor components such as healthy cells, immune cells, resources, Allee effects, and phenotypic plasticity are included?
self_contained_problem:
Consider adaptive cancer therapy, defined as dynamic, patient-specific modulation of drug dose or dose timing that deliberately preserves a population of treatment-sensitive tumor cells in order to competitively suppress treatment-resistant tumor cells and thereby delay therapeutic failure. Model a tumor as a population (or interacting collection of populations) of sensitive cells S(t) and resistant cells R(t), evolving under a controllable therapy schedule u(t). It is commonly hypothesized that adaptive therapy delays the emergence of resistance when three conditions hold: (a) resistance carries a fitness cost in the absence of therapy, (b) resistant cells are suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and (c) therapy reduces the population of sensitive cells.

Address the following questions rigorously.

1. Determine the precise set of conditions on a sensitive/resistant tumor model and its therapy protocol that are necessary, and the set that are sufficient, for adaptive therapy to delay the emergence of resistance compared with standard continuous maximum-tolerated-dose therapy. In particular, formalize and assess whether conditions (a)–(c) above are each necessary.

2. Propose and justify an appropriate definition of therapeutic success. Specifically, examine the three candidate objectives: (i) lowering the time-averaged therapeutic dose, (ii) delaying the time to emergence/expansion of resistant cells, and (iii) reducing total tumor burden over the treatment horizon. Decide whether any single therapy protocol can simultaneously optimize all three objectives, or whether trade-offs are unavoidable.

3. Investigate whether the conclusions drawn from minimal two-compartment sensitive/resistant models remain valid when the model is augmented to include additional realistic components of tumors, including: healthy (non-cancerous) host cells, immune cell populations interacting with the tumor, shared limiting resources (such as oxygen, nutrients, or space), Allee effects (positive density dependence at low population sizes), and phenotypic plasticity allowing reversible switching between sensitive and resistant states. Identify which of these mechanisms preserves, modifies, or invalidates the conditions identified in (1) and the conclusions of (2).
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in a 2022/2023 survey on adaptive therapy. Partial answers exist: Strobl et al. (Cancer Research, 2021) show that a resistance cost is not strictly necessary when tumors are near carrying capacity and resistance is rare, and identify four key modulating factors (initial resistant fraction, proximity to carrying capacity, resistant proliferation rate, turnover). Subsequent works (2024–2025) on treatment-pausing thresholds and stochastic/deterministic cycle stability further refine the conditions. However, a complete characterization of necessary/sufficient conditions across extended models (immune, healthy cells, Allee, plasticity) and a unifying notion of therapeutic success remain unresolved.

original_question: What role should phenotypic plasticity and drug-induced mutations play in adaptive cancer therapy? Since treatment can induce or select resistant cellular states, phenotype switching between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant states can be reversible, and treatment holidays may re-sensitize resistant populations, when and how should adaptive therapy protocols account for switching rates, treatment-induced resistance, cancer-type and patient-level variability in plasticity, and the need to identify plasticity in an individual tumor before deciding whether and how to use adaptive therapy?

paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
original_question: For a cancer patient who may be eligible for either aggressive continuous therapy aimed at cure or adaptive therapy aimed at long-term containment, how should clinicians and modelers decide between treat-to-cure and treat-to-contain strategies before treatment begins? What disease characteristics, eco-evolutionary factors, biomarkers, resistant-cell frequencies, competition and tradeoffs, tumor burden, toxicity, quality of life, and practical monitoring constraints are needed to stratify patients into a continuous-therapy cohort versus an adaptive-therapy cohort, especially because a failed curative attempt can leave too many resistant cancer cells for later adaptive control?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a mathematical model of a tumor consisting of two competing subpopulations: sensitive cells of density S(t) and resistant cells of density R(t), evolving under a Lotka–Volterra-type dynamic

    dS/dt = r_S S (1 - (S + a_{SR} R)/K) - d(u(t)) S,
    dR/dt = r_R R (1 - (R + a_{RS} S)/K),

where r_S, r_R > 0 are intrinsic growth rates, a_{SR}, a_{RS} > 0 are competition coefficients, K > 0 is the carrying capacity, and u(t) ∈ [0, u_max] is the drug dose with d(·) a non-decreasing kill function acting only on sensitive cells. Assume an initial state (S_0, R_0) with R_0 ≥ 1 (at least one resistant cell). Two treatment strategies are considered:

  (i) Continuous (treat-to-cure) therapy: u(t) ≡ u_max until S(t) + R(t) falls below a detection threshold ε; success is defined as eradication, i.e. S(t) + R(t) = 0 in finite time.

  (ii) Adaptive (treat-to-contain) therapy: u(t) is chosen as a feedback control of the observable total burden N(t) = S(t) + R(t) (e.g., on/off switching at thresholds N_on, N_off), with the objective of keeping N(t) bounded for all t ≥ 0 while maximizing a quality-of-life functional Q[u].

Problem. Identify a decidable, model-based stratification rule — i.e., a measurable function

    Φ : (r_S, r_R, a_{SR}, a_{RS}, K, S_0, R_0, d(·), toxicity parameters, monitoring noise σ) ⟼ {cure, contain},

based only on pre-treatment observables (such as tumor burden, estimated resistant-cell frequency R_0/(S_0+R_0), competition coefficients inferred from biomarkers, and bounds on the kill function), such that:

  (a) Whenever Φ outputs "cure", strategy (i) achieves eradication with probability at least 1 - α under the stochastic version of the model with monitoring noise σ;
  (b) Whenever Φ outputs "contain", strategy (ii) keeps E[N(t)] bounded for all t and achieves expected quality-of-life Q strictly larger than that achievable by (i) following a failed curative attempt (i.e., the residual resistant population after (i) is too large to be contained);
  (c) The rule Φ is optimal in the sense that no other pre-treatment decision rule, using the same observables, achieves a strictly better trade-off between cure probability, expected survival time, and Q.

Determine whether such a stratification rule Φ exists, characterize the regions of parameter space (in terms of resistant-cell frequency, competitive ability of resistant cells, drug efficacy, and tumor burden) on which each output is optimal, and exhibit explicit thresholds separating the "treat-to-cure" and "treat-to-contain" regimes.
status_search_result: This question of pre-treatment stratification between curative and containment (adaptive therapy) strategies is highlighted as an open clinical and mathematical-modeling question in recent surveys on adaptive therapy. While various Lotka–Volterra and game-theoretic models have proposed candidate criteria (e.g., resistant-cell fraction, competition strength), no universally validated stratification rule has been established as of 2026.

paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
context_brief: Using models to design wet-lab tests
original_question: How can mathematical modeling support wet-lab testing of adaptive cancer therapy so that experiments validate theory, assess safety, and guide protocol design for patients? In particular, how should experiments be designed to measure competitive suppression in a cancer; how should drug resistance be represented by mixing pre-evolved resistant and sensitive cells, allowing resistance to evolve during the experiment, using clone tracking, or another approach; and how should treatment algorithms from mathematical or experimental models be translated to clinical practice despite pharmacokinetics, differing animal and patient time scales, toxicity, machine failures, weekends or holidays, and other deviations from planned schedules?
self_contained_problem:
Develop a mathematical-modeling framework to support wet-lab testing of adaptive cancer therapy (treatment strategies that exploit competition between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cancer cell populations by modulating dose to maintain a controlled tumor burden rather than maximizing cell kill). Specifically, address the following three interconnected problems:

(a) Competitive suppression assays. Propose and analyze experimental designs (e.g., co-culture or in vivo mixed-population experiments) together with mathematical models that allow one to quantify the degree to which drug-sensitive cells competitively suppress drug-resistant cells in a given cancer. The design should produce identifiable model parameters (e.g., competition coefficients in a Lotka–Volterra-type system dS/dt = r_S S(1 − (S + α_{SR}R)/K), dR/dt = r_R R(1 − (R + α_{RS}S)/K) − δ(t)·(·), where δ(t) encodes drug effect) that predict whether adaptive scheduling can prolong tumor control compared with continuous maximum-tolerated-dose therapy.

(b) Representation of resistance. Determine, from a modeling and experimental-design standpoint, which representation of drug resistance is most informative and predictive: (i) seeding fixed proportions of pre-evolved resistant cells with sensitive cells, (ii) allowing resistance to evolve de novo during the experiment under selective pressure, (iii) using clone-tracking technologies (e.g., DNA barcoding or lineage tracing) to follow subclonal dynamics, or (iv) an alternative formulation. Provide criteria (identifiability, predictive accuracy on held-out treatment schedules, biological realism) for choosing among these.

(c) Translation to clinical protocols. Given a treatment algorithm derived from in vitro or in vivo mathematical models, formulate a principled procedure for converting it into a clinically deployable protocol that accounts for: pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic differences between model systems and patients; differing intrinsic time scales between animal models and human disease; dose-limiting toxicity; and real-world deviations from planned schedules such as missed doses due to equipment failure, weekends, or holidays. The procedure should include robustness guarantees (e.g., performance bounds under stochastic schedule perturbations) on the resulting clinical protocol.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research direction posed in a survey on adaptive cancer therapy. While individual components (Lotka–Volterra competition models, barcoded clone-tracking experiments, PK/PD bridging) have been studied, no comprehensive, validated framework integrating experimental design for competitive suppression, optimal resistance representation, and robust clinical translation under schedule perturbations currently exists. The question remains open as a programmatic research agenda.

paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
original_question: Is real-time patient-specific prediction feasible for adaptive therapy, and what monitoring, model calibration, validation, sensitivity analysis, identifiability analysis, and biomarker quality are required before predictions should guide dose modulation? Given a clinical marker such as prostate-specific antigen, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, urine markers, imaging, or another disease-specific biomarker, when can a mathematical model accurately describe patient-specific dynamics well enough to predict subsequent response, and when should it be rejected because it cannot describe the data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a patient undergoing adaptive cancer therapy, in which the dose or scheduling of treatment is dynamically modulated in response to longitudinal measurements of a disease-specific biomarker (for example, prostate-specific antigen, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cell counts, urine markers, or quantitative imaging). Let y(t) denote the time series of such a biomarker, and suppose one wishes to use a mathematical model M (with parameter vector θ ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ^p) of tumor–treatment dynamics to forecast the patient's future biomarker trajectory and, in particular, the time of disease progression, in real time.

Formulate and resolve the following questions:

(a) Identify general necessary conditions on the sampling frequency and noise level of y(t), on the structural and practical identifiability of θ given the observation map, on calibration and validation protocols (e.g., out-of-sample prediction error, sensitivity analysis of forecasts to θ), and on the quality of the biomarker as a surrogate for tumor burden, under which patient-specific real-time prediction of progression times is feasible with quantifiable uncertainty suitable to guide dose modulation.

(b) Provide a decision rule (a goodness-of-fit / model-adequacy criterion) that, given the calibration data of a single patient, determines when the model M may legitimately be used to issue forecasts, and when M must be rejected as unable to describe that patient's dynamics.

(c) For at least one concrete choice of biomarker and corresponding mechanistic model, demonstrate prospectively (not merely retrospectively) that the resulting predictions are sufficiently accurate and calibrated to inform clinical dose modulation.
status_search_result: The feasibility of real-time, patient-specific prediction for adaptive cancer therapy remains an active open research question. Recent works on PSA-based prostate cancer adaptive therapy and ctDNA-informed models report progress on retrospective calibration and identifiability, but prospective clinical validation enabling forecast-driven dose modulation has not been established. No definitive solution is reported in the literature.

paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
original_question: Can mathematical models reliably drive individual cancer treatment decisions in adaptive or evolution-based therapy? What must change in patient-data collection, prediction under uncertainty, interdisciplinary communication, and decision-support workflows so that predictive mathematical models can track patient-specific tumor dynamics, compare available treatment options using mechanisms such as virtual-patient cohorts in a Phase i framework, and provide clinically useful recommendations at scale?
self_contained_problem:
Formulate a rigorous framework, and determine whether one can construct, predictive mathematical models of tumor dynamics with the following properties, sufficient to drive individualized adaptive (evolution-based) cancer therapy decisions at scale:

(a) Patient-specific state model. For each patient p, let x_p(t) ∈ R^n denote a tumor state vector (e.g., subclone burdens, biomarker levels, microenvironmental variables) evolving according to a parametric dynamical system dx_p/dt = F(x_p, u; θ_p), where u(t) is the treatment input and θ_p ∈ Θ are patient-specific parameters. Specify minimal longitudinal measurement protocols y_p(t_k) = h(x_p(t_k)) + ε_k under which θ_p and the latent state x_p(t) are practically identifiable before clinical progression occurs.

(b) Prediction under uncertainty. Given a posterior π(θ_p, x_p | y_{1:k}) obtained from sequential Bayesian inference, characterize sufficient conditions on F, h, and the observation schedule such that predicted time-to-progression and response under any admissible treatment policy u(·) have credible intervals narrow enough to discriminate among candidate policies with a prescribed error rate α.

(c) Virtual patient Phase-i comparison. Define a procedure that, for each individual patient p, generates a virtual cohort {θ_p^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N from π(θ_p | y_{1:k}), simulates outcomes under each candidate treatment policy, and outputs a ranking with guaranteed coverage (e.g., a confidence set of near-optimal policies) under model misspecification bounded in a specified metric.

(d) Decision-support guarantees. Prove or disprove the existence of such a triple (model class F, measurement protocol h, inference-and-decision algorithm A) that simultaneously: (i) is identifiable from clinically feasible data; (ii) produces calibrated predictions whose miscoverage is uniformly bounded across a heterogeneous patient population; and (iii) yields treatment recommendations whose expected clinical utility provably dominates standard-of-care policies.

State precise hypotheses on F, Θ, the noise model, and the population distribution under which (a)–(d) admit a positive solution, or exhibit fundamental obstructions (identifiability failure, uncertainty propagation lower bounds, or decision-theoretic impossibility) that prevent it.
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic challenge in mathematical oncology: building clinically deployable, patient-specific predictive models for adaptive therapy. Current literature (virtual-patient/Phase-i trial frameworks, adaptive prostate cancer trials by Zhang/Gatenby, and ongoing reviews) treats this as an active open research program rather than a resolved problem; no general framework yet provides identifiability, calibrated uncertainty, and decision-theoretic guarantees at scale.

context_brief: Yau conjecture on positive holomorphic sectional curvature
original_question: If a compact Kahler manifold X has positive holomorphic sectional curvature, must X be projective and rationally connected?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. The holomorphic sectional curvature $H$ of $X$ is the restriction of the sectional curvature to complex lines in the tangent spaces; explicitly, for a nonzero tangent vector $v$ of type $(1,0)$, $H(v) = R(v,\bar v, v, \bar v)/\|v\|^4$, where $R$ is the curvature tensor of the Kähler metric. Say that $X$ has positive holomorphic sectional curvature if $H(v) > 0$ for every nonzero $(1,0)$ tangent vector $v$ at every point of $X$. Recall that $X$ is called projective if it admits a holomorphic embedding into some complex projective space, and rationally connected if any two points of $X$ can be joined by a chain of rational curves.

Prove or disprove: every compact Kähler manifold $X$ that admits a Kähler metric of positive holomorphic sectional curvature is projective and rationally connected.
status_search_result: The conjecture, due to Yau (Problem 47 in his 1982 problem list), was resolved affirmatively by Xiaokui Yang in 2018, who proved that a compact Kähler manifold with positive holomorphic sectional curvature is projective and rationally connected, using the notion of RC-positivity.

Yau.", "claim": "Yang proved Yau's conjecture that compact Kähler manifolds with positive holomorphic sectional curvature are projective and rationally connected."}]

context_brief: Extending the semi-positive curvature structure theorem
original_question: Can the structure theorem proved for smooth projective varieties with semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature, including the locally trivial MRC fibration and the splitting description of the universal cover, be generalized to compact Kahler manifolds?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold admitting a Kähler metric of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature (i.e., for every nonzero tangent vector $v$ of type $(1,0)$, the holomorphic sectional curvature $H(v) \ge 0$). For a smooth projective variety, the following structure theorem is known: there exists a maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration $\varphi: X \dashrightarrow Y$ which is everywhere defined, smooth, and locally trivial (with rationally connected fiber $F$ admitting a Kähler metric of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature), $Y$ has identically zero holomorphic sectional curvature, and the universal cover $\widetilde{X}$ splits holomorphically and isometrically as a product $\mathbb{C}^k \times \widetilde{F}$ (so in particular the MRC fibration lifts to the trivial product fibration after passing to the universal cover).

Problem: Does the same structure theorem hold for an arbitrary compact Kähler manifold $X$ (not assumed projective) carrying a Kähler metric of semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature? More precisely, must $X$ admit a smooth locally trivial MRC fibration $\varphi: X \to Y$ onto a compact Kähler manifold $Y$ of identically zero holomorphic sectional curvature, with rationally connected fiber, such that the universal cover of $X$ splits holomorphically and isometrically as $\mathbb{C}^k \times \widetilde{F}$?
status_search_result: The problem of extending the projective structure theorem for semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature to the compact Kähler setting appears to remain a research question being actively pursued. Recent preprints (2024–2025) by Matsumura and by Zhang–Zhang study the fundamental groups and partial semi-positivity in the Kähler case, and a related structure/splitting theorem has been obtained for compact Kähler manifolds with non-negative mixed curvature. However, no source clearly states a complete generalization of the full projective structure theorem (MRC locally trivial fibration plus universal cover splitting) to all compact Kähler manifolds. Status appears partially resolved.

context_brief: Truly flat tangent vectors and induced fibrations
original_question: Let (X, g) be a compact Kahler manifold with semi-positive or semi-negative holomorphic sectional curvature, and let V be the set of appropriate truly flat tangent vectors. Does V determine an integrable subbundle of TX? Can one find a complementary subbundle W with TX = W (+) V? In the semi-positive case, can one construct an MRC fibration f: X -> Y with W = TX/Y? In the semi-negative case, can one construct the Iitaka fibration f: X -> Z associated with K_X with V = TX/Z?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,g)$ be a compact Kähler manifold. The holomorphic sectional curvature of $g$ in the direction of a nonzero tangent vector $v \in T_xX$ is $H(v) = R(v,\bar v,v,\bar v)/|v|^4$, where $R$ is the curvature tensor of the Chern (equivalently Levi-Civita) connection of $g$. Assume that $g$ has either semi-positive holomorphic sectional curvature ($H(v)\ge 0$ for all $v$) or semi-negative holomorphic sectional curvature ($H(v)\le 0$ for all $v$).

Call a tangent vector $v\in T_xX$ "truly flat" (in the appropriate sense for the sign condition) if $H$ vanishes to sufficiently high order along $v$, so that $v$ lies in the zero set of the obstruction to strict positivity (respectively strict negativity) of $H$. Let $V\subset TX$ denote the set of such truly flat tangent vectors.

Answer the following:

(a) Does $V$ form an integrable holomorphic subbundle of $TX$?

(b) Does there exist a holomorphic subbundle $W\subset TX$ giving a holomorphic splitting $TX = W\oplus V$?

(c) In the semi-positive case, does there exist a maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration $f:X\to Y$ such that $W$ coincides with the relative tangent bundle $T_{X/Y}$?

(d) In the semi-negative case, does there exist an Iitaka fibration $f:X\to Z$ associated with the canonical bundle $K_X$ such that $V$ coincides with the relative tangent bundle $T_{X/Z}$?

status_search_result: This problem is posed as an open research problem concerning the structure of compact Kähler manifolds with sign-definite holomorphic sectional curvature. Related work (e.g., Heier–Lu–Wong–Yang and Matsumura on semi-negative/semi-positive HSC and their connections to MRC and Iitaka fibrations) provides partial structural results, but a full answer establishing integrability of the truly-flat distribution, the holomorphic splitting, and identification with the MRC/Iitaka fibration in the stated generality does not appear in the literature retrieved. Status remains open as posed.

context_brief: Local triviality for MRC fibrations with pseudo-effective tangent bundle
original_question: If X is a smooth projective variety with pseudo-effective tangent bundle and phi: X -> Y is its holomorphic MRC fibration, must phi be locally trivial?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety whose tangent bundle $T_X$ is pseudo-effective (i.e., the tautological line bundle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(T_X)}(1)$ on the projectivization $\mathbb{P}(T_X)$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle). (b) Prove or disprove: the Albanese map $\alpha\colon X \to \mathrm{Alb}(X)$ is a maximally rationally connected (MRC) fibration of $X$ (that is, its general fibers are rationally connected and any rational curve in $X$ meeting a general fiber is contained in it).

context_brief: Slope rationally connected quotient structure theorem
original_question: Let (X, Delta) be a klt pair with smooth X and nef -(K_X + Delta). Does there exist an orbifold morphism rho: (X, Delta) -> (R, Delta_R) such that (R, Delta_R) is a klt pair with smooth R and c_1(K_R + Delta_R) = 0, the general orbifold fibers are slope rationally connected, and the fibration is locally trivial with respect to pairs?

Let $(X,\Delta)$ be a klt (Kawamata log terminal) pair such that $X$ is a smooth complex projective variety and $-(K_X+\Delta)$ is nef. Does there exist an orbifold morphism

satisfying all of the following:

2. the general orbifold fiber $(X_r,\Delta_r)$ of $\rho$ is slope rationally connected (i.e., for a general pair of points there is an orbifold rational curve whose pullback of $T_{X_r}(-\Delta_r)$ — equivalently, the orbifold tangent sheaf — is ample, or, in the standard formulation, the orbifold fiber admits no positive-slope quotient of its orbifold cotangent sheaf with respect to any movable class);

Here an orbifold morphism $\rho:(X,\Delta)\to(R,\Delta_R)$ is a surjective morphism $\rho:X\to R$ compatible with the boundary divisors in the orbifold sense, and the general orbifold fiber $(X_r,\Delta_r)$ is the pair obtained by restricting $\Delta$ (minus its vertical part) to a general fiber $X_r=\rho^{-1}(r)$.

paper_title: Progress in Nuclear Astrophysics: a multi-disciplinary field with still many open questions
original_question: How can nuclear mass models for exotic neutron-rich nuclei be improved so that r-process calculations use masses and derived neutron-capture rates that remain accurate far from experimentally known nuclei? In the paper, current models can disagree by up to about ±5 MeV near important shell closures, causing neutron-capture rates to differ by 3 to 5 orders of magnitude, and the authors explicitly call for improved relativistic and non-relativistic mean-field models, beyond-mean-field corrections, and better treatment of odd-A and odd-odd nuclei together with broader agreement with other observables such as charge radii, neutron skins, fission barriers, spectroscopic data, nuclear-matter properties, and neutron-star properties.
self_contained_problem:
Develop a theoretical nuclear mass model capable of predicting atomic masses M(Z,N) of exotic neutron-rich nuclei (in particular near the neutron shell closures N = 126 and N = 184) with sufficient accuracy to be used in rapid neutron-capture (r-process) nucleosynthesis simulations. Concretely, construct a self-consistent mean-field (relativistic or non-relativistic, e.g. Skyrme-Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov, Gogny-HFB, or covariant density-functional) framework, augmented by beyond-mean-field corrections (such as quadrupole and octupole correlations obtained from the Generator Coordinate Method, and a proper treatment of odd-A and odd-odd nuclei including time-reversal symmetry breaking), such that:

1. The model reproduces all experimentally known atomic masses within current measurement uncertainties.
2. Predictions of unknown masses M(Z,N) for neutron-rich nuclei relevant to the r-process agree across independent parameterizations to substantially better than the current spread of approximately ±5 MeV near N = 126 and N = 184, so that the resulting (n,γ) neutron-capture rates (computed, e.g., via Hauser–Feshbach statistical theory using these masses as input) do not vary by the present 3–5 orders of magnitude between models.
3. The same model simultaneously reproduces, within accepted experimental error bars, additional nuclear (pseudo-)observables: charge radii, neutron-skin thicknesses, fission barriers and shape isomers, spectroscopic data such as 2⁺ excitation energies and moments of inertia, properties of infinite symmetric and pure neutron matter from ab initio calculations, and global neutron-star observables such as the maximum gravitational mass and the mass–radius relation.

Provide such a model (or prove its existence/non-existence under the constraints above) and quantify the residual uncertainty in r-process abundance predictions stemming from nuclear masses.
category_tag: nuclear mass models for r-process nucleosynthesis
status_search_result: This is a long-standing open challenge in nuclear astrophysics. Recent literature (2023–2025) on mass models (BSkG3, relativistic DFT, machine-learning-augmented mass tables) continues to report mass deviations of several MeV for very neutron-rich nuclei near N=126 and N=184, with corresponding order-of-magnitude spreads in (n,γ) rates, indicating the problem remains open.

paper_title: The Branch-Cut Cosmology: evidences and open questions
original_question: In branch-cut cosmology, how should the apparent cosmic anisotropy associated with the smoothness problem of small temperature fluctuations be explained consistently, especially in the final stage of contraction where the authors say a negative value of the dimensionless thermodynamic parameter epsilon reverses the scaling behavior of the anisotropy-related ratio while the remaining ratios stay locked in?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cosmological model in which the spatial scale factor is replaced by a complex, branch-cut analytic continuation of the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker scale factor, so that the universe undergoes a contracting phase followed by an expanding phase joined across a horizontal branch cut (no singular Big Bang). In an anisotropic Bianchi-type generalization of this background, introduce the dimensionless ratios that measure, in units of the total energy density, the contributions of (i) spatial curvature, (ii) matter, (iii) radiation, and (iv) shear anisotropy, as functions of a thermodynamic-like dimensionless parameter ε that characterizes the equation of state of an effective fluid driving the contraction/expansion. Assume that during the final stage of contraction the curvature, matter, and radiation ratios remain "locked in" (i.e. effectively constant in their relative scaling), while the anisotropy-related ratio scales as a power of the scale factor whose sign is governed by ε, so that taking ε<0 (interpreted as a dark-matter-like component) reverses the scaling behavior of the anisotropy ratio.

Problem. Within this framework, give a fully consistent dynamical explanation of how the smoothness (near-isotropy) of the cosmic temperature fluctuations can arise: specifically, derive conditions on ε and on the locked-in ratios under which the anisotropy ratio is driven to arbitrarily small values at the end of the contracting phase and remains small throughout the subsequent expansion, and show that such conditions are compatible with the analytic structure of the branch-cut scale factor and with the observed level of CMB temperature fluctuations.
status_search_result: Branch-cut cosmology is a recent proposal and the smoothness/anisotropy issue in its contracting phase is explicitly flagged by its proponents as lacking a consistent explanation. No follow-up work appears to have resolved this; the question seems to remain open.

paper_title: The Branch-Cut Cosmology: evidences and open questions
original_question: How should branch-cut cosmology be reformulated quantum mechanically, rather than only through leading-order classical equations of motion, so that the intrinsically quantum evolutionary domain near the primordial transition is described more faithfully?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the framework of "branch-cut cosmology," in which the cosmological scale factor a(t) of a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker-type universe is analytically continued to a multi-valued complex function defined on a Riemann surface with a branch cut, so that the classical primordial singularity is replaced by a finite branch-cut transition region connecting a contracting pre-bounce sheet to an expanding post-bounce sheet. At leading order, the dynamics of the (complexified) scale factor are governed by classical Einstein-type equations of motion obtained from a Hořava–Lifshitz-style gravitational action (with higher spatial-derivative curvature terms) coupled, possibly, to a scalar inflaton field.

Provide a fully quantum-mechanical reformulation of this model. Concretely:

1. Starting from a Hořava–Lifshitz gravitational Lagrangian density coupled to matter, perform an ADM (Arnowitt–Deser–Misner) decomposition adapted to the branch-cut geometry and derive the corresponding Hamiltonian constraint H = 0 in which the dynamical variable is the complex branch-cut scale factor β(t) and its conjugate momentum π_β.

2. Promote β and π_β to operators satisfying canonical commutation relations, choose an operator-ordering prescription (with explicit ordering parameters), and obtain the resulting Wheeler–DeWitt-type equation Ĥ Ψ(β) = 0 — equivalently, a Schrödinger-type equation with a (generically non-linear) effective potential — governing the wave function Ψ of the universe on the branch-cut Riemann surface.

3. Specify boundary/matching conditions for Ψ across the branch cut connecting the contracting and expanding sheets, and demonstrate that the resulting quantum evolution describes a non-singular quantum transition (a "quantum leap") between the two phases consistent with the Bekenstein entropy bound.

4. Show that, in an appropriate semiclassical/WKB limit, the quantum description reduces to the leading-order classical branch-cut equations of motion, and analyze quantum corrections to observables in the primordial transition region.
status_search_result: Subsequent works (2022–2024) by Hess, Zen Vasconcellos, Hadjimichef, Bodmann, de Freitas Pacheco and collaborators have developed Wheeler–DeWitt quantum formulations of branch-cut cosmology: a topological canonical quantum-mechanics approach (Astron. Nachr. 2023; arXiv:2212.03832), a Wheeler–DeWitt approach with operator-ordering parameters (Universe 9 (2023) 278), a non-commutative Wheeler–DeWitt extension (Universe 9 (2023) 428), and applications to primordial gravitational waves (arXiv:2401.06902). These provide concrete partial quantum reformulations along the lines requested, although a complete, fully observationally tested quantum theory of the branch-cut transition is still under development.

paper_title: The Branch-Cut Cosmology: evidences and open questions
original_question: What are the cosmological consequences in branch-cut cosmology of abandoning a symmetric treatment of the dimensionless thermodynamics connection epsilon(t), and of choosing a different ordering for the values taken by epsilon(t) during the universe's evolution?
self_contained_problem: In the branch-cut cosmology framework, the evolution of the universe is described in terms of a complex scale factor obtained by analytic continuation, and the thermodynamic content is encoded through a dimensionless connection function ε(t) that interpolates between regimes of the cosmic evolution. In the standard formulation, ε(t) is assumed to satisfy a symmetric prescription (i.e. ε(t) is treated symmetrically with respect to the branch-cut transition, with a fixed ordering of its values along the cosmic history). Investigate the cosmological consequences of relaxing this assumption: specifically, (i) adopt a non-symmetric prescription for the dimensionless thermodynamic connection ε(t) across the branch-cut transition, and (ii) consider alternative orderings of the values taken by ε(t) during the universe's evolution. Determine the resulting modifications to the cosmological dynamics (Hubble parameter, energy density, entropy production, and horizon structure) and identify which choices, if any, remain compatible with observational constraints.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicitly open direction for future investigation within the branch-cut cosmology program. No publication appears to have systematically addressed the consequences of a non-symmetric treatment or alternative orderings of ε(t); the topic is niche and confined to a small set of works developing branch-cut cosmology.

paper_title: The Branch-Cut Cosmology: evidences and open questions
original_question: What concrete predictions does branch-cut cosmology make for the primordial energy-density fluctuation spectrum that seeds later structure formation, and can Cosmic Microwave Background measurements from Planck constrain or test those predictions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the branch-cut cosmology framework, a nonsingular extension of standard Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker cosmology in which the scale factor a(t) is analytically continued onto a Riemann surface so that the cosmological singularity at t = 0 is replaced by a branch cut. Concretely, the usual scale factor a(t) is replaced by a complex-valued function a_β(t) depending on a dimensionless parameter β ∈ (0, 1] such that, in the limit β → 1, one recovers the standard cosmological scale factor, while for β < 1 the function a_β(t) is everywhere nonzero and develops a branch-cut structure that removes the Big Bang singularity. Assuming the usual minimally coupled inflaton-like scalar field dynamics on this analytically extended background, with quantum fluctuations of the energy density propagating on the branch-cut geometry:

(a) Derive an explicit prediction for the primordial scalar power spectrum P_ζ(k) of energy-density fluctuations that seed cosmological structure formation in the branch-cut cosmology, expressed as a function of comoving wavenumber k and of the model parameter β, including its scalar spectral index n_s(β) and any running α_s(β) = dn_s/d ln k.

(b) Determine whether the resulting P_ζ(k), n_s(β), and α_s(β) are compatible with the Cosmic Microwave Background temperature, polarization, and lensing constraints reported by the Planck satellite mission, in particular the measured values of n_s and the upper bound on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r, and identify the range of β (if any) for which the branch-cut prediction is observationally viable.
status_search_result: Branch-cut cosmology is an active but niche research program, and while subsequent works have begun to compare its predictions with CMB and structure-formation data, a definitive, fully worked-out primordial scalar spectrum with quantitative Planck-based constraints on the model parameter β has not been firmly established in the literature. The question as posed is therefore best characterized as open.

paper_title: The Branch-Cut Cosmology: evidences and open questions
original_question: Within branch-cut cosmology and its multiverse picture, how are the homogeneity of primordial radiation and the average density of matter established strongly enough to support the later formation of the structures observed in the universe today?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cosmological model, called branch-cut cosmology, in which the conventional initial singularity of the standard Big Bang scenario is replaced by a Riemann-surface branch cut in the complexified scale factor. In this framework the early universe is described not by a single classical spacetime but by a multiverse-like collection of sheets joined along the branch cut, each carrying its own primordial radiation field and matter distribution. Assume the dynamics on each sheet is governed by a Friedmann-type evolution equation analytically continued through the branch cut, and that primordial radiation and matter are transported between sheets according to the multi-sheeted geometry.

Within this setting, give a quantitative mechanism that establishes:

(a) the spatial homogeneity of the primordial radiation field across each sheet of the branch-cut multiverse to a level consistent with the observed isotropy of the cosmic microwave background (relative temperature fluctuations of order 10^{-5}); and

(b) a sufficiently uniform average matter density, together with a power spectrum of small perturbations on top of it, such that gravitational instability during the subsequent evolution reproduces the large-scale structure (galaxies, clusters, filaments and voids) observed in the present universe.

Formulate explicitly the equations governing the propagation of perturbations across the branch cut, derive the resulting two-point correlation function of density fluctuations at the end of the primordial epoch, and show that the homogeneity and uniformity conditions in (a) and (b) follow from the geometric structure of the branch-cut multiverse rather than from an inflationary phase.
status_search_result: Branch-cut cosmology is a relatively recent proposal; the question of how homogeneity of primordial radiation and uniform average matter density are achieved—without invoking standard inflation—is explicitly listed as an open question in the program. No published derivation establishing these properties quantitatively within branch-cut cosmology appears to exist.

paper_title: Recent progress and open problems in the Bergman space
original_question: Let D be the open unit disk and L^2_a(D) the Bergman space of square-area-integrable analytic functions on D. A sequence A of points in D is an L^2_a(D) zero sequence when some function in L^2_a(D) vanishes precisely on A, counting multiplicities. Characterize exactly which sequences in D are zero sequences for L^2_a(D).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space consisting of all analytic functions $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$$\|f\|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2 \, dA(z) < \infty,$$
where $dA$ denotes Lebesgue area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. A sequence $A = \{a_n\} \subset \mathbb{D}$ (with multiplicities) is called an $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ zero sequence if there exists a non-zero function $f \in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ whose zero set, counted with multiplicities, coincides exactly with $A$.

Give a complete characterization, in terms of the geometric/potential-theoretic distribution of the points $\{a_n\}$ in $\mathbb{D}$, of those sequences which are $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ zero sequences.
status_search_result: A complete geometric characterization of zero sequences for the unweighted Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ remains open. Significant partial results exist: Horowitz (1974/77) gave sufficient conditions and factorization, Luecking (1996) characterized zero sets for weighted Bergman spaces under certain conditions, and more recent work (e.g., Pau–Peláez–Perälä, 2019, and others) has extended such results to weighted settings with doubling or Bekollé–Bonami weights. However, an exact, intrinsic characterization of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ zero sequences is still not known.

paper_title: Recent progress and open problems in the Bergman space
original_question: For an inner divisor phi in L^2_a(D), let Phi_phi be the potential associated with phi, satisfying Delta Phi_phi = |phi|^2 - 1 in D and vanishing on the boundary circle, with the boundary gradient condition used for inner divisors. The known isometry for f in H^2(D) is ||phi f||^2_L2 = ||f||^2_L2 + integral_D |f'(z)|^2 Phi_phi(z) dS(z). Determine precisely for which inner divisors phi this isometry extends to every f in L^2_a(D), allowing the value +infinity on both sides.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk and let $dS$ denote normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. Define the Bergman space
$$L^2_a(\mathbb{D})=\Big\{f\in\mathrm{Hol}(\mathbb{D}):\|f\|^2_{L^2_a}=\int_\mathbb{D}|f(z)|^2\,dS(z)<\infty\Big\},$$
and the Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ of holomorphic $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ with $\sup_{0<r<1}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{i\theta})|^2\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}<\infty$.

A function $\varphi\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called an inner divisor (in the Bergman sense) if it has unit norm and 
$$\int_\mathbb{D} (|\varphi(z)|^2-1)\, q(z)\,dS(z)=0$$
for every bounded holomorphic $q$ in the invariant subspace generated by $\varphi$ (equivalently, $\varphi$ is the extremal/canonical divisor of its zero-based invariant subspace).

For such $\varphi$, let $\Phi_\varphi:\overline{\mathbb{D}}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the unique function satisfying
$$\Delta\Phi_\varphi(z)=|\varphi(z)|^2-1\quad\text{on }\mathbb{D},\qquad \Phi_\varphi\big|_{\partial\mathbb{D}}=0,$$
together with the natural boundary condition on the gradient appropriate for inner divisors (so that $\Phi_\varphi\ge 0$ on $\mathbb{D}$).

It is known that for every $f\in H^2(\mathbb{D})$,
$$\|\varphi f\|^2_{L^2_a(\mathbb{D})}=\|f\|^2_{L^2_a(\mathbb{D})}+\int_\mathbb{D}|f'(z)|^2\,\Phi_\varphi(z)\,dS(z). \qquad (\ast)$$

Determine precisely the class of inner divisors $\varphi\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ for which the identity $(\ast)$ extends to all $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$, where both sides are allowed to take the value $+\infty$.

original_question: Let A and B be finite zero sequences in D with A contained in B, and let phi_A and phi_B be their associated Bergman zero divisors. Does the argument of the quotient phi_B(z)/phi_A(z) increase monotonically as z travels counterclockwise around the unit circle? In the special case where B differs from A by one point, is phi_B/phi_A a star-shaped univalent function on D?

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $A^2=A^2(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty$, where $dA$ is normalized area measure. For a finite sequence $A=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of points in $\mathbb{D}$ (counted with multiplicity), the associated Bergman zero divisor (canonical, or contractive, divisor) $\varphi_A$ is the unique extremal solution of the problem
$$\varphi_A(0)=\max\{\operatorname{Re} f(0):\ f\in A^2,\ \|f\|=1,\ f(a_j)=0\ \text{for all } j\},$$
normalized so $\varphi_A(0)>0$. The function $\varphi_A$ extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ in the cases considered below, so $\arg\varphi_A(e^{i\theta})$ is well defined.

Suppose $A\subset B$ are two finite zero sequences in $\mathbb{D}$ (with $A$ a sub-multiset of $B$), and let $\varphi_A,\varphi_B$ be their associated Bergman zero divisors.

(a) Prove or disprove: as $z=e^{i\theta}$ traverses the unit circle once counterclockwise (i.e.\ $\theta$ increases from $0$ to $2\pi$), the argument $\arg\bigl(\varphi_B(z)/\varphi_A(z)\bigr)$ is a monotonically nondecreasing function of $\theta$.

self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space of holomorphic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with
$$\|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty,$$
where $dA$ is the normalized area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. A sequence $A=\{a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ (with multiplicities) is called a zero sequence for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ if there exists a nonzero $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ whose zero set (counted with multiplicity) contains $A$. Define
$$I(A)=\{f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D}):f\text{ vanishes on }A\text{ (with multiplicity)}\},$$
which is a closed subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ invariant under multiplication by $z$. Let $\varphi_A\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ denote the extremal (canonical) zero divisor associated with $A$, namely the unique solution of the extremal problem
$$\sup\{\operatorname{Re} f(0_A):f\in I(A),\ \|f\|=1\},$$
where $0_A$ is the lowest-order nontrivial Taylor coefficient functional determined by $A$ (so that $\varphi_A$ has unit norm in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ and vanishes on $A$).

The multiplier space $M(H^2,L^2_a)$ consists of holomorphic functions $\varphi:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $\varphi f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ for every $f\in H^2(\mathbb{D})$, normed by

A function $G\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called an inner divisor (more precisely an $L^2_a$-inner function) if $\|G\|_{L^2_a}=1$ and $\int_{\mathbb{D}}(|G(z)|^2-1)q(z)\,dA(z)=0$ for every bounded harmonic function $q$ on $\mathbb{D}$ (equivalently, $G$ is the canonical extremal divisor associated with an invariant subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$). paper_title: Recent progress and open problems in the Bergman space
original_question: Let A^-infinity be the algebra of analytic functions on D satisfying a growth bound |f(z)| <= C(1 - |z|^2)^(-N) for some positive constants C and N. If f belongs to L^2_a(D) and is cyclic in A^-infinity, meaning it generates a dense ideal there, must f also be cyclic in L^2_a(D)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk. Define:

(a) The Bergman space $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ consisting of analytic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with
$$\|f\|^2_{L^2_a}=\int_{\mathbb{D}} |f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty,$$
where $dA$ is normalized area measure. A function $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is called cyclic in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ if the closed subspace generated by $\{z^n f(z):n=0,1,2,\dots\}$ equals $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$.

(b) The Korenblum algebra
$$A^{-\infty}=\Big\{f\in\mathrm{Hol}(\mathbb{D}):\exists\, C,N>0\text{ such that }|f(z)|\le C(1-|z|^2)^{-N}\text{ for all }z\in\mathbb{D}\Big\},$$
endowed with its natural inductive limit topology. A function $f\in A^{-\infty}$ is called cyclic in $A^{-\infty}$ if the ideal $f\cdot A^{-\infty}$ is dense in $A^{-\infty}$.

It is known that any $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ which is cyclic in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is also cyclic in $A^{-\infty}$.

Question: Does the converse hold? That is, if $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ is cyclic in $A^{-\infty}$, must $f$ be cyclic in $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$?

The problem appears still open.

context_brief: Bergman-type kernels for logarithmically subharmonic weights
original_question: Let omega be a logarithmically subharmonic weight on D that reproduces the origin. Is the reproducing kernel k of the weighted Bergman space L^2_a(D,omega) a Bergman-type kernel, meaning a reproducing kernel of the McCullough-Richter form k(z,lambda) = (1 - conjugate(psi(lambda)) psi(z))^(-1)(1 - v(z,lambda)) for an analytic psi with psi(0)=0 and psi'(0) nonzero and a positive definite kernel v with v(0,0)=0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk, and let $\omega:\mathbb{D}\to(0,\infty)$ be a logarithmically subharmonic weight (i.e., $\log\omega$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb{D}$), normalized so that the origin is a reproducing point in the sense that $\int_{\mathbb{D}} f(z)\,\omega(z)\,dA(z) = f(0)$ whenever $f$ is holomorphic and integrable against $\omega\,dA$ (here $dA$ is normalized area measure). Consider the weighted Bergman space
$$L^2_a(\mathbb{D},\omega)=\Big\{f\text{ holomorphic on }\mathbb{D}:\ \|f\|^2_\omega=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\omega(z)\,dA(z)<\infty\Big\},$$
and let $k(z,\lambda)$ denote its reproducing kernel.

original_question: Should resilience require a system to return to a previous equilibrium, or can recovery mean reaching a different or gradually changed state? The question is especially relevant for ecological systems and volatile social organizations whose states evolve and may lack a well-defined reference equilibrium.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a dynamical system modeling a complex adaptive system (for instance an ecological community or a social organization) given by a state trajectory x(t) in some state space X, subject to perturbations. Classically, the system is called resilient at an equilibrium x* if, after a perturbation that displaces the state away from x*, the trajectory returns to x* as t tends to infinity. However, many real systems are non-stationary: their underlying dynamics evolve over time, they may possess multiple stable states, or they may lack any well-defined reference equilibrium at all (evolving systems never re-attain exactly identical states; highly volatile organizations admit no canonical reference state).

(a) does not require the system to return to a single fixed equilibrium x*,
(b) admits recovery to a different stable state, or to a gradually drifting reference trajectory x*(t), as a legitimate form of resilient response,
(c) reduces to the classical equilibrium-return notion in the time-invariant, single-attractor case,
(d) is operational for systems whose reference state is not a priori defined, in the sense that resilience can be detected or quantified from the observed trajectory and perturbation alone.

In particular, determine whether such a definition can be given uniformly across classes of models (deterministic ODEs, stochastic processes, agent-based models), and characterize the conditions under which it agrees with, or strictly extends, classical equilibrium-based resilience.

The literature on ecological and social resilience (Holling's engineering vs. ecological resilience, and more recent "resilience of non-autonomous systems" and "pullback attractor" approaches) shows that multiple competing definitions exist but no consensus mathematical framework has been established. The problem is therefore considered open as a modeling/definitional question.

The macroscopic behavior of the organization is assumed to emerge from local interactions (bottom-up modeling), permitting self-organization and exhibiting path dependence, so that the trajectory of the system depends on its history and not solely on present external conditions. paper_title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
original_question: What differences between network representations matter when modeling social organizations? The question should compare representations such as direct interaction networks, signed-relation networks, bipartite and multi-edge networks, knowledge graphs, multilayer or multiplex networks, and hypergraphs for group interactions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider an organization modeled as a set of agents together with relations among them. Several network representations can be used to encode such an organization:

1. Direct interaction networks: simple graphs G=(V,E) where edges represent observed interactions between pairs of agents.
2. Signed-relation networks: graphs in which each edge (i,j) carries a weight ω_{ij} ∈ ℝ whose sign indicates a positive or negative social relation (e.g., trust vs. distrust, cooperation vs. antagonism).
3. Bipartite and multi-edge networks: graphs G=(V_1∪V_2,E) with E⊆V_1×V_2 (agents linked to affiliations, events, or artifacts), possibly with multiple parallel edges between the same pair.
4. Knowledge graphs: directed labeled multigraphs whose edges are typed relations (predicates) between entities, from which one may extract one-mode projections.
5. Multilayer / multiplex networks: a family {G_α=(V,E_α)}_{α∈L} of graphs on a common (or aligned) vertex set indexed by layers α (different relation types or contexts), together with inter-layer couplings.
6. Hypergraphs: pairs H=(V,𝓔) with 𝓔⊆2^V, where each hyperedge e∈𝓔 represents a group interaction among an arbitrary subset of agents.

Problem. Identify and characterize the structural and dynamical differences between these network representations that are essential when modeling the resilience of social organizations. Specifically:

(a) For each pair of representations above, exhibit organizational features (e.g., signed balance, group-level interactions, role asymmetries, multi-relational coupling) that can be expressed in one representation but are lost or distorted under projection to the other.

(b) Determine which representation is minimally sufficient to capture (i) signed social relations ω_{ij} with positive and negative components, (ii) genuine k-body group interactions for k≥3 that are not reducible to pairwise interactions, and (iii) the coexistence of multiple relation types between the same agents.

(c) Compare how a dynamical process (e.g., a contagion, opinion, or stress-propagation model) defined on a hypergraph differs quantitatively from the same process defined on the pairwise projection of that hypergraph or on a multilayer reformulation, and identify invariants of the organization's resilience that depend on the chosen representation.
status_search_result: The question is a broad conceptual/open research problem about which network representation best captures features relevant to organizational resilience. While individual aspects (e.g., higher-order interactions via hypergraphs, multilayer dynamics, signed networks) have substantial literature showing representation-dependent behavior, no single definitive resolution exists; the problem as posed remains open in its general form.

Consider a social system modeled as a time-evolving multilayer network in which a set of agents A = {a_1, ..., a_n} interact over time. Assume the following data structures may be observed:

(i) Relational data: a sequence of (possibly signed) interaction graphs G_t = (A, E_t, w_t, s_t), where E_t ⊆ A × A is the set of directed dyadic interactions at time t, w_t : E_t → ℝ_{>0} assigns interaction intensities, and s_t : E_t → {+1, −1} assigns a sign (positive or negative relation).
(ii) Longitudinal data: observations of these graphs at discrete times t = 1, 2, ..., T, allowing reconstruction of trajectories of dyads and of individual agents.
(iii) Multivariate data: attribute vectors x_i(t) ∈ ℝ^d for each agent a_i recording features such as activity, role, or context, plus exogenous shock indicators ξ(t).

From such data, define operational estimators for:
 • the robustness R(t) of the system, intended as its capacity to maintain a reference structural/functional state under perturbations;
 • the adaptivity A(t), intended as its capacity to reorganize interactions in response to perturbations;

The problem is: determine the minimal sufficient set of relational, longitudinal, and multivariate observables — including signed relations, inferred interaction propensities p_{ij}(t) (probabilities that agents i and j interact), and temporal centrality measures C_i(t) — from which the quantities R(t), A(t), and Res(t) can be consistently estimated for a generic social system. paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
original_question: How can physical-layer security schemes be developed to secure uplink satellite communication from terrestrial or aerial devices to satellites, when the uplink is vulnerable to spoofing, message alteration, and denial-of-service attacks, carries large volumes of user data in broadband satellite systems, and must operate under performance and power constraints across heterogeneous devices and scenarios?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a satellite communication system whose uplink channel carries data from a heterogeneous population of terrestrial and aerial transmitters (e.g., handheld terminals, IoT sensors, UAVs, ground gateways) to one or more satellites in low, medium, or geostationary orbit. Each transmitter i has a finite transmit-power budget P_i, a hardware/computational complexity bound C_i, and a minimum throughput requirement R_i. The uplink is subject to (i) eavesdropping by passive adversaries, (ii) spoofing in which an adversary impersonates a legitimate transmitter, (iii) message alteration in which an adversary modifies a transmitted codeword, and (iv) denial-of-service attacks (jamming) that inject interference into the uplink band. Channel state information about the legitimate user-to-satellite link may be partial, while channel information about the adversaries is unknown beyond statistical models.

Within the framework of physical-layer security (which uses channel coding, beamforming/precoding, artificial-noise injection, cooperative jamming, secret-key generation from channel reciprocity, and authentication based on physical channel features rather than upper-layer cryptography), formulate and design a scheme that simultaneously:

1. Achieves a positive secrecy rate R_s(i) ≥ R_i^{sec} for each legitimate transmitter i against the eavesdropping model, subject to P_i and C_i.
2. Provides a physical-layer authentication test, based on measurable channel features, whose false-acceptance probability against spoofing and message-alteration attacks is at most ε_FA and whose false-rejection probability for legitimate users is at most ε_FR.
3. Maintains a guaranteed availability (probability of successful decoding) of at least 1 − δ under a specified jamming model with adversary power budget P_J.
4. Operates uniformly across the heterogeneity of devices and orbital scenarios (LEO/MEO/GEO with their associated Doppler, latency, and path-loss regimes).

Characterize the fundamental trade-off region among the tuples (R_s, ε_FA, ε_FR, δ, P_i, P_J) achievable by any such scheme, and exhibit an explicit construction (coding, precoding, and authentication procedure) that attains a point inside this region under realistic satellite channel models (Rician/shadowed-Rician fading, large Doppler shifts, long propagation delays).

paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
original_question: How can physical-layer security strategies be developed specifically for inter-satellite communication, including both radio-frequency and optical inter-satellite links, when such links are increasingly attackable in low-earth-orbit constellations, remain understudied in the literature, and exhibit distinctive physical-layer characteristics such as fading, Doppler shift, and weather-condition effects that may be exploitable for security, while optical inter-satellite links still lack proposed defenses against threats such as eavesdropping?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation in which pairs of satellites communicate over inter-satellite links (ISLs). Two link types are present: (i) radio-frequency (RF) ISLs, modeled by a time-varying channel with parameters capturing small-scale fading, large Doppler shifts due to relative orbital motion, and atmospheric/weather-induced attenuation when links graze the atmosphere; and (ii) free-space optical (FSO) ISLs, modeled by a line-of-sight channel with pointing/acquisition/tracking errors and atmospheric turbulence effects. An eavesdropper, located either on another satellite, on an aerial platform, or on the ground, attempts to intercept the legitimate transmission without active cooperation.

Within the framework of physical-layer security (PLS), where the security metric is the achievable secrecy rate
   C_s = [ log_2(1 + SNR_legit) − log_2(1 + SNR_eve) ]^+,
formulate concrete PLS strategies (e.g., beamforming, artificial noise injection, cooperative jamming, secret key generation from reciprocal channel features, or coding schemes) that explicitly exploit the distinctive physical-layer characteristics of inter-satellite links — namely the fading statistics, Doppler shift, and weather-induced effects on RF ISLs, and the narrow-beam, turbulence-affected nature of optical ISLs — to maximize C_s (or an equivalent secrecy outage / secrecy capacity metric) against eavesdropping and related passive attacks. Provide, in particular, a defense scheme for optical inter-satellite links against eavesdropping with provable secrecy guarantees.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers on satellite PLS (2023–2025) consistently identify inter-satellite link security, especially for optical ISLs, as an under-explored area with few concrete PLS schemes proposed; the problem remains broadly open, though some initial work on RF ISL secrecy and FSO eavesdropping models has appeared.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: How can a reconfigurable intelligent surface element be completely deactivated so that its reflection is nulled with respect to all angles, and what physically realizable RIS design or control model would make that all-angle nulling possible for channel-training methods that rely on turning elements off?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of $N$ subwavelength reflecting elements arranged on a planar aperture. Each element $n$ acts as a passive scatterer whose response to an incident plane wave depends on the angle of incidence $\theta_i$, the angle of reflection $\theta_r$, the polarization, and the frequency, and is characterized by a (generally angle-dependent) reflection coefficient $\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega)$ controllable through a set of tunable parameters (e.g., bias voltages applied to varactors or PIN diodes that change the local surface impedance).

Many channel-training and channel-estimation schemes for RIS-aided wireless systems require the ability to "switch off" individual elements, meaning that the element should contribute no scattered field regardless of the directions of the incoming and outgoing waves. Formally, we say element $n$ is all-angle nulled if there exists a setting of its tunable parameters for which
$$\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega) = 0 \qquad \text{for all admissible } (\theta_i,\theta_r,\text{polarization}),$$
so that the element produces no scattered field for every incidence/reflection geometry within the operating band.

Problem. Determine whether a physically realizable RIS hardware architecture and associated control model exist that achieves all-angle nulling of an individual RIS element in the sense above. If so, describe such an architecture (specifying the unit-cell structure, the tunable mechanism, and the control rule) and prove that the resulting $\Gamma_n$ vanishes identically over all incidence and reflection angles, polarizations, and the operating frequency band. If not, characterize the fundamental electromagnetic obstructions that prevent such an all-angle null, and quantify the best achievable angular and bandwidth uniformity of the suppression $|\Gamma_n(\theta_i,\theta_r;\omega)|$ over a passive (or active) tunable unit cell.
status_search_result: Recent work on RIS-aided spatial nulling (2024–2025) addresses nulling in specific directions and characterizes the existence of unimodular reflection weights producing perfect nulls in chosen directions, but acknowledges that an RIS element's response is intrinsically angle-, polarization-, and frequency-dependent. No source verifies a physically realizable design that nulls reflection from a single element across all angles simultaneously, so the question of true all-angle element deactivation appears to remain open.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: When RIS reflection coefficients are updated only infrequently and the practical implementation therefore requires coding across many coherence intervals of the slower channel, should RIS configuration and beamforming be optimized for outage capacity or throughput rather than ergodic capacity, and how should that optimization be formulated?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication system in which a transmitter communicates with a receiver via a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of N passive reflecting elements. The cascaded channel is modeled in two time scales:

- A fast-varying component h_f ∈ C^N that changes independently in each coherence block of length T_f symbols.
- A slow-varying component h_s ∈ C^N (e.g., large-scale fading or the RIS-related geometry) that remains constant over L consecutive fast coherence blocks.

Let θ = (θ_1, …, θ_N) ∈ Θ ⊂ C^N denote the vector of RIS reflection coefficients (|θ_n| = 1), and let w denote the transmit beamforming vector with ||w||² ≤ P. The instantaneous received SNR in a fast block with fading h_f is
   γ(θ, w; h_f, h_s) = |(h_s ⊙ h_f)^H diag(θ) w|² / σ²,
and the corresponding instantaneous mutual information is C(θ, w; h_f, h_s) = log₂(1 + γ).

Suppose that the RIS reflection vector θ can be updated only on the slow time scale (once per L fast blocks), so that θ must be chosen as a function of h_s alone, while w may adapt per fast block. Assume an outer code spans many fast coherence blocks within a slow block.

Formulate and solve the following joint optimization problems:

(a) ε-Outage capacity: For a target outage probability ε ∈ (0,1), determine
   C_out(ε) = sup_{θ(h_s)} sup_{w(·)} { R : Pr_{h_f}[ C(θ(h_s), w(h_f); h_f, h_s) < R ] ≤ ε },
and characterize the optimal slow-scale RIS configuration θ*(h_s) and fast-scale beamformer w*(h_f).

(b) Throughput maximization: Determine
   T* = sup_{θ(h_s), w(·)} E_{h_f}[ C(θ(h_s), w(h_f); h_f, h_s) · 1{C ≥ R_th} ],
or, equivalently, the maximum goodput (1−ε)·R achievable under outage constraint ε.

Specifically, provide: (i) the explicit form of the optimal θ*(h_s) under standard fading distributions (e.g., Rayleigh, Rician) for h_f; (ii) conditions under which optimizing for outage capacity or throughput yields a strictly different RIS configuration than optimizing for the ergodic capacity E[C]; and (iii) quantification of the performance gap between these criteria as functions of N, L, ε, and the fading statistics.
status_search_result: The question is framed as a direction for future work concerning RIS optimization under infrequent reconfiguration, where outage capacity or throughput would be more suitable metrics than ergodic capacity. A targeted web search did not surface a definitive treatment that jointly optimizes slow-scale RIS configuration and fast-scale beamforming explicitly for outage capacity/throughput under the two-time-scale model in full generality; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: Under exactly what physical, angular, and surface-design conditions are RIS-induced channels reciprocal or non-reciprocal, and what validated theory or experimental evidence is needed to support communication-system models that assume a non-reciprocal RIS?
self_contained_problem:
A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) is a planar array of N sub-wavelength scattering elements, each of which can be configured to impose a controllable complex reflection coefficient on an incident electromagnetic wave. Let an incident plane wave arrive at the surface from direction (θ_i, φ_i) with polarization p_i, and let the scattered field be observed in direction (θ_r, φ_r) with polarization p_r. Model the RIS as a linear two-port (or multi-port) device with a scattering operator S(θ_i, φ_i, p_i; θ_r, φ_r, p_r; Φ), where Φ = diag(e^{jϕ_1}, …, e^{jϕ_N}) encodes the per-element configuration, possibly augmented by lumped passive/active loads, magnetic biasing, or time-modulated impedances.

The RIS-induced channel is said to be reciprocal if, for every configuration Φ and every pair of directions/polarizations,
   S(θ_i, φ_i, p_i; θ_r, φ_r, p_r; Φ) = S(θ_r, φ_r, p_r; θ_i, φ_i, p_i; Φ),
and non-reciprocal otherwise.

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on
 (a) the physical realization of the unit cells (material constitutive relations, presence of magneto-optical, time-varying, or nonlinear components, active circuitry),
 (b) the angular geometry of incidence and reflection (including specular versus anomalous reflection regimes and near-field versus far-field operation), and
 (c) the surface design parameters (element spacing relative to wavelength, mutual coupling, load termination network, configuration Φ),
under which the scattering operator S satisfies the reciprocity identity above. Furthermore, for cases in which the identity fails, formulate a rigorously derived communication-channel model H_{RIS}(Φ) for a non-reciprocal RIS that is consistent with Maxwell's equations and energy-conservation constraints, and identify the experimentally measurable quantities that would distinguish reciprocal from non-reciprocal regimes.
status_search_result: Recent literature on reconfigurable intelligent surfaces continues to debate the conditions for channel reciprocity. Standard passive, linear, time-invariant, isotropic RIS designs are generally argued to be reciprocal by Lorentz reciprocity, but anomalous-reflection metasurfaces, space-time-modulated, magnetically biased, or actively loaded RIS designs have been proposed as non-reciprocal, with conflicting modeling assumptions in the communications literature. As of 2026 no consensus theorem or definitive experimental validation has settled the necessary and sufficient conditions, so the question remains open.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: Can hardware structures that provide near-independent control of reflection amplitude and phase be shown to work effectively for RIS-aided communication systems, rather than only in related reflectarray or metasurface settings?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication system aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS): a planar array of $N$ passive (or nearly passive) reflecting elements placed between a transmitter and a receiver, where the $n$-th element imposes a complex reflection coefficient $r_n = a_n e^{j\phi_n}$, with amplitude $a_n \in [0,1]$ and phase $\phi_n \in [0,2\pi)$, on the impinging electromagnetic wave. In most current designs the achievable pair $(a_n,\phi_n)$ is coupled: the amplitude is a (typically non-monotonic) function of the phase due to the physics of the underlying tunable element (e.g., varactor or PIN-diode loaded unit cell), which limits the achievable beamforming and channel-shaping performance.

Design and analyze a unit-cell hardware structure for an RIS such that:
1. Each element $n$ can be independently tuned to any pair $(a_n,\phi_n)$ in a prescribed two-dimensional region $\mathcal{R} \subseteq [0,1]\times[0,2\pi)$, with amplitude and phase essentially decoupled across $\mathcal{R}$.
2. The design operates over a bandwidth and at carrier frequencies relevant to wireless communication (e.g., sub-6 GHz or mm-wave bands), with insertion loss, response time, and power consumption compatible with real-time RIS-aided communication.
3. Using such elements in an $N$-element RIS, one can demonstrate—analytically and experimentally—measurable gains in channel estimation accuracy, achievable rate, or beamforming flexibility for an RIS-aided communication link, compared to phase-only or coupled amplitude-phase RIS designs.

Prove (or experimentally establish) that the resulting near-independent amplitude-phase control unit cells, which to date have been demonstrated mainly in reflectarray and metasurface contexts, can be effectively integrated into and benefit RIS-aided wireless communication systems.
status_search_result: Recent works (2022–2025) demonstrate RIS unit cells with near-independent amplitude and phase control, including a mm-wave (28 GHz) cell with 0–0.5 amplitude tuning and full 360° phase range using combined PIN-diode and varactor structures, and sub-6 GHz prototypes showing independent amplitude/phase coding for beam manipulation. These results indicate the question is partially solved at the unit-cell and prototype level, though comprehensive integration and end-to-end communication-system gains remain an active research area.
