paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: What channel models and channel-estimation techniques are appropriate for RIS-aided near-field communication, where a large RIS violates the far-field planar-wave assumption and different RIS elements experience different angles and polarization conditions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication system aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS): a planar array of N passive reflecting elements whose individual reflection coefficients (phase shifts, and possibly amplitudes) can be configured to shape the propagation environment between a transmitter and a receiver. When the RIS aperture is large relative to the wavelength and to the distances involved, a receiver or transmitter may lie within the Rayleigh (near-field) region of the surface. In this regime the standard far-field planar-wave assumption fails: the wavefronts impinging on the surface are curved (spherical), and the angles of arrival/departure, path lengths, and polarization states differ from one RIS element to another, so that the channel cannot be described by a single steering vector parametrized by a single direction.

Formalize the following research problem:

(a) Propose a tractable mathematical channel model for the cascaded transmitter–RIS–receiver link in the near field of a large RIS, accounting for (i) element-dependent spherical wavefront curvature (e.g., per-element distance and angle), (ii) element-dependent polarization mismatch, and (iii) possible mutual coupling, such that the model reduces to the standard far-field planar-wave RIS channel model in the appropriate asymptotic limit.

(b) Design and analyze a channel-estimation algorithm that, given pilot symbols transmitted under a chosen sequence of RIS configurations, recovers the parameters of the proposed near-field channel model with provable guarantees (e.g., identifiability, sample/pilot complexity, mean-squared-error scaling) that exploit the structure (such as spherical-domain sparsity) of the near-field channel.

Determine appropriate models and estimators meeting (a) and (b), and characterize the trade-offs between pilot overhead, RIS size, near-field/far-field regime, and estimation accuracy.
status_search_result: Multiple recent works (2022–2025) have proposed near-field RIS channel models based on spherical wavefronts and Fresnel approximations, and have developed estimation algorithms using compressive sensing in the polar/spherical domain, joint channel estimation and localization (NF-JCEL), and methods accounting for beam-squint in wideband XL-RIS systems. However, no single comprehensive model jointly handling spherical wavefronts, per-element polarization, mutual coupling, and wideband effects with provable estimation guarantees has been established; the area remains an active research direction.

paper_title: Concrete examples of the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations: numerical results for the heat semigroup and open questions on them (with appendix: full list of pictures and Python code)
original_question: Let UC_b(R,R) be the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on R with the sup norm. Given arbitrary a,b,c in UC_b(R,R) with a(x) bounded below by a positive constant, let L be the second-order variable-coefficient differential operator (Lf)(x)=a(x)f''(x)+b(x)f'(x)+c(x)f(x) on C_b^∞(R,R), whose closure generates a C_0-semigroup e^{tL}. Does there exist an explicitly computable family C(t) of bounded linear operators on UC_b(R,R), expressed directly in terms of a,b,c,f,x and not using e^{tL} even implicitly, such that C is a Chernoff function for L and, on some dense subspace D, the approximation error satisfies ||e^{tL}f-C(t/n)^n f|| ≤ M/q^n for constants M>0 and q>1 for all sufficiently large n? If such superfast Chernoff approximations do not exist, what obstruction proves their impossibility?
self_contained_problem:
Let $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}$, equipped with the supremum norm $\|\cdot\|$. Fix functions $a,b,c \in UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ with $\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}} a(x) > 0$. On the domain $C_b^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ of bounded smooth functions with bounded derivatives of all orders, define the second-order variable-coefficient differential operator
\[ (Lf)(x) = a(x)f''(x) + b(x)f'(x) + c(x)f(x). \]
Assume that the closure of $L$ generates a strongly continuous semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$.

Recall that a family $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ of bounded linear operators on $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ is called a Chernoff function for $L$ if $C(0)=I$, $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|C(t)\|<\infty$ for every $T>0$, $C(t)f$ is continuous in $t$ for every $f$, and $\lim_{t\to 0^+}(C(t)f-f)/t = Lf$ for $f$ in a core of $L$; in this case Chernoff's theorem yields $e^{tL}f = \lim_{n\to\infty} C(t/n)^n f$.

Question. Do there exist a family $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ of bounded linear operators on $UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ and a dense linear subspace $D \subset UC_b(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ such that:

(i) $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ is a Chernoff function for $L$;

(ii) there is an explicit formula $(C(t)f)(x) = F(a,b,c,f,x;t)$ depending only on the coefficients $a,b,c$, on $f$, and on $x,t$, and in particular not involving the semigroup $e^{tL}$ (neither explicitly nor in any hidden way);

(iii) there exist constants $M>0$, $q>1$, and $n_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $f\in D$ and every $t$ in a fixed bounded interval,
\[ \|e^{tL}f - C(t/n)^n f\| \le \frac{M}{q^n} \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0? \]

If no such "superfast" Chernoff approximation exists, exhibit an obstruction proving its impossibility.
status_search_result: The problem appears on a published list of open problems in one-parameter semigroup theory and is reiterated in recent works (2023) on Chernoff approximations. Known fast-converging Chernoff approximations either rely on the semigroup itself (circulus vitiosus) or are restricted to constant-coefficient/model examples (heat and transport equations); no explicit superfast Chernoff function for general variable coefficients has been exhibited, and no impossibility result is known. The status is open.

paper_title: Concrete examples of the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations: numerical results for the heat semigroup and open questions on them (with appendix: full list of pictures and Python code)
original_question: For the heat equation u_t(t,x)=u_xx(t,x) on the real line, work in the Banach space UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm. Let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. For t=1/2, compare the exact solution e^{tL}u0 with Chernoff products G(t/n)^n u0 and S(t/n)^n u0, where G is first-order Chernoff tangent to L and S is second-order Chernoff tangent to L. Write d_n^G=||e^{tL}u0-G(t/n)^n u0|| and d_n^S=||e^{tL}u0-S(t/n)^n u0||, and estimate log d_n approximately as alpha log n plus beta, where alpha is the order of decreasing error and beta is the free term. Why do the sampled errors d_n^G and d_n^S oscillate around their fitted power-law trends as n changes, forming waves rather than lying on a monotone or nearly straight log-log curve? What theoretical feature of the Chernoff products, the heat semigroup, the selected initial conditions, or the finite-n sampling causes this oscillatory error behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Let $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the sup norm $\|f\|=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f(x)|$. Consider the heat equation $u_t(t,x)=u_{xx}(t,x)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, whose generator $Lf=f''$ produces the strongly continuous heat semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$. Define the bounded linear operators
$$(G(t)f)(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}f(x)+\tfrac{1}{4}f(x+2\sqrt{t})+\tfrac{1}{4}f(x-2\sqrt{t}),$$
$$(S(t)f)(x)=\tfrac{2}{3}f(x)+\tfrac{1}{6}f(x+\sqrt{6t})+\tfrac{1}{6}f(x-\sqrt{6t}).$$
Here $G$ is Chernoff-tangent to $L$ to first order and $S$ to second order, so by Chernoff's theorem, for every $u_0\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ and every $t\ge 0$,
$$d_n^G(t):=\|e^{tL}u_0-G(t/n)^n u_0\|\to 0,\qquad d_n^S(t):=\|e^{tL}u_0-S(t/n)^n u_0\|\to 0$$
as $n\to\infty$. Fix $t=1/2$ and a smooth bounded initial datum $u_0$ (e.g.\ $u_0(x)=\sin x$, $\cos x$, $e^{-x^2}$, or similar). For large $n$ one observes numerically that
$$\log d_n^G\approx \alpha_G\log n+\beta_G,\qquad \log d_n^S\approx \alpha_S\log n+\beta_S,$$
but, plotted against $\log n$, the sequences $\log d_n^G$ and $\log d_n^S$ do not lie on these straight lines: they oscillate around the fitted trend in a wave-like manner rather than following a monotone or nearly linear log–log curve.

Provide a rigorous theoretical explanation of this oscillatory behaviour. Specifically, identify which features of the Chernoff products $G(t/n)^n$ and $S(t/n)^n$, of the heat semigroup $e^{tL}$, of the chosen initial conditions, or of the discrete sampling in $n$ are responsible for the periodic-like waves observed in $n\mapsto\log d_n^G$ and $n\mapsto\log d_n^S$ around their power-law trends.
status_search_result: The oscillation phenomenon was posed as an unexplained numerical observation among a list of open questions on the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations to the heat semigroup. Subsequent work (e.g., Galkin–Remizov on tangency-order based rates, and a 2024 Israel J. No source located identifies a theoretical mechanism explaining the oscillations, so the question appears still open.

original_question: For the heat equation u_t(t,x)=u_xx(t,x) on the real line, work in the Banach space UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm. Let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. self_contained_problem:
Consider the heat equation u_t(t,x) = u_{xx}(t,x) for (t,x) ∈ [0,∞) × ℝ on the Banach space F = UC_b(ℝ) of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on ℝ with the sup norm ‖f‖ = sup_{x∈ℝ}|f(x)|. The operator L f = f'' generates the heat C_0-semigroup (e^{tL})_{t≥0} on F.

Define two families of bounded linear operators on F by

  (G(t)f)(x) = (1/2) f(x) + (1/4) f(x + 2√t) + (1/4) f(x − 2√t),
  (S(t)f)(x) = (2/3) f(x) + (1/6) f(x + √(6t)) + (1/6) f(x − √(6t)),

so that G is Chernoff-tangent to L of first order and S is Chernoff-tangent to L of second order. By Chernoff's theorem, for every t > 0 and every u_0 ∈ F,

  d_n^G(t,u_0) := ‖e^{tL} u_0 − G(t/n)^n u_0‖ → 0,
  d_n^S(t,u_0) := ‖e^{tL} u_0 − S(t/n)^n u_0‖ → 0 as n → ∞.

Fix t = 1/2 and, for each parameter ξ ∈ (0,1), consider the two families of initial data

  u_0^{(sin)}(x) = |sin x|^ξ,    u_0^{(exp)}(x) = exp(−|x|^ξ),

both of which lie in F and belong to the Hölder class of exponent ξ. Empirically one finds a power-law decay

  log d_n^G ≈ α_G(ξ) log n + β_G(ξ),   log d_n^S ≈ α_S(ξ) log n + β_S(ξ),

Consider the heat equation u_t(t,x) = u_{xx}(t,x) on the real line, posed in the Banach space F = UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous functions f: R → R, equipped with the sup norm ||f|| = sup_{x in R} |f(x)|.   (G(t)f)(x) = (1/2) f(x) + (1/4) f(x + 2 sqrt(t)) + (1/4) f(x - 2 sqrt(t)),
  (S(t)f)(x) = (2/3) f(x) + (1/6) f(x + sqrt(6 t)) + (1/6) f(x - sqrt(6 t)).

These satisfy G(0) = S(0) = I and are tangent to L at 0 of orders 1 and 2 respectively, so by Chernoff's theorem, for every fixed t > 0 and every u_0 in F,

  d_n^G := || e^{tL} u_0 - G(t/n)^n u_0 ||  →  0,
  d_n^S := || e^{tL} u_0 - S(t/n)^n u_0 ||  →  0  as n → ∞.

Fix t = 1/2 and model the asymptotic decay numerically by

  log d_n^G ≈ α_G log n + β_G,    log d_n^S ≈ α_S log n + β_S,

calling α the order of decreasing error and β the free term.

  (Trigonometric family)  u_0(x) = |sin x|^ξ,
  (Exponential family)    u_0(x) = exp(-|x|^ξ).

 (i) For the trigonometric family, α_S depends approximately linearly on ξ, while α_G shows no comparable dependence on ξ.
 (ii) For the exponential family, neither α_G nor α_S depends appreciably on ξ.

paper_title: An Overview of Compact Star Populations and Some of Its Open Problems
original_question: What evolutionary relationships connect the observed neutron-star subpopulations, including ordinary radio pulsars, central compact objects, X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs), Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), magnetars, and other hidden neutron stars, and which of these classes are genuinely distinct populations versus temporary evolutionary stages of the same underlying objects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the observed Galactic population of isolated neutron stars, which is empirically partitioned into several classes distinguished by their emission properties, spin periods, period derivatives, magnetic field strengths, surface temperatures, and ages. These classes include: (i) ordinary radio pulsars (rotation-powered neutron stars emitting coherent radio pulsations); (ii) central compact objects (CCOs), thermally emitting X-ray point sources located near the centers of supernova remnants, with no detected radio emission and inferred weak dipolar magnetic fields; (iii) X-ray Dim Isolated Neutron Stars (XDINSs, the "Magnificent Seven"), nearby isolated neutron stars showing purely thermal soft X-ray spectra, long spin periods (several seconds), and no radio counterparts; (iv) Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), neutron stars detected only through sporadic single radio bursts rather than persistent pulsations; (v) magnetars (anomalous X-ray pulsars and soft gamma repeaters), neutron stars whose X-ray luminosity exceeds their rotational energy loss and which are powered by the decay of ultra-strong magnetic fields (B ≳ 10^14 G); and (vi) additional "hidden" classes of neutron stars that evade standard radio surveys.

Determine the evolutionary relationships connecting these subpopulations. Specifically, identify which of the above classes correspond to genuinely distinct populations of neutron stars with different formation channels or progenitor properties, and which instead represent transient evolutionary phases through which a single underlying type of neutron star passes during its lifetime. Provide a unified evolutionary scheme (for example, a directed graph of transitions among classes parameterized by age, magnetic field strength and its decay, spin period, and temperature) consistent with the observed number densities, kinematic ages, period and period-derivative distributions, magnetic field estimates, and thermal luminosities of each class, and consistent with the Galactic core-collapse supernova rate.
status_search_result: Recent reviews of neutron-star populations indicate that unification among radio pulsars, magnetars, XDINSs, CCOs and RRATs remains an active open problem. Magnetar-like behavior in some pulsars and high-B pulsars suggests partial unification, and magnetic field decay models link magnetars to XDINSs, but no consensus evolutionary scheme reproduces all observed populations simultaneously.

original_question: Does the compact-object mass distribution contain a true lower black-hole mass gap between about 2 and 5 solar masses, or is that interval only partially depleted, with some objects and formation channels populating at least part of the 2.5–5 solar-mass range?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the mass distribution of stellar-mass compact remnants (neutron stars and black holes) formed via stellar evolution and observed through electromagnetic and gravitational-wave channels. Empirically, neutron-star masses cluster below roughly 2.5 solar masses while observed stellar black holes are typically found at or above about 5 solar masses, suggesting a possible "lower mass gap" in the interval from approximately 2 to 5 solar masses (or, more conservatively, 2.5 to 5 solar masses).

Question: Does the underlying compact-object mass distribution contain a true gap in the interval [2, 5] solar masses (equivalently, is this interval essentially unpopulated), or is the interval only partially depleted, in the sense that there exist compact objects, formed through standard or alternative formation channels (such as core-collapse supernovae with different convective timescales, binary interactions, accretion-induced collapse, or hierarchical/dynamical processes), whose masses lie within the 2.5–5 solar-mass range with non-negligible probability? In particular, determine (i) whether a strict gap exists, (ii) if not, the lower edge above which any depletion begins, and (iii) the formation channels capable of populating the 2.5–5 solar-mass range.
status_search_result: The existence and structure of the lower black-hole mass gap (roughly 2–5 solar masses) remains an active and unresolved question. Recent gravitational-wave detections such as GW190425 and GW230529, together with electromagnetic discoveries of mass-gap candidates in wide binaries (e.g., the 2024 Nature Astronomy report), have produced objects with masses inside the putative gap, shifting debate toward whether the gap is real but partially filled or absent altogether. As of 2025–2026, the literature still treats the question as open.

context_brief: Flow-level control for measure differential equations
original_question: For measure differential equations on a manifold, where the non-variational setting uses probability vector fields that have only an abelian monoid structure rather than a Lie algebra structure, can one develop a mathematically useful control theory at the level of the induced flows instead of at the level of solutions, by leveraging geometric control techniques?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\mathcal{P}(M)$ denote the space of Borel probability measures on $M$. A probability vector field (PVF) on $M$ is a Borel map $V:\mathcal{P}(M)\to \mathcal{P}(TM)$ such that for every $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(M)$ the pushforward of $V(\mu)$ by the canonical projection $\pi:TM\to M$ equals $\mu$. A measure differential equation (MDE) driven by a PVF $V$ is the evolution problem of finding a continuous curve $t\mapsto \mu_t\in\mathcal{P}(M)$ satisfying, in the sense of distributions,
$$\partial_t \mu_t + \mathrm{div}_x\!\big(\,\textstyle\int_{T_x M} v\, dV(\mu_t)(x,v)\,\big) = 0,$$
or more generally the generalized notion of solution in which $\mu_t$ is obtained as a limit of Euler-type discrete schemes built from $V$. Under composition of the associated time-$t$ flows on $\mathcal{P}(M)$, the family of PVFs carries only the algebraic structure of an abelian monoid (with composition of induced flows as the operation), and does not in general carry a Lie algebra structure analogous to the one available for smooth vector fields on $M$.

A controlled MDE is the data of a family $\{V_u\}_{u\in U}$ of PVFs parameterized by a control set $U$, together with admissible controls $u:[0,T]\to U$, generating flows $\Phi_t^{u(\cdot)}:\mathcal{P}(M)\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ on the space of measures.

Problem. Develop a mathematically substantive control theory for such controlled MDEs at the level of the induced flows $\Phi_t^{u(\cdot)}$ on $\mathcal{P}(M)$ (rather than at the level of individual solution curves), using geometric control techniques. Specifically:

(a) Define suitable notions of accessibility, controllability, and reachable sets for the semigroup of flows generated by a family of PVFs, in a setting where only an abelian monoid (and not a Lie algebra) structure is available.

(b) Establish analogues of the Chow–Rashevskii / orbit theorems and Krener-type accessibility results characterizing the reachable set $\mathcal{R}_T(\mu_0)=\{\Phi_T^{u(\cdot)}\mu_0 : u(\cdot)\text{ admissible}\}$ in terms of intrinsic geometric invariants of the family $\{V_u\}_{u\in U}$.

(c) Identify sufficient conditions on the family $\{V_u\}$ under which the flow-level control system is (approximately) controllable on $\mathcal{P}(M)$, and exhibit nontrivial examples in which these conditions can be verified.

The question is posed as a research direction and no general controllability/accessibility results in this setting were located.

context_brief: Kantorovich formulation and parsimonious optimal control
original_question: In the Kantorovich formulation of multi-agent control, where solutions are represented as measures on the space of continuous curves and related to the classical Lagrangian and Eulerian formulations, how can one characterize sparse or parsimonious controls and derive necessary and sufficient optimality conditions within that framework?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-agent control system formulated in three equivalent ways:

1. (Lagrangian) A population of agents is described by trajectories $t\mapsto x_i(t)\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $i=1,\dots,N$, satisfying $\dot x_i(t)=v_F(t,x_i(t),\mu^N_t)+u_i(t)$, where $\mu^N_t=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i(t)}$, $v_F:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is a given interaction field, and $u_i\in L^2([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$ are controls.

2. (Eulerian) The mean-field limit is described by a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ together with a Borel velocity field $w:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ that decomposes as $w(t,x)=v_F(t,x,\mu_t)+u(t,x)$, satisfying the continuity equation $\partial_t\mu_t+\mathrm{div}(w\,\mu_t)=0$ in the sense of distributions, with prescribed initial datum $\mu_0$.

3. (Kantorovich) Solutions are represented as probability measures $\eta\in\mathcal{P}(\Gamma)$ on the space $\Gamma=C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$ of continuous curves, concentrated on absolutely continuous curves $\gamma$ that satisfy $\dot\gamma(t)=v_F(t,\gamma(t),(e_t)_\#\eta)+u_\eta(t,\gamma)$ for $\eta$-a.e. $\gamma$, where $e_t:\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is the evaluation map $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(t)$, and $u_\eta$ is a control law that may depend on the curve.

Given a cost functional of the form
$$\mathcal{J}(\eta,u_\eta)=\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Gamma L(t,\gamma(t),(e_t)_\#\eta,u_\eta(t,\gamma))\,d\eta(\gamma)\,dt + \int_\Gamma\Psi(\gamma)\,d\eta(\gamma),$$
together with a sparsity-promoting term (for instance an $L^1$-type penalization of the control in a suitable sense), address the following:

(a) Provide a precise notion of "sparse" or "parsimonious" control within the Kantorovich formulation, namely a notion that captures the idea that only a small (in measure) portion of the population is actively controlled at any given time, and that is consistent under the equivalences with the Lagrangian and Eulerian formulations.

(b) Derive necessary optimality conditions (in the form of a Pontryagin-type maximum principle on $\mathcal{P}(\Gamma)$) for minimizers of $\mathcal{J}$ in the Kantorovich formulation, including the case with sparsity-promoting penalizations.

(c) Identify sufficient conditions (such as convexity/semiconcavity hypotheses on $L$, $\Psi$, and $v_F$) under which the necessary conditions in (b) are also sufficient for optimality.

Related work establishes equivalence and Γ-convergence among Lagrangian, Eulerian and Kantorovich formulations, and separately treats sparse controls in the Lagrangian/Eulerian mean-field setting, but a combined treatment in the Kantorovich framework appears not to be available, so the problem is regarded as open.

context_brief: Characterization problem for congruence lattices of patch lattices
original_question: Let D be a finite distributive lattice that is the glued sum D^h u B2 of a finite distributive lattice D^h with B2, and let L be a patch lattice, meaning a rectangular lattice whose corners are dual atoms; equivalently, patch lattices are exactly those rectangular lattices L for which Con L is a glued sum of a finite distributive lattice Con^h L with B2. Which properties of the finite distributive lattice Con^h L characterize exactly when D is the congruence lattice of a patch lattice L?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions:

- A finite lattice L is called rectangular if it is planar, semimodular, and has exactly two doubly irreducible elements on its boundary, called its left corner and right corner; these corners are complementary elements. A rectangular lattice L is a patch lattice if its left and right corners are both dual atoms of L (i.e., are covered by the top element 1_L).

- For lattices, the glued sum A ⊔ B of two bounded lattices A and B is the lattice obtained by identifying the top element of A with the bottom element of B. Let B_2 denote the four-element Boolean lattice.

- The congruence lattice Con L of a finite lattice L is a finite distributive lattice. It is known that a rectangular lattice L is a patch lattice if and only if Con L can be written as a glued sum Con L = Con^h L ⊔ B_2 for some finite distributive lattice Con^h L (intuitively, Con^h L is Con L with its "hat" B_2 removed).

Problem: Determine necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed purely in terms of intrinsic properties of a finite distributive lattice D^h, for the finite distributive lattice D = D^h ⊔ B_2 to be isomorphic to Con L for some patch lattice L. Equivalently, characterize the class of finite distributive lattices that arise as Con^h L when L ranges over all patch lattices.
status_search_result: The Patch Problem is posed as an open characterization problem in Grätzer's work on congruences of finite lattices. Searches turned up Grätzer's monograph "The Congruences of a Finite Lattice: A Proof-by-Picture Approach" (latest edition 2023) and related notes, but no published solution characterizing congruence lattices of patch lattices in terms of Con^h L. Status is consistent with the problem remaining open.

original_question: In the same fixed-budget best arm identification setting, does there exist an algorithm, other than uniform sampling itself, that performs uniformly no worse than uniform sampling for every bandit instance mu in S? The comparison is the asymptotic fixed-budget error exponent discussed in the paper, namely whether the algorithm can achieve a lower or equal value of lim sup_{n->infinity} n / log(1/p_{mu,n}) than the uniform-sampling benchmark for every instance.
self_contained_problem:
Let S be a class of multi-armed bandit instances with K≥2 arms, where each instance μ=(μ_1,…,μ_K)∈S specifies the reward distribution of every arm and has a unique best arm a*(μ)=argmax_i μ_i. In the fixed-budget best-arm identification setting, an algorithm interacts with an instance μ for n rounds: at each round t=1,…,n it selects an arm A_t (possibly depending on past observations and internal randomness), observes a reward drawn from the corresponding distribution, and after round n outputs a guess â_n of the best arm. Let p_{μ,n} := P_μ(â_n ≠ a*(μ)) denote the probability of misidentification. Define the asymptotic error exponent of an algorithm on instance μ as

   E(μ) := limsup_{n→∞}  n / log(1/p_{μ,n}).

A smaller value of E(μ) corresponds to faster (better) asymptotic decay of the error probability. The "uniform sampling" algorithm draws each arm equally often (in round-robin or i.i.d. uniform fashion) and outputs the empirical best arm at time n; let E^{unif}(μ) be its error exponent on μ.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm π, different from uniform sampling, such that

   E^π(μ) ≤ E^{unif}(μ)   for every instance μ ∈ S,

i.e., an algorithm that performs uniformly no worse than the uniform-sampling benchmark on every bandit instance in the class S?
status_search_result: Subsequent work has addressed the problem in restricted settings. Degenne (COLT 2023, "On the existence of a complexity in fixed budget bandit identification") shows that for several classes (including two-armed Bernoulli bandits / A/B testing) no adaptive algorithm can strictly outperform uniform sampling on all instances, and more generally that any putative instance-uniform complexity must be attained by a static (non-adaptive) procedure. The strict version (no algorithm strictly beats uniform on every instance) is thus resolved negatively in some structured settings, but the general question of whether some non-uniform algorithm attains error exponent ≤ uniform on every instance of a general class S remains open in full generality.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: Let CTCS(n) be the continuous-time critical beta-splitting random tree on n leaves, obtained by recursively splitting a clade of m leaves into subclades of sizes i and m-i with probabilities proportional to 1/(i(m-i)), and let D_n^(1) and D_n^(2) be the time-heights of two leaves whose positions in the interval/cycle representation are r_n apart. If log r_n / log n -> alpha in [0,1], prove that the correlation coefficient rho(n,r_n) between these two leaf heights converges to 1-alpha.
self_contained_problem:
Define the continuous-time critical beta-splitting random tree on $n$ leaves, denoted $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$, as follows. Starting from a single clade containing all $n$ leaves, each clade of size $m\ge 2$ persists for an exponential holding time of rate $h_{m-1} = \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/j$, after which it splits into two subclades of sizes $i$ and $m-i$ ($1\le i\le m-1$) with probability
\[
q(m,i) \;=\; \frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{i(m-i)}\cdot\frac{m}{2}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{1\le i\le m-1\}\cdot\tfrac{1}{?}\,,
\]
i.e. proportional to $1/(i(m-i))$ (with the appropriate symmetric normalization so that probabilities sum to one); subclades evolve independently in the same manner, and clades of size $1$ are leaves and do not split further. The time-height of a leaf is the sum of the holding times of the clades containing it (equivalently, the time at which that leaf is created).

Use the natural ``interval'' (or cyclic) representation in which the $n$ leaves are placed in a fixed linear order $1,2,\dots,n$ induced by the recursive splitting. For $1\le r\le n-1$, let $D_n^{(1)}$ and $D_n^{(2)}$ denote the time-heights of two leaves whose positions in this order are at distance $r_n$ apart, and let
\[
\rho(n,r_n) \;=\; \mathrm{Corr}\bigl(D_n^{(1)},\,D_n^{(2)}\bigr).
\]

Prove that whenever $r_n$ is a sequence of integers with $1\le r_n\le n-1$ and
\[
\frac{\log r_n}{\log n} \longrightarrow \alpha \in [0,1] \qquad (n\to\infty),
\]
one has
\[
\rho(n,r_n)\;\longrightarrow\;1-\alpha.
\]
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an explicit open problem in the overview paper on the critical beta-splitting random tree and subsequent works (Aldous–Pittel on heights, Aldous–Janson on Mellin analysis, and a contraction-based approach) treat related limit theorems for single-leaf heights but do not appear to resolve this two-leaf correlation conjecture. No published proof of the limit $\rho(n,r_n)\to 1-\alpha$ was located.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: Let D*_n be the maximum leaf height of CTCS(n), the continuous-time critical beta-splitting tree on n leaves. Prove that D*_n / log n converges in probability to a constant c, and determine that constant.
self_contained_problem:
Define the continuous-time critical beta-splitting tree CTCS(n) on n leaves as follows. For each integer m ≥ 2, let q(n,i) := (n/i(n-i)) / H_{n-1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ n-1, where H_{n-1} = sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 1/j; this is a probability distribution on {1,...,n-1} (it is symmetric: q(n,i)=q(n,n-i)). Starting with a single block of size n, recursively split each block of size m ≥ 2 into two blocks of sizes (i, m-i) with probability q(m,i), independently across blocks. Assign to each block of size m an independent exponential holding time with rate 1/(m-1) (equivalently, the time between successive splits at a node corresponding to a block of size m is Exponential(1/(m-1))); blocks of size 1 (leaves) do not split. This yields a continuous-time rooted binary tree with n leaves, where the height of a leaf is the total elapsed time from the root to that leaf.

Let D*_n denote the maximum leaf height of CTCS(n), i.e. the height of the deepest leaf.

Prove that there exists a constant c ∈ (0, ∞) such that
   D*_n / log n  →  c   in probability  as  n → ∞,
and identify the value of c.
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. The companion paper on heights establishes only tail bounds showing P(D*_n ≥ (2+ε) log n) ≤ n^(-ρε) for some ρ > 0, and explicitly states convergence of D*_n/log n to a constant as a conjecture. Subsequent works (including the 2024 contraction paper and the 2025 CLT paper) address the height of a uniformly random leaf D_n (proving D_n/log n → 1/ζ(2) = 6/π^2 in probability with a CLT), but do not resolve the maximum leaf height question.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
context_brief: Variance and CLT for fringe-clade counts
original_question: Fix a finite clade shape χ in DTCS(n), and let N_n(χ) be the number of copies of χ appearing as fringe clades in the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree. Prove that n^{-1} Var(N_n(χ)) converges to a finite limit σ^2(χ), and prove the corresponding central limit theorem for N_n(χ).
self_contained_problem:
Consider the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n) on $n\ge 2$ leaves, defined recursively as follows: starting from the root clade of size $n$, a clade of size $m\ge 2$ is split into two child clades of sizes $i$ and $m-i$ (with $1\le i\le m-1$) with probability
$$q(m,i)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{i}\cdot\frac{m-i+i}{?}\quad\text{i.e.}\quad q(m,i)=\frac{m}{2h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{i(m-i)},$$
where $h_{m-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}1/j$, and the split is performed independently across clades until every clade has size 1 (a leaf). The resulting object is a rooted binary tree with $n$ labelled (or unlabelled) leaves.

A finite clade shape $\chi$ of size $i$ is an isomorphism class of such a tree on $i$ leaves. For each internal node $v$ of DTCS(n), the subtree rooted at $v$ (a "fringe clade") has some shape; let $N_n(\chi)$ denote the number of internal nodes of DTCS(n) whose fringe clade has shape $\chi$. It is known that there exists a constant $p(\chi)>0$ such that
$$n^{-1}\mathbb{E}[N_n(\chi)]\to p(\chi)/i\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.$$

Prove the following two assertions:
(a) The limit $\sigma^2(\chi):=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\mathrm{Var}(N_n(\chi))$ exists and is finite.
(b) The central limit theorem holds: as $n\to\infty$,
$$\frac{N_n(\chi)-\mathbb{E}[N_n(\chi)]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(N_n(\chi))}}\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\mathcal{N}(0,1).$$
category_tag: Random trees and central limit theorems
status_search_result: A 2025 preprint on the harmonic descent chain and applications to critical beta-splitting trees explicitly states that it answers Open Problems 5 and 6, establishing a CLT for the fringe-clade counts $N_n(\chi)$ (with appropriate centering and variance scaling) for every finite clade shape $\chi$. Thus the problem appears solved.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: For DTCS(n), the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree, study the combinatorics of fringe clades by determining the distribution of the number K_n of distinct clade shapes that appear at least once, the size of the largest clade shape that appears more than once, and the size of the smallest clade shape that does not appear at all.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the discrete-time critical beta-splitting random tree DTCS(n) on n ≥ 2 leaves, defined recursively as follows. Start with a root clade of size n. A clade of size m ≥ 2 is split into two child clades of sizes i and m − i (1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1) with probability
  q(m, i) = (1 / h_{m−1}) · 1/(i (m − i)),
where h_{m−1} = Σ_{j=1}^{m−1} 1/(j(m−j)) is the normalizing constant. Each child clade is recursively split by the same rule, and clades of size 1 are leaves. The resulting rooted binary tree has n leaves.

A "clade shape" χ is the unlabeled rooted binary tree shape of a subtree rooted at some internal node (a fringe subtree). For a realization of DTCS(n) and a clade shape χ, let N_n(χ) denote the number of internal nodes of DTCS(n) whose fringe subtree has shape χ. Define:

(a) K_n = Σ_χ 1{N_n(χ) ≥ 1}, the number of distinct clade shapes that appear at least once in DTCS(n).

(b) L_n = max{|χ| : N_n(χ) ≥ 2}, the size (number of leaves) of the largest clade shape that appears more than once in DTCS(n).

(c) S_n = min{|χ| : N_n(χ) = 0}, the size of the smallest clade shape that does not appear at all in DTCS(n).

Determine the distributions (and/or asymptotic behavior as n → ∞) of the random variables K_n, L_n, and S_n.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem about the combinatorics of fringe clades in the critical beta-splitting model. Subsequent work on this model (e.g., a third installment on the exchangeable partition representation and the fringe tree, and a contraction-based approach to critical beta-splitting) develops fringe-tree limit theory but does not appear to resolve the specific distributional questions about K_n (number of distinct clade shapes), the largest repeated clade shape, or the smallest missing clade shape. No published resolution was found.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
context_brief: Joint law of size-m clade counts
original_question: For each m, let N_m^(n) be the number of clades of size m in DTCS(n). Determine the joint distribution of the family (N_m^(n), 2 ≤ m ≤ n) well enough to compute covariances among clade counts and to derive central limit theorems for statistics built from these counts.
self_contained_problem:
Define the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n) as the random rooted binary tree obtained by the following recursive construction. Start with the root labelled by the integer n. Whenever a node is labelled by an integer m ≥ 2, split it into two children labelled L and m − L, where L is an independent random variable on {1, 2, …, m − 1} with distribution

  P(L = i) = (1 / a(m)) · 1/(i (m − i)),  for i = 1, …, m − 1,

where a(m) = ∑_{i=1}^{m−1} 1/(i(m − i)) is the normalizing constant. Nodes labelled 1 are leaves. A clade of the tree is the set of leaves descended from any internal node, and the size of a clade is the integer label of that node. For each integer m with 2 ≤ m ≤ n, let N_m^{(n)} denote the number of clades of size m in DTCS(n).

It is known that E[N_m^{(n)}] = (n/m) · a(n, m) for an explicit kernel a(n, m). The problem is to determine the joint distribution of the random vector

  (N_m^{(n)} : 2 ≤ m ≤ n)

in sufficient detail to (i) compute the asymptotic covariances Cov(N_{m_1}^{(n)}, N_{m_2}^{(n)}) as n → ∞ for fixed or scaling indices m_1, m_2, and (ii) derive central limit theorems for linear (and more general) statistics built from the clade counts (N_m^{(n)}).
status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) on the critical beta-splitting tree has established CLTs for heights of uniformly chosen leaves and joint convergence for height-related statistics, but the specific problem of determining the joint distribution of clade counts (N_m^{(n)}) with asymptotic covariances and CLTs for linear statistics does not appear to have been resolved in the available literature.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
context_brief: Larger empirical tests of the model
original_question: Repeat, on a much larger empirical scale and for additional balance or fringe-related indices, the paper's data comparisons between the critical beta-splitting model and real phylogenetic trees, including the empirical studies of splitting behavior and fringe distributions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the critical beta-splitting random tree model on n leaves, defined as follows. Starting from a root clade of size n, recursively split each clade of size m ≥ 2 into two sub-clades of sizes i and m − i (1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1) with probability

  q(m, i) = (1/Z_m) · 1/(i(m − i)),     Z_m = sum_{j=1}^{m-1} 1/(j(m − j)),

independently of all other splits, continuing until every clade has size 1. The resulting random binary rooted tree T_n has n leaves. From this model one can derive, as n → ∞, a limiting "fringe distribution" describing the law of the subtree rooted at the parent of a uniformly chosen leaf (and its iterates), as well as distributions of standard tree shape statistics (balance/imbalance indices such as Colless, Sackin, cherry counts, and other fringe-based or split-size functionals).

Carry out a large-scale empirical comparison between the critical beta-splitting model and large databases of real phylogenetic trees, addressing the following:

1. For a substantial corpus of empirical phylogenies (across many taxa and tree sizes), compute the empirical distribution of split sizes (the size of the smaller daughter clade as a function of parent clade size m) and compare with the law q(m, ·) of the critical beta-splitting model.

2. Compute empirical fringe-subtree frequencies (frequencies of small subtree shapes near random leaves) for these phylogenies and compare with the limiting fringe distribution of the critical beta-splitting model.

3. Extend the comparison to additional balance / shape / fringe-related indices beyond those already studied (e.g., Colless, Sackin, total cophenetic, cherry counts, generalized fringe statistics), and quantify the goodness-of-fit of the critical beta-splitting model relative to alternatives (such as the Yule–Harding model and the broader beta-splitting family with parameter β).

Provide statistically meaningful conclusions about for which indices, and on which scales of tree size, the critical beta-splitting model fits real phylogenetic data, and where systematic deviations occur.
status_search_result: The problem is an empirical/data-analysis open problem posed alongside the critical beta-splitting random tree program. Subsequent theoretical work on the model (e.g., the exchangeable partition representation and fringe-tree paper from 2024, and the heights paper) develops the limiting fringe distribution and related theory, but no published large-scale empirical re-examination across many balance/fringe indices comparing the critical beta-splitting model with real phylogenetic databases appears to have been carried out. Status appears still open.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: For the explicit inductive growth algorithm of CTCS(n), in which one picks a uniform random bud, moves upward toward it, and either inserts a side-bud or extends the target bud into a new Exponential(1)-length branch, determine whether there exists a useful martingale that can be exploited to analyze the model.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following family of random rooted binary trees with edge lengths, denoted CTCS(n) for integers n ≥ 1. The model is determined by the following discrete recursive splitting rule together with continuous-time edge lengths: for m ≥ 2, a clade of m leaves is split into two sub-clades of sizes i and m−i (with 1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability proportional to 1/(i(m−i)); each clade of m leaves is held for an Exponential(1/(m−1)) time before splitting (for m = 1 the leaf is held forever). The resulting random tree on n leaves with real edge lengths is CTCS(n).

The family (CTCS(n), n ≥ 1) admits an explicit inductive growth algorithm that constructs CTCS(n+1) from CTCS(n) as follows. Call each leaf of the current tree a "bud." Given CTCS(n):
 1. Pick a uniformly random bud and consider the path from the root to that bud.
 2. Move upward along this path; at each internal edge, with appropriate probability either:
    (a) insert a new side-bud (a new branch carrying a new leaf, attached at an interior point of the path with an Exponential(1)-length pendant edge), or
    (b) continue moving up; if the chosen bud is reached without insertion, extend the target bud by appending a new Exponential(1)-length branch terminating at a new leaf.
This procedure produces a sample of CTCS(n+1) and is consistent with the delete-a-random-leaf-and-prune dynamics on the family.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: For the standard cladogram drawing of DTCS(n), study the drawn width profile W(h), where W(h) counts the number of vertical lines crossing the strip (h,h+1), equivalently the number of clades whose draw-height is at most h and that arise from a split of a clade whose draw-height is at least h+1.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the discrete-time critical beta-splitting random tree on $n$ leaves, denoted $\mathrm{DTCS}(n)$, defined recursively as follows. Start with the set $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ at the root. At each internal node labelled by a set $S$ with $|S|=m\ge 2$, choose a split size $i\in\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}$ with probability
$$q(m,i)=\frac{1}{Z_m}\cdot\frac{1}{i(m-i)},\qquad Z_m=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{j(m-j)},$$
partition $S$ uniformly at random into a subset of size $i$ (the "left child clade") and a subset of size $m-i$ (the "right child clade"), and recurse independently on each child. The recursion terminates at singletons (leaves).

A "clade" is the leaf-set associated with any node of the tree. Draw $\mathrm{DTCS}(n)$ as a standard cladogram in the plane as follows. Each clade $C$ is drawn as a horizontal line segment at integer height equal to its draw-height, defined recursively by: a singleton clade has draw-height $0$, and a clade arising as the parent of two child clades has draw-height $1+\max(h_L,h_R)$, where $h_L,h_R$ are the draw-heights of its two children. Each internal node (split) is drawn so that the parent clade's horizontal segment connects to its two children's segments by vertical line segments running between the parent's height and each child's height.

For an integer $h\ge 0$, define the drawn width profile
$$W(h)=\#\{\text{vertical line segments of the cladogram that cross the horizontal strip } \mathbb{R}\times(h,h+1)\},$$
equivalently the number of clades $C$ of $\mathrm{DTCS}(n)$ such that the draw-height of $C$ is at most $h$ while the draw-height of the parent clade of $C$ is at least $h+1$.

Study the process $(W(h):h\ge 0)$. In particular, determine its asymptotic distributional behavior as $n\to\infty$ (after any necessary rescaling of $h$ and of $W$), describe its mean, fluctuations, and any scaling limit as a stochastic process in $h$.
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an open problem in the 2023 survey on the critical beta-splitting random tree, and subsequent works (e.g., the 2024 paper on the exchangeable partition representation and fringe tree, and the 2024 contraction-method paper) develop related aspects but do not address the drawn width profile process W(h). No published resolution was located.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: Consider the fringe process given by the local weak limit of DTCS(n) from a random leaf. Study the scaling limit of its branchpoints after rescaling, in the point-process sense suggested by the paper.
self_contained_problem:
Let DTCS(n) denote the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree on n leaves, defined recursively as follows. Start with a single clade of n leaves. A clade containing m ≥ 2 leaves is split into two sub-clades of sizes i and m−i (1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability

  q(m,i) = (1/Z_m) · 1/(i(m−i)),  where Z_m = sum_{j=1}^{m−1} 1/(j(m−j)),

and splitting continues independently within each resulting sub-clade until every clade is a single leaf. The resulting rooted binary tree carries an integer "height" on each internal node equal to the number of ancestral splits separating the node from the root.

Pick a leaf v uniformly at random from DTCS(n) and consider the rooted, marked subtree visible from v along its ancestral spine: as n → ∞, the joint law of the spine of v together with the sequence of subtrees branching off the spine has a local weak limit, the fringe process. In this fringe process the ancestors of v form an infinite path on which "branchpoints" occur at certain integer heights, and at each branchpoint a sibling subtree is attached.

Represent the fringe process as a point process on ℝ_{≥0} (or on a suitable mark space) whose points are the heights of the branchpoints (decorated by the corresponding sibling subtree). Identify the appropriate rescaling of the height coordinate (and of the attached subtrees) under which this point process of branchpoint positions converges in distribution, and describe the resulting limit point process explicitly.
status_search_result: A subsequent work (arXiv:2412.09655) gives an explicit description of the limit fringe distribution of the critical beta-splitting tree relative to a random leaf, but it is not clear from public sources whether the rescaled point process of branchpoint positions in the fringe process has been fully analyzed and its scaling limit identified. No published resolution of this specific scaling-limit problem was found.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
original_question: Clarify the exact mathematical relationship between CTCS(∞), the exchangeable-partition limit of the critical beta-splitting model, and the beta(2,1) coalescent, beyond the paper's observed coincidences involving the same subordinator and parallel asymptotics for collision or hop-count statistics.
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup.

(a) Critical beta-splitting and CTCS(∞). For each integer n ≥ 2, define a random binary tree on n labeled leaves by the following recursive splitting rule: a clade containing m ≥ 2 leaves is partitioned into two sub-clades of sizes i and m − i with probability
  q(m, i) = (1/Z_m) · 1/(i(m − i)),  1 ≤ i ≤ m − 1,
where Z_m = ∑_{i=1}^{m−1} 1/(i(m − i)). Iterating until all clades are singletons yields the discrete critical beta-splitting tree. Endow each internal node v that splits a clade of size m with a real-valued "time" coordinate such that times along any root-to-leaf path are decreasing, with edge lengths chosen according to the natural continuous-time embedding (the clade of size m holds for an independent waiting time before splitting). Call the resulting random metric tree on n leaves CTCS(n). The family (CTCS(n))_{n≥2} is consistent under the operation "delete a uniformly chosen leaf and contract the resulting degree-2 vertex," and admits a projective limit CTCS(∞), an exchangeable random structure encoding the partitions of N obtained by removing all edges at times above a given threshold.

(b) The beta(2, 1) coalescent. Let Λ be the probability measure on [0, 1] with density f(x) = 2(1 − x) (the Beta(1, 2) density). The Λ-coalescent associated to Λ, in the case Λ = Beta(2, 1) (i.e. f(x) = 2(1 − x)), is the exchangeable coalescent process Π(t) on partitions of N whose rate of merging any specified k of the b current blocks into one is
  λ_{b,k} = ∫_0^1 x^{k−2}(1 − x)^{b−k} Λ(dx),  2 ≤ k ≤ b.
This coalescent comes-down-from-infinity and is associated with a stable-type subordinator.

Both CTCS(∞) and the beta(2, 1) coalescent are known to share the same underlying subordinator and to produce matching asymptotics for several functionals (e.g. collision counts and hop counts).

Problem. Determine the precise mathematical relationship between CTCS(∞) and the beta(2, 1) coalescent. Specifically, exhibit an explicit coupling, time-change, or functional transformation that maps one exchangeable structure to the other (or prove that no such coupling exists), and identify which joint distributional features of the two processes coincide and which differ.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in the literature on the critical beta-splitting random tree. Subsequent work on the critical beta-splitting model (e.g., the 2024 "Critical beta-splitting, via contraction" paper) does not announce an elucidation of the precise CTCS(∞)–beta(2,1)-coalescent connection, so the problem appears to remain open as of 2026.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
context_brief: Dowker complexes and ε-nets on metric graphs
original_question: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted simple graph, let d_G be the geodesic distance on V induced by G, and let ε>0. A subset L⊂V is an ε-net if (i) every vertex v∈V lies within distance ε of some landmark u∈L and (ii) every two distinct landmarks u_i,u_j∈L satisfy d_G(u_i,u_j)>ε. Determine optimal upper and lower bounds for the number of elements of an ε-net for G.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G = (V, E, \omega)$ be a finite weighted simple graph, where $\omega : E \to (0, \infty)$ assigns a positive weight to each edge. For $u, v \in V$, let $d_G(u, v)$ denote the geodesic distance, i.e., the minimum over all paths from $u$ to $v$ of the sum of the weights of the edges in the path (with $d_G(v, v) = 0$). Fix $\varepsilon > 0$. A subset $L \subseteq V$ is called an $\varepsilon$-net of $G$ if:
(i) ($\varepsilon$-sample) for every $v \in V$, there exists $u \in L$ with $d_G(v, u) \le \varepsilon$;
(ii) ($\varepsilon$-sparse) for every pair of distinct $u_i, u_j \in L$, $d_G(u_i, u_j) > \varepsilon$.

Determine optimal upper and lower bounds, in terms of $G$ and $\varepsilon$, for the cardinality $|L|$ of an $\varepsilon$-net of $G$. That is, find the tight worst-case maximum and minimum possible sizes of an $\varepsilon$-net for a weighted simple graph with given combinatorial/metric parameters.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in a 2023 compilation of open problems in applied combinatorics. A web search did not surface any subsequent work providing optimal upper and lower bounds for the cardinality of an ε-net on a weighted simple graph, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
original_question: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted simple graph, let W=V be the witness set, and let L⊂V be an ε-net. The Dowker complex Dow_α(W,L) is the simplicial complex on the landmark set L whose simplices are the subsets σ⊂L for which there exists a witness w∈W satisfying d_G(w,l)≤α for every l∈σ. Determine how to choose ε and how to select the ε-net L so that, for sufficiently large α, the one-dimensional persistence diagram PD_1(Dow_α(W,L)) has cardinality equal to the genus of G. Assuming such an ε-net is given, find a bound for the bottleneck distance d_B(PD_1(VR_α(G)), PD_1(Dow_α(W,L))) in terms of the cycle lengths of G and ε.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G = (V, E, \omega)$ be a weighted simple graph with positive edge weights $\omega: E \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, and let $d_G : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ denote the induced shortest-path (geodesic) distance on $V$. For $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-net is a subset $L \subset V$ such that (i) for every $v \in V$ there exists $\ell \in L$ with $d_G(v,\ell) \le \varepsilon$, and (ii) $d_G(\ell, \ell') > \varepsilon$ for all distinct $\ell, \ell' \in L$.

For $\alpha \ge 0$, define the Vietoris–Rips complex $\operatorname{VR}_\alpha(G)$ as the abstract simplicial complex on vertex set $V$ whose simplices are the finite subsets $\sigma \subset V$ with $d_G(v,v') \le \alpha$ for all $v,v' \in \sigma$. Let $W = V$ (the "witness" set). Define the Dowker complex
$$\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W, L) = \{ \sigma \subset L : \exists\, w \in W \text{ with } d_G(w,\ell) \le \alpha \text{ for every } \ell \in \sigma \}.$$

As $\alpha$ varies, both $\{\operatorname{VR}_\alpha(G)\}_\alpha$ and $\{\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W,L)\}_\alpha$ form filtrations of simplicial complexes; let $\operatorname{PD}_1(\cdot)$ denote the resulting one-dimensional persistence diagram. Let $d_B$ denote the bottleneck distance between persistence diagrams, and let $g(G)$ denote the (orientable) genus of the graph $G$.

(i) Determine a rule prescribing a value $\varepsilon > 0$ and a procedure for selecting an $\varepsilon$-net $L \subset V$ such that, for all sufficiently large $\alpha$,
$$\#\,\operatorname{PD}_1(\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W, L)) \;=\; g(G).$$

(ii) Under the assumption that $L$ is an $\varepsilon$-net satisfying (i), establish an explicit upper bound for
$$d_B\bigl(\operatorname{PD}_1(\operatorname{VR}_\alpha(G)),\, \operatorname{PD}_1(\operatorname{Dow}_\alpha(W, L))\bigr)$$
expressed in terms of $\varepsilon$ and the lengths of cycles of $G$.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in a 2023 survey on open problems in applied combinatorics. Web searches reveal related stability results for Dowker and Vietoris–Rips persistence diagrams and applications of Dowker complexes, but no source addresses this specific question of choosing an ε-net so that the cardinality of PD_1 of the Dowker complex equals the genus of the graph, nor a bottleneck-distance bound in terms of cycle lengths and ε. No subsequent work resolving the problem was located.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
original_question: Fix positive integers n and t, an integer m with 1≤m≤2^n−1, and an n×m binary matrix A whose columns a_1,…,a_m are distinct nonzero vectors in {0,1}^n. For an n×t binary matrix x=(x_1^T,…,x_t^T), define the i-th expressiveness indicator by m_i^A(x)=Σ_{j=1}^t <a_i,x_j>_2, where the inner product is taken in GF(2) and the outer sum is taken over the integers. If x and y are sampled uniformly at random, the computational problem asks for P((m_i(x)=m_i(y)) for all i). For fixed m and k≤m, determine this probability when A consists of all binary vectors of weight at most k.
self_contained_problem:
Fix positive integers $n$ and $t$, and an integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le n$. Let $A$ be the $n \times m$ binary matrix whose columns are exactly all distinct nonzero vectors of $\{0,1\}^n$ having Hamming weight at most $k$; here $m = \sum_{j=1}^{k}\binom{n}{j}$. Denote the columns of $A$ by $a_1,\dots,a_m \in \{0,1\}^n$.

For an $n \times t$ binary matrix $x$ with columns $x_1,\dots,x_t \in \{0,1\}^n$, define the $i$-th expressiveness indicator by
$$m_i^A(x) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{t} \langle a_i, x_j\rangle_{2},$$
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ denotes the inner product in $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ (so each summand lies in $\{0,1\}$) and the outer sum is taken in $\mathbb{Z}$ (so $m_i^A(x) \in \{0,1,\dots,t\}$).

Let $x$ and $y$ be independent $n \times t$ binary matrices, each chosen uniformly at random from $\{0,1\}^{n\times t}$. Determine, as an explicit function of $n$, $t$, and $k$, the collision probability
$$P\!\left(\,m_i^A(x) = m_i^A(y)\ \text{for all } 1\le i\le m\,\right).$$
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in a 2023 survey on open problems in applied combinatorics. A web search did not turn up a published resolution; related work on commutative quantum-circuit expressiveness (e.g., arXiv:2404.19727, arXiv:2410.19173) studies the general framework but does not address the weight-at-most-$k$ case explicitly. The status appears to remain open.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
original_question: In the same computational problem where A is an n×m binary matrix with distinct nonzero columns and one must compute P((m_i(x)=m_i(y)) for all i) for uniformly random n×t binary matrices x and y, determine whether this computational problem is NP-complete when A is arbitrary.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \{0,1\}^{n \times m}$ be a binary matrix whose $m$ columns $a_1,\dots,a_m \in \{0,1\}^n$ are pairwise distinct and all nonzero. For an integer $t \ge 1$ and a binary matrix $x \in \{0,1\}^{n \times t}$, define, for each $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, the function
$$m_i(x) := a_i^{\mathsf T} x \pmod 2 \in \{0,1\}^{t},$$
i.e.\ the $t$-bit vector obtained by taking the inner product (modulo $2$) of column $a_i$ with each of the $t$ columns of $x$.

Consider the following computational problem. 

\textbf{Input:} A binary matrix $A \in \{0,1\}^{n \times m}$ with distinct nonzero columns, and a positive integer $t$ (encoded in unary, say).

\textbf{Output:} The probability
$$p(A,t) \;=\; \Pr_{x,y}\!\left[\, m_i(x) = m_i(y) \text{ for every } i \in \{1,\dots,m\} \,\right],$$
where $x$ and $y$ are sampled independently and uniformly at random from $\{0,1\}^{n \times t}$.

\textbf{Question:} Is the computation of $p(A,t)$ (or its natural decision version) NP-complete when $A$ is allowed to be arbitrary?

status_search_result: The problem is listed among seven open problems in applied combinatorics (2023). No subsequent work resolving the NP-completeness status of this expressiveness computation problem was located.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
context_brief: 4-uniform hypergraph s-t cuts with convex split penalty
original_question: Let H=(V,E) be a 4-uniform hypergraph with source node s and sink node t. For a bipartition {S,̄S} with s∈S and t∈̄S, let ∂_i(S) be the set of hyperedges having exactly i vertices on the smaller side of the cut, and assign penalty w_i≥0 to each hyperedge in ∂_i(S), with w_0=0. The cardinality-based hypergraph s-t cut problem minimizes Σ_i w_i |∂_i(S)| subject to s∈S and t∈̄S. When w_1=1, determine the computational complexity of this problem in the regime w_2>2.
self_contained_problem: Let H=(V,E) be a 4-uniform hypergraph (every hyperedge e∈E satisfies |e|=4) with two distinguished vertices s,t∈V. For a bipartition {S, V∖S} with s∈S and t∈V∖S, and for each hyperedge e∈E, define the split index of e by min{|e∩S|, |e∩(V∖S)|} ∈ {0,1,2}. For i∈{0,1,2}, let ∂_i(S) = { e∈E : min{|e∩S|, |e∩(V∖S)|} = i }. Fix nonnegative weights w_0, w_1, w_2 with w_0=0, and define the cut cost f(S) = w_0|∂_0(S)| + w_1|∂_1(S)| + w_2|∂_2(S)|. The cardinality-based 4-uniform hypergraph s-t cut problem asks to compute min{ f(S) : s∈S ⊆ V, t∉S }. Fix w_1 = 1. Determine the computational complexity of this minimization problem in the parameter regime w_2 > 2.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
original_question: Let G=(V,E) be a directed acyclic graph. In front-elimination of an edge (i,j), one removes that edge and adds edges from i to every successor of j; in back-elimination, one removes (i,j) and adds edges from every predecessor of i to j. A complete edge elimination sequence is a sequence of such eliminations that transforms G into the corresponding bipartite DAG representation of the Jacobian, and its cost is the sum of the individual elimination costs. Given G and an integer k≥0, determine whether there exists a complete edge elimination sequence whose total cost is at most k.
self_contained_problem:
Let G=(V,E) be a directed acyclic graph in which each edge (i,j)∈E carries a numerical weight (the local partial derivative of the elementary operation at vertex j with respect to its predecessor i). For an edge (i,j)∈E, define two elimination operations:

- Front-elimination of (i,j): remove the edge (i,j); then, for every successor k of j (i.e., every k with (j,k)∈E at the current moment), add an edge (i,k) whose weight is incremented by the product of the weights of (i,j) and (j,k); if (i,k) already exists its weight is updated by summing. The cost of this operation is the number of successors of j.
- Back-elimination of (i,j): remove (i,j); then, for every predecessor h of i, add an edge (h,j) whose weight is incremented by the product of the weights of (h,i) and (i,j); if (h,j) already exists its weight is updated. The cost is the number of predecessors of i.

Call a sequence of front- and back-eliminations a complete edge elimination sequence if its application transforms G into the bipartite directed acyclic graph whose only edges go directly from minimal (input) vertices to maximal (output) vertices, with edge weights equal to the entries of the Jacobian of the function represented by G. The cost of such a sequence is the sum of the costs of its individual eliminations.

Decide the following problem: given a directed acyclic graph G as above and a non-negative integer k, does there exist a complete edge elimination sequence for G whose total cost is at most k? In particular, determine the computational complexity of this decision problem.
status_search_result: The related vertex-elimination version (Optimal Jacobian Accumulation) was shown NP-complete by Naumann (2008), and a 2025 preprint extends NP-completeness to Structural Optimal Jacobian Accumulation and Minimum Edge Count under vertex elimination. The edge-elimination decision problem as stated, however, does not appear to have been resolved in the literature; it is still listed as an open problem in surveys of applied combinatorics and AD.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
context_brief: DAG reversal under memory and cost constraints
original_question: Let G be a directed acyclic graph arising from a numerical program, and suppose one wants to reverse G while using persistent memory of size at most M and computational cost at most O, where persistent memory stores values that cannot be recomputed for free and computational cost counts the work needed to recover overwritten intermediate values during reversal. Given integers M≥n and O≥0, determine whether G can be reversed within persistent memory at most M and computational cost at most O.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a directed acyclic graph with |V| = n vertices, modeling the data flow of a straight-line numerical program: each vertex represents an intermediate value, and an edge u → v indicates that the value at v depends directly on the value at u.

A "reversal" of G is a schedule that outputs the values associated with the vertices of G in reverse topological order, subject to the following rules:
- At any moment in time, a subset of vertex values is held in "persistent memory"; values not in persistent memory have been discarded and, if needed again, must be recomputed from currently stored values by following the edges of G.
- The "persistent memory" usage at any time is the number of values simultaneously stored.
- The "computational cost" of the schedule is the total number of (re)computations of vertex values performed during the reversal (each evaluation of a vertex from its predecessors counts as one unit of cost).

Given G together with two integers M ≥ n and O ≥ 0, decide whether there exists a reversal schedule of G that uses persistent memory of size at most M at all times and incurs total computational cost at most O.

Provide an algorithm (or a characterization) that decides this question, and analyze its complexity.
status_search_result: The DAG Reversal decision problem has been shown to be NP-complete (Naumann, "DAG reversal is NP-complete", J. Discrete Algorithms, 2009), so no polynomial-time decision algorithm is expected. However, the problem is still considered open in the sense of finding efficient exact algorithms, good approximation algorithms, and characterizations for structurally restricted DAGs; ongoing work focuses on special cases and heuristics for practical (e.g., automatic differentiation) instances.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
original_question: Let G=(V,E) be a graph and let k≥0. A set Z⊂V is an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set if, for every set E' of at most k edges, Z remains a zero-forcing set for the graph (V,E\E'). For sparse graphs resembling power-grid networks, determine whether one can give a structural characterization of the minimum-size (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing sets, in particular for graphs with few cycles or for sparse graphs of large diameter.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with $n=|V|$. Recall the standard zero-forcing color-change rule: starting from a set $Z\subseteq V$ of initially blue vertices (all others being white), repeatedly apply the rule that if a blue vertex has exactly one white neighbor, then that white neighbor becomes blue. The set $Z$ is a zero-forcing set for $G$ if iterating this rule eventually colors all of $V$ blue.

Fix an integer $k\ge 0$. A set $Z\subseteq V$ is called an $(n-k)$-contingent zero-forcing set for $G$ if, for every set $E'\subseteq E$ with $|E'|\le k$, the set $Z$ is still a zero-forcing set for the graph $G'=(V,E\setminus E')$. Let $Z_{n-k}(G)$ denote the minimum cardinality of such a set.

Problem: Provide a structural characterization of the minimum-size $(n-k)$-contingent zero-forcing sets for sparse graph classes. In particular:
(a) characterize these minimum sets for graphs with few cycles (e.g., trees, unicyclic graphs, and more generally graphs whose cyclomatic number is bounded);
(b) characterize these minimum sets for sparse graphs of large diameter.
status_search_result: No published structural characterization of minimum $(n-k)$-contingent zero-forcing sets for sparse graphs with few cycles or large diameter was found. Related work studies constrained / leaky / failed zero forcing variants and resilient strong structural controllability, but none provides such a characterization. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
context_brief: Typical contingent zero-forcing size in power-grid-like graphs
original_question: Let G be a graph with structural properties characteristic of power grids, and let k≥0. A set Z⊂V is an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set if it remains zero-forcing after deletion of any set of at most k edges. Determine the typical size of a minimum (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set, expressed in terms of the numbers of vertices and edges, for graphs with power-grid-like structure.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph on n = |V| vertices. The standard zero-forcing process on G with initial set Z ⊆ V proceeds as follows: each vertex of Z is colored blue, all others white; repeatedly, if a blue vertex v has exactly one white neighbor u, then u is colored blue (the "color-change rule"). The set Z is a zero-forcing set if iterating this rule eventually colors every vertex of V blue.

For an integer k ≥ 0, call Z ⊆ V an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set of G if, for every subset E₀ ⊆ E with |E₀| ≤ k, the set Z is a zero-forcing set of the edge-deleted graph G − E₀ = (V, E ∖ E₀). Let Z_{n−k}(G) denote the minimum cardinality of an (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing set of G.

Consider random or deterministic families of graphs that model the structural properties characteristic of electrical power-grid networks (e.g., sparse graphs with heavy-tailed or bounded degree distributions, planar or near-planar embeddings, and small treewidth typical of transmission networks). Determine the typical (asymptotic) value of Z_{n−k}(G) for such graphs as a function of the number of vertices n and the number of edges m = |E| (and of k).
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an open problem in a 2023 survey on applied combinatorics. Web searches return general material on N−k contingency analysis in power systems but no results that determine, asymptotically or otherwise, the typical minimum size of (n−k)-contingent zero-forcing sets in power-grid-like graphs. No published resolution was found.

original_question: For products of projective spaces (and, more generally, other interesting classes of varieties), classify special line bundles in the sense that there exists r ≥ 1 for which r generic double points fail to impose independent conditions on the line bundle.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $L$ be a line bundle on $X$. For a point $p \in X$, a "double point" at $p$ is the zero-dimensional subscheme defined by the square $\mathfrak{m}_p^2$ of the maximal ideal of $p$. Given $r \ge 1$ and generic points $p_1, \dots, p_r \in X$, let $Z_r \subset X$ be the disjoint union of the corresponding double points. One says that $r$ generic double points impose independent conditions on $L$ if the natural restriction map
$$H^0(X, L) \longrightarrow H^0(X, L \otimes \mathcal{O}_{Z_r})$$
is of maximal rank, i.e. surjective or injective (equivalently, $\dim H^0(X, L \otimes \mathcal{I}_{Z_r}) = \max\{0,\; h^0(X,L) - r(\dim X + 1)\}$). The line bundle $L$ is called special if there exists some $r \ge 1$ for which $r$ generic double points fail to impose independent conditions on $L$.

Problem: Classify all special line bundles on a product of projective spaces $\mathbb{P}^{n_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{P}^{n_k}$. More generally, give such a classification for other natural classes of smooth projective varieties.
status_search_result: The problem of classifying special line bundles (in the sense of generic double points failing to impose independent conditions, related to the classical polynomial interpolation / Alexander–Hirschowitz-type problems) is a long-standing open problem. While the Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem solves the case of $\mathbb{P}^n$ with the standard line bundles, the analogous classification for products of projective spaces and other varieties remains open in general; only partial results (e.g., for specific bidegrees on $\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1$, $\mathbb{P}^n \times \mathbb{P}^m$ in low dimensions, or specific Segre–Veronese settings) are known. Web search did not surface a complete classification.

original_question: For a homogeneous polynomial f ∈ S^dV, let X be a minimal apolar scheme for f (that is, deg(X)=cR_X(f) in the apolar setting). Must the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity satisfy reg(X) ≤ d?
self_contained_problem:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $S = \mathrm{Sym}^\bullet V$ be the symmetric algebra on $V$, identified with a polynomial ring. For a homogeneous polynomial $f \in S^d V$ of degree $d$, recall the apolarity pairing: the dual ring $T = \mathrm{Sym}^\bullet V^*$ acts on $S$ by contraction (partial differentiation), and the apolar ideal of $f$ is
$$f^\perp = \{\,\partial \in T : \partial \circ f = 0\,\} \subset T.$$
A closed subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}(V^*) = \mathrm{Proj}(T)$ is called apolar to $f$ if its homogeneous (saturated) ideal $I_X$ is contained in $f^\perp$. The cactus rank $cR(f)$ of $f$ is the minimum of $\deg(X)$ over all zero-dimensional apolar schemes $X$, and a zero-dimensional apolar scheme $X$ achieving $\deg(X) = cR(f)$ is called a minimal apolar scheme for $f$.

Let $\mathrm{reg}(X)$ denote the Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of $X$ (i.e., of its saturated homogeneous ideal, or equivalently of its structure sheaf).

Question: For every homogeneous polynomial $f \in S^d V$ and every minimal apolar scheme $X$ for $f$, does one have
$$\mathrm{reg}(X) \le d \, ?$$
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a 2023 survey on the geometry of tensors. Web searches did not turn up a published resolution (either a proof for all minimal apolar schemes or a counterexample). The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: For f ∈ S^dV, let X be the scheme associated to a generalized additive decomposition (GAD) of minimal length. Is reg(X) ≤ d? More generally, which conditions on f guarantee existence of a GAD whose associated scheme has low regularity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, and let $S^{\bullet}V = \bigoplus_{d \ge 0} S^d V$ denote the symmetric algebra on $V$, whose elements of degree $d$ are identified with degree-$d$ homogeneous polynomials (forms). For a form $f \in S^d V$, a generalized additive decomposition (GAD) of $f$ is an expression
$$ f \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ell_i^{\,d - m_i}\, g_i, $$
where $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_r \in V$ are pairwise non-proportional linear forms, $1 \le m_i \le d$, and each $g_i \in S^{m_i}V$ is a form of degree $m_i$. To such a GAD one associates a $0$-dimensional subscheme $X \subset \mathbb{P}(V^*)$, supported at the points $[\ell_i]$, whose local component at $[\ell_i]$ is the scheme defined by the apolar ideal of $g_i$ (viewed after a change of coordinates centered at $[\ell_i]$). The length of the GAD is $\mathrm{length}(X) = \sum_i \dim_K (S^{\bullet}V / \mathrm{Ann}(g_i))$, and a GAD is said to be of minimal length if no GAD of $f$ has smaller length. The Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of $X$ is denoted $\mathrm{reg}(X)$.

(a) For every $f \in S^d V$ and every $0$-dimensional scheme $X$ arising from a GAD of $f$ of minimal length, does the inequality $\mathrm{reg}(X) \le d$ hold?

(b) More generally, determine sufficient conditions on $f \in S^d V$ that guarantee the existence of a GAD of $f$ whose associated scheme $X$ has low Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity (e.g. $\mathrm{reg}(X) \le d$).
status_search_result: Subsequent work on schemes evinced by generalized additive decompositions establishes the bound reg(X) ≤ d in special cases: minimal-length tangential decompositions always evince d-regular schemes, and irredundant apolar schemes of length at most 2d+1 are d-regular. However, irredundant schemes apolar to a form need not be d-regular in general, so the question for arbitrary minimal-length GADs is not fully settled, and the general characterization in part (b) remains open.

original_question: Classify low-dimensional varieties whose second and/or third secant variety has minimal degree; more generally, for a fixed r, construct varieties X such that σ_r(X) is a hypersurface of the smallest possible degree.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Work over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For a non-degenerate irreducible projective variety X ⊂ P^N, the r-th secant variety σ_r(X) is the Zariski closure of the union of linear spans of r-tuples of points of X:
   σ_r(X) = closure of ⋃ ⟨x_1,...,x_r⟩, where x_1,...,x_r ∈ X.
When σ_r(X) is a hypersurface in P^N (i.e. has codimension one), one says it is of minimal degree if its degree attains the smallest value possible given the dimension and embedding data. (A variety Y ⊂ P^N of codimension c has minimal degree if deg(Y) = c + 1; this is the lower bound for non-degenerate varieties.)

Problem.
(a) Classify all non-degenerate irreducible projective varieties X of small dimension whose second secant variety σ_2(X) is a hypersurface of minimal degree, and analogously for the third secant variety σ_3(X).
(b) More generally, given an integer r ≥ 2, construct non-degenerate irreducible projective varieties X ⊂ P^N such that σ_r(X) is a hypersurface of the smallest possible degree.
status_search_result: A general classification of varieties whose higher secant variety is a hypersurface of minimal degree does not appear in the literature. Partial results exist: del Pezzo–Bertini classifies varieties of minimal degree; recent work (e.g. determinantal characterizations of higher secant varieties of minimal degree, and characterizations of secant varieties of Severi varieties among cubic hypersurfaces) gives structural results in special cases, but a full low-dimensional classification and a general construction for arbitrary r are not established.
