paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
original_question: How do a loosely bound eta-nucleon molecular interpretation and a compact quark-state interpretation of S11(1535) behave differently when additional baryons are present, and can a systematic theoretical approach be developed for eta-deuteron and eta-helium-3 systems that uses those differences to test the nature of S11(1535)?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the nucleon resonance S11(1535), a spin-1/2, isospin-1/2, negative-parity baryon resonance lying close to and strongly coupled to the eta-nucleon (ηN) channel. Two competing pictures of its internal structure are:

(i) a loosely bound ηN (and KΛ, KΣ) hadronic "molecule," generated dynamically as a quasi-bound state of meson–baryon channels by coupled-channel hadronic interactions; and

(ii) a compact three-quark (or genuine quark-model) excited baryon state of small spatial extent.

In the single-nucleon sector the two pictures can be tuned to reproduce essentially the same ηN scattering amplitude near threshold and the same pole position, so they are difficult to distinguish from πN → ηN and γN → ηN data alone. However, in environments containing additional baryons the two pictures are expected to behave differently: a loosely bound molecule should be substantially modified (e.g., Pauli blocking of its nucleon component, dispersive effects on its meson component, level rearrangement) when embedded in a few-nucleon system, whereas a compact quark state should be comparatively inert and behave more like a point-like resonance whose properties are dressed only by standard nuclear medium effects.

Problem. Develop a systematic theoretical framework for the η-deuteron (ηd) and η-helium-3 (η³He) systems that:

(a) treats the η meson, the nucleons, and the S11(1535) resonance as explicit degrees of freedom, and incorporates both structural hypotheses (i) and (ii) for S11(1535) on an equal footing within the same few-body scattering formalism (e.g., Faddeev/Faddeev–Yakubovsky or AGS-type equations with a coupled ηN–πN–S11 subsystem);

(b) yields predictions for low-energy ηd and η³He observables — including the complex η-nucleus scattering lengths, near-threshold elastic and inelastic cross sections, possible quasi-bound or virtual η-mesic states, and the energy dependence of the production amplitudes near threshold — as functions of which hypothesis (i) or (ii) is adopted for S11(1535);

(c) identifies observables in ηd and η³He for which the molecule and compact-quark interpretations give quantitatively or qualitatively distinguishable predictions, thereby providing experimentally accessible tests of the nature of S11(1535).

Construct such a framework and determine whether the resulting differences between the two interpretations are large enough, given current and foreseeable experimental precision, to discriminate between them.

paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
context_brief: Extracting eta-nucleus scattering from production data
original_question: How can scattering lengths or other eta-nucleus scattering parameters be quantitatively and reliably extracted from eta-production data when final-state interactions, effective-range corrections, and inelastic channels are present? A solution should go beyond using the Watson-Migdal scattering-length formula only qualitatively, because the direct proportionality between production and elastic scattering energy dependences holds only when the scattering length is much larger than the effective range, and because no closed-form final-state-interaction expression is available in the presence of inelasticities.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the production reaction A + B → η + X, where η denotes the eta meson and X denotes a nuclear final state, measured near the η-X production threshold. Let q denote the relative η-X momentum in the final state, and let f_η(q) be the η-X elastic scattering amplitude with low-energy expansion

   q cot δ(q) = 1/a + (1/2) r_0 q^2 + O(q^4),

where a is the (in general complex) η-X scattering length and r_0 is the effective range. The Watson–Migdal prescription approximates the production amplitude as M(q) ≈ M_0 · f_η(q), giving a direct proportionality between the energy dependence of the production cross section and that of elastic η-X scattering only when |a| is much larger than |r_0|.

Develop a quantitative and reliable method to extract the η-X scattering parameters (scattering length a, effective range r_0, and analogous complex low-energy parameters) from measured η-production data subject to the following complications simultaneously:

   (i) The final-state η-X interaction must be included beyond the leading scattering-length approximation, accounting for effective-range corrections when |a| and |r_0| are comparable.
   (ii) Inelastic channels (e.g., πN, ππN openings coupled to ηN, or breakup channels for nuclear targets) are open at the relevant energies, so that no closed-form Watson–Migdal-type final-state interaction factor is known.
   (iii) The production operator (the "short-distance" part M_0) may itself depend on q and must be disentangled from the final-state interaction in a controlled, model-independent way.

The problem is to construct such an extraction scheme and to quantify rigorously the theoretical uncertainty it incurs on a and r_0.
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., reviews on η-nucleus interactions through 2013 and analyses of γd → π⁰ηd through 2022) continues to report scattering-length determinations with significant model-dependence and large uncertainties, with different K-matrix and coupled-channel approaches yielding incompatible values (real parts ranging from ~0.2 fm to ~0.9 fm). No closed-form, model-independent extraction handling effective-range corrections together with inelasticities has been established; the problem appears still open.

paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
original_question: Why can the imaginary part of the eta-helium-3 scattering length be compatible with zero even though the pi-nucleon to eta-nucleon channel couples significantly near threshold and might suggest an imaginary part of order at least one fermi? The proposed resolution to assess is whether Pauli-principle blocking of the pi-NN intermediate state suppresses the most prominent inelastic channel in eta-deuteron and, to some extent, eta-helium-3 systems.
self_contained_problem: Consider the low-energy elastic scattering of an η-meson on a ³He nucleus, characterized by a complex scattering length a(η³He) = Re a + i Im a. Near threshold the η-nucleon system couples strongly to the πN channel, and on naive grounds one would expect that this strong coupling, propagated through πNN intermediate states inside the nucleus, would force Im a(η³He) to be of order at least 1 fm. Empirical analyses of near-threshold η³He production data, however, are compatible with Im a(η³He) ≈ 0.\n\nAssess the following proposed resolution: the antisymmetrization of the two-nucleon final state in the dominant inelastic intermediate channel ηNN → πNN forces the πNN system into quantum numbers that are largely forbidden by the Pauli principle near threshold, so that this otherwise prominent inelastic channel is strongly suppressed in η-deuteron and (to a lesser extent) η-³He systems. Show, within a coupled-channel few-body framework for the η-³He system, that Pauli blocking of the πNN intermediate state suppresses Im a(η³He) sufficiently to render it consistent with zero, and quantify the residual contribution from channels not affected by this blocking.
status_search_result: Theoretical few-body and optical-potential studies of η-³He near-threshold scattering have argued that Pauli blocking of πNN intermediate states substantially suppresses absorption, consistent with small empirical Im a(η³He). However, extractions of Im a(η³He) from data remain model-dependent and values nonzero in magnitude still appear in some analyses, so the question is best characterized as partially resolved rather than definitively closed.

paper_title: Hadronic production of η–mesons: recent results and open questions
context_brief: Eta-helium-3 bound state versus virtual state
original_question: Does the eta-helium-3 system realize a near-threshold eta-nucleus bound state or a virtual state? A resolution should determine the sign of the real part of the eta-helium-3 scattering length using sufficiently accurate below-threshold data, such as inelastic-channel measurements or high-statistics gamma helium-3 to pi-zero p X data, because existing analyses of TAPS/MAMI data favored the virtual-state scenario but could not exclude a bound state.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the near-threshold interaction of an η meson with a ³He nucleus. The s-wave η–³He scattering length a = Re(a) + i Im(a) governs the low-energy behavior of the elastic amplitude; a pole of the amplitude on the physical sheet corresponds to a genuine bound state of the η–³He system, while a pole on the unphysical sheet corresponds to a virtual (antibound) state. Existing final-state-interaction analyses of η-production data near threshold determine |Re(a)| ≈ 4 fm with appreciable Im(a), but are insensitive to the sign of Re(a); a negative sign would indicate a virtual state, while a positive sign (with sufficient magnitude) would indicate a true near-threshold bound state.

Problem. Determine whether the η–³He system supports a genuine near-threshold bound state or only a virtual state, equivalently: determine the sign of Re(a) for the η–³He s-wave scattering length, using sufficiently accurate sub-threshold information (for example, inelastic-channel cross sections such as γ ³He → π⁰ p X, or other observables sensitive to the analytic structure below threshold).
status_search_result: As of recent searches (WASA-at-COSY 2020 results and a 2023 few-body theoretical study), the question remains unresolved. WASA-at-COSY analyses of pd→³He 2γ/6γ found only a slight indication of a possible bound-state signal and could not decisively distinguish bound from virtual scenarios. Final-state-interaction analyses fix |Re(a)| ≈ 4.2 fm but cannot determine the sign of Re(a). Theoretical few-body calculations probing η³He continue to debate the binding question.

paper_title: Open questions and perspectives for hadron electromagnetic form factors in space-like and time-like regions.
context_brief: Impact of revised nucleon form factors on light-nucleus descriptions
original_question: Given polarization measurements of elastic electron-proton scattering that show a large deviation of the ratio G_E/G_M from the older dipole-scaling expectation G_E(Q^2) = G_M(Q^2)/μ_p ≃ G_D, what are the consequences for descriptions of light nuclei, such as the deuteron or helium-3, that use nucleon electromagnetic form factors as inputs?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. For elastic electron–nucleon scattering, the nucleon electromagnetic structure is encoded in two form factors per nucleon: the Sachs electric form factor G_E(Q^2) and the Sachs magnetic form factor G_M(Q^2), where Q^2 is the negative of the squared four-momentum transfer. Historically, Rosenbluth-separation measurements on the proton suggested the dipole-scaling behavior

  G_E^p(Q^2) ≈ G_M^p(Q^2)/μ_p ≈ G_D(Q^2),   G_D(Q^2) = (1 + Q^2[GeV^2]/0.71)^{-2},

with μ_p the proton magnetic moment. Polarization-transfer measurements of elastic e–p scattering instead yield a ratio μ_p G_E^p(Q^2)/G_M^p(Q^2) that decreases significantly (approximately linearly) with increasing Q^2 over the few-GeV^2 range, in clear disagreement with the dipole-scaling assumption.

Light nuclei such as the deuteron (^2H) and helium-3 (^3He) are commonly described theoretically by combining a nuclear wave function (from a nucleon–nucleon interaction model, possibly supplemented by two- and three-body currents and relativistic corrections) with the single-nucleon electromagnetic form factors G_E^{p,n}(Q^2), G_M^{p,n}(Q^2) entering through the one-body electromagnetic current operator. Elastic electron scattering observables of these nuclei (e.g. the deuteron form factors A(Q^2), B(Q^2), and tensor polarization T_{20}(Q^2); the ^3He charge and magnetic form factors F_C(Q^2), F_M(Q^2)) thus depend explicitly on the nucleon form factors used as input.

Problem. Determine, quantitatively and qualitatively, the consequences for theoretical predictions of elastic electromagnetic observables of light nuclei — in particular the deuteron and ^3He — when the proton form factors used as nucleon-level inputs are taken consistent with the polarization-transfer behavior (μ_p G_E^p/G_M^p decreasing with Q^2) rather than with the older dipole-scaling assumption G_E^p ≈ G_M^p/μ_p ≈ G_D. Specifically:

(a) Identify and compute the modifications induced in the predicted deuteron observables A(Q^2), B(Q^2), and T_{20}(Q^2), and in the ^3He elastic charge and magnetic form factors F_C(Q^2) and F_M(Q^2), over the momentum-transfer range where the polarization data deviate appreciably from dipole scaling.

(b) Assess how such input changes affect the extraction of the neutron electromagnetic form factors G_E^n(Q^2) and G_M^n(Q^2) from quasi-elastic or elastic electron scattering on deuteron and ^3He targets, where nuclear corrections are required because no free-neutron target exists.

(c) Determine to what extent the resulting discrepancies (if any) between theory and data on light nuclei can be absorbed into meson-exchange currents, relativistic corrections, or modifications of nucleon structure in the nuclear medium, versus indicating genuine new physics in the nuclear electromagnetic current.
status_search_result: The question is an active research direction rather than a settled mathematical theorem. Reviews and analyses of nucleon form factors (e.g., dispersion-theoretical analyses and global fits) continue to refine the inputs used in deuteron and ^3He calculations, and extractions of the neutron form factors from ^2H and ^3He targets are still being updated. No single definitive answer fully quantifies the consequences across all observables, and the topic remains under continuing theoretical and experimental investigation.

paper_title: Open questions and perspectives for hadron electromagnetic form factors in space-like and time-like regions.
context_brief: Two-photon exchange as an explanation of Rosenbluth-polarization discrepancy
original_question: Is two-photon exchange in elastic electron-proton scattering responsible for the discrepancy between proton electromagnetic form factors extracted by Rosenbluth separation of unpolarized cross-section data and those extracted by the polarization method from the ratio of longitudinal to transverse recoil-proton polarizations?
self_contained_problem:
In elastic electron–proton scattering $e^- p \to e^- p$, the proton's electromagnetic structure is characterized by the Sachs electric and magnetic form factors $G_E^p(Q^2)$ and $G_M^p(Q^2)$, where $Q^2$ is the squared four-momentum transfer. Under the standard assumption that the reaction proceeds dominantly by one-photon exchange, two experimental methods to extract these form factors are:

(i) the Rosenbluth (longitudinal–transverse) separation, in which the reduced unpolarized differential cross section is written as
$$\sigma_R(Q^2,\varepsilon) \;=\; \tau\, G_M^p(Q^2)^2 \;+\; \varepsilon\, G_E^p(Q^2)^2,$$
with $\tau = Q^2/(4 M_p^2)$ and $\varepsilon$ the virtual-photon longitudinal polarization parameter, and the two form factors are extracted from the linear dependence on $\varepsilon$ at fixed $Q^2$;

(ii) the polarization-transfer method, in which a longitudinally polarized electron beam scatters from an unpolarized proton target and the ratio of the transferred recoil-proton transverse and longitudinal polarization components determines the ratio
$$\frac{G_E^p(Q^2)}{G_M^p(Q^2)} \;\propto\; -\frac{P_t}{P_l}\,\sqrt{\frac{\tau(1+\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}}.$$

At momentum transfers $Q^2$ of a few GeV$^2$ and above, these two methods yield significantly different results for $G_E^p/G_M^p$.

Beyond one-photon exchange, the next correction is the two-photon exchange (TPE) amplitude, suppressed nominally by one power of the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ but with potentially enhanced kinematic dependence.

Question: Is the inclusion of two-photon exchange contributions in elastic electron–proton scattering quantitatively responsible for the observed discrepancy between $G_E^p/G_M^p$ extracted by the Rosenbluth method and that extracted by the polarization-transfer method?
status_search_result: Theoretical calculations and phenomenological analyses have established that hadronic two-photon exchange corrections, kinematically enhanced in the Rosenbluth method but suppressed in the polarization-transfer method, can largely account for the discrepancy in $G_E^p/G_M^p$ extractions. Three dedicated experiments comparing $e^+p$ and $e^-p$ elastic scattering (VEPP-3, CLAS, OLYMPUS), as well as recent positron-beam Super-Rosenbluth measurements, have confirmed the existence of a small TPE effect of the expected order. However, the precision and kinematic reach remain insufficient to definitively confirm the theoretical treatments or to show that TPE quantitatively closes the discrepancy at all $Q^2$. The question is therefore partially resolved.

context_brief: Possible zero crossing of the proton electric form factor
original_question: Does the proton electric form factor G_Ep(Q^2), as inferred from polarization-transfer measurements of the ratio G_Ep/G_Mp, cross zero and become negative at higher momentum transfer, for example in measurements extending the proton form-factor ratio up to Q^2 = 9 GeV^2?

Let $G_{E_p}(Q^2)$ and $G_{M_p}(Q^2)$ denote the proton electric (Sachs) and magnetic form factors, respectively, as functions of the squared four-momentum transfer $Q^2 \ge 0$. These are defined through the parametrization of the proton electromagnetic current matrix element
$$\langle p'|J^\mu|pangle =  ar u(p')\Big[\gamma^\mu F_1(Q^2) +  rac{i\sigma^{\mu
u}q_
u}{2M_p}F_2(Q^2)\Big]u(p),\quad q=p'-p,\ Q^2=-q^2,$$
with $G_{E_p}=F_1-	au F_2$, $G_{M_p}=F_1+F_2$, $	au=Q^2/(4M_p^2)$, and the normalization $G_{E_p}(0)=1$, $G_{M_p}(0)=\mu_p$.

$$R(Q^2):=\mu_p\, rac{G_{E_p}(Q^2)}{G_{M_p}(Q^2)},$$
and existing measurements show that $R(Q^2)$ decreases approximately linearly with $Q^2$ over the range so far explored.

paper_title: Open questions and perspectives for hadron electromagnetic form factors in space-like and time-like regions.
context_brief: Completeness and precision of radiative corrections
original_question: Can a complete and sufficiently precise calculation of radiative corrections, including all contributions and interference terms and their effects on electric and magnetic contributions to the reduced cross section, be developed for elastic electron-proton form-factor measurements so that Rosenbluth cross-section extractions and polarization-ratio measurements can be interpreted consistently at large Q^2?
self_contained_problem:
Consider elastic electron–proton scattering, $e^- p \to e^- p$, parametrized by the squared four-momentum transfer $Q^2 = -q^2 > 0$. In the one-photon-exchange (Born) approximation, the unpolarized cross section is the Rosenbluth formula
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right)_{\text{Mott}}\frac{1}{\varepsilon(1+\tau)}\Big[\tau\, G_M^2(Q^2) + \varepsilon\, G_E^2(Q^2)\Big],$$
where $\tau = Q^2/(4M_p^2)$, $\varepsilon$ is the virtual-photon longitudinal polarization, and $G_E, G_M$ are the proton electric and magnetic Sachs form factors. The ratio $G_E/G_M$ can be measured (i) via a Rosenbluth (longitudinal–transverse) separation of the reduced cross section, or (ii) via polarization-transfer experiments that measure the ratio of recoil-proton transverse to longitudinal polarizations.

At large $Q^2$ the electric contribution to the unpolarized cross section is kinematically suppressed relative to the magnetic one, and the experimentally applied radiative corrections (real and virtual photon emission, vacuum polarization, soft and hard two-photon exchange, lepton–proton bremsstrahlung interference, etc.) reach magnitudes of order $30$–$40\%$. In standard practice, radiative corrections are not applied to the polarization-transfer extraction under the assumption that they cancel in the polarization ratio, even though no complete calculation of all such contributions and their mutual interferences has been performed.

Problem. Develop a complete and quantitatively controlled calculation of the radiative corrections to elastic $ep$ scattering — including all contributions and their interference terms, and tracking separately their effects on the electric and magnetic pieces of the reduced cross section as well as on the polarization observables — such that:
(a) the Rosenbluth extraction of $G_E/G_M$ and the polarization-transfer extraction of $G_E/G_M$ become consistent at large $Q^2$;
(b) the non-cancellation of radiative effects in the polarization ratio is quantified;
(c) the residual theoretical uncertainty is small compared to the experimental precision of current and planned measurements.
Either construct such a calculation, or prove obstructions to its existence within QED plus a controlled hadronic model.
status_search_result: The discrepancy between Rosenbluth and polarization-transfer extractions of the proton form factor ratio at large Q^2 is widely attributed to two-photon-exchange and related higher-order radiative corrections, but as of 2024 a complete calculation including all interference terms is not available. Recent dedicated experiments (OLYMPUS at DESY, CLAS12, VEPP-3) confirm a small TPE effect at moderate Q^2 but do not validate theoretical treatments at large Q^2, and the proposed TPEX experiment aims to extend the kinematic range. Theory and experiment in this area remain active, and the question is regarded as open.

paper_title: On Two Open Problems in Convex Analysis
context_brief: Extreme points of bounded closed convex sets in Banach spaces.
original_question: Let C be a bounded closed convex subset of a Banach space E, let x0 be an extreme point of C, let y* be an element of the dual space E*, and let ε > 0. Must there always exist a constant M ≥ 0 such that, for every u and v in C, the inequality M||u + v - 2x0|| ≥ ⟨v - x0, y*⟩ - ε holds?
self_contained_problem:
Let $E$ be a (real) Banach space with continuous dual $E^*$, and let $C \subset E$ be a bounded closed convex subset. Let $x_0 \in C$ be an extreme point of $C$ (i.e., $x_0$ cannot be written as $\tfrac12(u+v)$ with $u,v \in C$ and $u \neq v$). Fix $y^* \in E^*$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.

Question: Does there necessarily exist a constant $M \geq 0$ such that, for all $u, v \in C$,
$$ M\,\|u + v - 2x_0\| \;\geq\; \langle v - x_0,\, y^*\rangle - \varepsilon \,?$$

If the answer is not always affirmative, characterize precisely those triples $(C, x_0)$ for which the above implication holds for every $y^* \in E^*$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$.
status_search_result: The question has been resolved. Without loss of generality assume $x_0 = 0$. $$Q(x-y) = (x_0 - y_0)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{d}(x_i - y_i)^2.$$

paper_title: Open Problems for Painlevé Equations
original_question: Give a complete classification and a unifying structural framework for the special properties of the Painlevé equations, including Hamiltonian formulations, exact solutions, Bäcklund transformations, associated isomonodromy or Lax-pair representations, and asymptotic descriptions together with the connection formulae relating them.
self_contained_problem:
The six Painlevé equations P_I,...,P_VI are the canonical second-order ordinary differential equations of the form w'' = F(z,w,w'), with F rational in w, w' and analytic in z, whose general solutions have no movable singularities other than poles (the Painlevé property), and which cannot be reduced to linear equations, to first-order equations, or to equations solvable in terms of classical special functions. They are:
  P_I:   w'' = 6w^2 + z,
  P_II:  w'' = 2w^3 + zw + α,
  P_III: w'' = (w')^2/w − w'/z + (αw^2+β)/z + γw^3 + δ/w,
  P_IV:  w'' = (w')^2/(2w) + (3/2)w^3 + 4zw^2 + 2(z^2−α)w + β/w,
  P_V:   w'' = ((1/(2w)) + 1/(w−1))(w')^2 − w'/z + (w−1)^2(αw + β/w)/z^2 + γw/z + δw(w+1)/(w−1),
  P_VI:  w'' = (1/2)(1/w + 1/(w−1) + 1/(w−z))(w')^2 − (1/z + 1/(z−1) + 1/(w−z))w' + (w(w−1)(w−z)/(z^2(z−1)^2))(α + βz/w^2 + γ(z−1)/(w−1)^2 + δz(z−1)/(w−z)^2),
where α,β,γ,δ are complex parameters.

Each of these equations is known to possess a collection of remarkable structures, including:
 (a) Hamiltonian representations as non-autonomous Hamiltonian systems,
 (b) families of exact solutions (rational, algebraic, and classical special-function solutions such as Airy, Bessel, Weber–Hermite, Whittaker, and hypergeometric solutions at distinguished parameter values),
 (c) Bäcklund transformations mapping solutions to solutions, often at shifted parameter values, generating affine Weyl group symmetries,
 (d) isomonodromic (Lax-pair) representations expressing each Painlevé equation as the compatibility condition of an associated pair of linear systems,
 (e) asymptotic expansions of solutions in the complex plane near the fixed singular points and near infinity, together with connection formulae relating the asymptotic data in different sectors.

Problem. Provide a complete classification of all such properties (Hamiltonian forms, exact special solutions, Bäcklund transformations, isomonodromic/Lax representations, asymptotic descriptions and their connection formulae) for the Painlevé equations P_I–P_VI, and a unifying structural framework from which these properties arise in a coherent and systematic way, rather than as the currently known fragmentary and case-by-case results.
status_search_result: This is a broad structural meta-problem in the theory of Painlevé equations. Results for individual equations are extensive (Okamoto Hamiltonians, Noumi–Yamada affine Weyl group symmetries, Jimbo–Miwa–Ueno isomonodromy, Its–Kapaev–Fokas–Novokshenov asymptotics), but no unifying classification framework encompassing all listed properties uniformly has been established. The problem remains open.

The best known lower bound is due to Edel , who has constructed progression-free sets in Fq of size (2:217:::)r by nding a particular example in rather large dimension and then taking a product of several copies of it. It would be of much interest to improve Meshulam's estimate, to show that any progression-free subset of Fq has size o(3r=r), and/or to determine whether there is an absolute constant c < 3 such that any progression-free subset of Fq has size, smaller than cr.

Let r be a positive integer and let F_q denote the finite field with q = 3^r elements, viewed as an abelian group under addition (equivalently, as the vector space F_3^r). Address the following:
(a) Improve Meshulam's bound by showing that every progression-free subset A ⊆ F_q satisfies |A| = o(3^r / r).
(b) Determine whether there exists an absolute constant c < 3 such that f(r) ≤ c^r for all sufficiently large r.
(c) More generally, determine the asymptotic growth rate of f(r) as r → ∞.

context_brief: Di erence sets in quadratic residues
original_question: Given a prime p 1 (mod 4), how large can a set A Fp be given that the di erence between any two elements of A is a quadratic residue modulo p? In other words, what is the clique number of the Paley graph over Fp? The existence of a set, possessing the property in question and of size (0:5+o(1)) log2 p, is established in . In the lower bound c log p log log log p is proved for in nitely many primes p. Finding a reasonable upper bound is an old problem on which noth- ing is known beyond the estimate jAj < pp. A simple elementary proof is as follows. Suppose that jAj > pp. Then for any x 2 Fp there exist a1; b1; a2; b2 2 A such that a1x + b1 = a2x + b2 and a1 6= a2. Consequently, x = (b1 b2)=(a2 a1) and since any x 2 Fp has a representation of this form, the set of all non-zero elements of A A is not contained in a multiplicative subgroup of Fp. This is probably a very hard problem: just observe that the estimate jAj < p" would imply that the least quadratic non-residue modulo p is smaller than p". One can consider the sumset A+A instead of the set of di erences, or ask the question for the multiplicative subgroups of Fp, other than the subgroup of quadratic residues, in the following spirit: given a proper subgroup H of the multiplicative group of Fq, what is the largest size of a subset A Fp with A A H? One can also ask whether there exists A Fp such that A + A = H, or such that the symmetric di erence of A + A and H is small.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and let $Q \subset \mathbb{F}_p^*$ denote the set of nonzero quadratic residues modulo $p$. Consider subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with the property that $a - a' \in Q$ for every pair of distinct $a, a' \in A$ (equivalently, $A$ is a clique in the Paley graph on $\mathbb{F}_p$, whose vertex set is $\mathbb{F}_p$ and whose edges join $x, y$ with $x - y \in Q$). Let $\omega(p)$ denote the maximum size of such a set $A$.

Known lower bounds give $\omega(p) \geq (1/2 + o(1)) \log_2 p$ in general, and $\omega(p) \geq c \, \log p \, \log\log\log p$ for infinitely many primes $p$. The only generally known upper bound is the elementary estimate $\omega(p) < \sqrt{p}$.

Problem: Determine improved upper bounds on $\omega(p)$. In particular, prove or disprove that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ one has $\omega(p) < p^{\varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently large primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and more generally describe the true asymptotic order of $\omega(p)$.

One may also pose the analogous questions with the difference set replaced by the sumset (i.e., $A + A \subseteq Q$, or $A + A = Q$, or $|(A+A) \triangle H|$ small), and with $Q$ replaced by an arbitrary proper multiplicative subgroup $H$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^*$: estimate the largest $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$ with $A - A \subseteq H \cup \{0\}$.
status_search_result: The trivial bound $\omega(p) < \sqrt{p}$ was improved by Hanson and Petridis (2019/2021) using Stepanov's method to $\omega(p) \leq \sqrt{(p-1)/2} + 1$ (i.e. roughly $\sqrt{p/2}$). original_question: What is a general theory of information flow in stochastic networks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a stochastic network modeled as a directed (or undirected) graph G = (V, E) in which each node v ∈ V is an information source or sink (or relay) and each edge e ∈ E is a noisy communication channel described by a conditional probability transition kernel p_e(y|x) between input and output alphabets. A set of source processes {X_s : s ∈ S} with prescribed joint distribution is to be transmitted to a set of sinks, where each sink t ∈ T demands a specified subset of the sources. A coding scheme assigns, at each node and each time step, a (possibly random) function of past observations to be transmitted on outgoing edges; decoders at sinks produce estimates of demanded sources. The capacity region of the network is the closure of all rate tuples for which arbitrarily small probability of error is achievable.

Develop a general theory of information flow in such stochastic networks. Concretely, give a single-letter (or otherwise computable) characterization of the capacity region of an arbitrary multi-source, multi-sink stochastic network with noisy channels, statistically dependent sources, and arbitrary demand structure, identifying the fundamental limits on simultaneously achievable communication rates and the optimal coding strategies (including the role of network coding, cooperation, feedback, and source–channel separation) that attain them.
status_search_result: The question of a general theory of information flow in stochastic (noisy, multi-terminal) networks is a long-standing open problem in network information theory. While special cases such as noiseless networks with single-source multicast (Ahlswede–Cai–Li–Yeung network coding theorem) and certain Gaussian/deterministic relay networks (Avestimehr–Diggavi–Tse approximate capacity) are well understood, the general multi-source/multi-sink noisy network capacity remains unresolved; standard textbooks (El Gamal–Kim) and surveys explicitly list it as open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Communication and Computation
original_question: Is there a duality between computation and communication?
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of information theory and theoretical computer science, communication is typically modeled by an encoder–channel–decoder system, in which a source message is mapped into a codeword, transmitted through a noisy channel, and decoded so as to recover the source with low error probability; the fundamental limits are characterized by Shannon's channel coding theorem and rate-distortion theory. Computation, on the other hand, is typically modeled by a Boolean circuit, Turing machine, or algorithm that maps inputs to outputs, with fundamental limits described in terms of time, space, or circuit-size complexity.

Formulate and establish (or refute) a precise duality principle between computation and communication. That is, exhibit an explicit correspondence under which: (i) every communication problem (a triple consisting of a source distribution, a channel, and a fidelity criterion) is associated with a dual computation problem (a function class, model of computation, and a resource measure), and conversely; (ii) optimal achievable rates / capacity-type quantities on the communication side correspond to optimal resource bounds (e.g. circuit size, depth, time, space) on the computation side, in a way that converts direct (achievability) theorems on one side into converse (lower bound) theorems on the other, and vice versa; and (iii) the correspondence is functorial in the sense that composition of channels corresponds to composition of computational reductions.

Either construct such a duality and prove the corresponding equivalence of fundamental limits, or prove that no such duality can exist by exhibiting an obstruction.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a broad conceptual open problem about a hypothetical duality between computation and communication. While there are partial analogies (e.g. between source/channel coding and circuit/communication complexity, or via interactive coding and information complexity), no general established duality theorem is known to formalize the correspondence, and no definitive negative result rules it out. The status appears open.

original_question: How can ranked-search techniques for distributed systems be extended so that they remain effective at the much larger scales expected in peer-to-peer data-sharing systems, while still exploiting the possibility of returning only the top k results instead of the full result set?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed data-sharing network modeled as a set of N nodes, each holding a local document collection, where N can be very large (e.g., 10^6 or more). Each document d has, for each query q drawn from some query space Q, a real-valued relevance score s(d,q). A ranked-search protocol is an algorithm that, given a query q issued at one node, returns the k documents in the entire network with the highest scores s(d,q), for a user-specified parameter k much smaller than the total number of relevant documents.

1. Correctness: with high probability the returned set equals (or has bounded approximation ratio to) the true global top-k by score s(·,q).
2. Scalability: the per-node communication, computation, and storage cost grows sublinearly (ideally polylogarithmically) in N, and the total network traffic per query is asymptotically smaller than the cost of retrieving the full result set.
3. Top-k exploitation: the protocol must take essential advantage of the bound k, so that its cost depends on k and decreases substantially when k is small compared to retrieving all matching documents.
4. Robustness: the protocol should remain effective under node churn, heterogeneous node capacities, and skewed score and document distributions across nodes.

Provide such a protocol and prove matching upper and lower bounds on its communication complexity as a function of N, k, and the score distribution, or prove that no protocol can simultaneously achieve all four properties.

Define peer autonomy as the degree of control a peer has over (i) which documents it stores locally, (ii) which queries it forwards or answers, and (iii) which neighbors it maintains in the overlay. Define efficiency as the expected cost (in messages, latency, or bandwidth) for successfully locating and retrieving a document. Existing designs typically fix a single point on the autonomy–efficiency tradeoff for the whole deployment: structured systems (e.g., distributed hash tables) achieve high efficiency at the cost of dictating document placement and routing, while unstructured systems preserve autonomy but incur higher search cost.

2. The system simultaneously supports documents with different choices of θ(d) within the same overlay, without partitioning the peers into separate subsystems.

paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
original_question: How should future peer-to-peer protocols for data sharing be designed so that adversaries cannot easily construct denial-of-service attacks by exploiting loosely constrained protocol features such as unconstrained responses, routing behavior, or resource allocation rules?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that interact according to a protocol P. The protocol P specifies, for each node, (i) how it responds to incoming messages (response rules), (ii) how it forwards or routes queries and data (routing rules), and (iii) how it allocates local resources such as bandwidth, storage, and CPU to handle requests (resource allocation rules). A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a strategy executed by a bounded coalition A of adversarial nodes (with |A| small relative to the total population) whose goal is to cause a disproportionate degradation of service availability for honest participants — formally, to drive some measurable performance metric (e.g., query success rate, average response latency, or fraction of reachable honest peers) below a chosen threshold while expending only o(1) of the resources required from the attacker compared to the damage inflicted on the system.

Say that a protocol feature is "loosely constrained" if it permits a node, upon receiving a single message of size s, to be obligated (by the protocol rules) to generate responses, forwarded traffic, or resource commitments whose total cost is ω(s), or if it permits an adversary to trigger arbitrarily many such actions without supplying a commensurate proof of work, identity, or prior interaction.

Problem. Design a P2P data-sharing protocol P satisfying the following properties simultaneously:

(1) Correctness/efficiency in the honest setting: with all nodes following P, the system supports data lookup, storage, and retrieval with polylogarithmic per-operation cost in the number of nodes.

(2) DoS resistance: for every adversarial coalition A of size at most a constant fraction ε of the network and every strategy A may follow within the syntactic rules of P, the ratio (damage inflicted on honest peers) / (resources expended by A) is bounded by a constant, where damage and resources are measured in a uniform cost model covering bandwidth, computation, and memory.

(3) No loosely constrained features: every response rule, routing rule, and resource-allocation rule of P must be tightly constrained in the sense above — i.e., the work induced on any honest node by a single adversarial message of size s is O(s), up to amortization by verifiable proofs.

Provide such a protocol together with a proof of its DoS resistance, or prove that no protocol can satisfy (1)–(3) simultaneously under standard cryptographic assumptions.
status_search_result: DoS resistance in peer-to-peer overlays remains an active research area with many partial mitigations (proof-of-work, admission control, secure routing in DHTs, rate limiting, reputation systems), but no general protocol design is known that simultaneously achieves polylogarithmic efficiency and provable constant-ratio DoS resistance against a constant fraction of adversaries while eliminating all loosely constrained features. The problem is generally regarded as open in the P2P security literature.

original_question: In a voting-based peer-to-peer file-authenticity mechanism, how can the protocol prevent spoofing of votes, spoofing of nodes, and spoofing of files, while still letting distributed participants collectively determine authenticity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer file-sharing network in which there is no trusted central authority. Each participating node may publish files and may cast votes attesting to the authenticity (i.e., the correctness of content and provenance) of files offered by other nodes. The collective authenticity judgment for a file is to be derived from the votes cast by the nodes.

Design a voting-based authenticity protocol for this setting that simultaneously achieves the following three security properties, under realistic adversarial assumptions in which a bounded fraction of nodes may be malicious and may collude:

1. Vote unforgeability: an adversary cannot inject votes that were not actually cast by legitimate, distinct participating nodes, nor duplicate, replay, or alter genuine votes.

2. Node non-spoofing (Sybil resistance): an adversary cannot create or impersonate an unbounded number of pseudonymous nodes in order to amplify its voting weight or impersonate honest participants.

3. File non-spoofing: an adversary cannot cause a file with different content to be accepted under the identifier or name of a genuine file, i.e., the file-to-identifier binding used in voting must be tamper-evident.

The problem is to specify identity, naming, and vote-aggregation mechanisms (and to prove their security) such that all three properties hold while still allowing the distributed set of participants to collectively determine file authenticity without relying on a trusted third party.

paper_title: Open Problems in Distributed Communities
original_question: In a dynamic distributed community that exchanges shared context information, how should replication and consistency be handled when centralized or well-known transaction managers may not be accessible? Specifically, what mechanisms, protocols, and data formats should govern information exchange, and how should the system decide whether, how, and where shared information is replicated so that improved access and persistence do not create unmanageable consistency problems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a dynamic distributed community modeled as a time-varying set of autonomous nodes that may join, leave, or become temporarily unreachable, and that exchange shared context information (state describing the participants and their interactions). Assume there is no centralized or globally well-known transaction manager available, and no a priori designated coordinator can be guaranteed to be reachable.

Design and analyze a framework for replication and consistency of the shared context information in such a community. Specifically:

1. Specify a set of mechanisms, communication protocols, and data formats by which nodes exchange shared context information.
2. Provide a decision procedure that determines, for each item of shared information, whether it should be replicated, how it should be replicated (e.g., full copy, partial copy, encoded fragments), and where (on which subset of nodes) replicas should reside, as a function of the current community membership, connectivity, and access patterns.
3. Prove that the resulting scheme simultaneously achieves:
   (a) improved availability and persistence of shared information relative to a non-replicated baseline,
   (b) a well-defined and tractable consistency guarantee (to be specified by the solution, e.g., eventual consistency, causal consistency, or a stronger criterion) that does not rely on the existence of centralized or well-known transaction managers, and
   (c) bounded resource overhead (communication, storage, and reconciliation cost) under realistic models of node churn and intermittent connectivity.

The problem is to exhibit such a framework together with the protocols, decision rules, and formal guarantees, or to prove impossibility results that delineate which combinations of availability, persistence, and consistency are achievable in this transaction-manager-free dynamic setting.

status_search_result: The question is a broad open research challenge concerning replication and consistency in dynamic distributed communities without transaction managers. While a large body of related work exists (e.g., CRDTs, gossip-based replication, eventual consistency, the CAP theorem, and Byzantine fault-tolerant replication), no single accepted solution addresses the full problem as posed, and the question remains an open-ended research agenda rather than a settled mathematical statement.

paper_title: Open problems in Gaussian fluid queueing theory
original_question: Consider a fluid queue with constant output rate c > 0 whose stationary buffer content process is Q(t), where the input is a centered Gaussian process X(t) with stationary increments, continuous sample paths, and variance function σ_X^2(t). Is the short-range or long-range dependence behavior of the input process X(·) inherited by the workload process Q(t), equivalently by the large-time behavior of the correlation function ρ(t)=Corr(Q(t),Q(0))?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{X(t):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ be a centered Gaussian stochastic process with stationary increments, almost surely continuous sample paths, and variance function $\sigma_X^2(t)=\mathrm{Var}(X(t))$. Fix a constant output rate $c>0$ such that the associated fluid queue is stable, and let $\{Q(t):t\geq 0\}$ denote the stationary buffer content (workload) process defined by
$$Q(t)=\sup_{s\leq t}\bigl(X(t)-X(s)-c(t-s)\bigr).$$
Define the workload correlation function $\rho(t)=\mathrm{Corr}(Q(t),Q(0))$ for $t\geq 0$.

Recall that $X$ is said to exhibit short-range dependence if its increment correlations are summable (or decay sufficiently fast, e.g. exponentially), and long-range dependence if they decay only polynomially and are non-summable.

Question: Is the short-range or long-range dependence property of the input process $X(\cdot)$ inherited by the workload process $Q(\cdot)$? Equivalently, does the large-$t$ decay rate of $\rho(t)$ match that of the covariance structure of $X$ — for instance, exponential decay of $\rho(t)$ when $X$ is short-range dependent, and polynomial decay of $\rho(t)$ at the same rate as the covariance of the increments of $X$ when $X$ is long-range dependent?
status_search_result: The question of whether the short/long-range dependence of a Gaussian input is inherited by the workload correlation function in a Gaussian fluid queue is identified as an open problem; only the Brownian queue case (exponential decay) is known, while the polynomial decay conjecture for long-range dependent inputs remains unresolved in general. Simulation-based studies and related work on Lévy-driven queues and tandem fluid queues address adjacent cases but do not settle the general Gaussian inheritance question.

paper_title: Open problems in Gaussian fluid queueing theory
original_question: Start the Gaussian fluid queue empty at time 0, so that the transient buffer content at time t is Q^tr(t)=sup_{s∈[0,t]}(X(s)−cs). For a fixed level u, determine the asymptotic behavior as t→∞ of γ(u,t)=P(Q>u)−P(Q^tr(t)>u), where Q denotes the stationary buffer content. In other words, how fast does the transient exceedance probability approach the stationary exceedance probability at a fixed threshold u?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X = \{X(t) : t \ge 0\}$ be a centered Gaussian process with stationary increments, $X(0)=0$, and almost surely continuous sample paths, with variance function $\sigma^2(t) = \mathrm{Var}\,X(t)$ satisfying the usual regularity assumptions ensuring stability of the associated fluid queue (in particular, the drift condition that guarantees a proper stationary buffer content). Fix a service rate $c>0$ such that $\mathbb{E} X(t) - ct \to -\infty$ as $t\to\infty$ (so that the queue is stable), and define the stationary buffer content
$$Q \;\stackrel{d}{=}\; \sup_{s \ge 0}\bigl(X(s) - cs\bigr).$$
Assume that the system starts empty at time $0$, so the transient buffer content at time $t>0$ satisfies
$$Q^{tr}(t) \;\stackrel{d}{=}\; \sup_{s \in [0,t]}\bigl(X(s) - cs\bigr).$$
For a fixed threshold $u>0$, define
$$\gamma(u,t) \;:=\; \mathbb{P}(Q > u) \;-\; \mathbb{P}(Q^{tr}(t) > u).$$
Determine the exact asymptotic behavior of $\gamma(u,t)$ as $t \to \infty$, with $u$ held fixed; that is, find an explicit function $f(u,t)$ such that $\gamma(u,t) \sim f(u,t)$ as $t \to \infty$.
status_search_result: The problem is explicitly listed as an open problem in the literature on Gaussian fluid queueing theory. Related work on Lévy-driven queues and speed of convergence to (quasi-)stationary distributions exists, but no source found establishes the exact fixed-$u$ asymptotics of $\gamma(u,t)$ for general centered Gaussian input with stationary increments. Status remains unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Open problems in Gaussian fluid queueing theory
original_question: Let H_η be the generalized Pickands constant associated with a centered Gaussian process η(t) with stationary increments, continuous sample paths, η(0)=0, and variance function σ_η^2(t), defined by the limit H_η = lim_{T→∞} H_η(T)/T where H_η(T)=E exp(max_{t∈[0,T]}(√2 η(t)−σ_η^2(t))). Find additional characterizations of H_η that can lead to more precise estimates of this constant.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\eta=\{\eta(t):t\ge 0\}$ be a centered Gaussian process with stationary increments, almost surely continuous sample paths, $\eta(0)=0$, and variance function $\sigma_\eta^2(t)=\mathrm{Var}(\eta(t))$. For $T>0$, define
$$H_\eta(T) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\,\exp\!\Big(\max_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\sqrt{2}\,\eta(t)-\sigma_\eta^2(t)\big)\Big),$$
and assume the limit
$$H_\eta \;=\; \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{H_\eta(T)}{T}$$
exists in $(0,\infty)$; this number is called the generalized Pickands constant associated with $\eta$.

The classical Pickands constant $\mathcal{H}_\alpha$ corresponds to the case $\eta(t)=B_\alpha(t)$, a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $\alpha/2\in(0,1]$, in which case $\sigma_\eta^2(t)=t^\alpha$. For general admissible $\eta$, only crude bounds on $H_\eta$ are known, and explicit values are available only in isolated cases (e.g.\ $\mathcal{H}_1=1$, $\mathcal{H}_2=1/\sqrt{\pi}$).

Problem: Find new equivalent characterizations or representations of the generalized Pickands constant $H_\eta$ (for instance, as expectations not involving a limit, variational formulas, or expressions in terms of auxiliary stochastic processes) that yield sharper quantitative estimates—upper bounds, lower bounds, or asymptotic expansions—for $H_\eta$ than those currently available.
status_search_result: Pickands constants and their generalizations remain a very active area, with progress on alternative representations (e.g., Dieker–Yakir-type expectation formulas, max-stable process representations) and on bounds and simulation methods. However, no closed-form expression or sharp characterization is known for general $\eta$, and obtaining sharper estimates for $H_\eta$ is still regarded as an open problem.

paper_title: Open problems in Gaussian fluid queueing theory
original_question: Develop a reliable and efficient simulation algorithm for estimating the generalized Pickands constant H_η. The method should avoid the instability of straightforward Monte Carlo schemes based directly on the defining representation of H_η(T)/T and should work for the class of Gaussian processes η considered in the paper.
self_contained_problem:
Let η = {η(t) : t ≥ 0} be a centered Gaussian process with stationary increments, almost surely continuous sample paths, η(0) = 0, and variance function σ²_η(t) = Var η(t) that is regularly varying at infinity with index in (0, 2). For T > 0, define
   H_η(T) = E[ exp( sup_{t ∈ [0,T]} ( η(t) − σ²_η(t)/2 ) ) ].
It is known that the limit
   H_η = lim_{T → ∞} H_η(T)/T
exists in (0, ∞); this is the generalized Pickands constant associated with η.

The problem is to construct a provably reliable and computationally efficient simulation (Monte Carlo) algorithm that produces consistent estimates of H_η with quantifiable error (bias and variance) for the whole class of admissible Gaussian processes η described above. The algorithm should avoid the instability of naive Monte Carlo schemes based directly on the ratio H_η(T)/T (whose variance blows up as T grows, while bias decreases), and should come with rigorous error bounds and a clear prescription for choosing its tuning parameters.
status_search_result: Dieker and Yakir (Bernoulli, 2014) introduced a representation of Pickands' constants as a plain expectation (no limit), yielding a reliable Monte Carlo estimator with explicit error analysis for the classical fractional-Brownian-motion Pickands constants H_α. This work is widely regarded as resolving the simulation problem in the classical case, and subsequent papers (e.g. on speed of convergence of discrete to continuous Pickands constants, and generalized/Berman-type extensions) have extended the methodology. A fully general, uniformly reliable simulation scheme covering all generalized Pickands constants H_η for arbitrary admissible Gaussian processes η is not established in a single definitive reference, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: What is the finite-sample performance of the k-nearest-neighbor decision rule when the training set is finite rather than infinite?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,Y)$ be a random pair taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{1,2,\dots,M\}$ with joint distribution $\mathbb{P}$, and let the regression/posterior functions be $\eta_j(x) = \mathbb{P}(Y=j \mid X=x)$ for $j=1,\dots,M$. The Bayes classifier is $g^*(x) = \arg\max_{j} \eta_j(x)$, with Bayes error $P_e^* = \mathbb{P}(g^*(X) \neq Y)$.

Given an i.i.d. training sample $D_n = \{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ from $\mathbb{P}$, and a positive integer $k \le n$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) decision rule $g_{n,k}$ classifies a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ by majority vote among the labels $Y_{(1)}(x),\dots,Y_{(k)}(x)$ of the $k$ training points whose features $X_{(i)}(x)$ are nearest to $x$ in Euclidean distance (ties broken by a fixed rule). Its conditional error probability is
$$P_e[k\text{-NN}](n) = \mathbb{P}\big(g_{n,k}(X) \neq Y \mid D_n\big),$$
and its expected error is $\mathbb{E}\,P_e[k\text{-NN}](n)$.

Provide a quantitative characterization of the finite-sample performance of the $k$-NN rule. Specifically, for general (or suitably specified) distributions $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{1,\dots,M\}$ and finite $n$, determine sharp non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on
$$\mathbb{E}\,P_e[k\text{-NN}](n) - P_e^*$$
as a function of $n$, $k$, the dimension $d$, and meaningful structural parameters of $\mathbb{P}$ (such as smoothness or margin conditions on $\eta_j$), and identify the choice of $k = k(n)$ that minimizes this finite-sample excess risk.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on finite-sample bounds for k-NN classification: non-asymptotic high-probability upper bounds in general metric spaces (Chaudhuri–Dasgupta), minimax-optimal rates of order n^{-4/(d+4)} under smoothness and margin (Tsybakov) conditions, and asymptotic expansions of k-NN risk are known. However, sharp distribution-free finite-sample characterizations and matching upper/lower bounds in full generality remain incomplete, so the broad question is best described as partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: In the k-nearest-neighbor rule, should all k neighbors contribute equally to the classification of an unknown pattern, or should they be weighted differently, and if so how should those neighbor weights be chosen?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,Y)$ be a random pair taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{1,\dots,c\}$ with unknown joint distribution, and let $\mathcal{D}_n = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be an i.i.d. sample from this distribution. For a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a fixed integer $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, let $x_{(1)}(x),\dots,x_{(k)}(x)$ denote the $k$ nearest neighbors of $x$ in $\mathcal{D}_n$ under a chosen metric $\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with corresponding labels $y_{(1)}(x),\dots,y_{(k)}(x)$ and distances $d_i(x) = \rho(x, x_{(i)}(x))$. A weighted $k$-nearest-neighbor rule assigns nonnegative weights $w_1(x),\dots,w_k(x)$ (possibly depending on $x$, on the distances $d_i(x)$, or on the index $i$) and classifies $x$ as
$$\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_{j \in \{1,\dots,c\}} \sum_{i=1}^{k} w_i(x)\,\mathbf{1}\{y_{(i)}(x) = j\}.$$
The uniform rule corresponds to $w_i(x) \equiv 1/k$.

Address the following: Is the uniform weighting $w_i \equiv 1/k$ optimal for minimizing the classification risk $P(\hat{Y}(X) \neq Y)$, or does there exist a weighting scheme $\{w_i(x)\}$ that strictly improves on it? In the latter case, give a principled prescription for choosing the weights $w_i(x)$ — as a function of the index $i$, the neighbor distances $d_i(x)$, the sample size $n$, the dimension $d$, the number of classes $c$, and properties of the underlying distribution — and characterize the optimality criterion (e.g., minimizing asymptotic or finite-sample misclassification probability, or excess risk over the Bayes rule) that the prescription satisfies.
status_search_result: The question of whether and how to weight k-NN neighbors has been studied extensively (e.g., Dudani's distance-weighted k-NN, Royall's work, and more recent results by Samworth (2012) on optimal weighted nearest neighbour classifiers, which derives asymptotically optimal weights minimizing the dominant terms of the regret). While substantial progress exists for specific asymptotic regimes and smooth-distribution settings, there is no universally accepted finite-sample optimal weighting scheme valid across all distributions, metrics, and dimensions, so the broader question is typically regarded as still open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: Which distance metric should be used when determining nearest neighbors in instance-based learning?
self_contained_problem:
Consider instance-based (memory-based) learning, in which a training set $S = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is stored, and predictions at a query point $x \in \mathcal{X}$ are made from the labels of the $k$ training instances $x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_k}$ minimizing $d(x, x_i)$ for some distance function $d : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. The performance of such a learner (e.g., its generalization error on an unknown data distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$) depends critically on the choice of $d$.

Problem. Provide a principled, general theory for selecting the distance metric $d$ used to determine nearest neighbors in instance-based learning. Specifically:

(a) Identify properties of the data distribution $\mathcal{D}$, the feature space $\mathcal{X}$ (which may mix numeric, ordinal, nominal, and structured attributes), and the target $\mathcal{Y}$ that determine when a given distance $d$ (for example, weighted Minkowski $d_p(x,x') = \big(\sum_j w_j |x_j - x'_j|^p\big)^{1/p}$, Mahalanobis $d_A(x,x') = \sqrt{(x-x')^\top A (x-x')}$ with $A \succeq 0$, value-difference metrics for nominal attributes, or learned metrics) is optimal or near-optimal for $k$-nearest-neighbor prediction.

(b) Give an algorithm that, from the training sample $S$ alone, selects or constructs a distance $d$ whose resulting $k$-NN rule attains generalization error close to $\inf_{d \in \mathcal{F}} \mathrm{err}_{\mathcal{D}}(k\text{-NN}_d)$ over a specified family $\mathcal{F}$ of admissible distances, with finite-sample guarantees.
status_search_result: The question of how to choose the distance metric in nearest-neighbor / instance-based learning is a longstanding open research direction. Many partial answers exist (Mahalanobis metric learning, LMNN, neighborhood components analysis, value-difference metric, deep metric learning, etc.), but no general theory prescribes the optimal metric for arbitrary data, and the problem is still treated as open in the literature on instance-based learning.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: How can a nearest-neighbor decision rule be made invariant to scaling of the measurements?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a feature space and let $T = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $x_i \in \mathcal{X}$ and $y_i$ a class label be a labeled training set. For a metric $\rho : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, the (1-)nearest-neighbor decision rule is the classifier
$$ f_{T,\rho}(x) \;=\; y_{i^*(x)}, \qquad i^*(x) \in \arg\min_{1 \leq i \leq n} \rho(x, x_i). $$
For any vector $s = (s_1, \dots, s_d) \in (0,\infty)^d$ of positive scale factors, let $D_s : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ denote the diagonal scaling $D_s(x) = (s_1 x_1, \dots, s_d x_d)$, and write $D_s(T) = \{(D_s(x_i), y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$.

Construct, in a fully data-driven way, a decision rule $g_T : \mathbb{R}^d \to \{\text{labels}\}$ depending only on the training set $T$, such that for every training set $T$, every query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and every $s \in (0,\infty)^d$,
$$ g_{D_s(T)}(D_s(x)) \;=\; g_T(x), $$
while $g_T$ retains the nearest-neighbor character (i.e., $g_T(x) = y_{i^*(x)}$ for some training index $i^*(x)$ chosen according to a notion of proximity that is intrinsically determined by $T$). In other words, design a nearest-neighbor classifier whose output is invariant under arbitrary coordinatewise rescalings of the measurements, and specify the proximity / metric construction that achieves this invariance.
status_search_result: Numerous approaches address scale sensitivity of nearest-neighbor classifiers, including feature standardization, Mahalanobis-distance learning, large-margin nearest-neighbor metric learning, and adaptive/dynamic feature-scaling schemes. These provide partial practical answers but there is no canonical fully-data-driven solution that is provably invariant under arbitrary coordinatewise rescalings while preserving nearest-neighbor semantics; the broader question is typically posed as an ongoing design challenge rather than a closed theorem, so the status is best described as unknown / informally open.

original_question: What is the smallest neural network that can implement nearest-neighbor decision rules?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S = \{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \{1, \dots, k\}$ be a finite labeled training set with all $x_i$ distinct. The nearest-neighbor decision rule $f_S : \mathbb{R}^d \to \{1, \dots, k\}$ is defined (up to ties on a measure-zero set) by 
$$f_S(x) = y_{i^*(x)}, \qquad i^*(x) \in \arg\min_{1 \le i \le n} \|x - x_i\|_2.$$
A feedforward neural network is a directed acyclic computational graph whose nodes (neurons) compute, on inputs $z \in \mathbb{R}^m$, an output of the form $\sigma(w^\top z + b)$ for some weights $w \in \mathbb{R}^m$, bias $b \in \mathbb{R}$, and a fixed activation function $\sigma$ (e.g. threshold, ReLU, or sigmoid). The size of the network is the total number of neurons (or, equivalently, one may also count layers, weights, and bit-precision of parameters).

Problem. Determine the smallest feedforward neural network (in terms of number of neurons, depth, and number of parameters) such that, for every finite labeled set $S$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, there exist parameter values making the network compute $f_S$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (except possibly on the measure-zero tie set). More precisely, characterize the minimum size, depth, and weight complexity—as functions of $n$, $d$, and $k$—of a neural network architecture that exactly realizes the nearest-neighbor classifier of any such training set.
category_tag: Neural network complexity of nearest-neighbor rules
status_search_result: Several constructions are known: a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier on n training points in R^d can be implemented by a 3-layer network of size O(nd), and synchronous neural architectures for k-NN have been proposed. Recent work on "Nearest Neighbor Representations of Neural Circuits" (2024) studies related complexity questions. However, tight lower bounds on the minimum number of neurons, depth, and weight precision required to realize arbitrary NN classifiers do not appear to be fully established, so the optimization aspect of the question remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: What is the computational complexity of computing the reduced training-set-consistent subset produced by Gates' reduced nearest neighbor rule after CNN post-processing?
self_contained_problem:
Let $T = \{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ be a labeled training set, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a finite set of class labels. For a subset $S \subseteq T$, the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{C}$ assigns to each point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the element of $S$ closest to $x$ in Euclidean distance (with ties broken by a fixed rule). The subset $S$ is said to be training-set-consistent with respect to $T$ if $\mathrm{NN}_S(x_i) = y_i$ for every $(x_i, y_i) \in T$.

Define the following two-stage reduction procedure on $T$:

1. (Condensed Nearest Neighbor, CNN) Initialize $S \subseteq T$ by Hart's procedure: start with one arbitrarily chosen element of $T$ placed in $S$, then iterate through the remaining points of $T$ (in a fixed order), adding to $S$ any point that is currently misclassified by $\mathrm{NN}_S$; repeat passes over $T$ until no more points are added.

2. (Reduced Nearest Neighbor, RNN, post-processing) Given the output $S$ of step 1, iterate through the points of $S$ (in a fixed order) and remove any point whose removal leaves a subset that is still training-set-consistent with $T$; continue until no further removal is possible. Let $S^\ast \subseteq S$ denote the resulting set.

Determine the computational complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, of computing $S^\ast$ from the input $T$.
status_search_result: Surveys of nearest-neighbor condensation techniques describe RNN as roughly twice as costly as CNN in practice, but no formal tight complexity bound for computing the RNN-reduced consistent subset after CNN post-processing was located in the search. The precise computational complexity appears to remain unresolved in the literature reviewed.

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: What is the computational complexity of finding the smallest-size training-set-consistent subset when the classification problem has exactly two classes?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane (or, more generally, in R^d for some d ≥ 2), and let c : P → {0, 1} be a 2-coloring of P (the two "classes"). A subset S ⊆ P is called training-set consistent (or a consistent subset) if, for every point p ∈ P, every nearest neighbor of p in S (with respect to Euclidean distance) has the same color as p. Equivalently, the nearest-neighbor classifier built from the labeled set (S, c|_S) correctly classifies every point of P.

The minimum consistent subset problem (MCS) asks, given (P, c), to determine a consistent subset S ⊆ P of smallest possible cardinality. It is known that for three or more color classes the corresponding decision problem ("is there a consistent subset of size at most k?") is NP-complete. 

Problem: Determine the computational complexity of the minimum consistent subset problem in the two-class case. Specifically, decide whether the decision version of MCS restricted to instances with exactly two colors is NP-complete, polynomial-time solvable, or of some intermediate complexity.
status_search_result: The two-class case was settled by Khodamoradi, Krishnamurti, and Roy (WALCOM 2018, "Consistent Subset Problem with Two Labels"), who proved that the minimum consistent subset problem is NP-complete already for two-colored point sets in R^d for every d ≥ 2, via a reduction from planar rectilinear monotone 3-SAT. Subsequent work (e.g., Biniaz–Cabello–Maheshwari–Smid, Algorithmica 2021) cites this as the resolution of the open two-class case left by Wilfong (1991).

paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
original_question: Can one design efficient algorithms for inserting and deleting vertices in useful proximity graphs such as the Gabriel graph, the relative-neighborhood graph, and the rectangular-influence graph, so that rotation-based or related error-estimation procedures can be carried out efficiently?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set of points in general position. Recall the following proximity graphs on $S$:

- The Gabriel graph $\mathrm{GG}(S)$: vertices $p,q \in S$ are joined by an edge iff the closed disk with diameter $pq$ contains no point of $S \setminus \{p,q\}$.
- The relative-neighborhood graph $\mathrm{RNG}(S)$: $p,q$ are joined iff the lune $\{x : \|x-p\| < \|p-q\|\} \cap \{x : \|x-q\| < \|p-q\|\}$ contains no point of $S \setminus \{p,q\}$.
- The rectangular-influence graph: $p,q$ are joined iff the axis-aligned rectangle having $p$ and $q$ as opposite corners contains no point of $S \setminus \{p,q\}$.

Design data structures and algorithms that maintain each of these three graphs under the operations of inserting a point into $S$ and deleting a point from $S$, with provably efficient (sub-linear amortized or polylogarithmic) update times per operation, while supporting the queries on graph adjacencies needed for rotation-based and related error-estimation procedures used in instance-based learning. Establish the best possible update-time bounds and matching lower bounds.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface algorithms specifically aimed at fully dynamic vertex insertion/deletion for the Gabriel graph, relative-neighborhood graph, and rectangular-influence graph with provable efficient update bounds. While these graphs are well-studied as subgraphs of the Delaunay triangulation (which itself admits dynamic algorithms), no definitive resolution to the combined question was located, so the status is best classified as unknown/partially addressed.

paper_title: Open Problems in Number Theory
context_brief: Central values of weight-2 newform L-functions
original_question: Let N be a sufficiently large prime, and let H_2^+(N) denote the set of weight-2 newforms of level Γ_0(N) whose functional equation has sign +1. For each f in H_2^+(N), let L(f,s) be its L-function. Iwaniec and Sarnak proved that, as N tends to infinity, at least 50% of the central values L(f,1) are larger than (log N)^(-2). Is it true that more than 50% of these central values are nonzero?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a prime number. Let $H_2^+(N)$ denote the set of normalized weight-2 holomorphic newforms $f$ for the congruence subgroup $\Gamma_0(N)$ whose completed $L$-function $\Lambda(f,s)$ satisfies a functional equation with sign $+1$ (i.e., even functional equation). For each $f \in H_2^+(N)$, let $L(f,s)$ denote its Hecke $L$-function, normalized so that the center of the critical strip is $s=1$ (equivalently, after the shift $s \mapsto s+1/2$, the central value is $L(f,1)$).

It is known that, as $N \to \infty$ through primes, at least $50\%$ of the values $\{L(f,1) : f \in H_2^+(N)\}$ exceed $(\log N)^{-2}$; in particular, at least $50\%$ of these central values are nonzero.

Problem: Prove that, as $N \to \infty$ through primes, strictly more than $50\%$ of the central values $L(f,1)$, for $f \in H_2^+(N)$, are nonzero. That is, show that
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\#\{f \in H_2^+(N) : L(f,1) \neq 0\}}{\#H_2^+(N)} > \frac{1}{2}.$$
status_search_result: The 50% non-vanishing result of Iwaniec–Sarnak (Israel J. Math., 2000) remains the benchmark. They showed that breaking the 50% barrier (with central values not too small) would rule out Landau–Siegel zeros, which is why the problem is regarded as very hard. Subsequent works (e.g., on prime power level by Balkanova–Frolenkov and others, and various one-level density investigations) have not surpassed 50% in this family. No proof of strict exceedance of 50% for weight-2 even newforms of prime level appears in the literature.

paper_title: Open Problems in Number Theory
context_brief: Generating series for rational points of arithmetic varieties
original_question: Let (V,L) be a projective manifold over a number field k together with a metrized ample sheaf, so that one has a height function h_L: V(k) → R and an associated height zeta function Z(V,L;s)=Σ_{x∈V(k)} h_L(x)^(-s). For varieties V that are not toric, the source says that this zeta function does not seem to have satisfactory analytic properties, unlike classical Hasse-Weil-Serre L-functions. Can one find a class of generating series that counts the rational points V(k) in a mathematically useful way and has good analytic behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be a number field and let $V$ be a smooth projective variety over $k$. Let $L$ be an ample line bundle on $V$ equipped with an adelic metric, giving rise to a height function $h_L : V(k) \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$. The associated height zeta function is the Dirichlet-type series
$$Z(V,L;s) \;=\; \sum_{x \in V(k)} h_L(x)^{-s},$$
which converges in some right half-plane whenever $V(k)$ is not too dense. For toric varieties and certain homogeneous spaces, $Z(V,L;s)$ is known to admit a meromorphic continuation with controlled poles, encoding precise asymptotics for the number of rational points of bounded height. However, for general (non-homogeneous) projective varieties $V$, the height zeta function $Z(V,L;s)$ is not expected to have good analytic properties (e.g. meromorphic continuation, functional equation, or a controlled set of poles) comparable to those of classical Hasse–Weil–Serre $L$-functions.

Problem: Construct a class of generating series associated with the pair $(V,L)$ over $k$, different from the naive height zeta function $Z(V,L;s)$, with the following properties:
(a) the series genuinely counts (or weights) the rational points $V(k)$, in a way that recovers meaningful arithmetic information such as asymptotics for points of bounded height;
(b) the series possesses good analytic behavior, including meromorphic continuation to a large region of $\mathbb{C}$, a precise description of its poles, and ideally a functional equation, holding for a class of varieties $V$ broader than toric or homogeneous ones.
status_search_result: This is a programmatic open question in the style of Manin's program on rational points. Refined conjectures (Batyrev–Manin, Peyre, Batyrev–Tschinkel) describe expected leading asymptotics, and height zeta functions have been analyzed for toric varieties, equivariant compactifications of algebraic groups, and certain fibrations. However, no general satisfactory class of "good" generating series for arbitrary non-homogeneous projective varieties is known, and the problem remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Number Theory
context_brief: Specialization ranks in families of abelian varieties
original_question: Suppose X is a curve over a field of characteristic 0 and π: A → X is an abelian scheme over X. Let Γ be a group of sections of π, and assume that no element of Γ factors through a subfamily of group varieties of relative dimension 1. For a geometric point P in X(ḱ), let Γ_P denote the fiber of Γ above P. Must there be only finitely many points P for which rank(Γ_P)=rank(Γ)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ with algebraic closure $\bar k$. Let $X$ be a smooth irreducible curve over $k$, and let $\pi\colon \mathcal{A}\to X$ be an abelian scheme. Denote by $\mathcal{A}(X)$ the group of sections of $\pi$, and let $\Gamma\subseteq \mathcal{A}(X)$ be a finitely generated subgroup. Assume that no nonzero element of $\Gamma$ factors through an abelian subscheme of $\mathcal{A}\to X$ whose fibers are of relative dimension one (equivalently, $\Gamma$ has no nonzero element lying in a one-dimensional abelian subscheme of $\mathcal{A}$ over $X$). 

For each geometric point $P\in X(\bar k)$, let $\Gamma_P\subseteq \mathcal{A}_P(\bar k)$ denote the image of $\Gamma$ under the specialization map $\sigma_P\colon \mathcal{A}(X)\to \mathcal{A}_P(\bar k)$ at $P$, and write $\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)$ for the rank of $\Gamma_P$ as a finitely generated abelian group. By Silverman's specialization theorem one has $\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)\ge \mathrm{rank}(\Gamma)$ for all but finitely many $P$.

Prove or disprove: there are only finitely many points $P\in X(\bar k)$ for which 
$$\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)=\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma).$$ 
Equivalently, for all but finitely many $P\in X(\bar k)$ one has $\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)>\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma)$.
category_tag: Specialization of ranks in families of abelian varieties
status_search_result: The question is a sharpening of Silverman's specialization theorem in families of abelian varieties over curves in characteristic 0, closely related to the circle of "unlikely intersections" results of Masser–Zannier and the relative Manin–Mumford / Pink–Zannier conjectures. General results of this strength (showing the rank strictly jumps at all but finitely many specializations, under a non-isotriviality / no-one-dimensional-factor hypothesis) do not appear in the literature; recent surveys and papers on specialization maps and unlikely intersections treat it as an open problem, with partial results in low dimensions and under additional hypotheses.
