paper_title: Open problems on graph eigenvalues studied with AutoGraphiX
original_question: Among all unicyclic graphs on n vertices, which graph has maximum energy E(G), defined as the sum of the absolute values of the adjacency eigenvalues? More specifically, is the maximum attained by the cycle C_n when n <= 7 and n is not 4, and also when n = 9, 10, 11, 13, or 15; by Lol_4,3 when n = 4; and by the lollipop graph Lol_n,6 for all other n, where Lol_n,g is formed by joining a cycle C_g to a path P_(n-g) by a single edge between a cycle vertex and a path endpoint?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a simple graph and let λ_1, λ_2, …, λ_n be the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix. The energy of G is defined by
   E(G) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} |λ_i|.
A graph is called unicyclic if it is connected and contains exactly one cycle (equivalently, has n vertices and n edges). For integers n ≥ g ≥ 3, the lollipop graph Lol_{n,g} is the unicyclic graph on n vertices obtained from a cycle C_g and a path P_{n−g} by adding a single edge between one vertex of the cycle and an endpoint of the path.

Determine the unicyclic graph on n vertices that maximizes E(G). Specifically, prove or disprove that the maximum is attained by:
 (a) the cycle C_n, when n ∈ {3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15};
 (b) the lollipop Lol_{4,3}, when n = 4;
 (c) the lollipop Lol_{n,6}, for all other values of n ≥ 8.
status_search_result: The conjecture on the maximum-energy unicyclic graph was completely settled by Huo, Li, and Shi (2011), "Complete solution to a conjecture on the maximal energy of unicyclic graphs" (Eur. J. Combin. / arXiv:1011.4658), using the Coulson integral formula and combinatorial estimates, confirming that Lol_{n,6} (denoted P_n^6 in their notation) is the maximizer for all n ∈ {8, 12, 14} and n ≥ 16, while C_n is the maximizer in the remaining listed cases and Lol_{4,3} when n = 4.

paper_title: Open problems on graph eigenvalues studied with AutoGraphiX
original_question: For every tricyclic graph G on n vertices with n = 20 or n >= 22, is the energy E(G) at most E(P_n^{6,6;6}), where P_n^{6,6;6} is the graph formed from three copies of C_6 and a path P_(n-18) by joining two of the 6-cycles to one endpoint of the path and the third 6-cycle to the other endpoint, one edge per attachment? Must equality occur only for G isomorphic to P_n^{6,6;6}?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite simple graph $G$, let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix, and define the graph energy by
$$E(G)=\sum_{i=1}^n |\lambda_i|.$$
A connected graph on $n$ vertices is called tricyclic if it has exactly $n+2$ edges. For integers $n\ge 19$, let $P_n^{6,6;6}$ denote the tricyclic graph constructed as follows: take three vertex-disjoint copies of the $6$-cycle $C_6$ and a path $P_{n-18}$ on $n-18$ vertices; attach two of the $6$-cycles to one endpoint of the path by adding one edge from each cycle to that endpoint, and attach the third $6$-cycle to the other endpoint of the path by adding one edge.

Prove or disprove: for every tricyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $n=20$ or $n\ge 22$,
$$E(G)\le E(P_n^{6,6;6}),$$
with equality if and only if $G\cong P_n^{6,6;6}$.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that while analogous conjectures for unicyclic and bipartite bicyclic graphs have been completely resolved (Huo–Li–Shi and collaborators), the tricyclic case remains open: partial results restrict the conjecture to bipartite tricyclic graphs with three vertex-disjoint cycles and verify it apart from a small number of subclasses, but no complete proof has been reported.

paper_title: Open problems on graph eigenvalues studied with AutoGraphiX
original_question: Let r and n be positive integers with n >= 6r + 4, and let p = floor(r/2) and q = ceil(r/2). If P_n^{p×6;q×6} denotes the graph obtained from r copies of C_6 and a path P_(n-6r) with endpoints u and v by joining u to one vertex in each of p of the 6-cycles and v to one vertex in each of the remaining q 6-cycles, one edge per attachment, does every connected r-cyclic graph G on n vertices satisfy E(G) <= E(P_n^{p×6;q×6})? Must equality occur only when G is isomorphic to P_n^{p×6;q×6}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a simple graph. The energy of $G$ is $E(G)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_i|$, where $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of $G$. A connected graph on $n$ vertices with $m$ edges is called $r$-cyclic if $m=n+r-1$ (equivalently, its cyclomatic number is $r$).

For positive integers $r$ and $n$ with $n\ge 6r+4$, set $p=\lfloor r/2\rfloor$ and $q=\lceil r/2\rceil$. Let $C_6^{(1)},\dots,C_6^{(r)}$ be $r$ vertex-disjoint copies of the 6-cycle, and let $P_{n-6r}$ be a path on $n-6r$ vertices with endpoints $u$ and $v$. Define the graph $P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}$ to be obtained from the disjoint union of $P_{n-6r}$ and the $r$ copies of $C_6$ by adding $r$ edges: from $u$ to exactly one vertex of each of $p$ of the 6-cycles, and from $v$ to exactly one vertex of each of the remaining $q$ 6-cycles (one edge per attached cycle). Note that $P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}$ is a connected $r$-cyclic graph on $n$ vertices.

Prove or disprove: for every connected $r$-cyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices,
$$E(G)\le E\bigl(P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}\bigr),$$
with equality if and only if $G\cong P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}$.
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open in general. It was formulated via AutoGraphiX experiments as a general $r$-cyclic extension of the maximum-energy conjectures for unicyclic, bicyclic, tricyclic and tetracyclic graphs. While the unicyclic case has been completely settled and partial progress exists for tricyclic and tetracyclic cases, no proof of the general $r$-cyclic statement for $n\ge 6r+4$ has been found in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems on k-orbit polytopes
original_question: Given a general k-orbit polytope together with a distinguished generating set for its automorphism group, describe a construction that rebuilds the polytope as a coset geometry of that group, in the same spirit that regular and chiral polytopes can be reconstructed from suitable generator data.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) are graded by rank from -1 to n, in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly one face of each rank, which is strongly flag-connected, and which satisfies the diamond condition: whenever F < G are faces with ranks differing by 2, there are exactly two faces strictly between F and G. The automorphism group Aut(P) acts freely on flags; P is called a k-orbit polytope if this action has exactly k orbits on flags. For a regular polytope (k=1), fixing a base flag Φ yields distinguished involutory generators ρ_0,...,ρ_{n-1} of Aut(P), and P can be reconstructed as the coset geometry on Aut(P) with respect to the parabolic subgroups generated by all ρ_i except one. An analogous coset-geometry reconstruction is known for chiral polytopes (a class of 2-orbit polytopes).

Problem. Let P be an arbitrary k-orbit abstract polytope (k ≥ 1) and let Γ = Aut(P) be equipped with a distinguished set of generators arising from the flag-orbit structure of P. Provide a general construction that recovers P as a coset geometry of Γ from this generator data alone, giving necessary and sufficient conditions (on the generators and on intersections of certain subgroups) under which an abstractly given group with such a generating set arises as the automorphism group of a k-orbit polytope reconstructable from those generators.
status_search_result: A 2023 paper by Hubard and Schulte ("All polytopes are coset geometries: Characterizing automorphism groups of k-orbit abstract polytopes") provides a general coset-geometry reconstruction of any abstract polytope from its automorphism group together with a distinguished generating set, and characterizes such groups by generator/intersection conditions. Specific small cases (k = 2 chiral, k = 3 polyhedra) have explicit detailed treatments. Hence the problem is largely resolved in general, though sharper case-by-case characterizations for higher k continue to be studied.

paper_title: Open problems on k-orbit polytopes
original_question: Characterize exactly which abstract polytopes P have monodromy group Mon(P) that is a string C-group, so that the minimal regular cover obtained from Mon(P) is itself polytopal.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set P of "faces", with a unique minimum face and a unique maximum face, in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly n+2 elements, P is strongly flag-connected, and the diamond condition holds: whenever F < G are faces with rank(G) − rank(F) = 2, there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G. For each i ∈ {0, 1, …, n−1} and each flag Φ of P, there is a unique flag Φ^i differing from Φ only in the face of rank i. The monodromy group Mon(P) is the subgroup of the symmetric group on the set F(P) of flags generated by the permutations σ_0, σ_1, …, σ_{n−1} defined by σ_i(Φ) = Φ^i.

A string C-group of rank n is a pair (G, {ρ_0, …, ρ_{n−1}}) where G is a group generated by involutions ρ_0, …, ρ_{n−1} that satisfy the string condition (ρ_i ρ_j)^2 = 1 whenever |i − j| ≥ 2 and the intersection condition ⟨ρ_i : i ∈ I⟩ ∩ ⟨ρ_i : i ∈ J⟩ = ⟨ρ_i : i ∈ I ∩ J⟩ for all I, J ⊆ {0, …, n−1}. When Mon(P) (with its distinguished generators σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}) is a string C-group, the abstract regular polytope associated with Mon(P) is the (unique) minimal regular cover of P; when Mon(P) fails the intersection condition, this construction does not yield a polytope.

Problem. Give a complete characterization of those abstract polytopes P for which Mon(P), with its distinguished generators σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}, is a string C-group (equivalently, for which the minimal regular cover of P obtained from Mon(P) is itself an abstract polytope).
status_search_result: The problem remains an active area of investigation. While Mon(P) is always a string C-group when P has rank ≤ 3, examples such as the tomotope show this fails for rank ≥ 4, and determining which polytopes are "C-connected" (i.e., have monodromy group satisfying the intersection condition) is described in the literature as an ongoing open research direction with no general characterization available.

paper_title: Open problems on k-orbit polytopes
original_question: Given a string group generated by involutions, determine the minimal string C-groups that cover it.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group and let $S = (\rho_0, \rho_1, \ldots, \rho_{n-1})$ be an ordered generating set of $G$ such that each $\rho_i$ is an involution and the involutions satisfy the string commuting property: $(\rho_i \rho_j)^2 = 1$ whenever $|i-j| \ge 2$. Such a pair $(G,S)$ is called a string group generated by involutions (sggi).

An sggi $(G,S)$ is called a string C-group if, in addition, it satisfies the intersection property: for every $I, J \subseteq \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$,
$$\langle \rho_i : i \in I\rangle \cap \langle \rho_j : j \in J\rangle = \langle \rho_k : k \in I \cap J\rangle.$$

Given two sggis $(G,S)$ and $(\widetilde G, \widetilde S)$ of the same rank $n$, we say that $(\widetilde G,\widetilde S)$ covers $(G,S)$ if the map $\widetilde \rho_i \mapsto \rho_i$ extends to a surjective group homomorphism $\widetilde G \to G$. A cover $(\widetilde G, \widetilde S)$ of $(G,S)$ that is a string C-group is called minimal if no proper quotient of $(\widetilde G,\widetilde S)$ (other than $(G,S)$ itself if it happens to be a string C-group) covers $(G,S)$ and is a string C-group.

Problem: Given an arbitrary string group generated by involutions $(G,S)$, determine all minimal string C-groups that cover $(G,S)$.
status_search_result: No published resolution of this problem was located. Related work develops the theory of string C-groups and computational tools (e.g., the SGGI Magma package) for sggis, and constructions of minimal common covers exist in special cases for regular polyhedra, but a general determination of minimal string C-group covers of an arbitrary sggi does not appear in the literature. The problem appears to remain open.

(i) G is connected, and

context_brief: symmetry type graphs of convex polytopes
original_question: Which symmetry type graphs occur among convex polytopes, both at the combinatorial level and at the geometric level?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

A convex polytope P in Euclidean space is a bounded intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces; it has a face lattice F(P) consisting of its faces (vertices, edges, …, facets, together with the empty face and P itself) ordered by inclusion. A flag of P is a maximal chain in F(P): one face of each dimension from −1 to dim P, pairwise incident. For each i ∈ {0, 1, …, dim P − 1}, every flag Φ has a unique i-adjacent flag Φ^i, obtained by replacing the i-dimensional face of Φ by the unique other face of that dimension lying between the (i−1)- and (i+1)-faces of Φ.

The combinatorial automorphism group Γ(P) is the group of order-preserving bijections of F(P), and the geometric symmetry group G(P) is the group of Euclidean isometries of the ambient space that map P to itself. Both groups act on the set of flags of P. The combinatorial symmetry type graph T_c(P) is the edge-colored multigraph whose vertices are the Γ(P)-orbits of flags, and in which two orbits O and O' are joined by an edge of color i whenever some flag in O is i-adjacent to some flag in O' (loops of color i are allowed when O = O'); the resulting graph is properly i-edge-colored in the sense that each vertex is incident with exactly one edge or loop of each color i ∈ {0, …, dim P − 1}. The geometric symmetry type graph T_g(P) is defined analogously using the orbits of G(P) acting on flags.

Problem. Characterize precisely which finite edge-colored multigraphs arise as combinatorial symmetry type graphs T_c(P) of convex polytopes P, and which arise as geometric symmetry type graphs T_g(P) of convex polytopes P. Equivalently, give necessary and sufficient conditions on such a graph T (with edge colors in {0, 1, …, n−1}, each vertex incident with exactly one edge of each color, and satisfying the standard 2-factor commutativity required of flag-graph quotients) for the existence of an n-dimensional convex polytope P whose combinatorial (respectively geometric) symmetry type graph equals T.

original_question: Fix Euclidean space E^d. For each symmetry type graph T, determine the largest rank n for which there exist finite n-polytopes, and separately infinite n-polytopes, admitting a faithful symmetric realization in E^d with symmetry type graph T.

Let $d\ge 1$ be a fixed integer, and let $\mathbb{E}^d$ denote Euclidean $d$-space with isometry group $\mathrm{Iso}(\mathbb{E}^d)$. An abstract $n$-polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is a ranked partially ordered set (with ranks $-1,0,1,\dots,n$) whose elements (called faces) satisfy the standard combinatorial axioms for abstract polytopes: it has a unique least face and unique greatest face, every maximal chain (flag) has exactly $n+2$ elements, $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected, and it satisfies the diamond condition (every section of rank $1$ has exactly two faces of the intermediate rank). The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts on the set of flags, and the symmetry type graph $T(\mathcal{P},\Gamma)$ of $\mathcal{P}$ under a subgroup $\Gamma\le\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ is the edge-labeled multigraph (with labels in $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$) whose vertices are the orbits of $\Gamma$ on flags and whose $i$-labeled edges record the $i$-adjacency of flags between orbits.

A realization of $\mathcal{P}$ in $\mathbb{E}^d$ is a mapping $\beta$ from the vertex set of $\mathcal{P}$ to $\mathbb{E}^d$ that extends recursively to all faces so that each $j$-face is sent to the set of $(j-1)$-faces it contains. The realization is called faithful if $\beta$ is injective on the faces of each rank, and symmetric if every automorphism in some chosen subgroup $\Gamma\le\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ is induced by an isometry of $\mathbb{E}^d$; in that case the symmetry type graph of the realization is defined to be $T(\mathcal{P},\Gamma)$.

(a) the largest integer $n$ for which there exists a finite abstract $n$-polytope admitting a faithful symmetric realization in $\mathbb{E}^d$ whose symmetry type graph equals $T$;

(b) the largest integer $n$ for which there exists an infinite abstract $n$-polytope admitting a faithful symmetric realization in $\mathbb{E}^d$ whose symmetry type graph equals $T$.

The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called two-orbit if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts on $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{P})$ with exactly two orbits (in particular it is not flag-transitive). 

Problem: Classify, up to isometry of $\mathbb{H}^3$, all two-orbit 4-polytopes in $\mathbb{H}^3$, i.e. determine all such hyperbolic tessellations whose symmetry group has exactly two orbits on flags.

paper_title: Open problems on k-orbit polytopes
context_brief: faithful Euclidean realizations with matching orbit count
original_question: Which k-orbit d-polytopes admit a faithful realization in Euclidean d-space E^d as geometrically k-orbit polytopes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be an abstract $d$-polytope, i.e. a ranked partially ordered set with a strict face structure satisfying the usual conditions (existence of a least and greatest face, the diamond condition, and strong flag-connectedness) and whose proper faces have ranks $0,1,\dots,d-1$. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts on the set of flags of $\mathcal{P}$; one says that $\mathcal{P}$ is a $k$-orbit polytope if this action has exactly $k$ orbits.

A (Euclidean) realization of $\mathcal{P}$ in $\mathbb{E}^d$ is a mapping $\beta$ that assigns to each vertex of $\mathcal{P}$ a point of $\mathbb{E}^d$, extended recursively to higher-rank faces by assigning to each face $F$ the set (or convex hull, in the convex case) of images of the vertices incident with $F$. The realization is called faithful when $\beta$ is one-to-one on the faces of every rank, so that the geometric figure obtained inherits the combinatorial structure of $\mathcal{P}$ without collapse. The symmetry group $G(\beta(\mathcal{P}))$ is the group of Euclidean isometries of $\mathbb{E}^d$ that permute the realized faces; the realization is called geometrically $k'$-orbit if $G(\beta(\mathcal{P}))$ acts on the flags of $\beta(\mathcal{P})$ with exactly $k'$ orbits.

Characterize the $k$-orbit abstract $d$-polytopes $\mathcal{P}$ that admit a faithful realization in $\mathbb{E}^d$ which is geometrically $k$-orbit, that is, for which the Euclidean symmetry group of the realization acts with exactly the same number $k$ of flag orbits as the combinatorial automorphism group of $\mathcal{P}$.
status_search_result: The problem appears in a published list of open problems on k-orbit polytopes and is stated as an open question. Searches reveal related results on realizations of abstract regular polytopes and dimension bounds, but no characterization of which k-orbit d-polytopes admit faithful geometrically k-orbit realizations in E^d has been found in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems on k-orbit polytopes
original_question: Develop a theory of k-orbit realizations of regular polytopes.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract n-polytope is a partially ordered set satisfying the standard axioms (bounded, graded with rank function taking values in {-1,0,...,n}, the diamond condition, and strong flag-connectedness). A flag is a maximal chain. The automorphism group acts on the set of flags; the polytope is called regular when this action is transitive, and k-orbit when there are exactly k flag orbits.

A realization of a regular abstract polytope P is a mapping β from the vertex set of P (the rank-0 elements) into a Euclidean space V such that every automorphism of P is induced by some isometry of V; this notion extends to a mapping of all faces into the lattice of affine subspaces of V. The set of all realizations of a fixed regular polytope, modulo congruence and trivial degeneracies, carries the structure of a closed convex cone whose extreme rays correspond to the irreducible orthogonal representations of the automorphism group, giving a rich theory of realizations for regular polytopes.

Problem. Develop an analogous theory of realizations for k-orbit abstract polytopes with k ≥ 2. That is, formulate an appropriate definition of a realization of a k-orbit abstract polytope (specifying how the automorphism group, or a suitable enlargement of it acting on flag orbits, must act by isometries on the image), describe the resulting space (or cone) of realizations, identify its extremal/irreducible elements and their relation to representations of the relevant group, and establish the structural results (such as decomposition into irreducible realizations and a Wythoffian/orbit-based construction) that parallel the established theory in the regular (1-orbit) case.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a research program asking for the development of a theory analogous to McMullen–Schulte's realization theory of regular polytopes, but for k-orbit polytopes. While partial progress exists on realizations in special cases (e.g., 2-orbit and 3-orbit polyhedra in ordinary space) and on representation-theoretic frameworks, no comprehensive theory of k-orbit realizations has been established. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: For the graph-model version of Isaacs' princess and monster game, where the searcher finds the hider once they are in the same place, solve the game on graphs other than the circle. In particular, determine the correct solution for the interval case, which the source says is not solved but only conjectured.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following zero-sum pursuit-evasion game (the "princess and monster" game) played on a connected graph G = (V, E) whose edges are isometric to closed intervals of given positive lengths, equipped with the induced shortest-path metric. Two players, a Searcher S (the monster) and a Hider H (the princess), each move continuously along G with speed at most 1. The game takes place in continuous time t ≥ 0. At t = 0 each player independently chooses a (possibly randomized) starting point in G, and thereafter each player chooses a (measurable) trajectory of speed at most 1; the Searcher does not see the Hider's position and the Hider does not see the Searcher's position. The capture time T is the first time t ≥ 0 at which the two players occupy the same point of G. The Searcher seeks to minimize, and the Hider to maximize, the expected capture time E[T]. Let V(G) denote the value of this game.

(a) For graphs G other than a single circle (a graph isometric to a circle of given total length L, for which the value is known to equal L/2 times an established constant), determine V(G) and optimal strategies for both players.

(b) In particular, solve the case in which G is a closed interval [0, 1] of length 1: determine the exact value V([0,1]) and exhibit optimal (or ε-optimal) mixed strategies for both the Searcher and the Hider.
status_search_result: The princess-and-monster game on a graph has been solved only for the circle. For the interval, Alpern, Fokkink, Lindelauf, and Olsder (SIAM J. Control Optim., 2008) showed the value V satisfies 15/11 ≤ V ≤ 13/9 (with V < 3/2), and derived properties of optimal strategies, but the exact value and optimal strategies remain unknown. No complete solution for the interval, or for general graphs, appears in the literature, so the problem is still open.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: Consider the princess and monster game on the interval [-1,1], where the monster moves continuously with maximum speed 1 and the princess may relocate with unbounded speed. Let M1 be the monster strategy that chooses an arbitrary initial point and direction, runs to one endpoint, and then back to the other endpoint; let M2 be the strategy that again chooses an arbitrary initial point and direction, runs until meeting the sweeper coming from that direction, then turns around, joins that sweeper, and finally traverses to the other endpoint; and let P be the class of princess strategies that either stay at an endpoint or start at a point in [-1+ε,-ε]∪[ε,1-ε], wait until the nearest-end sweeper is ε-close, then run to the middle and back to an endpoint. Is it true that against any mixed strategy supported on M1∪M2 there exists an optimal princess response supported on P, so that the interval game reduces to the stated optimization problem?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Princess-and-Monster pursuit-evasion game played on the closed interval [-1,1]. The Monster moves continuously along the interval with speed at most 1; the Princess may relocate instantaneously to any point (her position is hidden). Neither player observes the other. The payoff to the Monster is the (first) capture time, defined as the first time t ≥ 0 at which the two players occupy the same point; the Monster minimizes and the Princess maximizes the expected capture time.

Define the following pure Monster strategies, parameterized by an initial point x₀ ∈ [-1,1] and a direction d ∈ {-1,+1}:
• M1(x₀,d): start at x₀, move at speed 1 in direction d until reaching the corresponding endpoint, then reverse and traverse to the opposite endpoint.
• M2(x₀,d): start at x₀, move at speed 1 in direction d until meeting the "sweeper" coming from that direction (i.e., a Monster trajectory of type M1 traveling toward the same endpoint), then turn around and join that sweeper to the endpoint in direction d, then reverse and traverse to the opposite endpoint.

Fix an infinitesimal ε > 0 and define the following pure Princess strategies, forming a class P:
• Stay forever at an endpoint -1 or +1.
• Choose an initial point y₀ ∈ [-1+ε, -ε] ∪ [ε, 1-ε], remain stationary until the M1-type sweeper that starts at the endpoint nearest to y₀ is within distance ε of y₀, then run at unbounded speed to the midpoint 0, and finally run back to the endpoint on the same side as y₀.

It is known that, against any mixed Princess strategy supported on P, there exists an optimal Monster response supported on M1 ∪ M2.

Question: Is the converse true? That is, against any mixed Monster strategy supported on M1 ∪ M2, does there exist an optimal Princess response supported on P? Equivalently, does the Princess-and-Monster game on [-1,1] reduce to the finite-dimensional optimization problem (solvable by discretization and linear programming) of finding a saddle point in mixed strategies on (M1 ∪ M2) × P?
status_search_result: The princess-and-monster game on an interval remains unsolved: while the value on a circle is known, on the interval only bounds (e.g., 15/11 ≤ V ≤ 13/9) are established, and the conjecture that optimal strategies are supported on the described classes M1 ∪ M2 and P (which would reduce the game to a finite linear program) is reported as unproven in subsequent literature including a numerical-approach paper and a 2023 thesis.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: In Gilbert's high-low search game, Blue chooses a secret number h, after each guess tells Red whether the guess is too high, too low, or correct, and may then change the secret number provided the new choice remains consistent with all previous answers. If V(n) is the value of the n-number game, is it true that V(n) - log2(n) converges to a constant c as n→∞, with c approximately 0.487?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two-player zero-sum search game with parameter $n \geq 1$. Blue secretly maintains a number $h \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. In each round, Red announces a guess $g \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, and Blue must truthfully answer "too high", "too low", or "correct" relative to some value $h$, but Blue is allowed to change $h$ between rounds as long as every answer given so far remains consistent with at least one fixed sequence of valid choices (equivalently, Blue maintains the set $S$ of remaining candidates; on a guess $g$, Blue chooses one of the responses "high", "low", or "correct" and updates $S$ to $\{x \in S : x < g\}$, $\{x \in S : x > g\}$, or $\{g\}$ respectively). The game ends when Red identifies the unique remaining value; the payoff to Blue (and the loss to Red) is the number of guesses Red used. Both players play optimally. Let $V(n)$ denote the value of this game starting from $S = \{1,\ldots,n\}$.

Determine whether
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(V(n) - \log_2 n\bigr) = c$$
exists, and whether $c \approx 0.487$.
status_search_result: Public search results indicate that Gilbert's high–low search game with a mutable secret remains studied as an unsolved problem, with the asymptotic behavior of V(n) − log₂ n stated as a conjecture rather than a theorem. No source found establishing the limit or the value c ≈ 0.487.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: In the same continuous high-low guessing game with h in [0,1], high/low feedback after each guess, and payoff Σ|g_n-h| to the hider, what is an optimal strategy for the hider?
self_contained_problem:
Two players, a Hider and a Guesser, play the following infinite-horizon game. The Hider secretly chooses a number $h \in [0,1]$ (possibly according to a randomized strategy, i.e., a probability distribution on $[0,1]$). The Guesser then makes a sequence of guesses $g_1, g_2, g_3, \ldots \in [0,1]$; after each guess $g_n$, the Guesser is told only whether $g_n > h$ ("too high") or $g_n < h$ ("too low"). (The event $g_n = h$ occurs with probability zero under any nonatomic distribution and is ignored.) The Guesser uses this high/low feedback to choose subsequent guesses, and aims to minimize the total payoff
$$P = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |g_n - h|,$$
which is paid to the Hider; the Hider aims to maximize the expected value of $P$.

Determine an optimal (in general, randomized) strategy for the Hider in this zero-sum game, i.e., a probability distribution on $[0,1]$ that attains
$$\sup_{\mu} \inf_{\text{Guesser strategies}} \mathbb{E}_{h \sim \mu}\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |g_n - h|\right].$$
status_search_result: The problem is described as an unsolved open problem in a compilation of open problems on search games at zbMATH (6687175), which explicitly states "An optimal strategy for the hider has never been determined." A web search did not surface any subsequent work resolving the optimal hider strategy for this continuous high-low guessing game with cumulative-distance payoff.

paper_title: Open Problems on Search Games
original_question: Consider the continuous high-low guessing framework restricted to two guesses, with payoff (g2-h)^2 to the hider. What are the optimal strategies in this two-guess quadratic-payoff game?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a two-person zero-sum game played as follows. A hider secretly chooses a real number h in [0,1] according to some probability distribution. A searcher, without knowing h, chooses two real numbers g_1, g_2 in [0,1] (the "guesses"), where g_2 may depend on information revealed after the first guess in the standard continuous high-low fashion: after the searcher announces g_1, the hider truthfully reveals whether h < g_1, h = g_1, or h > g_1, and then the searcher selects g_2. The payoff from the searcher to the hider is

    (g_2 − h)^2.

The searcher wants to minimize, and the hider wants to maximize, the expected payoff. Determine the value of this game and describe an optimal (possibly mixed) strategy for the hider and an optimal strategy for the searcher.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Consider two Lagrangian fibrations phi: M 4 → B and phi′: M ′4 → B′. Assume that B and B′ are affinely equivalent in the sense that there exists an affine d iffeomorphism psi: B → B′. Is it true that under these assumptions the corresponding Lagr angian fibrations are symplectomorphic? In the local and semi-global setting, we may ask a similar question for a Lagrangian fibration in a neigh- bourhood of a singular point or of a singular fiber. According to the E liasson theorem [72, 166, 169], in the non-degenerate case, there are no local symplectic invarian ts. In other words, non-degenerate singular points of the same topological (algebraic) type are locally fib erwise symplectomorphic. The case of non-degenerate singular fibers has been discussed in [65, 2 25, 185, 186] for basic singularities of elliptic, hyperbolic, and focus types. One of the main observation s made in these papers is that every action variable can be written in the form I = Ising + Ireg, where the singular part Ising is the same for all singularities of a given topological type (due to Eliasson's result) and Ireg is a smooth function which can be arbitrary. This regular part (or its Taylor exp ansion) in many cases may serve as a complete symplectic invariant in semi-global setting. Let us now discuss what happens in the case of degenerate singular ities.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\phi: M^4 \to B$ and $\phi': M'^4 \to B'$ be two Lagrangian fibrations of four-dimensional symplectic manifolds (so each fiber is a smooth Lagrangian submanifold). The bases $B$ and $B'$ carry the natural integral affine structures induced by action variables (away from singular values). Assume that $B$ and $B'$ are affinely equivalent, i.e., there exists an affine diffeomorphism $\psi: B \to B'$ that preserves the integral affine structure (and, in the singular setting, the stratification by singular values together with the topological types of singularities).

Question: Does there necessarily exist a fiberwise symplectomorphism $\Phi: M \to M'$ covering $\psi$, that is, with $\phi' \circ \Phi = \psi \circ \phi$?

Formulate and answer the same question in the following local and semi-global settings:
(a) globally, for $\phi$ and $\phi'$ defined on all of $M^4$ and $M'^4$;
(b) locally, in a neighborhood of a singular point of the fibration;
(c) semi-globally, in a saturated neighborhood of a singular fiber.

In particular, determine whether affine equivalence of the bases is a complete symplectic invariant of the Lagrangian fibration in each of the settings (a), (b), and (c), including the case of degenerate singularities.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a 2018 survey of finite-dimensional integrable systems. Subsequent work (e.g., on symplectic invariants for parabolic orbits and cusp singularities, and on hypersemitoric systems) addresses particular non-degenerate and some degenerate singular cases via the "I_sing + I_reg" decomposition, but no general affirmative or negative answer in the global or degenerate semi-global setting appears to have been established.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Assume that we know explicit formulas for the action variabl es I1,..., In so that we are able to analyse their asymptotic behaviour in a neighb ourhood of a singular fiber. Can we recover the topology of this singularity from the asymptoti c behaviour (or at least to distinguish between different types of singularities)? For example, we know that, in the case of non-degenerate hyperbolic singularities, the singular part Ising is of the form h ln h +.... Is this property characteristic for non-degenerate hyperbolic singularities? The case of one d egree of freedom is understood in [99]. For degenerate singularities, this question becomes, of course, m ore interesting and important. Another interesting problem would be a description of singularities, b oth in local and semi-global setting, which may occur in algebraically integrable systems. There is no commonly accepted definition of algebraic integrability (see discussion on this subject and relevan t definitions in [220]) and the answer may depend on the approach used. In the most natural setting, a lgebraic integrability assumes that the commuting functions F1,..., Fn are polynomials and one can naturally complexify all the related objects (including the phase space, symplectic or Poisson structu re, and time) so that the integrable system under consideration becomes the real part of a certain co mplex integrable system. The crucial additional condition on this complex system is that its general comple x fibers are isomorphic to affine parts of Abelian varieties (see [220]) which imposes rather strong to pological conditions on singularities. For instance, in the case of one degree of freedom, it implies that th e Milnor number of a singular point cannot be greater than 2. In other words, singularities of alg ebraically integrable systems are expected to be very special.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M^{2n}, \omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold and let $F = (F_1, \dots, F_n) : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a completely integrable system, i.e., the functions $F_1, \dots, F_n$ are smooth, functionally independent on an open dense set, and pairwise Poisson-commute: $\{F_i, F_j\} = 0$. Near a regular fiber, Arnold–Liouville coordinates yield action variables $I_1(c), \dots, I_n(c)$, where $c = (c_1, \dots, c_n)$ ranges over values of $F$ in a punctured neighbourhood of a critical value corresponding to a singular fiber $F^{-1}(c_0)$.

Assume explicit formulas for the action variables $I_k(c)$ are available, so that their asymptotic expansion as $c \to c_0$ can be analysed. Decompose $I_k$ as $I_k = I_k^{reg} + I_k^{sing}$, where $I_k^{reg}$ is real-analytic at $c_0$ and $I_k^{sing}$ carries the non-smooth part.

(a) Determine to what extent the topology of the singular fiber and of its tubular neighbourhood (the local and semi-local topological type of the singularity, in the sense of the Eliasson–Williamson classification and its degenerate generalizations) is reconstructible from the asymptotic behaviour of $I_k^{sing}(c)$ as $c \to c_0$. In particular, can different topological types of singularities always be distinguished by these asymptotics?

(b) It is known that, for one degree of freedom, a non-degenerate hyperbolic singularity produces a singular part of the form $I^{sing}(h) = h \ln h + \dots$ near the critical value $h = 0$. Prove or disprove: in arbitrary dimension $n$, the appearance of an $h \ln h$-type term in $I_k^{sing}$ is a characteristic property of non-degenerate hyperbolic singularities (and singularities containing a hyperbolic block).

(c) Investigate the analogous question for degenerate singularities: classify the possible asymptotic forms of action variables near degenerate singular fibers and relate them to the topology of the singularity.

(d) Describe which local and semi-local singularities can occur in algebraically integrable systems, in the following sense: $F_1, \dots, F_n$ are polynomials on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, the system admits a complexification to a complex integrable system whose generic complex fibers are isomorphic to affine parts of abelian varieties. (For one degree of freedom this restricts the Milnor number of a singular point to be at most $2$.) Provide a classification of admissible singularity types in this algebraic setting.
status_search_result: The question is listed as an open problem in a 2018 survey on finite-dimensional integrable systems by Bolsinov, Izosimov, and Tsonev (zbMath 7030249). I found no subsequent work resolving the higher-dimensional characterization of non-degenerate hyperbolic singularities via action-variable asymptotics, nor a complete classification of singularities in algebraically integrable systems. The one-degree-of-freedom case is treated in earlier literature, but the multidimensional and degenerate cases appear to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Extend the classification of semitoric systems F = (J, H) in [185, 186] to allow for F having non-degenerate singularities with hyperbolic bloc ks (a version of this problem was mentioned in various forms in [188]). The first step in this direction is in Dullin et al [70], see also a general approach to the symplectic classification problem in Zung [238]. Note that, in contrast with the semitoric case, even the topology o f a small neighbourhood of a singular fiber can be quite complicated, see e.g. [23, 37, 121, 151, 158, 159, 160, 183, 236, 237, 238]. There are also a number of interesting problems at the intersection of integrable systems and Hamil- tonian compact group actions, the following being one of them.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a connected symplectic $4$-manifold, and let $F=(J,H):M\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. a smooth map whose components Poisson-commute and are functionally independent almost everywhere. Recall that a singular point $p\in M$ of $F$ is non-degenerate (in the Williamson sense) if the linearizations $dJ_p$, $dH_p$ generate a Cartan subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\mathrm{sp}(T_pM,\omega_p)$; in dimension four such a subalgebra decomposes as a direct sum of blocks of four possible types: elliptic, hyperbolic, focus–focus, and (in the corank-one case) regular.

A semitoric system is such an $F=(J,H)$ in which $J$ is proper and generates an effective Hamiltonian $S^1$-action, all singular points are non-degenerate, and no singular point has a hyperbolic block. Semitoric systems have been classified up to isomorphism by a list of symplectic invariants (number of focus–focus points, the Taylor-series invariant at each focus–focus point, the polygon invariant, the height invariant, and the twisting-index invariant).

Problem. Extend this classification to the class of integrable systems $F=(J,H)$ on $4$-dimensional symplectic manifolds for which $J$ still generates a proper Hamiltonian $S^1$-action and all singularities are non-degenerate, but where singular points with hyperbolic blocks are allowed. More precisely: produce a complete list of symplectic invariants, together with a realization theorem, classifying such systems up to isomorphism (where two systems $F_1$, $F_2$ are isomorphic if there exists a symplectomorphism $\varphi$ with $\varphi^*J_2=J_1$ and $\varphi^*H_2=f(J_1,H_1)$ for some smooth function $f$ with $\partial f/\partial H_1>0$).
status_search_result: The problem of extending the Pelayo–Vũ Ngọc semitoric classification to allow hyperbolic blocks is the subject of active recent research. Hohloch and Palmer introduced "hypersemitoric systems" as a natural framework, and recent preprints (e.g. "Towards hypersemitoric systems", 2023, and "On the affine invariant of simple hypersemitoric systems", 2024) develop partial invariants (polygon/affine invariants, treatments of parabolic and transversally-hyperbolic singularities, Hopf-bifurcation constructions). A complete symplectic classification analogous to the semitoric case is not yet established, so the problem appears partially solved.

original_question: Study the topology and geometry of these singular fibers and t heir small neighbourhoods. First results in this directions are due to D. Bouloc [40], where the ben ding flows of 3D polygons and the system on the 2-Grasmannian manifold were studied, and by Bouloc et al [41] for the Gelfand-Cetlin system. The natural conjecture is that, in most cases, the degenerate s ingular fibers are still smooth manifolds or orbifolds and, moreover, they are isotropic (or even Lagrangia n). They represent a new interesting class of singularities in integrable systems for which almost all traditio nal questions remain open (symplectic invariants, normal forms, stability). Another problem is related to the so called SYZ model of mirror symme try. In the case of Lagrangian fibrations on Calabi-Yau manifolds (see for example [47, 96, 97]) of co mplex dimension 3 (real dimension 6) there are 1-dimensional families of singularities of focus-focus t ype (which are well-understood from 1Another common spellings are Zetlin and Zeitlin. 7 the point of view of integrable systems), but there is also, for each system, a finite number of special singular fibers "at the intersection" of these families of focus-foc us singularities, and these special singular fibers are still a mystery.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a symplectic manifold equipped with a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. a smooth map $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ whose components Poisson-commute and are functionally independent on a dense open subset. A fiber $F^{-1}(c)$ is called singular if some $df_i$ fail to be linearly independent on it; a singular fiber is called degenerate when it is not modelled on the standard non-degenerate (elliptic, hyperbolic, focus-focus) building blocks of Williamson type.

(a) Investigate the topology and local geometry of degenerate singular fibers of completely integrable Hamiltonian systems and of small saturated neighbourhoods of such fibers. In particular, prove or disprove the following conjecture: for a generic / "most" completely integrable systems arising in the literature (such as bending flows on moduli spaces of $3$-dimensional polygons, the integrable system on the Grassmannian of $2$-planes, and the Gelfand–Cetlin system on coadjoint orbits of $U(n)$), every degenerate singular fiber is a smooth manifold or orbifold and is, moreover, an isotropic submanifold of $(M,\omega)$ — possibly even a Lagrangian submanifold when its dimension equals $n$. Develop the corresponding theory of symplectic invariants, symplectic normal forms, and stability under perturbation for these new classes of degenerate singularities.

(b) In the SYZ setting of mirror symmetry, let $\pi:X^{6}\to B^{3}$ be a Lagrangian torus fibration of a Calabi–Yau $3$-fold. Generic singularities of $\pi$ form $1$-dimensional strata of focus-focus type, but at finitely many isolated points of $B$ several such strata meet, producing special "intersection" singular fibers. Describe the topology, symplectic local model, and invariants of these special degenerate singular fibers occurring at intersections of focus-focus strata.
status_search_result: The conjecture has been confirmed in several specific examples since being posed: Bouloc handled the bending flows on 3D polygon spaces and the Grassmannian Gr(2,n) system; Bouloc–Miranda–Zung and Cho–Kim–Oh studied the Gelfand–Cetlin system on u(n)*, showing the singular fibers are smooth isotropic submanifolds (with Lagrangian "diamond" fibers); Cho–Kim handled the SO(n)-type Gelfand–Cetlin systems. The general conjecture for arbitrary integrable systems, the symplectic invariants/normal forms/stability theory of these degenerate fibers, and the description of the special intersection fibers in SYZ Calabi–Yau 3-fold fibrations remain open.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: If the geodesic flow of a Riemannian metric on the torus T 2 admits a nontrivial integral that is polynomial of degree 3 in momenta, then the m etric admits a Killing vector field. An easier version of this conjecture, which is also interesting, is as f ollows:
self_contained_problem:
Let $(T^2, g)$ be the two-dimensional torus equipped with a smooth Riemannian metric $g$. The geodesic flow of $g$ is the Hamiltonian flow on the cotangent bundle $T^*T^2$ generated by the Hamiltonian $H(x,p) = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{ij}(x) p_i p_j$. A smooth function $F: T^*T^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is called an integral of the geodesic flow if $\{F, H\} = 0$, where $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is the canonical Poisson bracket. The integral $F$ is said to be polynomial of degree $n$ in the momenta if, in any local cotangent coordinates, $F(x,p) = \sum_{i_1,\dots,i_n} a^{i_1\cdots i_n}(x)\, p_{i_1}\cdots p_{i_n} + (\text{lower-order terms in } p)$ with the top-degree part not identically zero. The integral is called nontrivial if it is functionally independent of $H$. A Killing vector field of $g$ is a vector field $X$ whose flow preserves $g$; equivalently, the function $p(X)$ on $T^*T^2$ is a linear-in-momenta integral of the geodesic flow.

Prove or disprove: if the geodesic flow of a Riemannian metric $g$ on $T^2$ admits a nontrivial integral that is polynomial of degree $3$ in the momenta, then $g$ admits a nontrivial Killing vector field.
status_search_result: The conjecture (often attributed to Bolotin–Kozlov and discussed by Kolokoltsov) remains open in full generality. Partial results exist: the conjecture has been verified for metrics close to a flat (or Liouville) metric, and recent works (e.g., on hydrodynamic-type systems and on third-rank Killing tensors on the 2-torus) provide partial progress, but no complete proof or counterexample is known.

original_question: If a natural Hamiltonian system with a nonconstant potential on a flat two-torus T 2 (i.e., g has zero curvature ) admits a polynomial integral of odd degree, then it admits a linear integral. If it admits a nontrivial in tegral of even degree, then it admits a nontrivial quadratic integral. As explained above, the cases d = 3, 4, 5 of this conjecture were proved in [12, 1, 171, 59]. If the potential U is a trigonometric polynomial, the problem was solved by N. Denisova an d V. Kozlov in [58]. Analogs of Conjectures 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 are also interesting if the metric g is semi-Riemannian (i.e., an indefinite metric of signature (1, 1)), which, of course, implies that our surface is a torus or a Klein bottle. Note that semi-Riemannian metrics on T 2 whose geodesic flows admit integrals which are linear or quadratic in momenta were described in [163] and, combining this re sult with [28], one obtains a description of all natural Hamiltonian systems on semi-Riemannian 2- tori with linear and quadratic integrals. As seen from the discussion above, in the case of the sphere S2, almost nothing is known about integrals of degree d ≥ 5, which suggests the following open problem:
self_contained_problem:
Let $T^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda$ be a flat two-torus equipped with a flat Riemannian metric $g$ (zero Gaussian curvature), and let $U: T^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth nonconstant potential. Consider the natural Hamiltonian system on the cotangent bundle $T^*T^2$ with Hamiltonian
$$H(x,p) = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{ij}(x) p_i p_j + U(x).$$
An integral of the system is a smooth function $F: T^*T^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\{H,F\}=0$; it is said to be polynomial of degree $d$ in momenta if $F(x,p) = \sum_{k=0}^{d} a_{i_1\cdots i_k}(x)\, p^{i_1}\cdots p^{i_k}$ with the top-degree component not identically zero. Such an $F$ is called nontrivial if it is functionally independent of $H$.

Prove or disprove the following:
(a) If the system admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of odd degree $d$, then it admits a nontrivial integral linear in momenta.
(b) If the system admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of even degree $d$, then it admits a nontrivial integral quadratic in momenta.
status_search_result: The conjecture is established only in low-degree cases: $d=3,4,5$ are proved, and the case of trigonometric-polynomial potentials is settled by Denisova–Kozlov. The general case for arbitrary degree remains open as of recent literature on polynomial integrals of natural systems on the 2-torus.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Construct new examples of natural Hamiltonian systems on hi gher dimensional mani- folds which are integrable in the class of integrals polynom ial in momenta. Another interesting direction of research might be relevant to Gen eral Relativity. Recall that the most famous solutions of the Einstein equation, Schwarzschild and Kerr m etrics, have integrable geodesic flow.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) manifold of dimension $n \geq 3$, and let $V \colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth potential. Consider the natural Hamiltonian system on the cotangent bundle $T^*M$ with Hamiltonian
$$H(q,p) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{ij}(q)\, p_i p_j \;+\; V(q),$$
where $(q,p)$ are canonical coordinates on $T^*M$. A function $F \colon T^*M \to \mathbb{R}$ is called polynomial in momenta of degree $d$ if, in any canonical chart,
$$F(q,p) \;=\; \sum_{|\alpha|\le d} a_\alpha(q)\, p^\alpha$$
with smooth coefficients $a_\alpha$. The system $(M,g,V)$ is said to be Liouville integrable in the class of integrals polynomial in momenta if there exist $n$ functions $F_1=H, F_2,\ldots,F_n$ on $T^*M$, each polynomial in momenta, that are functionally independent almost everywhere and pairwise Poisson-commuting: $\{F_i,F_j\}=0$.

Problem: Construct new explicit examples of natural Hamiltonian systems $(M,g,V)$ with $\dim M \geq 3$ that are Liouville integrable in this class of integrals polynomial in momenta and are not equivalent (by isometry, scaling, or reduction) to known examples. In particular, investigate whether new integrable natural systems can be produced in the setting of Lorentzian metrics arising in General Relativity, beyond the geodesic integrability of the Schwarzschild and Kerr metrics, by adjoining nontrivial potentials $V$ while preserving the existence of a complete set of polynomial-in-momenta first integrals.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a research direction asking for the construction of new examples rather than as a single conjecture to prove or disprove. While many classes of integrable natural Hamiltonian systems with polynomial integrals are known in dimension 2 and some in higher dimensions, the construction of new higher-dimensional examples (and integrable extensions of relativistic metrics like Schwarzschild/Kerr with potential) remains an active area of research with no definitive resolution. Status is best described as open/ongoing.

original_question: In the Riemannian case, is every 1-homogeneous manifold locally homo- geneous? The question was positively answered for dimensions 3, 4. The natural analogs of this conjecture for metrics of non-Riemannian signature are wrong. Notice that, in ter ms of polynomial integrals, local homogeneity is equivalent to the existence of linear integrals of the g eodesic flow that at each point span the tangent space.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth connected Riemannian manifold. Call $(M,g)$ locally homogeneous if for every pair of points $p,q\in M$ there exist open neighborhoods $U\ni p$, $V\ni q$ and an isometry $\varphi:(U,g|_U)\to(V,g|_V)$ with $\varphi(p)=q$. Call $(M,g)$ $1$-homogeneous if for every pair of points $p,q\in M$ there exists a local isometry between neighborhoods of $p$ and $q$ matching the metric and its first covariant derivatives at the basepoints; equivalently (in terms of geodesic flow), there exist linear-in-momenta first integrals of the geodesic flow whose values at each point of $M$ span the tangent space.

Question: Must every $1$-homogeneous Riemannian manifold be locally homogeneous?

It is known that the answer is affirmative in dimensions $3$ and $4$, while the analogous statement fails for indefinite (pseudo-Riemannian) metrics. Determine whether the implication "$1$-homogeneous $\Rightarrow$ locally homogeneous" holds for Riemannian manifolds of all dimensions.
status_search_result: No source was found resolving the conjecture in general dimensions. Results were established affirmatively for dimensions 3 and 4, and counterexamples exist in pseudo-Riemannian signature, but the general Riemannian case appears still open.

original_question: If a neighbourhood of the boundary of the billiard table Ω ⊂ R2 is foliated by caustics, then the billiard curve γ is an ellipse. We also formulate a generalized conjecture: if an open subset of the convex billiard table is foliated by caustics, then this table is elliptic. A polynomial version of Birkhoff's conjecture concerns the case wh en the integral of the billiard map is polynomial in the velocity. In the case of outer billiards, one modifies t hese conjectures in an obvious way (since outer billiards are affine-equivariant, there is no differenc e between ellipses and circles, and circles are integrable due to symmetry). The state of the art of the (smooth) Birkhoff conjecture is as follo ws. The special case of the conjecture in which the caustics of the billiard trajectories foliate Ω, except for one point, was proved by M. Bialy [13]; later he extended this result to the elliptic and hyperbolic planes [1 6]. Bialy also proved a version of this result for magnetic billiards in constant magnetic field on surfa ces of constant curvature [14]. Recently, substantial progress toward Birkhoff's conjecture was made by V. Kaloshin and his co-authors [5, 127, 117]: they proved the Birkhoff conjecture for small pertu rbations of ellipses. The general case remains open, and it is one of the foremost problems in this field.
self_contained_problem:
Let Ω ⊂ ℝ² be a strictly convex planar domain with smooth boundary γ. The (Birkhoff) billiard in Ω is the dynamical system describing the free motion of a point particle inside Ω that reflects off γ according to the law "angle of incidence equals angle of reflection." A smooth closed curve Γ ⊂ Ω is called a caustic of the billiard if every billiard trajectory tangent to Γ remains tangent to Γ after each reflection off γ.

Conjecture (Birkhoff): If there exists an open neighbourhood U of γ inside Ω such that U \ γ is foliated by caustics of the billiard in Ω, then γ is an ellipse.

Prove or disprove this conjecture. Also consider the generalized form: if some open subset of Ω is foliated by caustics of the billiard, must γ be an ellipse?
status_search_result: The smooth Birkhoff conjecture remains open in full generality. Major partial progress includes Bialy's theorem (boundary foliated except possibly one point), the local version proved by Avila–De Simoi–Kaloshin and Kaloshin–Sorrentino (small perturbations of ellipses must be ellipses), and complete proofs of the polynomial version by Bialy–Mironov and Glutsyuk. New integrable examples (e.g., billiards inside cones, 2025) suggest the landscape is still being mapped, but the original conjecture for general smooth convex tables is unresolved.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Prove the algebraic version of Birkhoff conjecture for outer billiards in a non-Euclidean surface of constant curvature. The next problem is a generalization of the previous one.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a complete simply connected two-dimensional Riemannian surface of constant curvature $K
eq 0$ — i.e. either the round sphere $S^2$ (when $K>0$) or the hyperbolic plane $H^2$ (when $K<0$). Let $\gamma\subset M$ be a smooth, strictly geodesically convex, closed curve bounding a domain $D$ whose complement contains no pair of points joined by a unique geodesic ambiguity (so that the outer billiard map is well-defined on an open subset of $M\setminus\overline{D}$).

The outer (dual) billiard map $T_\gamma$ associated with $\gamma$ is defined as follows. For a point $p$ in a suitable neighborhood of $\gamma$ in $M\setminus\overline{D}$, let $\ell_p$ be the (oriented) geodesic from $p$ that is tangent to $\gamma$ at a point $q(p)$, chosen by a fixed orientation convention. Then $T_\gamma(p)$ is the point on $\ell_p$ such that $q(p)$ is the geodesic midpoint of the segment from $p$ to $T_\gamma(p)$.

The outer billiard $T_\gamma$ is said to be polynomially integrable (algebraically integrable) if there exists a non-constant function $F:U	o\mathbb{R}$, defined on an invariant open neighborhood $U$ of $\gamma$, such that:
(i) $F\circ T_\gamma = F$ on $U$;
(ii) in any (and hence every) standard embedding of $M$ as a quadric in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (the sphere $\{x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1/K\}$ for $K>0$, or the upper sheet of the hyperboloid $\{x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2=1/K\}$ for $K<0$), the function $F$ is the restriction to $U$ of a polynomial in the ambient coordinates $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$.

Problem. Prove that if the outer billiard $T_\gamma$ associated with a closed strictly geodesically convex smooth curve $\gamma$ on $M$ is polynomially integrable in the above sense, then $\gamma$ is a conic in $M$, i.e. the intersection of the quadric model of $M$ with an affine quadric in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (equivalently, a geodesic circle, an ellipse, or another classical conic of constant curvature geometry).
status_search_result: The corresponding algebraic Birkhoff conjecture for inner (Birkhoff) billiards on surfaces of constant curvature has been established by Bialy–Mironov and Glutsyuk. The algebraic version of the Birkhoff conjecture for outer billiards is known in the affine (flat) plane (Tabachnikov), but for outer billiards on the sphere and hyperbolic plane it appears to remain open; the listed problem and recent work on "Integrable outer billiards and rigidity" continue to address it without a full resolution.

original_question: Are there plane billiards, other than ellipses, that posses s rational caustics with two different values of the rotation numbers? Same question for o uter billiards. Kaloshin and J. Zhang [129] studied the case of 1 /2 and 1 /3 caustics. They proved that, for a certain class of analytic deformations of a circle, the coexistence of such c austics implies that the deformation is trivial. Here is a weaker version of the previous problem. Let q0 ≥ 2 be an integer. A billiard table is called q0-rationally integrable is it possesses p/q-rational caustics for all 0 < p/q < 1/q0 (see [117]).
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A plane billiard is a strictly convex bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. The billiard map $T$ acts on oriented chords (or, equivalently, on the cylinder of boundary point/inward direction pairs) by the law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. A smooth convex curve $\Gamma \subset \Omega$ is called a caustic if every billiard trajectory tangent to $\Gamma$ remains tangent to $\Gamma$ after each reflection. To each caustic $\Gamma$ one associates a rotation number $\rho(\Gamma) \in (0,1/2]$ describing the average rotation per reflection of trajectories tangent to $\Gamma$. A caustic is called rational with rotation number $p/q$ (in lowest terms, $0<p/q<1/2$) if $\rho(\Gamma)=p/q$; equivalently, the trajectories tangent to $\Gamma$ are closed polygons of period $q$ winding $p$ times around $\Gamma$.

It is classical that every ellipse possesses rational caustics (confocal ellipses) for every admissible rotation number $p/q$.

An outer (dual) billiard about a strictly convex closed curve $\gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is the map of the exterior defined as follows: for a point $x$ outside $\gamma$, let $\ell$ be the tangent line from $x$ to $\gamma$ (oriented so that $\gamma$ lies to the right), touching $\gamma$ at $y$; then the image of $x$ is the reflection of $x$ through $y$. Caustics and rational caustics for outer billiards are defined analogously, as invariant curves carrying rotation number $p/q$.

Questions.
(a) Does there exist a plane (Birkhoff) billiard table, not bounded by an ellipse, that possesses rational caustics with at least two distinct rotation numbers $p_1/q_1 \ne p_2/q_2$?

(b) Same question for outer billiards: does there exist a strictly convex closed curve $\gamma$, not an ellipse, whose outer billiard map admits rational invariant caustics with at least two distinct rotation numbers?

(c) (Weaker version.) For an integer $q_0 \ge 2$, call a billiard table $q_0$-rationally integrable if it possesses a $p/q$-rational caustic for every rational $0 < p/q < 1/q_0$. Must every $q_0$-rationally integrable plane billiard be an ellipse?
status_search_result: The general problem remains open. Partial results exist: Kaloshin and J. Zhang showed that, for a class of analytic deformations of the circle, the coexistence of 1/2 and 1/3 rational caustics forces the deformation to be trivial; subsequent work (e.g. Koudjinan and others) extended non-coexistence results for 2- and 3-rational caustics near the circle, while studies of nearly circular billiards suggest possible families with coexisting 1/3 and 1/5 caustics at higher order. Kaloshin–Sorrentino proved a local rigidity theorem for integrable deformations of an ellipse. No example of a non-elliptic billiard with two rational caustics is known, and the full conjecture (including for outer billiards and the $q_0$-rationally integrable variant) is unresolved.

original_question: (M. Bialy) Assume that a plane billiard has a family of rotational invar iant circles with all the rotation numbers in the interval (0, 1/2). Then the billiard table is an ellipse. A variation on Innami's result is the following question, suggested by V. Kaloshin:
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a strictly convex planar domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$, and consider the associated Birkhoff billiard map $T$ defined on the phase cylinder of inward unit tangent vectors based on $\partial\Omega$, parametrized so that the canonical rotation number takes values in $[0,1/2]$ (rotation number $1/2$ corresponding to the boundary itself). A rotational invariant circle of $T$ is an essential (non-contractible) $T$-invariant closed curve in the phase cylinder; on such a curve the dynamics is conjugate to a rigid rotation with a well-defined rotation number.

Conjecture: Suppose that the billiard map associated with $\Omega$ admits a family of rotational invariant circles whose rotation numbers fill the entire open interval $(0, 1/2)$. Prove that $\partial\Omega$ must be an ellipse.
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open in general. Significant partial progress has been made: Bialy and Mironov established the Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture for centrally symmetric C²-smooth convex planar billiards (Annals of Mathematics, 2022), and proved that if a neighborhood of the boundary admits a C¹-smooth foliation by convex caustics with rotation numbers in (0, 1/4], then the boundary is an ellipse. Kaloshin and collaborators have proved the Birkhoff conjecture for domains nearly centrally symmetric or close to an ellipse. The full conjecture as stated (requiring all rotation numbers in (0, 1/2)) has not been fully resolved.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: (M. Bialy) Are there multi-dimensional convex billiards, other than e llipsoids, having invariant hypersurfaces in the phase space? Same question f or multi-dimensional outer billiards. A common feature of families of integrable maps is that they commute (Bianchi permutability). 17 Consider two confocal ellipses: the billiard reflections define two tra nsformations on the set of oriented lines that intersect both ellipses. These transformations commute, see [209]. The converse was recently proved by A. Glutsyuk [89], as a consequence of his classification of 4 -reflective complex planar billiards. For outer billiards, an analogous theorem is that if the outer billiard tr ansformations on two nested curves commute then the curves are concentric homothetic ellipse s [205]. It would be interesting to find a proof of Glutsyuk's result via a more geometric approach of [20 5]. In higher dimensions (greater than two), the billiard transformatio ns, induced by two confocal ellip- soids, commute as well (see, e.g., [64]).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \ge 3$ be a smooth strictly convex bounded domain. The billiard map $T_\Omega$ acts on the phase space $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ of oriented lines intersecting $\Omega$ (equivalently, on inward unit vectors based at $\partial\Omega$) by the standard law of elastic reflection: an incoming oriented line hits $\partial\Omega$ at a point $p$ and is reflected so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection with respect to the outward normal at $p$. An invariant hypersurface for $T_\Omega$ is a smooth codimension-one submanifold $\Sigma \subset \mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ with $T_\Omega(\Sigma) = \Sigma$.

It is classical that if $\Omega$ is an ellipsoid, then $T_\Omega$ admits a foliation by invariant hypersurfaces (the families of lines tangent to confocal quadrics).

Question (a): Do there exist smooth strictly convex bounded domains $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge 3$, other than ellipsoids, such that the billiard map $T_\Omega$ possesses an invariant hypersurface in its phase space?

Question (b): Analogously, let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ be a smooth strictly convex bounded domain and let $T_K^{\text{out}}$ denote its outer (dual) billiard map, defined on the exterior of $K$ via the symplectic structure: for a point $x$ outside $K$, $T_K^{\text{out}}(x)$ is the reflection of $x$ through the point of tangency of the (suitably defined) supporting affine hyperplane to $K$ from $x$. Are there examples of such $K$, other than ellipsoids, for which $T_K^{\text{out}}$ admits an invariant hypersurface in phase space?
status_search_result: The question remains largely open for inner (Birkhoff) billiards in dimensions ≥ 3: classical Berger–Gruber rigidity shows that only ellipsoids admit convex caustics, but the broader existence of invariant hypersurfaces in phase space (not necessarily corresponding to caustics) is unresolved, and no non-ellipsoidal examples are known. For the outer (symplectic) billiard version, recent work (2025) of Bialy–Tabachnikov on symplectically self-polar convex bodies provides the first non-trivial examples of invariant hypersurfaces beyond ellipsoids, partially answering the outer-billiard part.
