original_question: (B. Khesin, F. Soloviev) The maps TI,I are integrable for all multi-indices I. Khesin and Soloviev also conjectured that all the maps TI,J (and even a more general type of maps, called universal pentagram maps) are Hamiltonian, that is, preserv e a certain non-trivial Poisson structure. See the recent paper by A. Izosimov on this subject [1 23]. Some of the maps considered by Khesin and Soloviev are included in the family of transformations desc ribed in [88]; they are examples of integrable cluster dynamics. 4.4 Noncommutative integrable maps This section concerns dynamical systems, with continuous or discr ete time, on associative but not commutative algebras, so that the variables involved do not commut e; the reader with an aversion to free non-commuting variables may think of matrices of an arbitrary size: see, e.g., [177, 165]. In this case, one speaks about noncommutative integrability, although this term has another, quite different, meaning as well (when the integrals form a non-Abelian Lie algebra with respect to the Poisson bracket). The overarching problem is to develop a comprehensive theory that would include noncommutative counterpart to the definition of integrability as given in Section 4.1. A s of now, the geometric aspects of the noncommutative theory are poorly understood, and one mo stly deals with the formal, algebraic part of the story. In what follows, we work with noncommutative La urent polynomials or power series in several variables. 19 Here is an example of a 2-dimensional noncommutative integrable map that illustrates the specifics and peculiarities of the noncommutative situation. This example was d iscovered by S. Duzhin and M. Kontsevich [139] and studied in [4, 232]: T: (x, y) ↦→ (xyx- 1, (1 + y- 1)x- 1). Here x and y are free non-commuting variables and the map can be understood a s a substitution in the ring of Laurent polynomials C<x, y, x- 1, y- 1>. The map T preserves the commutator xyx- 1y- 1. In the commutative case, when xy = yx, the map becomes T: (x, y) ↦→ (y, (1 + y- 1)x- 1), but the integral xyx- 1y- 1 degenerates to a constant. On the other hand, in the commutativ e case, one has an integral I = x + y + x- 1 + y- 1 + x- 1y- 1, whose level curves are elliptic curves, and the map has an invariant a rea form ( xy)- 1dx ∧ dy, so it is completely integrable in the sense of Section 4.1. In the noncommutative case, the Laurent polynomial I is transformed by T as follows I ↦→ xIx- 1. If the variables represent matrices (of an arbitrary size), then tr I k is an integral of the transformation T for every positive integer k. In the general case, when x, y are formal variables, one defines trace on the algebra of Laurent polynomials C<x, y, x- 1, y- 1> as an equivalence class of the cyclic permutations of factors of a polynomial. On the other hand, in the intermediate ("quantum") case, when xy = qyx, with q commuting with everything, the map T has the integral Iq = x + qy + qx- 1 + y- 1 + x- 1y- 1, whose q → 1 limit is I. The map T is a discrete symmetry of the system of differential equations ˙x = xy - xy- 1 - y- 1, ˙y = - yx + yx- 1 + x- 1. Once again, we consider these differential equations in the formal s ense, as Laurent series whose coefficients depend on a parameter, and we are not concerned with the questions of existence and uniqueness of solutions. This system of ODEs admits a Lax presentation with a spectral para meter (that commutes with everything); the entries of the Lax matrix are noncommutative La urent polynomials in x and y, and the conjugacy class of the Lax matrix does not change under the m ap T. The map T belongs to a family of maps Tk: (x, y) ↦→ (xyx- 1, (1 + yk)x- 1). 20 For k ≥ 1, these maps satisfy the Laurent phenomenon: both components of all the iterations belong to the noncommutative ring of Laurent polynomials in x, y (for k ≥ 3, the maps Tk are not integrable). This theorem, also conjectured by S. Duzhin and M. Kontsevich [139 ], was first proved in [217] and, independently, in [61], and later, by different methods, in [9, 150] (th ese papers also tackle different variations of the S. Duzhin and M. Kontsevich conjectures). In th e commutative setting, the Laurent phenomenon is well known in the theory of cluster algebras and is rela ted with integrability of cluster dynamical systems. We now switch gears and discuss an open problem concerning noncom mutative versions of the penta- gram maps described in the previous section. These maps belong to t he realm of projective geometry, so one needs a noncommutative version of projective geometry an d, in particular, of the cross-ratio of a quadruple of points on the projective line. A fundamental notion of noncommutative algebra is quasi-determin ant [80, 81, 82], a noncommutative analog of the determinant (quasi-determinants play a role in the stu dy of noncommutative integrability, see [73, 62]). Using quasi-determinants, V. Retakh [194] defined th e cross-ratio and described its properties. Let us present the relevant definitions. Let A be a 2 × n matrix whose entries a1i and a2i, i = 1,..., n, are elements of an associative ring R over a field. For 1 ≤ i, j, k ≤ n, define the quasi-Pl ucker coordinates of the matrix A qk ij(A) = ( a1i - a1ka- 1 2k a2i)- 1(a1j - a1ka- 1 2k a2j), where we assume that all the inversions are defined (quasi-Pl ucker coordinates can be defined for k × n matrices as well). Let x, y, z, t be four 2-vectors with components in R. These vectors form the columns of a 2 × 4 matrix A, and one defines the cross-ratio [x, y, z, t] = qy zt(A)qx tz(A). In the commutative case, assuming that the second components o f the vectors equal 1, one obtains a familiar definition of the cross-ratio (or, better said, one of its six d efinitions): [x, y, z, t] = (z - x)(t - y) (z - y)(t - x). The non-commutative cross-ratio shares some properties with its commutative counterpart. For ex- ample, [Gxλ1, Gyλ2, Gzλ3, Gtλ4] = λ- 1 3 [x, y, z, t]λ3, where G is a 2 × 2 matrix over R, and λi ∈ R, i = 1, 2, 3, 4. Having a definition of noncommutative cross-ratio, one may define a nd study noncommutative analogs of the pentagram maps. To be concrete, consider the following 1-d imensional version of the pentagram map, introduced in [79] and called the leapfrog map. Let S- = (S- 1, S- 2,...) and S- = (S1, S2,...) be a pair of n-gons in the projective line. The leapfrog map (S-, S) ↦→ (S, S+) is defined as follows. For every i, there exists a unique projective involution that 21 sends the triple ( Si- 1, Si, Si+1) to the triple ( Si+1, Si, Si- 1); this transformation sends S- i to S+ i (that is, the point S- i "jumps" over Si, in the projective metric on the segment [ Si- 1, Si+1], and becomes S+ i - thus the name of the map). In other words, one has [ Si- 1, Si, Si+1, S- i ] = [ Si+1, Si, Si- 1, S+ i ]. The theory of noncommutative cross-ratios implies that there exis ts a projective transformation ( Si- 1, Si, Si+1, S- i ) ↦→( Si+1, Si, Si- 1, S+ i ) if and only if (Si+1 - Si)- 1 ( S- i - Si ) ( S- i - Si- 1 ) - 1 (Si+1 - Si- 1) = r- 1 (Si- 1 - Si)- 1 ( S+ i - Si ) ( S+ i - Si+1 ) - 1 (Si- 1 - Si+1) r where r ∈ R is invertible. In the commutative case, this becomes the formula defi ning the leapfrog map. It was proved in [79] that the leapfrog map is completely integrable: it has an invariant Poisson structure and a complete collection of Poisson commuting integrals; in the appendix to [79], A. Izosimov constructed a tri-Hamiltonian structure for this map.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Fix integers d ≥ 2 and n with n sufficiently large. A twisted n-gon in the projective space RP^d is a sequence v = (v_i)_{i ∈ Z} of points in RP^d such that v_{i+n} = M(v_i) for some fixed projective monodromy M ∈ PGL_{d+1}(R) and such that every d+1 consecutive points are in general position. Let P_{n,d} denote the moduli space of twisted n-gons modulo projective equivalence.

For each pair of multi-indices I = (i_1, …, i_{d-1}) and J = (j_1, …, j_{d-1}) of positive integers, the generalized pentagram map T_{I,J} : P_{n,d} ⇢ P_{n,d} is defined as follows. To each vertex v_k of a twisted n-gon associate the "I-diagonal hyperplane" P_k^I, namely the projective hyperplane spanned by the d points v_k, v_{k+i_1}, v_{k+i_1+i_2}, …, v_{k+i_1+…+i_{d-1}}. The "J-shifted" image vertex (T_{I,J} v)_k is then defined as the intersection of d consecutive I-diagonal hyperplanes P_k^I, P_{k+j_1}^I, P_{k+j_1+j_2}^I, …, P_{k+j_1+…+j_{d-1}}^I. The classical Schwartz pentagram map corresponds to d = 2 and I = J = (2).

For d = 2 there is a known invariant symplectic structure and the maps T_{I,I} are known to be completely integrable. In higher dimensions the situation is open in general.

Problem (Khesin–Soloviev).
(a) Prove that for every dimension d ≥ 2 and every multi-index I, the map T_{I,I} on P_{n,d} is completely integrable in the Liouville–Arnold sense: it preserves an invariant Poisson structure on P_{n,d} together with a maximal family of functionally independent, Poisson-commuting first integrals.
(b) More generally, prove that every map T_{I,J} (and every "universal pentagram map" obtained by analogous diagonal/intersection constructions in RP^d) is Hamiltonian, i.e. preserves a non-trivial Poisson structure on the corresponding moduli space of twisted polygons.
status_search_result: The conjecture has been substantially advanced but is not fully settled. Izosimov, using a Poisson–Lie group of pseudo-difference operators, established invariant Poisson structures for the pentagram map and its known integrable multidimensional generalizations, addressing a major part of the Hamiltonian claim. Izosimov and Khesin proved integrability of long-diagonal pentagram maps in RP^d, which encompasses many of the T_{I,J} cases. A complete proof for all T_{I,J} and the most general "universal pentagram maps" does not yet appear in the literature, so the conjecture is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems, questions and challenges in finite-dimensional integrable systems
original_question: Consider the action of Aut(V, J ) on V. Describe the partition of V into Aut(V, J )- orbits. More generally, describe the action of Aut(V, J ) on the set of all k-dimensional subspaces U ⊂ V (orbits, invariants, fixed points). Notice that fixed points of this action (i.e., Aut(V, J )- invariant subspaces) are important, as they correspond to w ell-defined (co)distributions in the context of Poisson pencils. A subspace L ⊂ V is said to be bi-Lagrangian if it is simultaneously isotropic with respect to both A and B and has maximal possible dimension (which is 1 2 (dim V + corank J)). The set LG( V, J ) of all bi-Lagrangian subspaces is called the bi-Lagrangian Grassmannian. A detailed description of 24 LG(V, J ) is an important open problem, see the discussion in [195]. It is importa nt that bi-Lagrangian subspaces always exist, so that LG( V, J ) is never empty. In general, this is a projective algebraic variety with rather non-trivial properties, which essentially depen d on the algebraic type of the pencil J. In particular, there might exists bi-Lagrangian subspaces of diffe rent algebraic types. In other words, LG( V, J ) may consist of several orbits of the automorphism group Aut( V, J ).
self_contained_problem:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$), and let $J = \{A_\lambda = A + \lambda B : \lambda \in \mathbb{P}^1\}$ be a pencil of skew-symmetric bilinear forms on $V$, where $A,B : V \times V \to \mathbb{F}$ are skew-symmetric. Define the automorphism group of the pencil by
$$\mathrm{Aut}(V,J) = \{ g \in GL(V) : g^*A = A \text{ and } g^*B = B \}.$$
The corank of the pencil is $\mathrm{corank}\, J := \min_{\lambda} \dim \ker A_\lambda$. A subspace $L \subset V$ is called bi-Lagrangian for $J$ if it is isotropic with respect to both $A$ and $B$ (i.e. $A(L,L) = B(L,L) = 0$) and has the maximal possible dimension
$$\dim L = \tfrac{1}{2}(\dim V + \mathrm{corank}\, J).$$
Let $LG(V,J)$ denote the set of all bi-Lagrangian subspaces of $V$; it is known to be a nonempty projective algebraic variety carrying a natural $\mathrm{Aut}(V,J)$-action.

(a) Describe the partition of $V$ into $\mathrm{Aut}(V,J)$-orbits.

(b) More generally, for each $1 \le k \le \dim V - 1$, describe the action of $\mathrm{Aut}(V,J)$ on the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_k(V)$ of $k$-dimensional subspaces of $V$: classify the orbits, find a complete system of invariants, and determine the fixed points (i.e. the $\mathrm{Aut}(V,J)$-invariant subspaces of $V$).

(c) Give a detailed description of the bi-Lagrangian Grassmannian $LG(V,J)$ as a projective algebraic variety, including its decomposition into $\mathrm{Aut}(V,J)$-orbits and the algebraic types of bi-Lagrangian subspaces it contains, in terms of the Jordan–Kronecker (algebraic) type of the pencil $J$.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research problem on the structure of the bi-Lagrangian Grassmannian of a Jordan–Kronecker pencil. No comprehensive classification appears to have been published; partial results exist in works of Bolsinov, Izosimov, and collaborators on Jordan–Kronecker invariants, but a full orbit/algebraic-type description of $LG(V,J)$ remains open.

original_question: Do bi-integrable systems exist for each algebraic type? This question is local in the sense that bi-integrable systems in quest ion "live" in a small neighbourhood of a generic point x ∈ M where the algebraic type of a given Poisson pencil is locally constant. However, for applications, we need smooth commuting functions that are glob ally defined on the whole manifold M. For two constant brackets {, }1 and {, }2 on a vector space V, bi-integrable systems can be easily constructed by means of bi-Poisson linear algebra: each bi-Lagran gian subspace can be interpreted as a bi-integrable Hamiltonian system with linear integrals. The first non- trivial example is the so-called "argument shift" pencil (see A.S. Mischenko and A.T. Fomenko [172]), generated by a linear and a constant brackets. We recall this construction. 25 5.2 Argument shift method and Jordan-Kronecker invariants of Lie alge- bras Let g∗ be the dual space of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra g. It is well known that g∗ possesses two natural compatible Poisson brackets. The first one is the standar d linear Lie-Poisson bracket {f, g}(x) = <x, [d f(x), dg(x)]>, (5.3) and the second one is a constant bracket given by {f, g}a(x) = <a, [d f(x), dg(x)]>, (5.4) where a ∈ g∗ is a fixed element. Here we assume a to be regular, although formula (5.4) makes sense for an arbitrary a. There are many examples of finite-dimensional Lie algebras for which we can construct a complete family of polynomials in bi-involution with respect to the brackets (5.3) and (5.4). In particular, the famous theorem by A.S. Mischenko and A.T. Fomenko [172] states th at such a family exists for every semisimple Lie algebra g and consists of shifts of Ad ∗ -invariant polynomials, i.e., function of the form fi(x + λa), where λ ∈ R and f1,..., fr are generators of the algebra of (co)-adjoint invariants. However, it is still an open question whether one can construct suc h a family for every finite-dimensional Lie algebra. In many examples (see [38]), the answer turns out to be positive, leading us to the following Generalised Argument Shift conjecture which was first stated in [38 ] and then mentioned and discussed in a number of papers [195, 36, 122, 34]:
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold equipped with two compatible Poisson structures $\{\,,\,\}_1$ and $\{\,,\,\}_2$ (i.e., every linear combination $\lambda_1\{\,,\,\}_1+\lambda_2\{\,,\,\}_2$ is again a Poisson bracket). The family $\mathcal{P}=\{\lambda_1\{\,,\,\}_1+\lambda_2\{\,,\,\}_2:(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\}$ is called a Poisson pencil on $M$.

For a generic point $x\in M$, the pair of skew-symmetric forms induced on $T_x^*M$ by the two brackets admits a Jordan–Kronecker canonical form, i.e., a decomposition into Jordan blocks (with eigenvalues $\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}$) and Kronecker blocks (of various odd sizes). The collection of these blocks (sizes and eigenvalues) is called the algebraic type of the pencil at $x$. On an open dense subset of $M$ the algebraic type is locally constant; this common type is the (generic) algebraic type of $\mathcal{P}$.

A bi-integrable system on $(M,\{\,,\,\}_1,\{\,,\,\}_2)$ is a family $\mathcal{F}$ of smooth functions on $M$, globally defined, that is:
(i) in bi-involution: $\{f,g\}_1=\{f,g\}_2=0$ for all $f,g\in\mathcal{F}$; and
(ii) complete in the sense that at a generic point the differentials of functions in $\mathcal{F}$ span a subspace of $T_x^*M$ which is bi-Lagrangian for the pair of forms, i.e., of maximal possible dimension compatible with bi-involution dictated by the algebraic type.

Problem. Determine whether, for every algebraic type of a Poisson pencil that can occur at a generic point, there exists a smooth manifold $M$ with a compatible pair $(\{\,,\,\}_1,\{\,,\,\}_2)$ of that generic algebraic type admitting a bi-integrable system $\mathcal{F}$ in the above sense, with the functions of $\mathcal{F}$ globally defined on the whole of $M$.

Searches reveal active study of Jordan–Kronecker decompositions of Poisson pencils and bi-Hamiltonian singularities (Bolsinov–Oshemkov, Bolsinov–Izosimov), but no global existence theorem for bi-integrable systems for arbitrary algebraic type. The status appears to remain open.

original_question: Study examples of "quadratic + linear" Poisson pencils. Compute their algebraic types and construct complete families of polynomials in bi-invol ution for such pencils. It is a very general question whether or not a given symplectic (Pois son) manifold M admits an integrable system with good properties. In particular, if M is a vector space endowed with a polynomial Poisson bracket, we are interested in integrable systems defined o n M by a collection of Poisson commuting polynomials. For a linear Poisson bracket (5.3), such a poly nomial integrable system always exists. This statement, known as Mischenko-Fomenko conj ecture, was proved by S. Sadetov [197] in 2004. What can we say about polynomial Poisson brackets of higher degrees?
self_contained_problem:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real (or complex) vector space equipped with a polynomial Poisson bracket $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$, that is, a Poisson bracket on $C^\infty(V)$ (or on the polynomial algebra $\mathbb{R}[V]$) such that the bracket of any two linear coordinate functions is a polynomial on $V$. Recall:

1. A "linear" Poisson bracket on $V$ corresponds to a Lie algebra structure on $V^*$: it is the canonical Lie–Poisson bracket on $\mathfrak{g}^* \cong V$. For such linear brackets, the Mischenko–Fomenko conjecture (proved by Sadetov) asserts that there always exists a complete family of polynomials on $V$ in involution, i.e. a polynomial integrable system.

2. A Poisson pencil is a one-parameter family $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_\lambda = \{\cdot,\cdot\}_1 + \lambda \{\cdot,\cdot\}_2$ of compatible Poisson brackets (any linear combination is again Poisson). A "quadratic + linear" pencil consists of a quadratic Poisson bracket $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_2$ (bracket of linear coordinates is homogeneous of degree $2$) compatible with a linear Poisson bracket $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_1$.

3. A family $\mathcal{F} \subset \mathbb{R}[V]$ of polynomials is said to be in bi-involution with respect to a Poisson pencil if $\{f,g\}_\lambda = 0$ for every $\lambda$ and every $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$. The family is complete (defines an integrable system) if at a generic point $x \in V$, $\dim\, d\mathcal{F}(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}(\dim V + \mathrm{corank}\,\{\cdot,\cdot\}_\lambda$ at $x)$ for generic $\lambda$.

Problem. (a) Investigate concrete examples of "quadratic + linear" Poisson pencils on vector spaces $V$, determine their algebraic types (i.e. the structure of the associated linear pencil of bivectors and the singular set), and for each such pencil construct an explicit complete family of polynomials in bi-involution.

(b) More generally, given a vector space $V$ equipped with a polynomial Poisson bracket of degree $\geq 2$, does there always exist a complete family of Poisson-commuting polynomials on $V$? In other words, does the analogue of the Mischenko–Fomenko theorem hold for polynomial Poisson brackets of higher degree?
status_search_result: The Mischenko–Fomenko conjecture for linear Poisson brackets was proved by Sadetov (2003/2004). The analogous question for polynomial Poisson brackets of higher degree, and the systematic study of "quadratic + linear" Poisson pencils with construction of complete bi-involutive families, remains an active research direction with only partial results (e.g., families of quadratic Poisson structures on gl(3)* compatible with the Lie–Poisson bracket due to Sokolov and others). No general result establishing existence of complete polynomial integrable systems for arbitrary higher-degree polynomial Poisson brackets has been reported.

original_question: Describe closed manifolds M which admit Nijenhuis operators L(x) that are alge- braically regular at each point x ∈ M.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth closed (compact, without boundary) manifold of dimension $n$. A Nijenhuis operator on $M$ is a smooth (1,1)-tensor field $L:TM\to TM$ whose Nijenhuis torsion
$$
\mathcal{N}_L(X,Y) := L^2[X,Y] - L[LX,Y] - L[X,LY] + [LX,LY]
$$
vanishes identically for all smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $M$. At a point $x\in M$, the operator $L(x):T_xM\to T_xM$ is called algebraically regular if its centralizer in $\mathrm{End}(T_xM)$ has the minimal possible dimension $n$, equivalently if the characteristic and minimal polynomials of $L(x)$ coincide (each eigenvalue of $L(x)$ corresponds to a single Jordan block). The operator $L$ is called algebraically regular on $M$ if $L(x)$ is algebraically regular for every $x\in M$.

Describe (i.e., classify, or give effective topological/geometric obstructions and constructions for) the closed manifolds $M$ that admit a Nijenhuis operator $L$ which is algebraically regular at every point of $M$.
status_search_result: The problem is part of an active research program in Nijenhuis geometry. Partial results exist: normal forms for gl-regular Nijenhuis operators (each eigenvalue a single Jordan block) have been obtained locally and near singular points, and some topological restrictions on closed surfaces are known, but a general description/classification of closed manifolds admitting algebraically regular Nijenhuis operators does not appear to have been achieved. Recent surveys of research problems in Nijenhuis geometry continue to list such questions as open.

Let $M$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) two-dimensional real analytic surface. A (1,1)-tensor field $L$ on $M$ is called a Nijenhuis operator if its Nijenhuis torsion
$$N_L(X,Y) = L^2[X,Y] - L[LX,Y] - L[X,LY] + [LX,LY]$$
vanishes identically for all smooth vector fields $X, Y$ on $M$.

(i) at every point of $M$ the two eigenvalues of $L$ are real, and
(ii) on an open dense subset of $M$ the two eigenvalues are distinct.

Equivalently, determine on which closed real analytic surfaces such operators exist and exhibit explicit constructions of them.

$$L = \begin{pmatrix} f_x - x & f_y \\ f_x(x - f_x) - f & -f_x \end{pmatrix},$$
so that admissibility of $\sigma_2 = f$ requires $\frac{f_x(x - f_x) - f}{f_y}$ to extend as a smooth function. The problem asks for global real analytic realizations of such structures.)

We assume that 0 is a singular point of Phi, that is, rank dPhi(0) < n, but almost all points x ∈ U (0) are regular. An operator L(x) with linear entries (5.6) is Nijenhuis if and only if bi jk are structure constants of a left-symmetric algebra. Recall that an algebra ( A, ∗) is called left-symmetric if the following identity holds: a ∗ (b ∗ c) - (a ∗ b) ∗ c = b ∗ (a ∗ c) - (b ∗ a) ∗ c, for all a, b, c ∈ A. original_question: Describe the structure of singularities of Phi = ( σ1,..., σn): M → Rn in terms of the singular points of the recursion operator R, their linearisations, and the corresponding left-symmet ric algebras. What are sufficient and/or necessary conditions fo r such singularities to be non-degenerate (in the sense of Eliasson [72])? Notice that, in this case, th e algebraic type of R is rather special: at a generic point, R is semisimple, but each of its eigenvalues has multiplicity 2.
self_contained_problem:
Let (M, ω) be a smooth symplectic manifold of dimension 2n equipped with a Nijenhuis recursion operator R: TM → TM, that is, a (1,1)-tensor field whose Nijenhuis torsion vanishes and which is compatible with ω in the sense required to generate a bi-Hamiltonian (or, more generally, Nijenhuis-Hamiltonian) integrable system. Let σ_1, …, σ_n denote the elementary symmetric functions of the (generically) eigenvalues of R, and assume that {σ_i, σ_j} = 0 for all i, j with respect to the Poisson bracket induced by ω, so that the map

    Φ = (σ_1, …, σ_n): M → R^n

is the momentum map of a completely integrable Hamiltonian system. Assume that at a generic point of M the operator R is semisimple and that each of its eigenvalues has algebraic multiplicity exactly 2.

A singular point p ∈ M of Φ is said to be non-degenerate in the sense of Eliasson if, denoting by k the rank of dΦ(p), the linearised system of the components of Φ that vanish to first order at p generates a Cartan subalgebra of the Lie algebra sp(2(n−k), R) of quadratic Hamiltonians on the symplectic transverse to the orbit through p.

At a singular point p of Φ one may consider:
  (i) p as a singular point of the recursion operator R (where the spectral or Jordan type of R degenerates),
  (ii) the linearisation of R at p,
  (iii) the left-symmetric algebra structure naturally attached to R at p (the algebra whose product is determined by the linearisation of R viewed as an endomorphism on the tangent space).

Problem.
(a) Describe the structure of the singularities of Φ in terms of the data (i)–(iii) above; i.e. give an explicit correspondence between the local geometry of the critical set of Φ and the singular behaviour of R together with its linearisation and associated left-symmetric algebra.
(b) Find sufficient conditions, expressed purely in terms of (i)–(iii), under which a singular point of Φ is non-degenerate in the sense of Eliasson.
(c) Find necessary conditions of the same kind, and ideally a combined necessary-and-sufficient criterion.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not reveal a published full resolution of this problem on singularities of integrable systems generated by a Nijenhuis recursion operator with double eigenvalues. The problem is stated as an open problem in the integrable-systems literature, and recent works on Nijenhuis geometry and bi-Hamiltonian singularities address related but more restricted settings (simple eigenvalues, or specific normal forms), without providing the requested general structural correspondence with left-symmetric algebras and Eliasson non-degeneracy.

original_question: Extend the action-angle theorem in a neighbourhood of a Liou ville torus at singular points of the Poisson structure for splittable integrable s ystems. We suspect that either stability of the transversal part of the Po isson manifold or the existence of associated toric actions will play a role in solving this problem for specia l classes of Poisson manifolds. This problem can be extended to its global version. Can we find action -angle coordinates globally? This problem was considered by Duistermaat in the symplectic case [68 ]. One of the main ingredients in his construction was the affine structure defined by the action va riables on the image of the moment map. In the regular Poisson setting, the image of the moment map is f oliated by affine manifolds. Understanding this foliation is a key point to understanding global ob structions. The following problem has been partially considered in [76].
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\pi)$ be a Poisson manifold of dimension $n$ and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_s):M\to\mathbb{R}^s$ be an integrable system on $(M,\pi)$ in the sense that the components $f_i$ pairwise Poisson-commute and define, on the regular part, a foliation by isotropic tori of maximal dimension. Assume the system is "splittable" at a point $p\in M$: in a neighbourhood of $p$ the Poisson structure $\pi$ admits a Weinstein-type splitting into a symplectic factor and a transverse Poisson factor that is compatible with the integrable system $F$, and assume that $p$ lies on a compact regular fibre (Liouville torus) of $F$ but is a singular point of the Poisson structure $\pi$ (i.e., the rank of $\pi$ drops at $p$).

(a) (Local problem.) Establish an action–angle theorem in a neighbourhood of the Liouville torus through $p$: find coordinates $(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r, p_1,\dots,p_r, z_1,\dots,z_{n-2r})$ in a tubular neighbourhood of the torus, where $\theta_i$ are angle coordinates on the torus, $p_i$ are action coordinates conjugate to the $\theta_i$, and the $z_j$ are transverse coordinates, in which $\pi$ takes a normal form and $F$ depends only on $(p_1,\dots,p_r,z_1,\dots,z_{n-2r})$. Identify the precise hypotheses (for example, stability of the transverse Poisson structure, or the existence of an associated effective torus action preserving $F$) under which such coordinates exist for natural classes of Poisson manifolds.

(b) (Global problem.) On a regular Poisson manifold $(M,\pi)$ carrying an integrable system $F$, the image of the moment-type map $F$ is foliated by affine manifolds carrying integral affine structures coming from action variables on each symplectic leaf. Determine the obstructions (cohomological/monodromy/Chern-class-type invariants associated with this affine foliation) to the existence of global action–angle coordinates, in analogy with Duistermaat's symplectic obstruction theory.

original_question: Which foliations with affine leaves can be described as the ima ge of the moment map? Notice that a similar problem is still open even in the symplectic setting: which closed manifolds Bn may serve as bases of locally trivial Lagrangian fibrations M 2n T n - → Bn, where M 2n is symplectic? Extensions of the affine structure to the singular setting are also d esirable. One instance when the affine structure on the leaves extends to an affine structure on th e image of the moment map for non-regular Poisson manifolds is the case of b-Poisson manifolds [107]. For these manifolds this affine structure is well-understood and classified via the Delzant theorem [106]. original_question: Find natural examples of integrable systems in classical me chanics with non-trivial Duistermaat-Chern classes.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a connected symplectic $2n$-manifold and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. the components $f_i$ are smooth functions in involution $\{f_i,f_j\}=0$ that are functionally independent on an open dense subset. Restrict to the set of regular values of $F$ whose fiber is a compact connected Lagrangian torus; by the Arnold–Liouville theorem $F$ defines a locally trivial Lagrangian $T^n$-fibration over this regular base $B^{\mathrm{reg}}$. Associated to this fibration are two Duistermaat invariants: the monodromy representation $\pi_1(B^{\mathrm{reg}})\to GL(n,\mathbb{Z})$, and, once the monodromy is killed (or after passing to an appropriate cover), the Lagrangian Chern class in $H^2(B^{\mathrm{reg}};\mathcal{Z})$ (with coefficients in the sheaf of integral affine sections) which obstructs the existence of a global Lagrangian section, the so-called Duistermaat–Chern class.

Problem: Exhibit a natural example of a completely integrable Hamiltonian system arising in classical mechanics (in the sense of a physically motivated system on a phase space coming from mechanics, e.g. rigid-body, celestial-mechanics, or molecular systems) whose Duistermaat–Chern class is non-trivial.
status_search_result: Available literature on monodromy and topology of integrable Hamiltonian systems indicates that while artificial examples with non-trivial Duistermaat–Chern class can be constructed (e.g. by twisting ruled symplectic 4-manifolds), no naturally occurring example from classical mechanics with a non-trivial Duistermaat–Chern class appears to be known. The problem is thus still open.

original_question: Given a set of semiclassical operators that verify conditio ns 1 and 2 above, can one detect the independence axiom 3 in a purely spe ctral way? More precisely, can one tell from asymptotics of joint eigenvalues or eigenfunctions of (P1,..., Pn) that the principal symbols are almost everywhere independent? A great achievement of microlocal analysis of pseudo-differential o perators is the formulation of com- plete Bohr-Sommerfeld rules to any order. Given a quantum integrable system, these rules are, in fact, some kind of integrality conditions (or cohomological conditions), de pending on a parameter E ∈ Rn, that are satisfied if and only if E is a joint eigenvalue of the system, modulo an arbitrarily small error of size O(hbar∞ ). Historically (both in physics and mathematics), these rules have bee n written for regular Lagrangian tori, i.e., E should stay in a small ball of regular values of the classical moment ma p. More recently, non-trivial extensions to some singular situations have been found, see [50, 229, 228]. In order to treat even more physical examples, and to appeal to t he geometry community, it is impor- tant to extend these rules to Berezin-Toeplitz quantisation on com pact K ahler manifolds. This was done recently for regular tori [48], and for one degree of freedom systems with Morse singularities, see [147, 146]. It should be possible to treat the focus-focus case as well, along the lines of [227].
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and let $P_1(\hbar), \dots, P_n(\hbar)$ be a family of self-adjoint semiclassical $\hbar$-pseudodifferential operators on $M$ (or on a quantizable Kähler manifold via Berezin–Toeplitz quantization) depending on a small parameter $\hbar \in (0,\hbar_0]$. Assume that:

1. The operators pairwise commute: $[P_i(\hbar), P_j(\hbar)] = 0$ for all $i,j$.
2. Each $P_i$ admits a principal symbol $p_i \in C^\infty(M;\mathbb{R})$, and the joint principal symbol map $F = (p_1, \dots, p_n) : M 	o \mathbb{R}^n$ is proper on each level (so the joint spectrum is discrete).

A classical integrability condition further requires:

3. The functions $p_1, \dots, p_n$ are almost everywhere independent, i.e.\ $dp_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dp_n 
eq 0$ on a dense open subset of $M$.

The joint spectrum $\mathrm{JointSpec}(P_1(\hbar), \dots, P_n(\hbar))$ is the set of $E = (E_1,\dots,E_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that there exists a nonzero common eigenvector $\psi$ with $P_i(\hbar)\psi = E_i \psi$ for all $i$.

Question: Suppose only conditions (1) and (2) are known. Is there a purely spectral criterion — formulated through the asymptotic behavior, as $\hbar 	o 0^+$, of the joint eigenvalues $E(\hbar)$ and/or the joint eigenfunctions of $(P_1(\hbar),\dots,P_n(\hbar))$ — that is equivalent to condition (3) (almost-everywhere independence of the principal symbols)?
status_search_result: No published resolution of this specific spectral-detection problem for the classical independence axiom in semiclassical quantum integrable systems was located. The problem is listed as an open problem attributed to S. Vũ Ngọc and no subsequent solution appears in available sources.

original_question: Define (and detect) the quantum Chern class. 7.2 Inverse problem for quantum integrable systems (commun icated by A. Pelayo and S. V u Ngo. c) The notion of quantum integrable system as a maximal set of commut ing quantum observables is fairly well established now. It is a very old notion, going back to Bohr, Somm erfeld and Einstein [71] in the early days of quantum mechanics. Nonetheless the theory didn't blo ssom at that time because of the lack of technical tools needed to solve interesting problems about q uantum integrable systems. For recent surveys discussing the spectral geometry of integrable s ystems, see [188, 181]. The most elementary results about the symplectic structure of cla ssical integrable systems, such as the existence of action-angle variable, did not fit well in Schr odinge r's quantum setting at that time because they involve the analysis of differential and pseudodifferen tial operators, only developed since the 1960s. This is a prominent part of analysis and PDE (the most mat hematical side of quantum mechanics), that goes by the name of "microlocal analysis". The microlocal analysis of action-angle variables starts with the pion eering works of Duistermaat [67] and Colin de Verdi` ere [51, 52], and was followed by many other authors (see [49] for further references). For compact symplectic manifolds, the study of quantum action-an gle variables is very recent, it goes back to Charles [48], using the theory of Toeplitz operators. Toeplit z operators give rise to a semiclas- sical algebra of operators with symbolic calculus and microlocalization properties, isomorphic (at a microlocal level) to the algebra of pseudodifferential operators (s ee Boutet de Monvel-Guillemin [42]). The classification of semitoric systems in [185, 186] (see Section 1) g oes a long way to answering the fascinating question "can one hear the shape of a semitoric system "? More precisely, the idea is to recover the classical semitoric invariants from the joint spectrum of a quantum integrable system, as much as possible.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a compact connected symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$, and let $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a smooth map whose components Poisson-commute, $\{F_i,F_j\}=0$, and which is a momentum map for an effective Hamiltonian action of $\mathbb{T}^n$ on $M$ (so $(M,\omega,F)$ is a symplectic-toric manifold). In this case the Delzant polytope $\Delta=F(M)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ together with the integer affine structure inherited from $\mathbb{Z}^n$ determines, via its outward primitive normal vectors at each facet, characteristic classes of $M$, in particular the Chern classes $c_k(TM)\in H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{Z})$.

A quantization of $(M,\omega,F)$ is given by a self-adjoint semiclassical operator family $(\hat F_{1,\hbar},\dots,\hat F_{n,\hbar})$, $\hbar\in(0,\hbar_0]$, of Berezin–Toeplitz (or pseudodifferential) type, acting on a family of Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_\hbar$, such that $[\hat F_{i,\hbar},\hat F_{j,\hbar}]=0$ and the principal symbols are $F_1,\dots,F_n$. The joint spectrum 
$$\Sigma_\hbar=\operatorname{JointSpec}(\hat F_{1,\hbar},\dots,\hat F_{n,\hbar})\subset\mathbb{R}^n$$
is, modulo $O(\hbar^\infty)$, an $\hbar$-dependent discrete subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Problem. Provide an intrinsic definition of a "quantum Chern class" attached to such a quantum integrable system, characterized by the following requirements:

(a) (Definition) For each $k\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ define an invariant $c_k^{\mathrm{q}}(\hat F_\hbar)$ of the quantum integrable system $(\hat F_{1,\hbar},\dots,\hat F_{n,\hbar})$, depending only on its unitary equivalence class up to $O(\hbar^\infty)$.

(b) (Semiclassical limit) Show that, in the semiclassical limit $\hbar\to 0$, the invariant $c_k^{\mathrm{q}}(\hat F_\hbar)$ recovers the classical Chern class $c_k(TM)\in H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ of the underlying symplectic-toric (or, more generally, semitoric) manifold.

(c) (Detection) Give an explicit constructive procedure that recovers $c_k^{\mathrm{q}}(\hat F_\hbar)$ from the asymptotics of the joint spectrum $\Sigma_\hbar$ as $\hbar\to 0$ alone, without knowing the operators $\hat F_{i,\hbar}$ a priori.

Carry this out in the toric setting, and extend the construction to the semitoric setting in dimension $4$ (where $n=2$ and one component $F_1$ generates an effective $S^1$-action while singularities may include focus-focus points).
status_search_result: A literature search does not return any work explicitly defining or detecting a "quantum Chern class" for quantum integrable systems. Related work by Pelayo, Vũ Ngọc, Le Floch and others has constructively recovered classical symplectic invariants of semitoric systems from joint semiclassical spectra, but the specific question of defining and spectrally detecting a quantum analogue of the Chern class appears to remain open.

self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega,F=(J,H))$ be a semitoric integrable system on a connected $4$-dimensional symplectic manifold; that is, $J$ and $H$ are smooth functions in involution, the momentum map $F:M\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is proper, $J$ generates an effective Hamiltonian $S^1$-action, and all singularities of $F$ are non-degenerate with no hyperbolic components. Assume $F$ has a focus-focus critical point $m\in M$ with critical value $c=F(m)\in\mathbb{R}^2$. Associated with such a focus-focus point is the Taylor series symplectic invariant: a formal power series $S^\infty\in\mathbb{R}[[X,Y]]$ (with $S^\infty(0,0)=0$ and $S^\infty$ defined modulo $2\pi X$) which is the semi-global symplectic invariant of the singular Lagrangian fibration of $F$ in a neighborhood of the focus-focus fiber $F^{-1}(c)$.

Consider a semiclassical quantization of the system by a pair of commuting self-adjoint (pseudodifferential or Berezin-Toeplitz) operators $\hat J(\hbar),\hat H(\hbar)$ whose principal symbols are $J,H$, and denote by
$$\Sigma(\hbar)=\operatorname{JointSpec}(\hat J(\hbar),\hat H(\hbar))\subset\mathbb{R}^2$$
their joint spectrum.

Problem. Give an explicit algorithm that recovers the Taylor series invariant $S^\infty$ associated with the focus-focus critical value $c$ directly from the asymptotic behaviour, as $\hbar\to 0^+$, of the part of the joint spectrum $\Sigma(\hbar)$ lying in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of $c$, using a singular Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rule at the focus-focus singularity.

original_question: What information about the principal symbols f1,..., fn of a quantum integrable system T1,hbar,..., Tn,hbar can be detected from their semiclasical joint spectrum? For instance, suppose that we know that a certain object - say, an integer z, or a matrix A - is a symplectic invariant of (M, omega, f1,..., fn). Can we compute this object from the semiclassical joint spe ctrum? An additional interesting problem, which is in fact closely related to Qu estion 2.5 is as follows:
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a connected symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$, and let $f_1,\dots,f_n:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be smooth functions whose Hamiltonian vector fields pairwise Poisson-commute and are linearly independent almost everywhere, so that $(M,\omega,f_1,\dots,f_n)$ is a classical integrable system. Suppose this system is quantized by an $n$-tuple of pairwise commuting self-adjoint semiclassical operators $T_{1,\hbar},\dots,T_{n,\hbar}$ (e.g. $\hbar$-pseudodifferential or Berezin–Toeplitz operators) whose principal symbols are $f_1,\dots,f_n$. The semiclassical joint spectrum is the family, indexed by $\hbar\to 0$, of joint eigenvalues
$$\mathrm{JointSpec}(T_{1,\hbar},\dots,T_{n,\hbar})=\{(\lambda_1(\hbar),\dots,\lambda_n(\hbar))\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,v\neq 0,\ T_{j,\hbar}v=\lambda_j(\hbar)v\ \forall j\}.$$

A symplectic invariant of $(M,\omega,f_1,\dots,f_n)$ is any quantity (e.g. an integer, a polygon, a matrix, a Taylor series) that depends only on the equivalence class of the system under symplectomorphisms intertwining the momentum maps up to allowed transformations.

Problem. Determine which information about the principal symbols $f_1,\dots,f_n$ can be recovered from the semiclassical joint spectrum of $T_{1,\hbar},\dots,T_{n,\hbar}$ as $\hbar\to 0$. More precisely: given a symplectic invariant of $(M,\omega,f_1,\dots,f_n)$ (such as a specific integer $z$ or matrix $A$), produce an explicit algorithm that computes this invariant from the semiclassical joint spectrum.

original_question: Can one make progress in counting the number of fixed points by studying the spectrum of the quantisation of mu: M → S1? This type of problem should be very relevant to the study of equilibriu m points of integrable systems but, for the moment, it is only a toy version to start with. The gener al case would involve quantisation and a study of the fixed point properties of an object (momentum m ap) of the form M → (S1)k × Rn, and this will likely be quite challenging. 7.3 Quantum integrability for polynomial in momenta integr als The approach to quantisation of natural Hamiltonian systems discu ssed in this section is, perhaps, the most traditional. Instead of a Hamiltonian of the form (3.1), i.e., H = K + U on a Riemannian manifold M, one considers the second order differential operator acting on C2-differentiable functions on M and given by ˆH:= ∆ + U, where ∆ = gij∇ i∇ j is the Beltrami-Laplace operator corresponding to g. Next, by a quantum integral we understand another differential operator ˆF that commutes with H: [ ˆH, ˆF ] = ˆH ◦ ˆF - ˆF ◦ ˆH = 0. (7.1) Sometimes one requires that the operator ˆF be self-adjoint. It is known and is easy to see that, for any operators ˆH and ˆF, the symbol of [ ˆH, ˆF ] is just the Poisson bracket of the symbols of ˆH and ˆF. We say that a polynomial in momenta integral F for (3.1) is quantisable if there exists a quantum integral ˆF for ˆH such that its symbol is F.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a compact connected symplectic manifold equipped with a Hamiltonian circle action whose momentum map is $\mu : M \to S^1$ (regarded as an $S^1$-valued Hamiltonian). The fixed point set of the $S^1$-action coincides with the set of critical points of $\mu$. Suppose one constructs a quantization of $\mu$, i.e.\ a self-adjoint operator $\widehat{\mu}$ acting on a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ associated with $(M,\omega)$ via a chosen quantization scheme (e.g.\ geometric or Berezin–Toeplitz quantization), whose principal symbol is $\mu$.

Question: Can one extract information about, and in particular count, the number of fixed points of the $S^1$-action on $M$ purely from spectral data of $\widehat{\mu}$ (such as its eigenvalues, their asymptotic distribution, or associated semiclassical invariants)?

More generally, given a Hamiltonian action of $T^k \times \mathbb{R}^n$ on $(M,\omega)$ with momentum map $\mu : M \to (S^1)^k \times \mathbb{R}^n$ and an appropriate joint quantization $\widehat{\mu}$, determine to what extent the spectrum (joint spectrum) of $\widehat{\mu}$ recovers the fixed point structure (number, indices, and local invariants of fixed points) of the underlying classical action, providing in particular a method to count equilibrium points of the corresponding integrable system.

original_question: Quantise the Mischenko-Fomenko algebra Fa ⊂ P (g) for an arbitrary finite-dimensional Lie algebra g (or find an obstruction to quantisation ). 7.4 Integrable systems and geometric quantisation As explained above, the idea of quantisation is to associate a repres entation space with a classical system in a functorial way, so that the observables (smooth func tions) become operators on a Hilbert space, and the classical Poisson bracket becomes the commutato r of operators. Here we would like to stress the role of Lagrangian foliations in Geometric Quantisation. Consider a symplectic manifold ( M 2n, omega) with an integral homology class [ omega]. Because of integrality of [ omega] ([233], [136]), there exists a complex line bundle L with a connection ∇ over M such that curv(∇ ) = omega. The pair ( L, ∇ ) is called a prequantum line bundle of (M 2n, omega). Having fixed these data, as a first candidate for the representation space, we consider th e set of sections s which are flat, meaning that ∇ X s = 0 in some privileged directions, given by polarisation (integrable Lagr angian distribution of the complexified tangent bundle). Any Lagrangian foliation of M 2n defines a polarisation, and thus integrable systems can be seen as real polarisations, and their tan gent directions can be used to solve the flatness equation ∇ X s = 0. It is convenient to extend the notion of polarisation to take singular ities into account. Thus a real polarisation P is a foliation whose generic leaves are Lagrangian submanifolds. 40 A leaf of a polarisation is called Bohr-Sommerfeld if the flat sections are defined along the leaf. In the classical case, when M 2n is a cotangent bundle with the leaves being the cotangent spaces, t his condition is fulfilled for all of them. However, if the leaves of a polarisa tion are compact, then this condition becomes nontrivial. As we will see next, the action-angle coordinates of integrable syst ems are useful for localisation of Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves, and a simple model of quantisation would he lp to count them. This coincides with Kostant's viewpoint on geometric quantisation (see [141]). As the simplest example, consider the surface M 2 = S1 × R endowed with the symplectic form omega = dt ∧ dθ. Take, as a prequantum line bundle L, the trivial bundle with connection 1-form Θ = tdθ, and as a distribution P = < ∂ ∂θ >. The flat sections satisfy ∇ X σ = X(σ) - i<θ, X>σ = 0. Thus σ(t, θ) = a(t)eitθ, and Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves are given by the condition t = 2πk, k ∈ Z, i.e., by the integral action coordinates, associated to the polarisation wit h the moment map t. This characterisation of Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves generalises for r egular fibrations: Theorem 7.13 (Guillemin-Sternberg, [100]). Assume the polarisation is a regular Lagrangian fibration with compact leaves over a simply connected base B. Then the Bohr-Sommerfeld set is discrete; and if the zero-fiber {(f1(p),..., fn(p)) = 0 ∈ Rn} ⊂ M 2n is a Bohr-Sommerfeld leaf, then the Bohr- Sommerfeld set is given by BS = {p ∈ M, (f1(p),..., fn(p)) ∈ Zn}, where f1,..., fn are global action coordinates on B. Let us now relate Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves with the geometric quant isation scheme. Denote by J the sheaf of (local) flat sections along the polarisation. Following Kostan t [141], we define the quantisation as the sheaf cohomology Q(M ) = ⨁ k≥ 0 H k(M, J ). The following theorem by Sniatycki [202] provides a bridge between this sheaf cohomology approach of Kostant and c ounting Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves: Theorem 7.14 (Sniatycki). If the leaf space Bn is Haussdorf and the natural projection π: M 2n → Bn is a fibration with compact fibers, then all the cohomology gro ups H k(M, J ) vanish, except for k = 1 2 dim M. Thus, Q(M 2n) = H n(M 2n, J ), and the dimension of the vector space H n(M 2n, J ) equals the number of Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves. This scheme works well for toric manifolds, where the base B may be identified with the image of the moment map associated with the torus action, i.e., the interior of the Delzant polytope and, more gen- erally, for Lagrangian fibrations with elliptic singularities [111]. The nex t step would be to generalise this scheme to the case of integrable systems with arbitrary non-d egenerate singularities. Unfortu- nately, hyperbolic and focus-focus singularities [112], [167] do not b ehave well under this scheme, and the dimension of H n(M 2n, J ) may become infinite even if the number of Bohr-Sommerfeld leaves is finite.

paper_title: Open problems
original_question: Study the various possible notions of relative irregularity for families of higher-dimensional varieties, under appropriate conditions on the fibres.
self_contained_problem:
For a fibration $f\colon X \to B$ from a smooth complex projective surface $X$ onto a smooth projective curve $B$, the relative irregularity is classically defined as $q_f := h^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X) - g(B)$, where $g(B)$ is the genus of $B$. This invariant plays a central role in the geometry of surface fibrations (e.g., in Xiao's conjecture and the Severi inequality).

Investigate analogous notions of relative irregularity for families $f\colon X \to B$ of higher-dimensional smooth projective varieties (i.e., where the general fibre $F$ has $\dim F \geq 2$), under suitable hypotheses on the fibres (for instance, fibres of general type, fibres of maximal Albanese dimension, or fibres with prescribed Hodge-theoretic properties). Formulate the possible definitions of relative irregularity in this higher-dimensional setting, compare them, establish their basic properties, and determine the inequalities or geometric constraints (analogous to those known in the surface case) that they must satisfy.
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Rita Pardini in 2018, asks for a systematic study rather than a single yes/no answer, so it is open-ended by nature. Related progress exists (e.g., a relative Severi inequality for fibrations of maximal Albanese dimension over curves has been established), but the broader programme of defining and studying various notions of relative irregularity for higher-dimensional families remains an active and incomplete area of research.

paper_title: Open problems
original_question: For a fibred surface f: S → B with genus g general fibre and with u_f the rank of the unitary flat summand U in the second Fujita decomposition of f_*ω_f, determine the general relation between u_f and the genus of the fibration. In particular, ask whether there is a Xiao-type lower bound for u_f, including in the isotrivial case.
self_contained_problem:
Let $f: S \to B$ be a fibred surface, that is, a surjective morphism with connected fibres from a smooth complex projective surface $S$ onto a smooth complex projective curve $B$, whose general fibre is a smooth curve of genus $g \geq 2$. Let $\omega_f$ denote the relative dualizing sheaf and consider the Hodge bundle $f_*\omega_f$, a vector bundle of rank $g$ on $B$. By the second Fujita decomposition, $f_*\omega_f$ admits a splitting $f_*\omega_f = A \oplus U$, where $A$ is a locally free sheaf with ample Hodge-theoretic part and $U$ is the maximal unitary flat summand (i.e., the maximal subbundle coming from a unitary representation of $\pi_1(B)$). Let $u_f := \mathrm{rk}(U)$.

(a) Determine the general relation between the unitary rank $u_f$ and the genus $g$ of the fibration. In particular, decide whether there exists a Xiao-type lower bound for $u_f$ in terms of $g$ and the invariants of $f$.

(b) Answer the same question in the isotrivial case, namely when all smooth fibres of $f$ are mutually isomorphic.
status_search_result: Recent work has produced upper bounds (e.g., u_f < g(5g-2)/(6g-3) for non-isotrivial fibrations, with maximal unitary rank u_f = g-1 forcing g ≤ 6) and slope/Clifford-index inequalities linking u_f and g, and there are constructions of locally non-trivial fibrations with maximal unitary rank. A definitive Xiao-type lower bound for u_f in terms of g (especially in the isotrivial case) does not appear to be established in full generality, so the problem is partially solved.

original_question: Find more k-gonal curves, beyond the known examples discussed in the source, that satisfy dim W^1_k(C) = 1, or prove general conditions characterizing curves with dim W^1_k(C) = 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective irreducible curve of genus $g$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For a positive integer $k$, say that $C$ is $k$-gonal if $k$ is the smallest integer such that $C$ admits a non-constant morphism $C \to \mathbb{P}^1$ of degree $k$. For integers $d \geq 0$ and $r \geq 0$, let
$$W^r_d(C) = \{ L \in \mathrm{Pic}^d(C) : h^0(C, L) \geq r+1 \},$$
endowed with its natural scheme structure as a determinantal subvariety of $\mathrm{Pic}^d(C)$. In particular, $W^1_k(C)$ parametrizes line bundles of degree $k$ on $C$ with at least a $2$-dimensional space of global sections, i.e.\ pencils of degree $k$.

Exhibit infinite families of $k$-gonal curves $C$ (beyond those already classically known) for which $\dim W^1_k(C) = 1$, or alternatively, formulate and prove geometric conditions on $C$ (in terms of its gonality pencil, the associated scrollar invariants, or its embedding into a Hirzebruch surface) that characterize the property $\dim W^1_k(C) = 1$.

original_question: Diaz proved that if Y is a complete subvariety of the moduli space M_g of curves of genus g ≥ 2, then dim Y ≤ g - 2. For an integer $d\ge 1$, let $S\mathbb{P}_d$ denote the moduli space of smooth surfaces of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$, that is, the geometric quotient of the open locus $U_d\subset \mathbb{P}(H^0(\mathbb{P}^3,\mathcal{O}(d)))$ parametrizing smooth surfaces by the natural action of $\mathrm{PGL}(4,\mathbb{C})$. paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Largest size of a q-ary code
original_question: For fixed code length n, minimum distance d, and finite field F_q, determine A(n, d), the largest integer M for which there exists a code C contained in F_q^n with exactly M codewords.
self_contained_problem:
Let $q \ge 2$ be a prime power and let $\mathbb{F}_q$ denote the finite field with $q$ elements. For vectors $x,y \in \mathbb{F}_q^n$, define the Hamming distance $d_H(x,y) := |\{i \in \{1,\dots,n\} : x_i \ne y_i\}|$. A $q$-ary code of length $n$ and minimum distance $d$ is a subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ such that $d_H(x,y) \ge d$ for every pair of distinct $x,y \in C$. Define
$$A_q(n,d) := \max\{\,|C| : C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n \text{ is a code with minimum distance at least } d\,\}.$$
Problem: For fixed integers $n \ge 1$, $1 \le d \le n$, and a fixed prime power $q$, determine the exact value of $A_q(n,d)$.
status_search_result: Determining $A_q(n,d)$ exactly is a long-standing central open problem in coding theory. Exact values are known only in restricted cases (e.g., MDS codes meeting the Singleton bound, perfect codes, small parameters); tables of best known upper and lower bounds are maintained (e.g., Brouwer's and Grassl's tables), but no general formula is known and the problem remains open.

context_brief: Largest code in a finite metric space
original_question: Given a finite metric space X^n with metric D, and fixed integers n and d, determine the largest integer M for which there exists a code C contained in X^n having minimum distance d and cardinality M.

A code is any subset $C \subseteq X^n$, and the minimum distance of $C$ is defined as $\min\{D(x,y) : x,y \in C,\ x \neq y\}$. Fix positive integers $n$ and $d$. It remains open in general; exact values of $A(n,d)$ for the Hamming metric are unknown for most parameter ranges, and only bounds (Singleton, Hamming, Plotkin, Elias–Bassalygo, linear programming, etc.) are known. No general closed-form solution exists.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
original_question: Does there exist a notion of duality for codes over non-Abelian groups that yields a MacWilliams formula, and if so is there at least some subclass of non-Abelian groups for which such a duality and MacWilliams formula can be made to work?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $n \geq 1$. A (group) code of length $n$ over $G$ is a subgroup $C \leq G^n$. When $G$ is abelian, the classical MacWilliams identity relates the complete weight enumerator of $C$ to that of its dual code $C^\perp \leq \widehat{G}^n$ (where $\widehat{G}$ is the Pontryagin dual), via the character table of $G$.

Question: Does there exist a notion of duality $C \mapsto C^\perp$ for codes $C \leq G^n$ over non-abelian finite groups $G$ that produces a MacWilliams-type identity, i.e., a linear transformation expressing a suitable weight enumerator of $C^\perp$ in terms of that of $C$ (and vice versa) so that the enumerators of $C$ and $C^\perp$ determine each other? If no such duality exists for all non-abelian finite groups, identify a non-trivial subclass of non-abelian finite groups for which such a duality together with a MacWilliams identity can be defined.
status_search_result: There are both negative and positive results. A negative result establishes that no traditional duality theory on all subgroups of $G^n$ can satisfy a MacWilliams identity for any non-abelian $G$. However, recent work has proposed alternative notions of duality for non-abelian group codes that do yield MacWilliams-type identities (and Greene-type theorems), reducing to the classical formulas when $G$ is abelian. Thus the original question is partially answered: pure subgroup duality fails, but modified frameworks succeed.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
original_question: Determine whether there is a theoretical upper limit on the design parameter t for which the Assmus-Mattson theorem can produce t-designs from linear codes, or else prove that no such limit exists by exhibiting codes that yield t-designs for arbitrarily large t.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A linear $[n,k,d]$ code $C$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, where $d$ denotes its minimum Hamming distance. Its dual code $C^\perp$ is defined with respect to the standard inner product and has minimum distance denoted $d^\perp$. For a codeword $c\in C$, its support is $\mathrm{supp}(c)=\{i:c_i\neq 0\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$. For each integer $w$, let $\mathcal{B}_w(C)$ denote the multiset of supports of codewords of $C$ of Hamming weight $w$ (taken up to scalar multiplication). A $t$-$(n,w,\lambda)$ design is a collection of $w$-element blocks from an $n$-element point set such that every $t$-element subset of points lies in exactly $\lambda$ blocks.
        
The Assmus–Mattson theorem asserts: let $C$ be an $[n,k,d]$ linear code over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with dual code $C^\perp$ of minimum distance $d^\perp$. Fix a positive integer $t<d$. If the number of nonzero weights in $C^\perp$ that are at most $n-t$ is at most $d-t$, then for every $w$ with $d\le w\le n$, the supports $\mathcal{B}_w(C)$ form (the blocks of) a $t$-design (and similarly for $C^\perp$).

Problem. Either:
(a) prove that there exists an absolute upper bound $T<\infty$ such that, for every prime power $q$, every length $n$, and every linear code $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, the largest value of $t$ for which the Assmus–Mattson theorem applied to $C$ produces a nontrivial $t$-design is at most $T$; or
(b) prove no such bound exists, by exhibiting, for every positive integer $t$, a linear code $C$ over some finite field for which the Assmus–Mattson theorem yields a $t$-design.
category_tag: Assmus-Mattson theorem and t-designs from codes
status_search_result: No proof of either a universal upper bound on $t$ or a construction giving arbitrarily large $t$ via the Assmus–Mattson theorem has been located. Recent literature (e.g., results bounding $t\le 5$ for certain four-weight binary codes, and Assmus–Mattson-type theorems extended to association schemes, rank-metric codes, and codes over $\mathbb{Z}_4$) studies specific classes but does not settle the general question, which appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Classification of optimal rank-metric variants over rings of order 4
original_question: Classify all linear codes over rings of order 4 that meet the corresponding rank bounds for Lee, Euclidean, or Bachoc weight, namely all MLDR, MEDR, and MBDR codes.
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a finite ring of order 4 (for instance Z/4Z or F_2[u]/(u^2) or F_4). Consider linear codes C ⊆ R^n. Three weight functions are considered on R:

(i) the Lee weight w_L,
(ii) the Euclidean weight w_E,
(iii) the Bachoc weight w_B.

For a codeword x ∈ R^n, define the corresponding distance d_•(x) as the sum of the per-coordinate weights, and for a code C set d_•(C) = min{d_•(x) : x ∈ C, x ≠ 0}. Each codeword x ∈ R^n also has a rank rk(x), defined (as in the rank-metric setting for codes over rings of order 4) via the matrix associated to x over the underlying prime field; the rank distance of a code is rk(C) = min{rk(x) : x ∈ C, x ≠ 0}.

Known bounds relate the Lee, Euclidean, and Bachoc distances of a linear code to its rank K and length n:
  (1)  d_L(C) ≤ Φ_L(n,K),
  (2)  d_E(C) ≤ Φ_E(n,K),
  (3)  d_B(C) ≤ Φ_B(n,K),
for explicit functions Φ_L, Φ_E, Φ_B (the rank-metric Singleton-type bounds for these weights).

A code attaining bound (1) is called a Maximum Lee Distance with respect to Rank (MLDR) code; attaining (2) gives a Maximum Euclidean Distance with respect to Rank (MEDR) code; attaining (3) gives a Maximum Bachoc Distance with respect to Rank (MBDR) code.

Problem: Find and classify, up to equivalence, all MLDR, MEDR, and MBDR linear codes over every ring of order 4.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Automorphism group of the putative [72,36,16] Type II code
original_question: Assuming a binary Type II self-dual [72, 36, 16] code exists, prove that its automorphism group is trivial.
self_contained_problem:
A binary linear code of length $n$ is a linear subspace $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$. The code $C$ is called self-dual if $C = C^\perp$ with respect to the standard inner product on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and it is called Type II (doubly-even) if it is self-dual and the Hamming weight of every codeword is divisible by $4$. The minimum distance of $C$ is $d(C) = \min\{\mathrm{wt}(c) : c \in C, c \neq 0\}$. The automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(C)$ consists of all coordinate permutations $\sigma \in S_n$ such that $\sigma(C) = C$.

Assume that a binary Type II self-dual code $C$ of length $72$, dimension $36$, and minimum distance $16$ exists. Prove that $\mathrm{Aut}(C)$ is trivial, i.e. $\mathrm{Aut}(C) = \{1\}$.
status_search_result: A sequence of works has progressively restricted the automorphism group of a putative extremal Type II [72,36,16] binary code. It has been shown that the group cannot contain various subgroups (S_3, A_4, D_8, Z_2×Z_4, Q_8, Z_10) and is not elementary abelian of order 8. Combining these results, Aut(C) has order at most 5; it is now known to be cyclic of order 1, 2, 3, or 5. The full conjecture that the automorphism group is trivial has not been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Extremal Type II Z_(2k)-codes producing extremal lattices
original_question: For lengths n that are multiples of 8, find a Type II self-dual code over Z_(2k), with 2k ≥ 2s + 2, whose minimum Euclidean weight d_E satisfies d_E/(2k) = 2s + 2, so that Construction A yields an extremal unimodular lattice.
self_contained_problem:
Let $k\ge 1$ and consider the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}=\mathbb{Z}/2k\mathbb{Z}$. For a vector $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{2k}^n$, define its Euclidean weight by
$$\mathrm{wt}_E(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n \min\{x_i^2,(2k-x_i)^2\},$$
where $x_i$ is identified with its representative in $\{0,1,\dots,2k-1\}$. A linear code $C\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{2k}^n$ is self-dual if $C=C^\perp$ with respect to the standard inner product modulo $2k$. The code $C$ is called Type II if it is self-dual and every codeword has Euclidean weight divisible by $4k$. Let $d_E(C)$ denote the minimum nonzero Euclidean weight of $C$.

Construction A assigns to such a code $C$ the lattice
$$\Lambda(C)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2k}}\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n : x \bmod 2k \in C\bigr\}.$$
If $C$ is Type II, then $\Lambda(C)$ is an even unimodular lattice of minimum norm $\min\{2k,\,d_E(C)/(2k)\}$. An even unimodular lattice in dimension $n$ (a multiple of $8$) is called extremal if its minimum norm equals $2\lfloor n/24\rfloor+2$.

Problem: Let $n$ be a positive multiple of $8$, and write $s=\lfloor n/24\rfloor$. Construct a Type II self-dual code $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$ of length $n$ with $2k\ge 2s+2$ such that
$$\frac{d_E(C)}{2k}=2s+2,$$
so that $\Lambda(C)$ is an extremal even unimodular lattice. Determine, for each such $n$ and each admissible $k$, whether such an extremal Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-code exists.
status_search_result: The problem is a general existence question; constructions are known in many specific cases (e.g., extremal Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-codes of length 24 for $k=4,\dots,20$ and length 32 for $k=4,\dots,10$, plus recent constructions for lengths 56 and 64 over $\mathbb{Z}_4$), but the general existence question for all multiples of 8 and admissible $k$ remains open. Results from 2022–2024 continue to address specific cases, indicating the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
original_question: Give a proof, without relying on a lengthy computer search, that every Type II [48, 24, 12] code is equivalent to q48, and determine whether q48 is in fact the unique [48, 24, 12] code even without the Type II restriction.
self_contained_problem:
A binary linear code of length $n$ and dimension $k$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$. Its minimum distance $d$ is the smallest Hamming weight of a nonzero codeword. The code is self-dual if $C = C^\perp$ under the standard inner product, and it is Type II (doubly even) if it is self-dual and every codeword has weight divisible by $4$. A $[48,24,12]$ code is a binary linear code with the indicated parameters. Two codes are equivalent if one is obtained from the other by a permutation of coordinates. Let $q_{48}$ denote the extended binary quadratic residue code of length $48$, which is a Type II $[48,24,12]$ code.

(a) Give a proof, not relying on a lengthy computer search, that every Type II $[48,24,12]$ binary linear code is equivalent to $q_{48}$.

(b) Determine whether $q_{48}$ is the unique (up to equivalence) binary linear $[48,24,12]$ code, without imposing the Type II restriction; that is, prove or disprove that every binary $[48,24,12]$ code is equivalent to $q_{48}$.
status_search_result: The Type II uniqueness of the [48,24,12] code (equivalence to the extended quadratic residue code q48) was established by Houghten, Lam, Thiel and Parker via a computer search, so part (a)—a proof without a lengthy computer search—appears to remain open. The general uniqueness question (without the Type II restriction) does not appear to have been resolved in the literature.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Classification of singly-even self-dual [48,24,10] codes of type W48,2
original_question: Classify all extremal singly-even self-dual [48, 24, 10] codes whose weight enumerator is W48,2 = 1 + 768y^10 + 8592y^12 + 57600y^14 + ··· and whose shadow enumerator begins S48,2 = 54y^8 + 16976y^12 + ···.
self_contained_problem:
A binary linear code $C$ of length $n$ is self-dual if $C = C^\perp$ with respect to the standard inner product on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$. It is singly-even (Type I) if all codeword weights are even but not all are divisible by 4. The shadow of a singly-even self-dual code $C$ is $S = C_0^\perp \setminus C$, where $C_0$ is the subcode of codewords of weight divisible by 4. A self-dual code of length $n$ and minimum distance $d$ is called extremal if $d$ attains the maximal value allowed by the Mallows–Sloane bound; for Type I codes of length $48$ this maximum is $10$.

It is known that there are exactly two possible weight enumerators for extremal singly-even self-dual $[48,24,10]$ codes. Consider the second one, namely
$$W(y) \;=\; 1 + 768\,y^{10} + 8592\,y^{12} + 57600\,y^{14} + \cdots,$$
together with the corresponding shadow weight enumerator
$$S(y) \;=\; 54\,y^{8} + 16976\,y^{12} + \cdots .$$

Classify, up to equivalence, all extremal singly-even self-dual binary $[48,24,10]$ codes whose Hamming weight enumerator equals $W(y)$ (equivalently, whose shadow enumerator equals $S(y)$).

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
original_question: Give a universal decoding algorithm for quasi-cyclic codes, where a code C is quasi-cyclic of index k if v ∈ C implies σ^k(v) ∈ C for the cyclic shift σ.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and let $\sigma:\mathbb{F}_q^n \to \mathbb{F}_q^n$ denote the cyclic shift $\sigma(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_{n-1}) = (v_{n-1},v_0,\ldots,v_{n-2})$. For a positive integer $k$ dividing $n$, a linear code $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ is called quasi-cyclic of index $k$ if $\sigma^k(v) \in C$ for every $v \in C$.

Provide a universal decoding algorithm for the class of quasi-cyclic codes: that is, exhibit an explicit algorithm which, given as input the parameters of an arbitrary quasi-cyclic code $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ of index $k$ (for example, a generator or parity-check matrix) together with a received word $y \in \mathbb{F}_q^n$, returns a codeword $c \in C$ minimizing the Hamming distance $d(y,c)$ (or, more generally, decodes up to half the minimum distance of $C$), with correctness and complexity guarantees that hold uniformly across the family of quasi-cyclic codes.
status_search_result: Recent literature indicates that no efficient universal decoding algorithm for general quasi-cyclic codes is known. The Quasi-Cyclic Syndrome Decoding Problem has been shown to be NP-complete (2023), and the BIKE/HQC code-based cryptosystems rely on the presumed hardness of decoding random quasi-cyclic codes. The problem appears still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Tightness of the binary Varshamov-Gilbert bound
original_question: For binary codes, is the Varshamov-Gilbert bound actually tight?
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $n$ and $d$, let $A_2(n,d)$ denote the maximum size of a binary code of length $n$ and minimum Hamming distance at least $d$; that is, the largest cardinality of a subset $C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$ such that any two distinct $x,y\in C$ differ in at least $d$ coordinates. For $0<\delta<1/2$, define the asymptotic rate function
$$R(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log_2 A_2(n,\lfloor \delta n\rfloor).$$
Let $H_2(\delta)=-\delta\log_2\delta-(1-\delta)\log_2(1-\delta)$ denote the binary entropy function. The (binary) Gilbert–Varshamov bound asserts that $R(\delta)\geq 1-H_2(\delta)$ for all $\delta\in(0,1/2)$.

Decide whether the Gilbert–Varshamov bound is asymptotically tight in the binary case: is it true that
$$R(\delta)=1-H_2(\delta)\quad\text{for all }\delta\in(0,1/2)\,?$$
status_search_result: The tightness of the binary Gilbert–Varshamov bound is a long-standing open problem in coding theory. For alphabets of size q ≥ 49, the Tsfasman–Vlăduț–Zink bound from algebraic-geometry codes improves on Gilbert–Varshamov, but no asymptotic improvement is known for binary codes, and it remains a conjecture (often attributed to Goppa) that the bound is asymptotically tight in the binary case. Recent expository sources (MIT open-problems notes; CMU lecture notes; surveys) continue to list this as open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
original_question: Do there exist perfect codes over alphabets whose size is not a prime power?
self_contained_problem:
Let q ≥ 2 be an integer (the alphabet size) and let A be a set with |A| = q. For words x, y ∈ A^n, let d(x,y) denote the Hamming distance, i.e. the number of coordinates in which x and y differ. A code C ⊆ A^n is called a perfect e-error-correcting code (or perfect code of radius e) if the Hamming balls of radius e centered at the codewords of C partition A^n; equivalently, every word in A^n lies in exactly one ball B(c, e) = { y ∈ A^n : d(y, c) ≤ e } with c ∈ C. Trivial perfect codes (the whole space A^n, single-codeword codes, and repetition codes of odd length over a binary alphabet, together with their natural generalizations) are excluded.

Question: Does there exist a nontrivial perfect code of length n ≥ 2 and radius e ≥ 1 over an alphabet of size q, where q is not a prime power?
status_search_result: The question is widely cited as folklore-open. For e ≥ 3 the parameters of perfect codes are fully classified, and for e = 2 nonexistence is known for q a prime power, for q = 2^r 3^s, and for a small finite list of additional q. Recent work (2024) using Diophantine techniques (e.g. generalized Ramanujan–Nagell equations) ruled out 172 further non-prime-power values of q, but a complete answer for arbitrary non-prime-power q remains unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
original_question: If K(n, R) denotes the smallest size of a covering code of length n and covering radius R, is it always true for R ≠ n that K(n + 2, R + 1) ≤ K(n, R)?
self_contained_problem:
For integers n ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ R ≤ n, a binary covering code of length n and covering radius R is a subset C ⊆ {0,1}^n such that every vector x ∈ {0,1}^n lies within Hamming distance R of some codeword c ∈ C. Let K(n, R) denote the smallest possible cardinality of such a code. 

Determine whether, for every pair of integers (n, R) with 0 ≤ R < n, the inequality
   K(n + 2, R + 1) ≤ K(n, R)
holds.
status_search_result: Search results indicate that the inequality K(n+2, R+1) ≤ K(n, R) is known to hold for sufficiently large n (via density/covering radius results in the covering-code literature), but a proof valid for all (n, R) with R ≠ n does not appear to be established, so the full conjecture appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Coding Theory
context_brief: Covering radius of first-order Reed-Muller codes
original_question: Determine the covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code R(1, m) when m is odd.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $m$, the first-order Reed–Muller code $R(1,m)$ is the binary linear code of length $2^m$ whose codewords are the truth tables (evaluations on $\mathbb{F}_2^m$) of all affine Boolean functions $f(x_1,\dots,x_m)=a_0+a_1x_1+\cdots+a_mx_m$ with $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb{F}_2$. The covering radius of a binary code $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is
$$\rho(C)=\max_{v\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}\min_{c\in C} d_H(v,c),$$
where $d_H$ denotes Hamming distance. Equivalently, $\rho(R(1,m))$ is the maximum, over all Boolean functions $f:\mathbb{F}_2^m\to\mathbb{F}_2$, of the Hamming distance from $f$ to the set of affine functions (the nonlinearity of $f$).

For even $m$, it is known that $\rho(R(1,m))=2^{m-1}-2^{m/2-1}$, the value being attained by bent functions.

Determine the exact value of $\rho(R(1,m))$ for all odd $m\ge 1$.
status_search_result: The exact value of the covering radius of $R(1,m)$ for odd $m$ (equivalently, the maximum nonlinearity of Boolean functions on an odd number of variables) is a long-standing open problem. Only small cases are settled; for general odd $m$ only bounds are known, with the classical lower bound $2^{m-1}-2^{(m-1)/2}$ and improved upper bounds such as $\rho(1,2k+1)\le 2\lfloor 2^{2k-1}-2^{2k-3/2}\rfloor$. The problem remains open as of recent surveys.
