paper_title: Gradings, Braidings, Representations, Paraparticles: Some Open Problems
original_question: Do the proposed Hamiltonians built from a monochromatic parabosonic field and a (p+1)-level system, with spectrum-generating algebra P_BF(1,1), P_FB(1,1), or a related mixed paraparticle algebra, yield exactly solvable generalizations of the Jaynes-Cummings model whose energy levels, eigenfunctions, transition rates, and other physical quantities can be computed and compared with theory and experiment?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. The standard Jaynes–Cummings model describes a single mode of a quantized bosonic field interacting with a two-level atom via the Hamiltonian
H_JC = ω a†a + (ω_0/2) σ_z + g(a σ_+ + a† σ_−),
where a, a† are bosonic ladder operators ([a,a†]=1) and σ_z, σ_± are the Pauli matrices for the two-level system. This model is exactly solvable: its spectrum, eigenstates, Rabi oscillations and transition rates admit closed-form expressions.

Generalization. Fix a positive integer p (the order of the paraparticle statistics). A monochromatic parabosonic field of order p is described by a pair of operators b, b† acting on a Fock-like representation and satisfying the trilinear (Green) parabose relations
[{b,b†},b] = −2 b,   [{b,b†},b†] = 2 b†,   [b,b]=[b†,b†]=0 (as trilinear relations),
which generate an osp(1|2)-type Lie superalgebra; on the order-p paraboson Fock space F_p one has b† b |n⟩ = n |n⟩ when n is even and = (n−1+p)|n⟩ when n is odd (or the analogous staircase formula), so the number operator has a deformed integer spectrum depending on p.

Let A be a (p+1)-level atomic system with orthonormal basis |0⟩,…,|p⟩, and let E_{ij} = |i⟩⟨j| be the matrix units acting on A. Consider the relative parastatistics algebras P_BF(1,1) and P_FB(1,1), the unital associative ⋆-algebras generated by one parabosonic pair (b, b†) and one parafermionic pair (f, f†) of order p, together with mixed trilinear (anti)commutation relations of either Bose–Fermi (BF) or Fermi–Bose (FB) type, and let P_MIX(1,1) denote any closely related mixed paraparticle algebra obtained from a Z_2-graded coloring/braiding of these relations.

Question. Construct Hamiltonians of Jaynes–Cummings type acting on F_p ⊗ A and having one of P_BF(1,1), P_FB(1,1), or a related mixed paraparticle algebra as a spectrum-generating algebra, for example of the schematic form
H = ω b†b + Σ_{k=0}^{p} ε_k E_{kk} + g Σ_k ( b T_k^- + b† T_k^+ ),
where the operators T_k^± on A are determined by the embedding of the (p+1)-level system into a parafermionic sector of the chosen algebra.

(a) Determine whether such Hamiltonians are exactly solvable, in the sense that their full spectrum and a complete set of eigenstates can be obtained in closed form by exploiting the chosen spectrum-generating algebra.
(b) When they are exactly solvable, compute explicitly the energy levels, the eigenfunctions, the generalized Rabi frequencies, the atomic and field transition rates, and the time-evolved expectation values of standard observables (atomic inversion, field intensity, photon number variance).
(c) Compare the resulting predictions with the p = 1 (ordinary Jaynes–Cummings) limit and identify physical regimes where the paraparticle order p produces measurable deviations from the standard model.
status_search_result: No published resolution was located. The problem is posed as an open program of constructing and exactly solving paraparticle generalizations of the Jaynes–Cummings model with spectrum-generating algebras P_BF(1,1), P_FB(1,1), or related mixed paraparticle algebras; no follow-up paper carrying out this full analysis was identified, so the current status is taken as unknown.

paper_title: Open problems on graph eigenvalues studied with AutoGraphiX
original_question: For every connected graph G on n at least 3 vertices, is the spectral spread s(G) = λ1(G) − λn(G) always at most sqrt(4qn − 3q^2 − 2q + 1), where q = floor(2n/3) and λ1(G), λn(G) are the largest and smallest adjacency eigenvalues of G? Equivalently, is the maximum spectral spread among connected n-vertex graphs attained exactly by the complete split graph CS(n,q), meaning a graph consisting of a q-vertex clique and an independent set on the remaining n−q vertices with every clique vertex adjacent to every independent-set vertex, with independent-set size ceil(n/3)?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a simple connected graph on n ≥ 3 vertices, with adjacency matrix A(G) and real eigenvalues λ1(G) ≥ λ2(G) ≥ … ≥ λn(G). Define the spectral spread of G by s(G) = λ1(G) − λn(G). For integers n ≥ 3 and 1 ≤ q ≤ n−1, let CS(n, q) denote the complete split graph consisting of a clique on q vertices and an independent set on the remaining n − q vertices, with every vertex of the clique adjacent to every vertex of the independent set. Let q = ⌊2n/3⌋, so that n − q = ⌈n/3⌉.

Prove or disprove: for every connected graph G on n ≥ 3 vertices,
  s(G) ≤ √(4qn − 3q² − 2q + 1),
with equality if and only if G ≅ CS(n, q). Equivalently, show that the maximum of s(G) over all connected graphs on n vertices is attained exactly by the complete split graph CS(n, ⌊2n/3⌋).
status_search_result: The conjecture (originally due to Gregory–Hershkowitz–Kirkland and rediscovered/refined via AutoGraphiX experiments) that the spread-maximizing connected graph on n vertices is the complete split graph CS(n, ⌊2n/3⌋) was proved for all sufficiently large n by Breen, Riasanovsky, Tait and Urschel using graph limits and numerical analysis. The statement is not yet known to hold for all n ≥ 3, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems on graph eigenvalues studied with AutoGraphiX
original_question: Among all unicyclic graphs on n vertices, is the maximum graph energy achieved by the cycle Cn for n ≤ 7 and for n = 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, while for all remaining values of n the maximum is achieved by the lollipop graph Lol(n,6), obtained by joining a cycle C6 to a path P(n−6) with a single edge from a cycle vertex to an endpoint of the path?
self_contained_problem: Let G be a simple graph with adjacency matrix A(G), and let λ_1, λ_2, …, λ_n denote the eigenvalues of A(G). The energy of G is defined by E(G) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} |λ_i|. A unicyclic graph is a connected graph containing exactly one cycle. For integers n ≥ 6 and 3 ≤ g ≤ n, the lollipop graph Lol(n,g) is obtained from a cycle C_g and a path P_{n-g} on n-g vertices by joining a single vertex of C_g to an endpoint of P_{n-g} by an edge (so Lol(n,g) has n vertices and exactly one cycle, of length g).\n\nDetermine, among all unicyclic graphs on n vertices, which graph has the maximum energy. Specifically, decide whether the following statement is true: the cycle C_n attains the maximum energy among unicyclic graphs on n vertices precisely for n ∈ {3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15}, while for all remaining values of n ≥ 4 (with n ≠ 4) the maximum is attained by the lollipop Lol(n,6).
status_search_result: The conjecture was completely resolved by Huo, Ji, and Li (2011). The maximum-energy unicyclic graph on n vertices is C_n for n ≤ 7 with n ≠ 4 and for n ∈ {9, 10, 11, 13, 15}; Lol(4,3) is the maximum for n = 4; and Lol(n,6) is the maximum for all remaining n. Thus the originally stated conjecture is correct except for the small case n = 4.

paper_title: Open problems on graph eigenvalues studied with AutoGraphiX
original_question: For every tricyclic graph G on n vertices with n = 20 or n at least 22, is the energy of G at most the energy of P_n^{6,6;6}, with equality only for P_n^{6,6;6}? Here P_n^{6,6;6} denotes the graph obtained from three copies of C6 and a path P(n−18) by adding a single edge from two of the 6-cycles to one endpoint of the path and a single edge from the third 6-cycle to the other endpoint.

The energy of a simple graph G is defined as E(G) = sum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix. A connected graph on n vertices is called tricyclic if it has exactly n+2 edges (equivalently, its cycle space has dimension 3).

For each integer n ≥ 20, define the graph P_n^{6,6;6} as follows. Take three vertex-disjoint copies of the 6-cycle C_6, call them H_1, H_2, H_3, and a path P_{n-18} on n−18 vertices with endpoints u and v. paper_title: Open Problems and Conjectures on Rational Systems in Three Dimensions
original_question: Consider the three-dimensional rational system, for n = 0, 1, ..., with nonnegative parameters and nonnegative initial conditions such that all denominators are positive: x_{n+1} = (alpha_1 + beta_1 x_n + gamma_1 y_n + delta_1 z_n)/(A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n + D_1 z_n), y_{n+1} = (alpha_2 + beta_2 x_n + gamma_2 y_n + delta_2 z_n)/(A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n + D_2 z_n), and z_{n+1} = (alpha_3 + beta_3 x_n + gamma_3 y_n + delta_3 z_n)/(A_3 + B_3 x_n + C_3 y_n + D_3 z_n). Across the 11,390,625 special cases of this system, what is the boundedness characterization of each special case, and are there general boundedness patterns analogous to those found in two-dimensional rational systems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the three-dimensional rational system of difference equations
  x_{n+1} = (α₁ + β₁ xₙ + γ₁ yₙ + δ₁ zₙ)/(A₁ + B₁ xₙ + C₁ yₙ + D₁ zₙ),
  y_{n+1} = (α₂ + β₂ xₙ + γ₂ yₙ + δ₂ zₙ)/(A₂ + B₂ xₙ + C₂ yₙ + D₂ zₙ),
  z_{n+1} = (α₃ + β₃ xₙ + γ₃ yₙ + δ₃ zₙ)/(A₃ + B₃ xₙ + C₃ yₙ + D₃ zₙ),
for n = 0, 1, 2, …, where all 24 parameters α_i, β_i, γ_i, δ_i, A_i, B_i, C_i, D_i (i = 1, 2, 3) are nonnegative real numbers and the initial conditions (x₀, y₀, z₀) are nonnegative reals chosen so that every denominator is positive for all n ≥ 0. A "special case" is obtained by setting some subset of the parameters in each numerator and denominator to zero (so that the numerator and denominator of each component are nonzero linear combinations), yielding a total of 11,390,625 distinct such special cases.

A solution {(xₙ, yₙ, zₙ)} is called bounded if there exists M < ∞ such that xₙ, yₙ, zₙ ≤ M for all n ≥ 0, and the special case is said to have the boundedness property when every admissible solution is bounded.

Problem: For each of the 11,390,625 special cases, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the (nonzero) parameters and the admissible initial conditions under which every solution is bounded. Moreover, identify general structural patterns characterizing boundedness across these special cases that are analogous to the boundedness classification known for the two-dimensional rational systems
  x_{n+1} = (α₁ + β₁ xₙ + γ₁ yₙ)/(A₁ + B₁ xₙ + C₁ yₙ),
  y_{n+1} = (α₂ + β₂ xₙ + γ₂ yₙ)/(A₂ + B₂ xₙ + C₂ yₙ).
status_search_result: Search results indicate ongoing work on boundedness of particular three-dimensional rational difference systems, with various authors treating isolated special cases (e.g., Alayachi 2021; Camouzis–Ladas work on rational systems). No complete classification of boundedness across all 11,390,625 special cases of the general three-dimensional first-order linear-fractional system has been found, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: For infinite polycyclic groups of high Hirsch length, determine whether there are algorithms that solve the conjugacy search problem effectively, and give computational complexity bounds for such algorithms if they exist. self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series
$$ G = G_0 \trianglerighteq G_1 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_n = \{1\} $$
with each quotient $G_i / G_{i+1}$ cyclic. The Hirsch length $h(G)$ is the number of indices $i$ for which $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is infinite cyclic; it is an invariant of $G$.

The conjugacy search problem in $G$ is: given elements $u, v \in G$ that are known to be conjugate (i.e., there exists $g \in G$ with $g^{-1} u g = v$), produce such an element $g$.

The problem is the following: for infinite polycyclic groups $G$ of arbitrarily large Hirsch length, given by a polycyclic presentation, does there exist an algorithm that solves the conjugacy search problem and runs in time bounded by a stated complexity function (e.g., polynomial in the input size and the Hirsch length)? status_search_result: The problem remains open in the regime of high Hirsch length. Known algorithms (e.g., Eick–Kahrobaei) have been implemented and work for small Hirsch length, but no efficient algorithm is known for large Hirsch length. There are families of polycyclic groups for which the uniform conjugacy problem is shown to be NP-complete (Hofheinz–Steinwandt-type constructions, and the arXiv:1403.4153 family), suggesting that no efficient algorithm exists in general; however a definitive resolution—either a worst-case efficient algorithm for arbitrary polycyclic groups, or a matching hardness result for the search version in the natural cryptographic setting—has not been established.

original_question: For general polycyclic groups used as platform groups in group-based cryptography, determine bounds on the dimensions of the smallest faithful linear embeddings and determine when faithful linear representations are known and small enough for linear decomposition or linear centralizer attacks to be tractable.

$$G = G_0 \triangleright G_1 \triangleright \cdots \triangleright G_n = \{1\}$$
such that each quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. A faithful linear representation of $G$ over a field $k$ is an injective group homomorphism $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$; the smallest such $d$ (over a specified family of fields, e.g. $\mathbb{C}$ or finite fields) is called the minimal faithful linear dimension of $G$, denoted $\mu(G)$.

Linear decomposition and linear centralizer attacks against group-based cryptosystems with platform group $G$ run in time polynomial in $\mu(G)$ (and in the size of the field of definition), provided one can effectively compute a faithful representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mu(G)}(k)$.

1. Determine explicit upper and lower bounds for $\mu(G)$ in terms of standard invariants of $G$ such as the Hirsch length $h(G)$, the number of generators, the derived length, and the orders of the finite cyclic factors $G_i/G_{i+1}$.

Characterize those polycyclic groups $G$ for which $\mu(G)$ is small enough (e.g. polynomially bounded in the chosen security parameter) that linear decomposition attacks and linear centralizer attacks against cryptosystems with platform group $G$ become tractable, and conversely identify infinite families of polycyclic groups for which $\mu(G)$ grows superpolynomially, so that such linear attacks are provably infeasible.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: In fully decentralized or peer-to-peer federated learning, where no central server orchestrates training and clients communicate over a possibly dynamic graph, what governance or trust mechanism should decide the model, algorithm, hyperparameters, and debugging responsibility for a learning task?
self_contained_problem: Consider a fully decentralized (peer-to-peer) federated learning system consisting of a set of clients $\{1,\dots,N\}$, each holding a local dataset $\mathcal{D}_i$, communicating over a (possibly time-varying) connected graph $G_t = (V, E_t)$ with no central coordinator. The clients wish to collaboratively train a model by exchanging messages only along edges of $G_t$. A "learning task specification" consists of: (i) the model class (architecture, parameter space), (ii) the training algorithm (e.g., decentralized SGD, gossip averaging, etc.), (iii) the hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, communication schedule, stopping criterion), and (iv) the assignment of responsibility for monitoring, debugging, and correcting failures during training. Design a formal governance / trust mechanism — i.e., a distributed protocol $\Pi$ executed on $G_t$, together with a decision rule $\mathcal{R}$ — such that the clients can collectively agree upon and update the learning task specification in a way that satisfies the following desiderata: (a) correctness: the agreed-upon specification is well-defined and consistent across all honest clients; (b) incentive compatibility: no client (or coalition of size below a specified threshold) can unilaterally impose a specification that benefits itself at the expense of others; (c) robustness: the mechanism tolerates a bounded fraction of Byzantine or unresponsive clients and adapts to changes in $G_t$; (d) accountability: every decision can be traced to an identifiable subset of clients who can be held responsible for debugging. Either exhibit such a mechanism $(\Pi, \mathcal{R})$ together with a proof of properties (a)–(d), or prove that no protocol satisfying (a)–(d) simultaneously can exist under stated assumptions on the communication and adversary models.
status_search_result: The question of governance and trust mechanisms in fully decentralized federated learning remains an active open research direction. Recent surveys and works on decentralized/peer-to-peer FL (often combining gossip protocols with blockchain or DAG-based consensus) propose partial solutions but no widely accepted formal mechanism simultaneously providing correctness, incentive compatibility, Byzantine robustness, and accountability has been established.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: For fully decentralized learning under non-IID client data, how can one understand convergence and design model-averaging policies that achieve the fastest convergence, especially when clients perform several local update steps before communication?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a fully decentralized optimization problem of the form

  minimize  F(x) = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n F_i(x),    F_i(x) = E_{ξ∼D_i}[ f(x; ξ) ],

where n clients (nodes) are arranged on a connected communication graph G=(V,E) and the local data distributions D_1,…,D_n are heterogeneous (non-IID), so that the local gradients ∇F_i may differ substantially from the global gradient ∇F. Communication is restricted to neighbors in G and is encoded by a sequence of symmetric doubly-stochastic mixing matrices {W_t} ⊂ R^{n×n} supported on G.

Each client i maintains a local model x_i^{(t)} ∈ R^d. In each communication round, every client performs H ≥ 1 local stochastic gradient steps,

  y_i^{(t,0)} = x_i^{(t)},
  y_i^{(t,h+1)} = y_i^{(t,h)} − η ∇f(y_i^{(t,h)}; ξ_i^{(t,h)}),  h = 0,…,H−1,

and then performs a gossip averaging step using the mixing matrix W_t:

  x_i^{(t+1)} = Σ_{j=1}^n (W_t)_{ij} · y_j^{(t,H)}.

Under standard assumptions on f (L-smoothness, possibly (non)convexity, bounded stochastic gradient variance σ^2, and a bounded heterogeneity measure such as (1/n)Σ_i ‖∇F_i(x) − ∇F(x)‖^2 ≤ ζ^2), address the following:

(a) Derive convergence guarantees (rates as functions of n, H, η, σ^2, ζ^2, and the spectral properties of the mixing matrices, such as the second-largest singular value ρ = ‖W − (1/n)11^T‖) that quantify how non-IID data and the number H of local steps affect the convergence of the iterates {x_i^{(t)}} toward a stationary point or minimizer of F.

(b) Determine model-averaging policies — i.e., choices of the (possibly time-varying) mixing matrices W_t supported on G, the local step count H, and the step size η — that achieve the fastest possible convergence rate in this setting, and identify lower bounds matching these rates so as to characterize the optimal averaging policy for decentralized learning with multiple local updates under client data heterogeneity.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made on understanding decentralized SGD convergence under non-IID data with local steps. Koloskova et al. (ICML 2020) gave a unified convergence theory for decentralized SGD with changing topology and local updates, and subsequent works (e.g., gradient-tracking variants, Huang et al. 2022, momentum-based unified frameworks 2024) have improved dependence on heterogeneity. However, fully characterizing optimal time-varying mixing policies and matching lower bounds, especially with many local steps under heterogeneity, remains an active area without a definitive closed answer.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Can compressed-communication and sparse-update methods developed for centrally orchestrated federated learning be translated to fully decentralized learning without harming convergence, while also enabling better privacy-utility trade-offs than local differential privacy alone?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a fully decentralized learning setting in which $n$ agents (nodes) are arranged on a connected undirected communication graph $G=(V,E)$, with $|V|=n$. Each agent $i\in V$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ and a local loss $F_i(	heta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim \mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(	heta;z)]$ for parameter $	heta\in\mathbb{R}^d$, and the agents collectively wish to minimize $F(	heta)= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n F_i(	heta)$. Communication is restricted to neighbors in $G$; there is no central server.

In each round $t$, every agent $i$ performs (possibly stochastic) local updates and then communicates with neighbors a message $m_{i	o j}^{(t)} = \mathcal{C}(g_i^{(t)})$, where $g_i^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is an update vector (e.g., a stochastic gradient or model delta) and $\mathcal{C}:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathcal{M}$ is a (possibly randomized) compression operator (such as quantization, top-$k$ sparsification, or sketching) with bounded message size $b(\mathcal{C})\ll d$ bits. Sparse-update methods further restrict $g_i^{(t)}$ to lie in a low-dimensional subset (a coordinate mask) chosen by each agent.

For privacy, an algorithm is said to satisfy local differential privacy with parameter $\varepsilon>0$ if, for every agent $i$, the entire transcript of messages $i$ sends to its neighbors is $\varepsilon$-DP with respect to $i$'s local dataset. More generally, one may consider distributed/network differential privacy, where the privacy guarantee is taken with respect to the view of any colluding subset of agents.

The problem has two parts.

(a) Construct a decentralized optimization algorithm using a compression operator $\mathcal{C}$ and/or sparse-update masks that, under standard assumptions (e.g., $L$-smoothness of each $F_i$, bounded gradient variance, mixing properties of the gossip matrix associated with $G$), achieves the same asymptotic convergence rate (in expectation, to a stationary point for nonconvex $F$, or to the optimum for convex $F$) as the corresponding uncompressed centrally orchestrated federated algorithm, while using only $O(b(\mathcal{C}))$ bits per agent per round.

(b) Show that such a decentralized compressed algorithm can be combined with a privacy mechanism so that, for a fixed end-to-end privacy budget $\varepsilon$ against an adversary controlling a strict subset of agents, the resulting privacy-utility trade-off (excess loss as a function of $\varepsilon$ and $n$) is strictly better than what is achievable by any algorithm satisfying $\varepsilon$-local differential privacy at each agent.

Provide such an algorithm together with matching upper and lower bounds, or prove that no such algorithm exists.
category_tag: decentralized federated learning with compression and differential privacy
status_search_result: The question is a stated open research direction in the federated learning literature. There has been substantial progress on compressed decentralized SGD (e.g., CHOCO-SGD, DeepSqueeze, Quantized Gossip), and on network/secure-aggregation differential privacy that outperforms local DP, but a fully unified solution matching centralized-FL convergence rates with provably better privacy-utility trade-offs in arbitrary decentralized topologies remains an active open research direction.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: For cross-silo federated learning, what formal privacy guarantees are appropriate when client organizations may control data from many users, may distrust other clients more than the server, and may require local or user-level differential privacy depending on the application?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cross-silo federated learning setting in which a fixed set of K client organizations (silos) jointly train a model via a central server. Each silo k holds a local dataset D_k consisting of records contributed by n_k end-users (so silo k can be viewed as a collection of user-level data). Communication proceeds in rounds: in each round the server sends a model to a subset of silos, each participating silo computes an update from its local data, and the server aggregates the updates to produce the next model. Assume the following threat model: (i) each silo is honest-but-curious and may attempt to infer information about data held by other silos; (ii) silos trust the server less than they would trust themselves but possibly more or less than they trust other silos; (iii) some applications require protection of individual users (user-level guarantees) whereas others require protection at the level of an entire silo's contribution.

Formulate a formal differential-privacy-style definition (or family of definitions) of privacy that simultaneously captures:

1. A notion of inter-silo privacy: the joint view of any coalition of silos (together with, optionally, the server) should be (ε, δ)-indistinguishable under change of a single user's record, or under change of an entire silo's dataset, depending on the application's required granularity.

2. A configurable trust model in which the server's view and each silo's view may be governed by different privacy parameters (ε_server, ε_silo, δ_server, δ_silo), reducing to local differential privacy when no party is trusted and to central differential privacy when the server is fully trusted.

3. A clear specification of the unit of privacy (single user vs. silo) and of neighboring datasets at the federation level.

Provide such a definition, prove its basic properties (post-processing, composition across rounds and across silos, group privacy with respect to multiple users within one silo), and exhibit a federated training mechanism that satisfies the definition with non-trivial utility guarantees for convex stochastic optimization.
status_search_result: The question of formalizing appropriate privacy notions for cross-silo federated learning under varied trust models and granularities (user-level vs. silo-level) is highlighted as not systematically explored. Subsequent works (e.g., on inter-silo record-level DP, ISRL-DP, and shuffle-model variants) have proposed partial formalizations and algorithms, but a unified, broadly accepted framework covering all listed trust configurations and granularities does not appear to be established, so the broad problem remains open.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How should real-world cross-client differences in federated datasets be characterized across feature-distribution skew, label-distribution skew, concept drift, concept shift, quantity skew, violations of independence, and dataset shift so that realistic non-IID benchmarks and mitigation strategies can be built?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which K clients, indexed by k = 1, …, K, each hold a local data distribution P_k(x, y) over an input space X and label space Y. Cross-client heterogeneity can be decomposed by writing P_k(x, y) = P_k(y | x) P_k(x) = P_k(x | y) P_k(y) and includes the following phenomena:

1. Feature-distribution skew (covariate shift): P_k(x) varies across k while P_k(y | x) is shared.
2. Label-distribution skew (prior probability shift): P_k(y) varies across k while P_k(x | y) is shared.
3. Concept drift (same label, different features): P_k(x | y) varies across k while P_k(y) is shared.
4. Concept shift (same features, different labels): P_k(y | x) varies across k while P_k(x) is shared.
5. Quantity skew: the number of samples n_k varies substantially across clients.
6. Violations of independence: within a client, samples need not be i.i.d., and across clients the availability or selection of clients may be correlated with their distributions (e.g., temporal, geographic, or device-type correlations).
7. General dataset shift: arbitrary combinations of the above.

Problem. Provide a rigorous, quantitative framework for characterizing real-world cross-client differences in federated datasets that simultaneously captures all seven phenomena above. The framework should:

(a) Define formal, measurable divergence quantities D_i({P_k}) for i = 1, …, 7 that isolate each form of skew (for example, by decomposing a joint heterogeneity measure such as Σ_k (n_k / Σ_j n_j) · KL(P_k ‖ P̄), where P̄ = Σ_k (n_k / Σ_j n_j) P_k, into components attributable to marginals, conditionals, sample sizes, and dependence structure);

(b) Yield procedures for estimating these quantities from finite client samples with provable consistency guarantees;

(c) Induce benchmark-generation protocols whereby, given target values of (D_1, …, D_7), one can synthesize federated partitions of standard centralized datasets that realize those values up to controlled error;

(d) Predict, via theorems relating (D_1, …, D_7) to optimization and generalization behavior, the performance degradation and convergence slowdown of canonical federated algorithms (such as FedAvg) relative to a centralized baseline, and identify which mitigation strategies (personalization, clustered FL, multi-task FL, robust aggregation, data augmentation) are provably effective for each individual skew type.

Construct such a framework, or prove obstructions showing that no single framework can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(d).
status_search_result: The problem of rigorously characterizing non-IID data across clients in federated learning—covering feature/label skew, concept drift/shift, quantity skew, independence violations, and dataset shift—remains an active open research area. Surveys and follow-up works since 2021 (e.g., works on non-IID FL benchmarks like LEAF, FedScale, NIID-Bench) propose partial taxonomies and synthetic benchmarks but no unified quantitative framework with provable guarantees across all seven categories has been established.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: For federated averaging and local-update stochastic gradient methods, can theory identify when local steps help or hurt convergence, close the gap to accelerated mini-batch SGD in IID settings, and handle asynchronous or straggler-tolerant variants under realistic federated constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the distributed stochastic optimization problem
  min_{x ∈ ℝ^d}  F(x) = (1/M) Σ_{i=1}^{M} F_i(x),  with  F_i(x) = E_{ξ∼D_i}[ f(x; ξ) ],
where M clients each hold a local data distribution D_i and can compute unbiased stochastic gradients g_i(x) with E[g_i(x)] = ∇F_i(x) and bounded variance E‖g_i(x) − ∇F_i(x)‖^2 ≤ σ^2. Each F_i is L-smooth, and one may additionally consider the (strongly) convex or nonconvex regimes. Heterogeneity may be quantified by sup_x (1/M) Σ_i ‖∇F_i(x) − ∇F(x)‖^2 ≤ ζ^2.

Federated averaging (FedAvg) / local-update SGD proceeds in rounds: in each round a subset S_t of clients is sampled; each selected client initializes from the server model x_t and performs K local stochastic gradient steps with stepsize η, producing x_{t,i}^{(K)}; the server then aggregates x_{t+1} = (1/|S_t|) Σ_{i∈S_t} x_{t,i}^{(K)}. Mini-batch SGD with batch size MK is the natural baseline (one synchronous step per round using MK stochastic gradients).

Address the following three questions for this family of algorithms:

(a) Provide matching upper and lower bounds on the worst-case convergence rate of local-update SGD/FedAvg as a function of M, K, T (number of rounds), L, σ^2, ζ^2, that determine precisely the regimes of (K, σ^2, ζ^2, L, …) in which performing K > 1 local steps strictly improves convergence over the mini-batch SGD baseline using MK gradients per round, and the regimes in which it strictly hurts.

(b) In the homogeneous (IID) setting where all F_i = F, determine whether the gap between known upper bounds for local SGD and the optimal rate of accelerated mini-batch SGD (with MK gradients per round) can be closed; either exhibit a local-update method (possibly with acceleration, momentum, or control variates) matching the accelerated mini-batch lower bound, or prove a separation showing no local-update method can attain it.

(c) Establish convergence guarantees for asynchronous and straggler-tolerant variants of FedAvg under realistic federated constraints — heterogeneous client availability, arbitrary and possibly adversarial delays, partial participation, communication compression, and statistical heterogeneity — with rates that explicitly account for delay distributions and participation biases, and which degrade gracefully (rather than diverge) as stragglers become extreme.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: tight upper and lower bounds for local SGD in the homogeneous convex setting (Woodworth et al. 2020) identify regimes where local steps help or hurt versus mini-batch SGD, and methods like SCAFFOLD and FedAC give improved or accelerated rates in some regimes. However, fully matching upper and lower bounds in the heterogeneous setting, closing the gap to accelerated mini-batch SGD in IID settings in all regimes, and rigorous guarantees for asynchronous/straggler-tolerant FedAvg under realistic federated constraints remain only partially resolved.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How can model-agnostic meta-learning and learning-to-learn methods be adapted to federated learning, including realistic benchmarks, theoretical guarantees, personalized-performance metrics, explanations for why globally optimized models may personalize poorly, treatment of concept drift, and possible non-parameter-transfer algorithms?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates training across a population of clients $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, where each client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ over an input-output space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ and the distributions $\mathcal{D}_i$ may be statistically heterogeneous (non-IID) and may drift over time. A model is parameterized by $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$, with a loss $\ell(\theta;x,y)$ and per-client risk $F_i(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(\theta;x,y)]$.

In the model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) / learning-to-learn formulation of personalization, the server seeks an initialization $\theta^\star$ such that, after a small number $k\geq 1$ of local adaptation steps $U_i^k(\theta)$ (e.g., gradient steps on $F_i$), the personalized parameters $\theta_i:=U_i^k(\theta^\star)$ achieve low local risk. A natural objective is
$$\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d}\ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N F_i\bigl(U_i^k(\theta)\bigr).$$
More generally, "non-parameter-transfer" personalization replaces $U_i^k$ by transfer mechanisms that do not consist solely of fine-tuning a shared parameter vector (e.g., hypernetworks, modular components, prototype/embedding transfer, or data-dependent personalization maps).

Develop a theory and methodology for federated meta-learning addressing all of the following:

(a) Construct realistic benchmark task distributions and evaluation protocols for federated meta-learning that reflect cross-device and cross-silo deployments, including non-IID clients, system heterogeneity, partial participation, communication constraints, and temporal concept drift in $\{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i,t}$.

(b) Establish theoretical guarantees (convergence rates, sample/communication complexity, and generalization bounds to held-out and to newly-arriving clients) for federated MAML-type algorithms under realistic assumptions on heterogeneity, stochastic gradients, partial participation, and Hessian access in the inner update.

(c) Define and analyze rigorous personalized-performance metrics that measure post-adaptation accuracy across the client population (including tail/worst-client behavior, fairness across clients, and few-shot adaptation on new clients), and prove their relation to the global meta-objective above.

(d) Provide a mathematical characterization explaining when and why a globally optimal model $\theta_G^\star\in\arg\min_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_i F_i(\theta)$ personalizes poorly, i.e., quantify the gap
$$\Delta\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_i F_i(\theta_G^\star)\;-\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_i F_i\bigl(U_i^k(\theta^\star)\bigr)$$
in terms of geometric or statistical properties of $\{F_i\}$ (curvature, task similarity, conditioning).

(e) Extend the framework to handle concept drift, where $\mathcal{D}_i$ is replaced by a time-varying $\mathcal{D}_{i,t}$, with provable tracking/adaptation guarantees.

(f) Design and analyze non-parameter-transfer federated meta-learning algorithms that go beyond a shared initialization, with formal guarantees comparable to (b)–(d).

Determine to what extent each of (a)–(f) admits a complete solution.
status_search_result: Partial progress exists: Fallah–Mokhtari–Ozdaglar (NeurIPS 2020) established convergence and first-order-optimality guarantees for Per-FedAvg, a MAML-based personalized federated learning algorithm, and Jiang et al. (2019) gave empirical MAML-based personalization results. Subsequent work (2023–2025) has produced clustered/co-meta-learning variants, hypernetwork-based personalization (pFedHN/pFedLA), and reinforcement-learning-style personalization addressing heterogeneity. However, comprehensive realistic benchmarks, tight theoretical guarantees under partial participation and concept drift, fairness-aware personalization metrics with provable links to the meta-objective, and provably effective non-parameter-transfer algorithms remain only partially addressed, so the overall program is still open in significant parts.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: For federated communication and compression, what are the optimal trade-offs between communication cost and accuracy, how can statistical lower-bound theory guide practical training methods, and can compression be co-designed with secure aggregation and differential privacy rather than treated separately?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which $n$ clients each hold a local dataset and collaborate, via a (possibly untrusted) server, to optimize a global model parameter $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ by minimizing $F(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} F_i(\theta)$, where $F_i$ is the local objective of client $i$. In each round, every client sends an encoded message $C_i(g_i) \in \{0,1\}^{b}$ (a compressed update derived from a local stochastic gradient or model delta $g_i$), and the server returns an aggregated update. Communication cost is measured by the per-round per-client bit budget $b$, and accuracy is measured by the expected suboptimality $\mathbb{E}[F(\hat\theta)] - \min_\theta F(\theta)$ after a prescribed number of rounds $T$.

Additionally require the protocol to satisfy:
(i) $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy of each client's data against the server and other clients, and
(ii) cryptographic secure aggregation, meaning the server only learns $\sum_i g_i$ (or a function of it) and not individual $C_i(g_i)$.

Address the following:

1. (Optimal trade-off) Determine the tight Pareto frontier between the per-client communication budget $b$ and the achievable optimization/statistical error for federated stochastic optimization over standard function classes (e.g., smooth convex, strongly convex, and non-convex with bounded variance gradients). Specifically, give matching upper and lower bounds on the minimax error as a function of $(n, d, T, b)$.

2. (Lower-bound–driven algorithms) Identify statistical/information-theoretic lower bounds (e.g., based on distributed estimation under communication constraints) that match practical training schemes, and exhibit explicit algorithms whose accuracy attains these bounds while remaining implementable at scale.

3. (Joint design) Construct a single protocol that simultaneously enforces (i) and (ii) together with compression to budget $b$, such that the end-to-end error does not exceed the sum of the unavoidable losses from compression and from privacy, and prove that decoupled designs (compression, then secure aggregation, then DP noise injection) are strictly suboptimal — or prove that some decoupled design is optimal up to constants.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers (2023–2025) continue to treat the joint design of compression, secure aggregation, and differential privacy as an active and unresolved research direction. Partial results exist (e.g., sketching-based compression compatible with DP, gradient-pruning + DP schemes, robust-compatible compression), but tight communication–accuracy trade-offs matching information-theoretic lower bounds in a unified DP + secure-aggregation framework are not established.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How should federated-learning functions be partitioned among trusted execution environments, ordinary cloud computation, and client devices so that key operations such as secure aggregation or shuffling limit server access to raw contributions without making the trusted computing base too large or impractical?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a central server coordinates training across a large population of client devices, each holding private data. The system has three classes of compute resources available:

(i) client devices, which hold raw user contributions (e.g., model updates) and have limited compute, memory, and network capacity;
(ii) ordinary (untrusted) server-side cloud computation, which is plentiful but must be assumed to be observable by an adversary controlling the server;
(iii) trusted execution environments (TEEs), available either on the server or on clients, which provide hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity for code and data inside an enclave but have restricted memory, restricted I/O bandwidth, and a security guarantee that degrades as the trusted computing base (TCB) — the size and complexity of the code and hardware that must be trusted — grows.

Let a federated-learning protocol be specified by a decomposition of its global computation F (including subroutines such as secure aggregation of client model updates, random shuffling of contributions, differentially private noise addition, model broadcast, and update application) into subroutines F_1, ..., F_k together with an assignment a : {1,...,k} → {client, untrusted-cloud, TEE} of each subroutine to one of the three resource classes.

Define:
- Server raw-access leakage L(a): the amount of information about individual client contributions that the (untrusted) server can observe under assignment a, formalised as the mutual information between the view of the untrusted-cloud component and the individual client inputs.
- TCB size T(a): the total code/hardware complexity that must be placed inside a TEE under assignment a.
- Practicality cost C(a): an aggregate of client compute, client communication, TEE memory/throughput usage, and overall wall-clock cost induced by a.

Problem. Determine principled partitioning strategies a* of federated-learning functions among clients, untrusted cloud computation, and TEEs such that:
(1) L(a*) is bounded by a prescribed leakage budget ε (in particular, the server cannot access raw individual contributions to operations such as secure aggregation or shuffling);
(2) T(a*) is kept small enough that the TEE security model remains credible;
(3) C(a*) is feasible for realistic client devices and TEE hardware.

Equivalently, characterise the Pareto frontier of (L, T, C) achievable by such partitions for canonical federated-learning workloads (cross-device aggregation, shuffled differential privacy, secure model distribution), and identify whether there exist partitioning schemes that simultaneously achieve negligible L, small constant-size T independent of the number of clients n, and per-client cost scaling as Õ(model size) with server cost scaling as Õ(n · model size).
category_tag: Federated learning with trusted execution environments
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open design/research problem about how to partition federated-learning computations across clients, untrusted servers, and trusted execution environments. It is a broad systems-and-cryptography research direction rather than a specific theorem-style conjecture; subsequent work (e.g., on TEE-based secure aggregation, shuffle-model DP, and hybrid TEE/MPC designs) has proposed point solutions, but no canonical resolution or established Pareto-optimal partitioning theory is known. The problem remains open in the sense of lacking a definitive, principled solution.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How can federated-learning implementations of differential privacy be audited for correctness, including black-box testing methods for systems whose organizations do not open-source their code?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ denote a randomized mechanism implemented as part of a federated learning system that claims to satisfy $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy: for all neighboring data sets $D, D'$ (differing in one client's record) and all measurable output sets $S$,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D)\in S]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D')\in S]+\delta.$$
Suppose the implementation of $\mathcal{M}$ is operated by an organization that does not release its source code, so the auditor only has black-box query access: the auditor may choose inputs (subject to realistic constraints on participation as a federated client) and observe the (possibly aggregated) outputs of $\mathcal{M}$, but cannot inspect internal state, randomness, or code.

Develop a methodology for auditing such a federated-learning implementation of differential privacy for correctness. Concretely:

1. Define a black-box auditing procedure $A$ that, given query access to $\mathcal{M}$ and a claimed privacy budget $(\varepsilon,\delta)$, outputs either "accept" or "reject" together with a statistical guarantee (e.g., a lower bound $\hat\varepsilon$ on the true privacy parameter with controlled Type I error).
2. Provide testing techniques applicable when the auditor cannot open-source-inspect the system, including the design of adversarial neighboring inputs (canaries), choice of test statistics, and methods that remain valid under the federated setting (multiple clients, secure aggregation, server-side noise).
3. Establish sample-complexity bounds and soundness/completeness guarantees showing that, under stated assumptions on the access model, common implementation bugs that violate $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP are detected with high probability.
status_search_result: Active research has produced multiple black-box and gray-box auditing methods for differentially private mechanisms (e.g., tight black-box auditing of DP-SGD, f-DP-based black-box estimation, sequential anytime-valid tests, and gray-box library audits). These provide partial answers — particularly for DP-SGD and standalone DP libraries — but a fully general, sample-efficient black-box auditing methodology tailored to closed-source federated learning systems with secure aggregation remains an active and only partially resolved problem.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Against an adversarial server, how can one construct efficient and robust secure aggregation that handles semi-honest setup assumptions, per-round aggregate leakage, sparse vectors, client input well-formedness, and client dropouts at large scale?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed computation setting with a central server S and a large set of clients C = {1, ..., n}, where each client i holds a private input vector x_i ∈ R^d (possibly sparse). A secure aggregation protocol is an interactive cryptographic protocol that allows S to learn the sum y = Σ_{i ∈ A} x_i over the set A ⊆ C of clients that successfully complete the protocol, while revealing no additional information about any individual x_i beyond what is implied by y and the adversary's view.

Assume the following adversarial model:
(a) The server S may be malicious (i.e., may deviate arbitrarily from the protocol), while a subset of clients may also be corrupted and colluding with S.
(b) The trusted-setup phase (e.g., distribution of cryptographic keys, public parameters) is only semi-honest: parties follow it honestly but the transcript may later leak to the adversary.
(c) The server obtains the aggregate output y in each round, and these per-round aggregates are considered acceptable leakage.
(d) Clients may drop out at arbitrary points during protocol execution, including adaptively.
(e) Inputs x_i are typically high-dimensional and sparse, and the protocol must enforce well-formedness of inputs (e.g., bounded norm, bounded sparsity, integer-valued in a prescribed range) so that malicious clients cannot poison the aggregate by submitting out-of-range vectors.

Design a secure aggregation protocol that simultaneously achieves the following:
1. Correctness: when honest parties follow the protocol, S obtains Σ_{i ∈ A} x_i for the set A of non-dropout honest clients.
2. Privacy against a malicious server colluding with a constant fraction of malicious clients, with security reducing only to semi-honest assumptions on the setup phase, and allowing only the per-round aggregate as leakage.
3. Robustness to an arbitrary (adaptive) pattern of client dropouts among the n clients, with output still correctly representing the sum of the surviving honest clients' inputs.
4. Verifiable input well-formedness: any contribution from a malicious client that does not lie in a prescribed admissible set (e.g., bounded ℓ∞- or ℓ2-norm, prescribed sparsity, prescribed quantization) is rejected.
5. Efficiency: per-client communication and computation, and server computation, scale at most polylogarithmically in n and quasi-linearly in the effective (sparse) input size, so that the protocol is practical for n on the order of 10^6 or more.

Provide such a protocol together with a proof of its security and complexity, or prove an impossibility/lower bound showing that no protocol can simultaneously achieve all of (1)–(5).
status_search_result: Secure aggregation against a malicious server with simultaneous handling of dropouts, sparse inputs, input well-formedness, and large-scale efficiency remains an active research area. Partial progress has been made (e.g., RoFL for input constraints, ACORN, Flamingo, SecAgg+, EIFFeL for malicious-server settings), but no single protocol has been shown to achieve all listed desiderata at the scale and efficiency demanded; the problem is generally regarded as still open.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: For distributed differential privacy mechanisms that use discrete finite-support noise because Gaussian mechanisms are incompatible with secure shuffling or secure aggregation implementations, how can privacy accounting be tailored to those discrete noise distributions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a distributed differential privacy setting in which $n$ parties each hold a private vector and wish to compute an aggregate (for instance, a sum) under $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy. Because the aggregation is performed through a cryptographic primitive — either a secure aggregation protocol that operates in a finite group $\mathbb{Z}_q^d$ with modular arithmetic, or a secure shuffler that permutes finitely encoded messages — the continuous Gaussian mechanism cannot be used: noise must be drawn from a distribution with discrete (and in practice finite) support so it is compatible with the underlying finite-precision, modular, or message-based protocol. Examples of such noises include the discrete Gaussian, discrete Laplace (two-sided geometric), Skellam, Pólya, and binomial distributions, possibly summed across the $n$ parties after local sampling.

Develop a rigorous privacy accounting framework for mechanisms of this form. Specifically, for a mechanism $M(x) = \big(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i + Z_i)\big) \bmod q$ (or the shuffled analogue), where each $Z_i$ is sampled from a prescribed discrete, finite-support distribution $\mathcal{D}$, determine:

1. Tight $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP and Rényi-DP bounds for $M$ as a function of $n$, $q$, the per-party sensitivity, the parameters of $\mathcal{D}$, and the fraction of colluding parties.
2. Composition theorems for repeated applications of $M$ (e.g., across training rounds) that account for the discrete nature of $\mathcal{D}$ and any data quantization or modular wrap-around effects, and that match the tightness of continuous Gaussian accountants in the appropriate regime.
3. Privacy amplification results combining $\mathcal{D}$ with subsampling and/or secure shuffling.

Provide accountants whose bounds are tight (not merely obtained by approximating $\mathcal{D}$ by a continuous Gaussian or Laplace) and that remain computable for the parameter ranges arising in large-scale distributed training.
status_search_result: Tailored privacy accounting for several discrete noise distributions has been developed, notably the distributed discrete Gaussian mechanism with Rényi-DP analysis accounting for modular summation and quantization (Kairouz et al., 2021), the Skellam mechanism, and follow-up work on securely sampling discrete Gaussian noise via MPC (CCS 2023) and benchmarks of secure sampling protocols (2024). These results address the original need for accountants tailored to discrete finite-support noises compatible with secure aggregation/shuffling, but the broader program — tight accountants for arbitrary discrete distributions, full composition with subsampling and shuffling, and matching central-Gaussian tightness across all regimes — remains an active area of research, so the problem is best characterized as partially solved.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How should federated-learning systems communicate privacy benefits and limitations to ordinary users, model user privacy preferences, decide who sets privacy and security parameters, and incorporate individual choices about desired privacy levels or allowable inferences?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a central server coordinates the training of a shared model across a population of clients $\mathcal{U} = \{u_1, \dots, u_N\}$, each holding private local data $D_i$. The system applies a privacy mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ (e.g., a $(\varepsilon_i,\delta_i)$-differentially private mechanism, secure aggregation, or a combination) with privacy parameters $	heta_i \in \Theta$ that may vary per user. Each user $u_i$ has a (possibly unknown) privacy preference modeled as a utility function $V_i : \Theta 	imes \mathcal{I} 	o \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{I}$ denotes the set of inferences an adversary could potentially make from released information; the user wishes to permit some inferences (those useful to the learning task) while disallowing others.

Develop a principled framework that simultaneously addresses the following:

1. (Communication of guarantees) Define a function $C : \Theta 	o \mathcal{R}$, where $\mathcal{R}$ is a space of human-interpretable representations, that conveys to a non-expert user both the privacy benefits and limitations of $\mathcal{M}$ with parameters $	heta_i$, in a way that is provably faithful to the underlying mathematical guarantee.

2. (Modeling preferences) Construct a model class $\{V_i^{\widehat{}} : i \in \mathcal{U}\}$ that approximates each user's true preference $V_i$ from a feasible elicitation procedure, with quantitative guarantees on approximation error.

3. (Parameter setting authority) Specify a decision protocol $\pi$ that determines whether $	heta_i$ is set by the user, by the service provider, by a third party, or by a combination, optimizing an explicit social welfare or game-theoretic objective $W(	heta_1,\dots,	heta_N)$ that balances utility of the learned model against per-user privacy loss.

4. (Incorporating individual choices) Design an aggregation/training algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that takes heterogeneous user-chosen privacy levels $\{	heta_i\}$ and allowed-inference sets $\{I_i \subseteq \mathcal{I}\}$ as input, and produces a model whose privacy guarantees with respect to each user $u_i$ provably respect $	heta_i$ and $I_i$, while maximizing expected model utility.

Provide existence, optimality, or impossibility results for such a framework $(C, \{V_i^{\widehat{}}\}, \pi, \mathcal{A})$.
status_search_result: This is a long-standing open research direction in federated learning, spanning differential privacy, mechanism design, and HCI. As of 2026 no unified mathematical framework addresses all four sub-problems with provable guarantees; partial progress exists on heterogeneous/personalized differential privacy and on privacy-utility tradeoff mechanisms, but communicating guarantees to users and eliciting preferences remain largely unresolved.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How should adversarial training and robust optimization be adapted to federated learning when samples may be seen only a few times, data are non-IID, perturbation bounds cannot be chosen by inspecting data centrally, and adversarial-example generation may exceed on-device memory or power budgets?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a global model is trained across a large, heterogeneous population of client devices. Each client holds a local dataset, and the local distributions are non-identically and non-independently distributed (non-IID) across clients. Training proceeds by repeated rounds in which a server distributes the current model to a subset of clients, each client performs local updates on its data, and the server aggregates the resulting updates. The setting has the following constraints:

(a) Any given training sample on a client may be visited only a small number of times during the entire training process.
(b) Raw client data cannot be inspected centrally, so global statistics needed to set hyperparameters (in particular, the magnitude of allowable adversarial perturbations) are not directly available.
(c) Each client device has bounded memory, compute, and power, which may be insufficient to run standard procedures for generating adversarial examples (e.g., multi-step projected gradient ascent inner loops) at training time.

Design a training procedure that performs adversarial training or, more generally, robust optimization in this federated setting, and provide formal guarantees on the adversarial robustness of the resulting global model. Specifically:

1. Define a notion of robust risk appropriate to the federated, non-IID setting, including how the per-client perturbation set should be chosen given that data cannot be examined centrally.
2. Specify an algorithm that produces adversarial perturbations and model updates under the per-sample visit limit and the on-device memory/compute constraints, and prove convergence of the algorithm to a stationary point of the chosen robust objective.
3. Establish bounds on the robust generalization error of the trained model in terms of the data heterogeneity, the number of times each sample is used, and the resources available on each client.

Either provide such a procedure with the stated guarantees, or prove obstructions showing that no algorithm satisfying the constraints can achieve nontrivial certified robustness in this regime.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers (2023–2025) on robust and adversarial federated learning explicitly list adapting adversarial training to federated settings under non-IID data, limited sample reuse, and tight on-device resource budgets as an ongoing research direction. Several partial methods (e.g., federated adversarial training variants, clustering-based defenses, dual adversarial schemes) exist, but no method addresses all the listed constraints simultaneously with formal robust-generalization guarantees, and recent systematic reviews continue to flag it as an open challenge.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: When secure aggregation is used for privacy in federated learning, how can systems still defend against adversarial attacks, develop efficient range proofs, and determine which nonlinear or Byzantine-robust aggregation methods can be computed efficiently under secure aggregation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which $n$ clients hold local model updates $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a central server wishes to learn only the aggregate $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ (or some function thereof) under a cryptographic secure aggregation protocol that hides every individual $x_i$ from the server and from other clients. Within this setting, address the following three problems:

(a) Adversarial robustness under secure aggregation. Design a protocol that defends against adversarial clients who submit arbitrarily corrupted updates $x_i$ aimed at degrading model accuracy or implanting backdoors, while preserving the privacy guarantee that no individual $x_i$ is revealed. Specify a threat model (e.g., up to a fraction $\beta < 1$ of malicious clients with full knowledge of the protocol), and prove correctness and privacy guarantees for the proposed defense.

(b) Efficient range proofs. Construct a cryptographic protocol that allows each client to prove, in zero knowledge to the server (or to a set of verifiers), that its encrypted contribution $x_i$ lies within a prescribed set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ (for example, that $\|x_i\|_p \le B$ for given $p$ and bound $B$), such that the per-client communication and computation, and the server's verification cost, are sublinear or otherwise practically efficient in $d$ and in $n$. Quantify the achievable trade-offs between proof size, soundness error, and computational cost.

(c) Nonlinear and Byzantine-robust aggregation under secure aggregation. Characterize which aggregation functions $f(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ — in particular nonlinear robust aggregators such as coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, geometric median, Krum, or Multi-Krum — can be computed under a secure aggregation protocol with communication and computation cost polynomial in $n$ and $d$ and with cryptographic privacy guarantees matching those of linear secure aggregation. For each such function, provide an explicit protocol with complexity bounds; for functions shown not to admit such efficient protocols, prove a corresponding lower bound or impossibility result.
status_search_result: Active research has produced partial solutions: frameworks such as ByzSFL, RiseFL, and PriRoAgg combine zero-knowledge proofs, hybrid commitments, and Lagrange-coded computing to provide Byzantine-robust secure aggregation and bounded-norm range proofs, while earlier work (e.g., Prio's SNIP, and "Secure Byzantine-Robust Machine Learning") gives limited input validation. However, no single approach achieves efficient secure aggregation simultaneously for arbitrary nonlinear robust aggregators with tight complexity bounds, and the general characterization of which robust aggregators admit efficient secure computation remains open.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How can fairness be measured and improved in federated learning when sensitive attributes such as race or gender are unavailable, including scalable use of distributionally robust optimization or multicalibration and new theoretical fairness definitions that do not rely on sensitive attributes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a global predictive model is trained across many decentralized clients, each holding a local data distribution, without exchanging raw data. Suppose that sensitive attributes (such as race or gender) are not observable at the server nor reliably at the clients, so that classical group-fairness criteria (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds) cannot be evaluated directly.

Address the following:

1. Propose rigorous theoretical definitions of fairness for a federated predictor that do not require access to sensitive attributes at training or evaluation time. The definitions should be well-posed in the presence of statistical heterogeneity across clients and should specialize to or imply standard group-fairness notions when sensitive attributes happen to be available.

2. Design scalable federated algorithms that measure and improve fairness under these definitions. In particular, develop either:
   (a) a distributionally robust optimization procedure that minimizes the worst-case risk over an appropriate ambiguity set of client or sub-population distributions, while remaining communication-efficient, privacy-preserving, and convergent under standard non-i.i.d. federated assumptions; or
   (b) a federated analogue of multicalibration, in which a predictor is required to be calibrated simultaneously on a rich, computationally identifiable family of subpopulations (defined without reference to sensitive attributes), together with provable convergence and sample-complexity guarantees.

3. Prove formal guarantees connecting the fairness criteria of (1) to the algorithms of (2), including bounds on the gap between worst-case and average client performance, and analyze the trade-offs with overall utility, communication cost, and differential privacy.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and papers (2024–2025) on fair federated learning explicitly note that evaluating and enforcing fairness without sensitive group information—particularly via scalable multicalibration or DRO—remains largely unexplored. While partial progress exists (e.g., SFFL, FedUFO, DRDM combining DRO with client-drift control), no comprehensive theoretical fairness framework dispensing with sensitive attributes has been established, indicating the problem is still open.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: To what extent does increasing stakeholder and data diversity through federated training improve model fairness, and how do required differential privacy mechanisms affect the fairness, performance, and diversity gains of such federated training?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a central model is trained collaboratively over $K$ clients, where client $k$ holds a local dataset $D_k$ drawn from a client-specific distribution $\mathcal{P}_k$ over an input–output space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$, with each example additionally carrying a sensitive attribute $a\in\mathcal{A}$ (e.g., a demographic group). Let $\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_k D_k$ denote the aggregated training distribution and let $\mathrm{Div}(\{\mathcal{P}_k\})$ be a measure of stakeholder/data diversity (for instance, the average pairwise total variation distance between the $\mathcal{P}_k$ or the coverage of $\mathcal{A}$ across clients). Let $h_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ be the trained global model, and define:
- a performance functional $U(h_\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{P}^\star}[\ell(h_\theta(x),y)]$ against a target distribution $\mathcal{P}^\star$;
- a group-fairness functional $F(h_\theta)$, such as the maximum gap in true-positive rates, demographic parity, or accuracy across values of $a$.

Assume the federated training protocol satisfies $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy with respect to either record-level or client-level adjacency, implemented via gradient clipping at norm $C$ and Gaussian noise of scale $\sigma$ at the aggregation step.

Provide a rigorous quantitative analysis of the following:

(a) Establish, as a function of $\mathrm{Div}(\{\mathcal{P}_k\})$, upper and lower bounds on the achievable fairness $F(h_\theta)$ when no privacy constraint is imposed ($\varepsilon=\infty$). In particular, identify conditions on the client distributions $\{\mathcal{P}_k\}$ under which increasing diversity provably reduces $F(h_\theta)$, and conditions under which it cannot.

(b) Characterize, for fixed diversity, the joint feasible region of triples $(U(h_\theta),F(h_\theta),\varepsilon)$ under $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP federated training with clipping parameter $C$ and noise scale $\sigma$. Quantify how decreasing $\varepsilon$ (stronger privacy) degrades $F$ and $U$, including the role of clipping in introducing disparate impact across groups $a\in\mathcal{A}$.

(c) Determine whether the fairness gains attributable to increased diversity can be preserved under non-trivial DP guarantees, or whether DP necessarily erases these gains; provide either an algorithm achieving such preservation with explicit rates, or an impossibility result.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers (2023–2025) consistently describe the interplay among diversity, fairness, differential privacy, and utility in federated learning as an active open research area. Authors note an inherent tension between DP mechanisms (clipping and noise) and fairness, and a lack of unified theory simultaneously addressing privacy, fairness, and performance. While partial algorithmic progress exists (e.g., zero-sum formulations and DP-fair methods), a comprehensive quantitative characterization remains unresolved.

original_question: How can cross-device federated-learning systems quantify and mitigate system-induced bias caused by availability profiles, device performance, network connectivity, CPU load, local dataset size, timeouts, and other factors that affect whether a device contributes to a round?

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Can a portable, fast, lightweight, flexible on-device runtime be built for federated learning so that end-user devices can serialize, receive, interpret or execute, and communicate machine-learning training computations without the limitations of large or unstable framework-specific runtimes?
self_contained_problem:
Design and demonstrate a portable, lightweight, and flexible on-device runtime system for federated learning with the following properties. The runtime must execute on heterogeneous end-user devices (e.g., mobile phones, embedded devices, browsers) with limited memory, compute, and energy budgets, and must support the full federated training loop, namely: (i) receiving from a server a serialized description of a machine-learning training computation (including model architecture, loss, optimizer step, and any client-side data-processing pipeline), (ii) deserializing and interpreting or executing that computation on locally held data to produce model updates, and (iii) communicating the resulting updates back to the server in a serialized form. The runtime should satisfy simultaneously:

1. Portability: a single runtime binary or specification that runs across major device platforms without per-platform reimplementation of the training logic.
2. Small footprint: binary size and memory usage substantially smaller than full-fledged machine-learning framework runtimes designed for datacenter use.
3. Stability: deterministic and reliable execution suitable for deployment to large populations of consumer devices.
4. Expressivity / flexibility: ability to represent and execute a broad class of model architectures, optimizers, and training procedures (not a fixed model family), with the computation specified by the server rather than hard-coded into the client.
5. Efficiency: training throughput on-device competitive with native implementations of the same computation.

Construct such a runtime, together with a serialization format for training computations and a precise specification of the supported class of computations, and prove (empirically and via formal guarantees on the serialization/execution semantics) that all of the above properties are met simultaneously; or, alternatively, establish an impossibility result showing that some subset of these requirements cannot be satisfied together under reasonable assumptions on device capabilities.
status_search_result: The problem is framed as an open systems challenge in federated learning. While various lightweight on-device ML runtimes (e.g., TensorFlow Lite, ExecuTorch, ONNX Runtime Mobile, Flower client, PyTorch Mobile) provide partial solutions—mostly for inference and limited on-device training—no single runtime is widely recognized as satisfying all of the portability, footprint, stability, flexibility, and efficiency requirements for arbitrary server-specified federated training computations. The problem appears to remain open as of 2026.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How can the federated-learning community develop new datasets that better represent real-world federated problems, including unbalanced and non-IID client partitions, scale-sensitive cross-device scenarios, metadata such as timestamps or geolocation, and feature-partitioned cross-silo datasets?
self_contained_problem:
Design a methodology for constructing benchmark datasets for federated learning that faithfully reflect realistic deployment conditions. A federated learning setting consists of a (possibly very large) collection of clients $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$, each holding a local dataset $D_i$ drawn from a client-specific distribution $P_i$ over a feature-label space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. Construct a family of benchmark datasets satisfying all of the following properties simultaneously:

1. (Unbalanced partitions) The sizes $|D_i|$ follow a heavy-tailed distribution across clients, reflecting real-world participation imbalance.
2. (Non-IID partitions) The local distributions $P_i$ differ across clients in label distribution, feature distribution, and/or conditional distribution $P_i(y\mid x)$, in ways quantifiably similar to those observed in real federated deployments.
3. (Cross-device scale sensitivity) The benchmark supports the cross-device regime, with $|I|$ on the order of $10^6$ or more clients, each holding a small $D_i$, and includes mechanisms to evaluate algorithms whose behavior is sensitive to the total number of participating clients.
4. (Metadata) Each example or each client carries auxiliary metadata such as timestamps and geolocation tags, enabling study of temporal drift, non-stationarity, and spatial heterogeneity.
5. (Feature-partitioned cross-silo data) The benchmark includes a vertical federated learning variant in which a fixed set of entities is described by disjoint feature subsets $\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal{X}_k$ held by distinct silos, with consistent entity-linking information.

Provide rigorous criteria (e.g., quantitative measures of non-IIDness, imbalance, and drift) under which a proposed dataset family is declared representative of real-world federated problems, and exhibit such a dataset family meeting these criteria.
status_search_result: This is an open research direction in federated learning. While several benchmark suites (LEAF, FedScale, FLamby, TFF datasets) have partially addressed unbalanced, non-IID, and cross-device settings, no single benchmark family is widely accepted as covering all listed properties (scale, metadata such as timestamps/geolocation, and vertical/feature-partitioned cross-silo data) with rigorous representativeness criteria. The problem remains open as a community goal.

paper_title: Padua points and “fake” nodes for polynomial approximation: old, new and open problems
original_question: Let Ω be a compact subset of R^d. For degree-m polynomials P bounded by 1 on Ω, define the Dubiner metric by μΩ(x,y)=sup (1/m)|arccos(P(x))-arccos(P(y))| over such P. Are nearly optimal interpolation point sets on Ω asymptotically equidistributed with respect to this Dubiner metric?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a compact set. For a positive integer $m$, let $\mathcal{P}_m$ denote the space of real polynomials of degree at most $m$ in $d$ variables. Define the Dubiner (pseudo)metric on $\Omega$ by
$$\mu_\Omega(x,y) \;=\; \sup\Big\{\tfrac{1}{m}\big|\arccos P(x) - \arccos P(y)\big| \;:\; m\ge 1,\; P\in\mathcal{P}_m,\; \|P\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le 1\Big\},$$
for $x,y\in\Omega$. For each $m$, let $N_m = \dim \mathcal{P}_m|_\Omega$ and let $X_m=\{x_1^{(m)},\dots,x_{N_m}^{(m)}\}\subset\Omega$ be a sequence of unisolvent interpolation arrays whose Lebesgue constants grow at most polynomially in $m$ ("nearly optimal" interpolation points). Consider the associated normalized counting (empirical) measures
$$\nu_m \;=\; \frac{1}{N_m}\sum_{j=1}^{N_m}\delta_{x_j^{(m)}}.$$
Prove or disprove: for every compact $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and every such nearly optimal sequence $(X_m)$, the measures $\nu_m$ converge weakly, as $m\to\infty$, to a measure that is equidistributed with respect to the Dubiner metric $\mu_\Omega$ on $\Omega$ (i.e., the points $X_m$ are asymptotically uniformly distributed in the Dubiner metric).
status_search_result: The conjecture, originally due to Dubiner, that nearly optimal polynomial interpolation point sets on a compact set in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are asymptotically equidistributed with respect to the Dubiner metric, remains open in general. Verifications are known only in special cases (e.g., the interval, the square via Padua-like points, spherical triangles), and the Dubiner metric itself is explicitly known only on a few domains. No general proof or disproof appears in the literature.
