original_question: Can one construct explicit families of local quasi-holomorphic curves from the complex disk into a quasi Riemann surface, for example when the ambient 2n-dimensional space is the sphere S^{2n}, so that local conformal-field-theoretic structure can be studied there?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $M$ be a smooth oriented Riemannian $2n$-dimensional manifold. Following the framework of quasi Riemann surfaces, one associates to $M$ a quasi Riemann surface $Q(M)$: a (typically infinite-dimensional) space built from integral $(n-1)$-currents on $M$, equipped with a skew-hermitian form and a complex structure $J$ that mimic, in higher dimension, the period pairing and the Hodge star on a Riemann surface. A quasi holomorphic curve in $Q(M)$ is a map $f : \Sigma \to Q(M)$ from an ordinary Riemann surface $\Sigma$ (or an open subset of the complex disk $D \subset \mathbb{C}$, in the local case) into $Q(M)$ that intertwines the complex structures and preserves the skew-hermitian forms on integral currents. Such curves serve as local probes that pull back functions, differential forms, and conformal tensors on $Q(M)$ to ordinary objects on the Riemann surface $\Sigma$, thereby giving local two-dimensional conformal-field-theoretic data on $Q(M)$.

Problem. Construct explicit families of local quasi holomorphic curves $f : D \to Q(M)$ from the complex disk $D$ into the quasi Riemann surface $Q(M)$ in the case
$$M = S^{2n},$$
the round $2n$-sphere. In particular, exhibit a family rich enough that pullback along the family represents functions, forms, and conformal tensors on $Q(S^{2n})$ as coherent collections of ordinary holomorphic data on Riemann surfaces, so that the local conformal-field-theoretic structure of $Q(S^{2n})$ can be analyzed concretely.
status_search_result: The notion of quasi Riemann surfaces and quasi holomorphic curves was introduced by Friedan, who explicitly states that constructing local quasi holomorphic curves, in particular for $M = S^{2n}$, is needed and remains to be carried out. original_question: Can standard two-dimensional conformal-field-theory constructions, such as orbifolding and perturbation theory, be reproduced or generalized on quasi Riemann surfaces so as to generate new theories of higher-dimensional defects?
self_contained_problem:
A quasi Riemann surface is a higher-dimensional generalization of a Riemann surface designed to support a notion of conformal field theory whose "fields" are extended (higher-dimensional) defect operators rather than point operators. On a quasi Riemann surface one expects an analogue of the algebra of local operators, operator product expansion, and partition/correlation functions, with the role of points played by submanifolds (defects).

Develop, on quasi Riemann surfaces, analogues of the standard two-dimensional conformal field theory constructions—specifically:

(a) Orbifolding: Given a quasi Riemann surface X equipped with the action of a (finite) symmetry group G of the underlying CFT-like structure, construct an "orbifold" CFT on X/G by (i) restricting to G-invariant defect operators, (ii) introducing twisted defect sectors labelled by conjugacy classes of G, and (iii) defining modular-invariant (or suitably consistent) partition and correlation functions summing over these sectors.

(b) Perturbation theory: Given a CFT-like structure on a quasi Riemann surface X together with a marginal or nearly marginal higher-dimensional defect operator O, define and compute order-by-order deformations of the correlation functions of the theory by O, in analogy with conformal perturbation theory in two dimensions.

The problem is to determine whether such constructions can be carried out rigorously on quasi Riemann surfaces, and to use them to produce new, nontrivial theories of higher-dimensional defects (i.e., new examples of defect CFTs in dimension greater than two), establishing their basic consistency properties (e.g., associativity of the defect OPE, invariance under the relevant symmetry group of the quasi Riemann surface, and finiteness of the perturbative expansion).

original_question: For a tournament, meaning an orientation of a complete graph, that contains at least one directed cycle, is there always an arc whose reversal decreases the total number of directed cycles?
self_contained_problem:
A tournament is an orientation of a finite complete graph; that is, a directed graph obtained by assigning a direction to every edge of a complete graph. A directed cycle in a tournament is a sequence of distinct vertices v_1, v_2, …, v_k, v_1 (k ≥ 3) such that each consecutive pair forms an arc in the tournament. Given a tournament T that contains at least one directed cycle, the reversal of an arc (u,v) is the operation of replacing (u,v) by (v,u), producing a new tournament T'. Let c(T) denote the total number of directed cycles in T (of all lengths).

Prove or disprove: for every tournament T with c(T) ≥ 1, there exists an arc e of T whose reversal yields a tournament T' with c(T') < c(T).
status_search_result: Ádám's original conjecture for general digraphs has known counterexamples, but the restriction to tournaments, posed by Reid and Beineke in 1978, is reported as still open in surveys on tournament problems. Recent work (e.g., a 2017 master's thesis on Ádám's conjecture and arc-reversal problems, and surveys by Bang-Jensen and Gutin) treats the tournament version as an unresolved problem, verifying partial cases (e.g., quasi-acyclic digraphs, certain connectivity classes).

original_question: Let D be a finite digraph with n vertices and minimum out-degree k. Must D contain a directed cycle of length at most ceil(n/k)?
self_contained_problem: Let $D$ be a finite digraph (no loops, at most one arc in each direction between any two vertices is not assumed, but parallel arcs in the same direction are disallowed) on $n$ vertices such that every vertex has out-degree at least $k$, where $k \geq 1$ is an integer. Prove or disprove: $D$ must contain a directed cycle of length at most $\lceil n/k \rceil$.
status_search_result: The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture remains open in general. paper_title: Selected Conjectures and Open Problems on Directed Graphs
original_question: Can the Caccetta-Haggkvist conjecture be verified for fixed small values of the minimum out-degree k, beginning with the currently first unsettled case k = 6?
self_contained_problem:
The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture asserts that every finite simple digraph on n vertices in which every vertex has out-degree at least n/k contains a directed cycle of length at most k. Equivalently, for every integer k ≥ 1, if D is a digraph on n vertices with minimum out-degree at least ⌈n/k⌉, then D contains a directed cycle of length at most k.

The conjecture is known to hold for k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The problem is to settle the conjecture for the next fixed value, k = 6: prove or disprove that every digraph on n vertices with minimum out-degree at least ⌈n/6⌉ contains a directed cycle of length at most 6. More generally, settle the conjecture for further fixed small values of k beyond k = 6.
status_search_result: The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture has been proved for k = 1, 2, 3 (Hamidoune) and k = 4, 5 (Hoàng–Reed), and for all sufficiently large k (k ≥ 224,539 via Shen-type bounds). The case k = 6 is the first unsettled fixed small case and does not appear to have been resolved in the literature; the standard open-problem repositories continue to list it as open.

original_question: Does the Caccetta-Haggkvist conjecture hold for Euler digraphs, meaning connected directed multigraphs in which every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree: does every such digraph with n vertices and minimum out-degree k contain a directed cycle of length at most ceil(n/k)?

Define the minimum out-degree of $D$ as $\delta^{+}(D)=\min_{x\in V}d^{+}(x)$, and the girth of $D$ as the length of a shortest directed cycle in $D$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: For every Euler digraph $D$ on $n$ vertices with minimum out-degree $k\ge 1$, $D$ contains a directed cycle of length at most $\lceil n/k\rceil$.

(This is the Caccetta–Häggkvist statement restricted to the class of Euler digraphs.)

paper_title: Selected Conjectures and Open Problems on Directed Graphs
original_question: Can the Bermond-Thomassen vertex-disjoint-cycles conjecture be verified for multipartite tournaments: does every multipartite tournament with minimum out-degree at least 2k - 1 contain k pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles?
self_contained_problem:
A multipartite tournament is an orientation of a complete multipartite graph: the vertex set is partitioned into independent classes, and between every two vertices in different classes there is exactly one directed edge (and no edges within a class). The minimum out-degree of a digraph D, denoted δ⁺(D), is the smallest out-degree over all its vertices. 

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every positive integer k, every multipartite tournament D with δ⁺(D) ≥ 2k − 1 contains k pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles.
status_search_result: The Bermond-Thomassen conjecture has been verified for tournaments (Bang-Jensen, Bessy, Thomassé) and for some subclasses of multipartite tournaments, including triangle-free multipartite tournaments and 3-partite tournaments. The full statement for arbitrary multipartite tournaments has not been established and recent work (e.g., a 2023 note on disjoint cycles in multipartite tournaments, and 2024 results on bipartite tournaments) continues to chip away at it. Hence the problem is partially solved.

original_question: Let G be a finite directed graph, and let lambda(G) be the number of vertices in a longest directed path of G. For every natural number q with 0 < q < lambda(G), must the vertices of G be partitionable into two vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs A and B such that lambda(A) equals q and lambda(B) equals lambda(G) - q?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph (digraph) on a vertex set $V(G)$. A directed path in $G$ is a sequence of distinct vertices $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$ such that $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an arc of $G$ for $i = 1, \dots, k-1$; its number of vertices is $k$. Define $\lambda(G)$ to be the maximum number of vertices in any directed path of $G$. For a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$, let $G[S]$ denote the induced subdigraph on $S$, and write $\lambda(S) := \lambda(G[S])$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every finite directed graph $G$ and every integer $q$ with $0 < q < \lambda(G)$, there exists a partition $V(G) = A \sqcup B$ into two disjoint (possibly empty) subsets such that
$$\lambda(A) = q \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda(B) = \lambda(G) - q.$$
status_search_result: This is the strong form of Berge's path partition conjecture for digraphs (1982). It is known to hold for q=1 (Gallai–Milgram), for q=2 (proved by Hartman), and for q ≥ λ(G)−3, as well as for acyclic digraphs and several restricted classes (e.g., claw-free digraphs). The full conjecture remains open for general digraphs.

context_brief: weighted and multigraph directed cut exponent
original_question: For acyclic directed multigraphs and weighted acyclic digraphs whose arc weights are at least 1, determine the exact asymptotic exponent for the error term above one quarter of the total arc count or total arc weight, closing the known gap between upper exponent 3/4 and lower exponent 3/5 for the corresponding functions h_mu and h_omega.
self_contained_problem:
A directed cut in a digraph $D=(V,A)$ is the set of arcs from $S$ to $V\setminus S$ for some $S\subseteq V$. For an acyclic directed multigraph $D$ with $m$ arcs (parallel arcs allowed), let $\mathrm{mc}(D)$ denote the maximum number of arcs in a directed cut of $D$, and define
$$h_\mu(m) = \min\{\mathrm{mc}(D) : D \text{ is an acyclic directed multigraph with } m \text{ arcs}\}.$$
For a weighted acyclic digraph $D$ with arc weight function $\omega:A\to[1,\infty)$ and total weight $w=\sum_{a\in A}\omega(a)$, let $\mathrm{mc}_\omega(D)$ denote the maximum total weight of a directed cut, and define
$$h_\omega(w) = \min\{\mathrm{mc}_\omega(D) : D \text{ is a weighted acyclic digraph with arc weights} \ge 1 \text{ and total weight } w\}.$$
It is known that
$$\tfrac{m}{4} + \Omega(m^{3/5}) \le h_\mu(m) \le \tfrac{m}{4} + O(m^{3/4}), \qquad \tfrac{w}{4} + \Omega(w^{3/5}) \le h_\omega(w) \le \tfrac{w}{4} + O(w^{3/4}).$$
Determine the exact asymptotic exponent $\alpha\in[3/5,\,3/4]$ such that $h_\mu(m) = m/4 + \Theta(m^\alpha)$ and $h_\omega(w) = w/4 + \Theta(w^\alpha)$.

original_question: For every n-vertex finite digraph D with sink set S, does D have a quasi-kernel Q satisfying |Q| <= (n + |S| - |N_D^-(S)|)/2, where N_D^-(S) is the set of vertices with arcs into S?

Let $D=(V,A)$ be a finite digraph with $n=|V|$ vertices. A vertex $v\in V$ is called a sink of $D$ if it has no out-neighbors in $D$; denote by $S\subseteq V$ the set of all sinks of $D$. For a set $X\subseteq V$, let $N_D^{-}(X)=\{u\in V : \exists\, x\in X \text{ with } (u,x)\in A\}$ denote the set of in-neighbors of $X$. A subset $Q\subseteq V$ is a quasi-kernel of $D$ if (i) $Q$ is independent (no two vertices of $Q$ are joined by an arc in either direction), and (ii) every vertex of $V\setminus Q$ can be reached from some vertex of $Q$ by a directed path of length at most $2$.

Prove or disprove: every finite digraph $D$ on $n$ vertices possesses a quasi-kernel $Q$ satisfying
$$|Q| \;\le\; \frac{n + |S| - |N_D^{-}(S)|}{2}.$$

paper_title: Selected Conjectures and Open Problems on Directed Graphs
original_question: Other than the directed cycle of length 4, does there exist a connected sink-free digraph of order n for which every quasi-kernel has size n/2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D=(V,A)$ be a finite simple digraph. A vertex $v\in V$ is called a sink if it has out-degree $0$; $D$ is sink-free if it has no sinks. A set $Q\subseteq V$ is independent if there is no arc between any two vertices of $Q$. A quasi-kernel of $D$ is an independent set $Q\subseteq V$ such that every vertex $u\in V\setminus Q$ can reach some vertex of $Q$ by a directed path of length at most $2$. The underlying graph of $D$ is the simple undirected graph obtained by ignoring orientations and multiplicities of arcs; $D$ is connected if its underlying graph is connected.

The directed cycle $\vec{C}_4$ on $4$ vertices is a connected sink-free digraph of order $4$ in which every quasi-kernel has size exactly $2 = n/2$.

Question: Does there exist a connected sink-free digraph $D$ of some order $n$, with $D \not\cong \vec{C}_4$, such that every quasi-kernel of $D$ has size exactly $n/2$?
status_search_result: A recent survey on the small quasi-kernel conjecture states that disjoint copies of directed 2-cycles and 4-cycles are the only known sink-free digraphs whose smallest quasi-kernel has size at least n/2, and presents only an asymptotic family (hairy regular tournaments) approaching the n/2 bound. No connected sink-free digraph other than the directed 4-cycle is reported in which every quasi-kernel has size exactly n/2, and the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Selected Conjectures and Open Problems on Directed Graphs
context_brief: Seymour conjecture for split and multipartite classes
original_question: Can Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture be verified for split oriented graphs and for multipartite tournaments? A split digraph has its vertices partitioned into a semicomplete part and an arc-less part, and a multipartite tournament is an orientation of a complete multipartite graph.
self_contained_problem:
A digraph is a directed graph without loops; an oriented graph is a digraph with no pair of mutually opposite arcs. A digraph is semicomplete if for every pair of distinct vertices u,v at least one of the arcs (u,v),(v,u) is present. A split digraph is a digraph D whose vertex set admits a partition V(D)=X∪Y such that the induced subdigraph D[X] is semicomplete and D[Y] is arc-less (has no arcs). A multipartite tournament is an orientation of a complete multipartite (undirected) graph.

For a vertex v of a digraph D, let N⁺(v) denote the set of out-neighbors of v, and let N⁺⁺(v) denote the set of vertices w ≠ v such that w ∉ N⁺(v) and there exists u ∈ N⁺(v) with (u,w) an arc of D. Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture asserts that every oriented graph D contains a vertex v with |N⁺⁺(v)| ≥ |N⁺(v)|.

Prove or disprove Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture in each of the following two restricted classes:
(a) split oriented graphs (oriented graphs that are split digraphs);
(b) multipartite tournaments.
status_search_result: The general Seymour second neighborhood conjecture remains open. For the two restricted classes, partial results are known: Seymour's conjecture has been verified for several subfamilies of split oriented graphs (e.g., when the semicomplete part induces a regular or almost-regular tournament, and via split–twin extensions), and there are results for related classes such as tournaments and oriented bipartite graphs, but the full statement for arbitrary split oriented graphs and for arbitrary multipartite tournaments has not been fully resolved.

paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
original_question: Let A be a commutative unital complex m-convex B0-algebra, meaning a completely metrizable locally convex algebra whose topology can be given by a sequence of submultiplicative seminorms. Must every multiplicative linear functional on A be continuous? Equivalently, must every codimension-one maximal ideal of A be closed?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a commutative, unital, complex topological algebra that is an m-convex B_0-algebra; that is, A is a completely metrizable locally convex topological vector space whose topology can be defined by a countable family of seminorms (p_n)_{n≥1} satisfying p_n(xy) ≤ p_n(x) p_n(y) for all x, y ∈ A and all n. (Equivalently, A is a commutative unital Fréchet algebra whose topology is given by a sequence of submultiplicative seminorms.)

Question: Must every multiplicative linear functional φ : A → ℂ be continuous? Equivalently, must every maximal ideal of A of codimension one be closed?
status_search_result: This is Michael's problem (1952), one of the most famous open problems in the theory of topological algebras. It remains widely regarded as open. Recent work (e.g., Esterle's 2023 paper on Picard–Borel ideals in Fréchet algebras and Michael's problem) treats it as still unresolved. A 2020 arXiv preprint claims an affirmative resolution, but this has not been accepted as a verified solution in the community.

original_question: Let A be a commutative complex unital B0-algebra, that is, a completely metrizable locally convex algebra. Must every multiplicative linear functional on A be continuous?
self_contained_problem: A B_0-algebra is a complex associative algebra A endowed with a topology making it a completely metrizable locally convex topological vector space such that multiplication A × A → A is jointly continuous. Equivalently, the topology of A is generated by a countable family of submultiplicative (or at least suitably compatible) seminorms with respect to which A is complete. Assume in addition that A is commutative and possesses a unit element e. A multiplicative linear functional on A is a nonzero linear map φ : A → C satisfying φ(xy) = φ(x)φ(y) for all x, y ∈ A.\n\nQuestion: Must every multiplicative linear functional φ on A be continuous?

paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
original_question: Suppose A is an F-algebra with continuous inversion on its group G(A) of invertible elements. Must A have no proper topologically invertible elements, where an element x is topologically invertible if there exists a net (z_α) in A with z_α x converging to the identity e, and where a proper topologically invertible element means an element of G^t(A) that is not actually invertible?
self_contained_problem: Let $A$ be an $F$-algebra, that is, a complete metrizable topological algebra over $\mathbb{C}$ whose topology is given by a translation-invariant metric and whose multiplication is jointly continuous, with unit $e$. Let $G(A)$ denote the (multiplicative) group of invertible elements of $A$. An element $x \in A$ is called topologically invertible if there exists a net $(z_\alpha) \subset A$ such that $\lim_\alpha z_\alpha x = e$; let $G^t(A)$ denote the set of all such elements, which is a multiplicative semigroup containing $G(A)$. An element of $G^t(A) \setminus G(A)$ is called a proper topologically invertible element. Assume further that the inversion map $x \mapsto x^{-1}$ is continuous on $G(A)$. Does it follow that $G^t(A) = G(A)$, i.e., that $A$ has no proper topologically invertible elements?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in the literature on dense ideals in topological algebras. Related work studies relationships between topologically invertible elements, topological zero divisors and invertibility in locally convex / locally pseudoconvex algebras, but no source found in the search resolves this specific implication for general F-algebras with continuous inversion.

paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
original_question: Let A be a topological algebra with the Arens property, meaning that A has no dense finitely generated ideal. If A0 is a closed subalgebra of A, must A0 also have the Arens property?
self_contained_problem:
A topological algebra is an associative algebra $A$ over $\mathbb{C}$ equipped with a (Hausdorff) vector space topology making the multiplication separately (or jointly) continuous. A (left/two-sided) ideal $I$ of $A$ is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements $x_1, \dots, x_n \in A$ such that $I = Ax_1 + \cdots + Ax_n$ (no closure is taken on the right-hand side). The algebra $A$ is said to have the Arens property if $A$ has no dense finitely generated proper ideal.

Question: Suppose $A$ is a topological algebra with the Arens property, and let $A_0 \subseteq A$ be a closed subalgebra of $A$. Must $A_0$ also have the Arens property?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in the survey on dense ideals in topological algebras. paper_title: Zero Sum Trees: A Survey of Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Zero-sum spanning tree conjecture for Z_m-colored complete graphs.
original_question: Let m be a positive integer, and let c be an edge-coloring of the complete graph K_{m+1} by elements of the cyclic group Z_m. Must there always exist a spanning tree T of K_{m+1} whose m edges e_1, e_2, ..., e_m have total color sum 0 in Z_m, that is, for which c(e_1) + c(e_2) + ... + c(e_m) = 0 in Z_m?
self_contained_problem:
Let m be a positive integer and let K_{m+1} denote the complete graph on m+1 vertices. Let Z_m = Z/mZ denote the cyclic group of order m, and let c : E(K_{m+1}) → Z_m be an arbitrary edge-coloring of K_{m+1} by elements of Z_m. Prove or disprove: there always exists a spanning tree T of K_{m+1}, with edge set {e_1, e_2, …, e_m}, such that
    c(e_1) + c(e_2) + ⋯ + c(e_m) ≡ 0  (mod m).
status_search_result: The conjecture was proved by Z. Füredi and D. Kleitman: for any Z_m-edge-coloring (equivalently, integer weights mod m) of K_{m+1}, there exists a spanning tree whose edge-sum is 0 mod m. A simpler proof and a generalization were later given by Schrijver and Seymour. The result is now a standard theorem in zero-sum Ramsey theory.
